parts.problemMd:
A vehicle drives along a straight horizontal road. In a time of 10 seconds, the driving force of its engine does 75000 J of work.

Find the average power developed by the engine during these 10 seconds, giving your answer in kilowatts.
parts.solutionMd:
Power is the rate at which work is done, so use average power $= \frac{\text{work done}}{\text{time taken}}$

$P = \frac{75000}{10} = 7500$

**[M1]**

There are 1000 W in 1 kW, so divide by 1000 to convert to kilowatts

$7500 \div 1000 = 7 . 5$

**Final answer:** $P = 7 . 5$** kW**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of average power $= \frac{\text{work done}}{\text{time taken}}$ with 75000 and 10.
> 
> **A1**: Correct answer of 7.5 kW. The question asks for kilowatts, so the unit kW must be stated; 7500 W on its own does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:
The engine continues to work at the same constant rate.

Find the work done by the engine in the next 1 minute.
parts.solutionMd:
Rearrange power $= \frac{\text{work done}}{\text{time taken}}$ to give work done $=$ power $\times$ time, with the time in seconds

$\text{Work done} = 7500 \times 60$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $\text{Work done} = 450000$** J**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of work done $=$ power $\times$ time, with 1 minute converted to 60 seconds. Follow through on the power from part (a).
> 
> **A1**: Correct value of 450000. An answer of 450 kJ is also accepted, with the unit kJ stated.

parts.problemMd:
A car travels 100 m along a straight horizontal road at constant speed, taking 25 seconds. The engine of the car exerts a constant driving force of 1300 N in the direction of motion.

(i) Find the work done by the driving force.

(ii) Hence find the power developed by the engine.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The driving force acts in the direction of motion, so use work done $=$ force $\times$ distance

$\text{Work done} = 1300 \times 100$

**Final answer:** $\text{Work done} = 130000$** J**

**[B1]**

(ii)

Power is the rate at which work is done, so divide the work done by the time taken

$P = \frac{130000}{25}$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $P = 5200$** W**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct work done of 130000.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of power $= \frac{\text{work done}}{\text{time taken}}$ with 25 seconds. Follow through on the work done.
> 
> **A1**: Correct power of 5200. An answer of 5.2 kW is also accepted, with the unit kW stated.

parts.problemMd: By first finding the speed of the car, find the power developed by the engine without using the work done.
parts.solutionMd:
The speed is constant, so it is the distance divided by the time

$v = \frac{100}{25} = 4$

**[M1]**

Use $P = F v$ with the driving force $F = 1300$

$P = 1300 \times 4$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $P = 5200$** W**

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Both routes give the same power because they are the same calculation.
> 
> - Work done divided by time is force times distance divided by time,
> - and distance divided by time is the speed,
> - so $\frac{Fd}{t} = F v$.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct speed from distance divided by time. This can be implied by later working.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $P = F v$ with 1300 and the speed.
> 
> **A1**: Correct power of 5200.

parts.problemMd: Show that $F = 38500$.
parts.solutionMd:
Convert the rate of working from kilowatts to watts

$P = 462 \times 1000 = 462000$

Use $P = F v$ with $v = 12$

$462000 = F \times 12$

**[M1]**

$F = \frac{462000}{12}$

$F = 38500$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $P = F v$ with $P = 462000$ and $v = 12$. Using 462 without converting to watts does not earn this mark.
> 
> **B1**: Correct working leading to $F = 38500$. As the value is given, the division must be seen.

parts.problemMd: Find $R$.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the completed force diagram from part (a)

![Completed diagram of the lorry on a slope inclined at 8 degrees to the horizontal. The driving force F N acts up the slope, the resistance R N acts down the slope, the normal contact force acts perpendicular to the slope and the weight 270000 N acts vertically downwards. Above the slope, the single-headed arrow is labelled 12 m s to the power minus 1 and the double-headed arrow is labelled 0 m s to the power minus 2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/power/assets/024-completed-diagram-of-the-lorry-on-a-slope-inclin.png)

The acceleration is zero, so the forces along the slope balance. Resolve parallel to the slope, taking up the slope as positive, with $F = 38500$

$38500 - R - 270000 \text{sin}  8 ^{\circ} = 0$

**[M1]**

$R = 38500 - 270000 \text{sin}  8 ^{\circ}$

$R = 923 . 262 \dots$

**Final answer:** $R = 923$** N (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law parallel to the slope with zero acceleration, three terms: the driving force, the resistance and the component of the weight. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 923.

parts.problemMd:
A car of mass 900 kg moves at a constant speed of 24 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ along a straight level road. There is a constant resistance to motion of magnitude 1200 N.

Find, in kW, the rate at which the engine of the car is working.
parts.solutionMd:
The speed is constant, so the acceleration is zero and the driving force $F$ N equals the resistance

$F = 1200$

Use $P = F v$ with $v = 24$

$P = 1200 \times 24 = 28800$

**[M1]**

Divide by 1000 to convert watts to kilowatts

**Final answer:** $P = 28 . 8$** kW**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $P = F v$ with the driving force equal to the resistance of 1200 N and $v = 24$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct answer of 28.8 kW. The question asks for kW, so the unit must be stated; 28800 W on its own does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:
The rate of working of the engine is increased to 41.2 kW, and the car moves at a new constant speed against a resistance to motion of magnitude 1450 N.

Find the new constant speed of the car.
parts.solutionMd:
At constant speed the driving force equals the resistance, so use $P = F v$ with $F = 1450$ and $P = 41200$

$41200 = 1450 v$

**[M1]**

$v = \frac{41200}{1450} = 28 . 413 \dots$

**Final answer:** $v = 28 . 4 \text{m s}^{-1}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $P = F v$ with the driving force equal to 1450 and the power converted to 41200 W.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 28.4.

parts.problemMd:
A van of mass 3000 kg accelerates from rest to 23 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ in 20 seconds along a straight horizontal road, with a constant driving force.

Find the average power developed by the engine during these 20 seconds in each of the following cases.

(i) All resistances to motion are ignored.

(ii) The work done against resistances to motion is 90000 J.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The van starts from rest and there is no resistance, so the work done by the driving force equals the gain in kinetic energy

$\text{Work done} = \frac{1}{2} \times 3000 \times 23^{2}$

**[M1]**

$\text{Work done} = 793500$

Use average power $= \frac{\text{work done}}{\text{time taken}}$

$P = \frac{793500}{20}$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $P = 39675$** W**

**[A1]**

(ii)

By the work-energy principle, the work done by the driving force now also covers the work done against the resistances

$\text{Work done} = 793500 + 90000 = 883500$

**[M1]**

$P = \frac{883500}{20}$

**Final answer:** $P = 44175$** W**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct kinetic energy gained, $\frac{1}{2} \times 3000 \times 23^{2}$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of average power $= \frac{\text{work done}}{\text{time taken}}$ with a time of 20 seconds.
> 
> **A1**: Correct average power of 39675. Answers which round to 39700, or 39.7 kW with the unit stated, are also accepted.
> 
> **M1**: Correct work done by the driving force, adding 90000 to the kinetic energy gained. Follow through on the kinetic energy.
> 
> **A1**: Correct average power of 44175. Answers which round to 44200, or 44.2 kW with the unit stated, are also accepted.
> 
> A method using the constant acceleration of 1.15 $\text{m s}^{-2}$ to find the distance of 230 m and the driving force, then work done $=$ force $\times$ distance, earns the same marks.

parts.problemMd:
A go-kart of mass 120 kg moves along a horizontal track against a constant resistance to motion of 410 N. The engine of the go-kart is working at a constant rate of 8 kW.

Write down the acceleration of the go-kart when it is moving at its maximum speed, and hence find this maximum speed.
parts.solutionMd:
At its maximum speed the go-kart can go no faster, so it is not accelerating

$a = 0$

**[B1]**

With no acceleration the driving force $F$ N equals the resistance

$F = 410$

Use $P = F v$ with $P = 8000$

$8000 = 410 v$

**[M1]**

$v = \frac{8000}{410} = 19 . 512 \dots$

**Final answer:** $v = 19 . 5 \text{m s}^{-1}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Acceleration of zero at the maximum speed.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $P = F v$ with the driving force equal to the resistance of 410 N and the power converted to 8000 W.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 19.5.

parts.problemMd:
At the instant when the go-kart is travelling with speed 16 $\text{m s}^{-1}$, find

(i) the driving force of the engine,

(ii) the acceleration of the go-kart.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Use $P = F v$ with $v = 16$

$8000 = F \times 16$

**Final answer:** $F = 500$** N**

**[B1]**

(ii)

Apply Newton's second law in the direction of motion

$500 - 410 = 120 a$

**[M1]**

$120 a = 90$

$a = 0 . 75 \text{m s}^{-2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct driving force of 500.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law with three terms: the driving force, the resistance and the mass times acceleration. Allow sign errors for this mark. Follow through on the driving force.
> 
> **A1**: Correct acceleration of 0.75.

parts.problemMd:
A cyclist travels up a straight road inclined at 5° to the horizontal, along a line of greatest slope. The cyclist works at a constant rate of 300 W, and all resistances to motion can be neglected.

At the instant when the speed of the cyclist is 2 $\text{m s}^{-1}$, the acceleration is 0.5 $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

Find the total mass of the cyclist and the bicycle.
parts.solutionMd:
Let the total mass be $m$ kg and the driving force be $F$ N, and draw the forces on the cyclist

![Force diagram for the cyclist and bicycle, drawn as a particle of mass m kg on a slope inclined at 5 degrees to the horizontal, moving up the slope. The driving force F N acts up the slope, the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the slope and the weight 10m N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/power/assets/018-force-diagram-for-the-cyclist-and-bicycle-drawn-.png)

Use $P = F v$ with $P = 300$ and $v = 2$

$300 = F \times 2$

$F = 150$

**[B1]**

Apply Newton's second law up the slope

$150 - 10 m \text{sin}  5 ^{\circ} = 0 . 5 m$

**[M1]**

Collect the terms in $m$

`150 = m\left(0.5 + 10\text{sin} \; 5°\right)`

$m = \frac{150}{0.5+10\text{sin}5^{\circ}} = 109 . 364 \dots$

**Final answer:** $m = 109$** kg (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct driving force of 150 from $P = F v$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law up the slope with three terms: the driving force, the component of the weight and the mass times acceleration. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 109.

parts.problemMd:
At the top of the hill the cyclist turns round and travels back down the same road, now working at a constant rate of 100 W. Resistances to motion can still be neglected.

Find the acceleration of the cyclist at the instant when the speed is 5 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
parts.solutionMd:
The cyclist now moves down the slope, so the driving force and the component of the weight both act down the slope

![Force diagram for the cyclist and bicycle, drawn as a particle of mass m kg on a slope inclined at 5 degrees to the horizontal, moving down the slope. The driving force F N acts down the slope, the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the slope and the weight 10m N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/power/assets/019-force-diagram-for-the-cyclist-and-bicycle-drawn-.png)

Use $P = F v$ with $P = 100$ and $v = 5$

$100 = F \times 5$

$F = 20$

**[B1]**

Apply Newton's second law down the slope, using the unrounded mass from part (a), $m = 109 . 364 \dots$

$20 + 109 . 364 \dots \times 10 \text{sin}  5 ^{\circ} = 109 . 364 \dots a$

**[M1]**

$a = 1 . 0544 \dots$

**Final answer:** $a = 1 . 05 \text{m s}^{-2}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct driving force of 20 from $P = F v$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law down the slope with three terms: the driving force, the component of the weight and the mass times acceleration. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only. Follow through on the mass from part (a).
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 1.05.

parts.problemMd:
A tractor of mass 4000 kg travels along a straight horizontal road with its engine working at a constant rate of 81 kW. There is a constant resistance to motion of 1000 N. The tractor is moving with speed 9 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ at the instant that it passes a chicken at the side of the road.

Find the acceleration of the tractor as it passes the chicken.
parts.solutionMd:
The rate of working is 81 kW, which is 81000 W, so use $P = F v$ with $v = 9$ to find the driving force $F$ N

$81000 = F \times 9$

$F = 9000$

**[B1]**

Apply Newton's second law in the direction of motion

$9000 - 1000 = 4000 a$

**[M1]**

$a = 2 \text{m s}^{-2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct driving force of 9000, with the power converted to watts.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law with three terms: the driving force, the resistance and the mass times acceleration. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct acceleration of 2.

parts.problemMd:
The tractor is moving with speed $v$$\text{m s}^{-1}$ at the instant that it passes a dog. At this instant the acceleration of the tractor is 1.2 $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

Find the value of $v$, giving your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.solutionMd:
The acceleration is known, so first use Newton's second law to find the driving force at this instant

$F - 1000 = 4000 \times 1 . 2$

**[M1]**

$F = 5800$

Use $P = F v$ with $P = 81000$

$81000 = 5800 v$

**[M1]**

$v = \frac{81000}{5800} = 13 . 965 \dots$

**Final answer:** $v = 14 . 0$** (1 d.p.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law with an acceleration of 1.2, three terms. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $P = F v$ with 81000 and the driving force found, to form an equation in $v$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value of 14.0, given to 1 decimal place as the question requires.

parts.problemMd:
A bus of mass 2400 kg moves along a straight horizontal road against a constant resistance to motion of 2000 N. The maximum speed of the bus on this road is 30 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Find the maximum power of the engine of the bus.
parts.solutionMd:
At its maximum speed the bus is not accelerating, so the driving force $F$ N equals the resistance

$F = 2000$

Use $P = F v$ with $v = 30$

$P = 2000 \times 30$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $P = 60000$** W**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $P = F v$ with the driving force equal to the resistance of 2000 N and $v = 30$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct maximum power of 60000. An answer of 60 kW is also accepted, with the unit kW stated.

parts.problemMd:
The engine of the bus is working at its maximum power.

Find the acceleration of the bus at the instant when its speed is 10 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Use $P = F v$ with the maximum power $P = 60000$ and $v = 10$

$60000 = F \times 10$

$F = 6000$

**[B1]**

Apply Newton's second law in the direction of motion

$6000 - 2000 = 2400 a$

**[M1]**

$a = \frac{4000}{2400} = 1 . 666 \dots$

**Final answer:** $a = 1 . 67 \text{m s}^{-2}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct driving force of 6000. Follow through on the power from part (a).
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law with three terms: the driving force, the resistance and the mass times acceleration. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 1.67. The exact value $\frac{5}{3}$ is also accepted.

parts.problemMd:
A motorcycle and its rider have a combined mass of 250 kg and travel along a straight horizontal road. The resistance to motion is $k v$ N, where $v$$\text{m s}^{-1}$ is the speed of the motorcycle and $k$ is a constant.

Show that, when the motorcycle is travelling at a constant speed, the power $P$ W developed by the engine is given by $P = k v^{2}$. Justify your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Let the driving force be $F$ N and apply Newton's second law

*The speed is constant, so the acceleration is zero and the resultant force on the motorcycle is zero*

$F - k v = 250 \times 0$

$F = k v$

**[B1]**

Use $P = F v$ with this driving force

$P = k v \times v$

**[M1]**

$P = k v^{2}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A correct justification that the acceleration is zero at constant speed, so that the driving force equals the resistance $k v$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $P = F v$ with the driving force $k v$.
> 
> **B1**: Correct working leading to $P = k v^{2}$. As the result is given, the product $k v \times v$ must be seen.

parts.problemMd:
The greatest speed that the motorcycle can reach is 50 $\text{m s}^{-1}$, and the greatest power that its engine can develop is 30 kW.

Find the value of $k$.
parts.solutionMd:
The greatest speed is reached at constant speed with the engine at its greatest power, so use $P = k v^{2}$ from part (a) with $P = 30000$ and $v = 50$

$30000 = k \times 50^{2}$

**[M1]**

$k = \frac{30000}{2500}$

$k = 12$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $P = k v^{2}$ with $v = 50$ and the power converted to 30000 W.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value of 12.

parts.problemMd: Find the maximum speed of the motorcycle when its engine is working at a constant rate of 12 kW.
parts.solutionMd:
The maximum speed at this power is reached at constant speed, so use $P = k v^{2}$ with $k = 12$ and $P = 12000$

$12000 = 12 v^{2}$

**[M1]**

$v^{2} = 1000$

$v = \sqrt{1000} = 31 . 622 \dots$

**Final answer:** $v = 31 . 6 \text{m s}^{-1}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $P = k v^{2}$ with the value of $k$ from part (b) and the power converted to 12000 W.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 31.6. The exact value $10 \sqrt{10}$ is also accepted.

parts.problemMd:
A train of mass 90000 kg travels up a straight track inclined at 1.5° to the horizontal, along a line of greatest slope. The engine of the train works at a constant rate of $P$ W, and there is a constant resistance to motion of 2000 N. The maximum speed of the train up the slope is 20 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

At the top of the slope the track becomes horizontal. The resistance to motion and the rate of working of the engine are unchanged.

Find

(i) the value of $P$,

(ii) the acceleration of the train at the instant when it reaches the horizontal track, travelling at 20 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Let the driving force be $F$ N and draw the forces on the train on the slope

![Force diagram for a train, drawn as a rectangle, on a track inclined at 1.5 degrees to the horizontal and moving up the slope. The driving force F N acts up the slope, the resistance 2000 N acts down the slope, the normal contact force acts perpendicular to the slope and the weight 900000 N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/power/assets/015-force-diagram-for-a-train-drawn-as-a-rectangle-o.png)

At the maximum speed the acceleration is zero, so resolve along the slope with the weight $90000 \times 10 = 900000$ N

$F - 2000 - 900000 \text{sin}  1 . 5 ^{\circ} = 0$

**[M1]**

$F = 2000 + 900000 \text{sin}  1 . 5 ^{\circ} = 25559 . 25 \dots$

Use $P = F v$ with $v = 20$

$P = 25559 . 25 \dots \times 20$

**[M1]**

$P = 511185 . 0 \dots$

**Final answer:** $P = 511000$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

The driving force is unchanged at $25559 . 25 \dots$ N, and there is no weight component on the horizontal track, so apply Newton's second law

$25559 . 25 \dots - 2000 = 90000 a$

**[M1]**

$a = \frac{23559.25\dots}{90000} = 0 . 261769 \dots$

**Final answer:** $a = 0 . 262 \text{m s}^{-2}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of zero acceleration at the maximum speed, with three terms along the slope: the driving force, the resistance and the component of the weight. The weight must use $g = 10$. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $P = F v$ with $v = 20$ and the driving force found.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 511000. An answer of 511 kW is also accepted, with the unit kW stated.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law on the horizontal track, using the same driving force and the resistance, with no weight component.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 0.262.

parts.problemMd:
The engine of a motorcycle works at its maximum power as the motorcycle moves along a straight horizontal racetrack. There is a constant resistance to motion of 400 N, and the maximum speed of the motorcycle is 60 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Find the maximum power of the engine.
parts.solutionMd:
At its maximum speed the motorcycle is no longer accelerating, so the resultant force is zero and the driving force $F$ N balances the resistance

$F - 400 = 0$

$F = 400$

**[M1]**

Use $P = F v$ with $v = 60$

$P = 400 \times 60$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $P = 24000$** W**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of zero acceleration at the maximum speed, so that the driving force equals the resistance of 400 N. This can be implied by later working.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $P = F v$ with the driving force and $v = 60$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct power of 24000. An answer of 24 kW is also accepted, with the unit kW stated.

parts.problemMd:
A car of mass 700 kg is travelling down a straight road inclined at 8° to the horizontal, along a line of greatest slope. The engine of the car is working at a constant rate of 9 kW and there is a constant resistance to motion of 1300 N.

Draw a diagram to show the forces acting on the car.
parts.solutionMd:
Let the driving force be $F$ N and the normal contact force be $R$ N, and use $g = 10$ for the weight

$W = 700 \times 10 = 7000$

The car moves down the slope, so the driving force acts down the slope and the resistance acts up the slope

![Force diagram for a car, drawn as a rectangle, on a slope inclined at 8 degrees to the horizontal and moving down the slope. The driving force F N acts down the slope, the resistance 1300 N acts up the slope, the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the slope and the weight 7000 N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/power/assets/020-force-diagram-for-a-car-drawn-as-a-rectangle-on-.png)

**[B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: All four forces shown in the correct directions: the weight vertically downwards, the normal contact force perpendicular to the slope, the driving force down the slope and the resistance up the slope.
> 
> **B1**: Forces correctly labelled, with the weight as 7000 N or 700g N and the resistance as 1300 N. Any letters may be used for the driving force and the normal contact force.

parts.problemMd:
At the instant when the car is travelling with speed $v$$\text{m s}^{-1}$, it has acceleration $a$$\text{m s}^{-2}$.

By considering an equation of motion, show that

$a = \frac{90-13v}{7v} + 10 \text{sin}  8 ^{\circ}$
parts.solutionMd:
Use the force diagram from part (a)

![Force diagram for a car, drawn as a rectangle, on a slope inclined at 8 degrees to the horizontal and moving down the slope. The driving force F N acts down the slope, the resistance 1300 N acts up the slope, the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the slope and the weight 7000 N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/power/assets/021-force-diagram-for-a-car-drawn-as-a-rectangle-on-.png)

The rate of working is 9 kW, which is 9000 W, so use $P = F v$ to write the driving force in terms of $v$

$F = \frac{9000}{v}$

**[B1]**

Apply Newton's second law along the slope, taking down the slope as positive

$F + 7000 \text{sin}  8 ^{\circ} - 1300 = 700 a$

**[M1]**

Substitute the expression for the driving force

$\frac{9000}{v} + 7000 \text{sin}  8 ^{\circ} - 1300 = 700 a$

Divide every term by 700

$a = \frac{9000}{700v} + \frac{7000\text{sin}8^{\circ}}{700} - \frac{1300}{700}$

$a = \frac{90}{7v} + 10 \text{sin}  8 ^{\circ} - \frac{13}{7}$

Write $\frac{13}{7}$ as $\frac{13v}{7v}$ so that the two fractions have the same denominator

$a = \frac{90}{7v} - \frac{13v}{7v} + 10 \text{sin}  8 ^{\circ}$

$a = \frac{90-13v}{7v} + 10 \text{sin}  8 ^{\circ}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct use of $P = F v$ to give the driving force as $\frac{9000}{v}$, with the power converted to watts.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law along the slope, with four terms: the driving force, the component of the weight, the resistance and the mass times acceleration. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **B1**: Correct working leading to the given result. As the result is given, the division by 700 and the combining of the fractions must be seen.

parts.problemMd: Find the acceleration of the car at the instant when it is travelling at a speed of 10 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Substitute $v = 10$ into the result from part (b), $a = \frac{90-13v}{7v} + 10 \text{sin}  8 ^{\circ}$

$a = \frac{90-13\times10}{7\times10} + 10 \text{sin}  8 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

$a = - \frac{4}{7} + 10 \text{sin}  8 ^{\circ}$

$a = 0 . 820302 \dots$

**Final answer:** $a = 0 . 820 \text{m s}^{-2}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 0.820.

parts.problemMd:
A train consists of an engine and five carriages, connected by couplings that can be modelled as light and inextensible. The train moves along a straight horizontal track. A constant resistance to motion of 2800 N acts on the engine and a constant resistance to motion of 500 N acts on each of the five carriages. The maximum speed of the train on the track is 35 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Find the maximum power of the engine.
parts.solutionMd:
Treat the whole train as a single body, so the forces in the couplings cancel out

![Diagram of a train on a horizontal track: an engine followed by five carriages in a line, joined by couplings. The driving force F N acts forwards on the engine, a resistance of 2800 N acts backwards on the engine, and a resistance of 500 N acts backwards on each carriage](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/power/assets/011-diagram-of-a-train-on-a-horizontal-track-an-engi.png)

Add the resistances on the engine and the five carriages

$\text{Total resistance} = 2800 + 5 \times 500 = 5300$

**[B1]**

At maximum speed the acceleration is zero, so the driving force equals the total resistance. Use $P = F v$ with $v = 35$

$P = 5300 \times 35$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $P = 185500$** W**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct total resistance of 5300 N.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $P = F v$ with the driving force equal to the total resistance and $v = 35$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct maximum power of 185500. Answers which round to 186000, or 185.5 kW or 186 kW with the unit stated, are also accepted.

parts.problemMd:

Find the acceleration of the train at the instant when its speed is 20 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
parts.solutionMd:

$F = 9275$

**[B1]**

Treat the train as one body with total mass $15000 + 5 \times 7000 = 50000$ kg, and apply Newton's second law

$9275 - 5300 = 50000 a$

**[M1]**

$a = \frac{3975}{50000}$

$a = 0 . 0795 \text{m s}^{-2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for the whole train with three terms, using the total mass of 50000 kg and the total resistance. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct acceleration of 0.0795.

parts.problemMd:
A lorry of mass 8000 kg is travelling along a straight horizontal road with its engine working at a constant rate of 44 kW.

By first finding the driving force, find the resistance to the motion of the lorry at the instant when its speed is 11 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and its acceleration is 0.4 $\text{m s}^{-2}$.
parts.solutionMd:
The rate of working is 44 kW, which is 44000 W, so use $P = F v$ with $v = 11$

$44000 = F \times 11$

$F = 4000$

**[B1]**

Apply Newton's second law in the direction of motion, with resistance $R$ N

$4000 - R = 8000 \times 0 . 4$

**[M1]**

$4000 - R = 3200$

**Final answer:** $R = 800$** N**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct driving force of 4000, from $P = F v$ with the power converted to watts.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law with three terms: the driving force, the resistance and the mass times acceleration. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct resistance of 800.

parts.problemMd:
The resistance to motion is constant.

(i) Find the speed of the lorry at the instant when its acceleration is 0.6 $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

(ii) Find the acceleration of the lorry at the instant when its speed is 20 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The acceleration is known, so first use Newton's second law to find the driving force at this instant

$F - 800 = 8000 \times 0 . 6$

**[M1]**

$F = 5600$

Now use $P = F v$ with $P = 44000$ to find the speed

$44000 = 5600 v$

**[M1]**

$v = \frac{44000}{5600} = 7 . 857 \dots$

**Final answer:** $v = 7 . 86 \text{m s}^{-1}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

The speed is known, so first use $P = F v$ to find the driving force at this instant

$44000 = F \times 20$

$F = 2200$

**[B1]**

Apply Newton's second law in the direction of motion

$2200 - 800 = 8000 a$

**[M1]**

$a = \frac{1400}{8000}$

$a = 0 . 175 \text{m s}^{-2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law with an acceleration of 0.6, three terms. Allow sign errors for this mark. Follow through on the resistance from part (a).
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $P = F v$ with 44000 and the driving force found, to form an equation in $v$.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 7.86. The exact value $\frac{55}{7}$ is also accepted.
> 
> **B1**: Correct driving force of 2200 at a speed of 20.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law with three terms, using the driving force at a speed of 20. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct acceleration of 0.175.

parts.problemMd: Use your answers to part (b) to describe the relationship between the speed and the acceleration of the lorry while its engine works at a constant rate of 44 kW.
parts.solutionMd:
Compare the results from part (b): an acceleration of 0.6 $\text{m s}^{-2}$ at a speed of 7.86 $\text{m s}^{-1}$, and an acceleration of 0.175 $\text{m s}^{-2}$ at a speed of 20 $\text{m s}^{-1}$

**Final answer:** **As the speed increases, the acceleration decreases**

**[B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This happens because the driving force is $\frac{44000}{v}$, which gets smaller as the speed increases while the resistance stays at 800 N. The acceleration falls to zero when the driving force equals the resistance, which is at the maximum speed of 55 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A correct description that the acceleration decreases as the speed increases, or equivalently that the acceleration increases as the speed decreases.

parts.problemMd:
A car of mass 850 kg moves up a straight road inclined at an angle $θ$ to the horizontal, along a line of greatest slope, where $\text{sin}  θ = \frac{1}{50}$. The engine of the car is working at a constant rate of 12.1 kW and the car is moving at a constant speed of $v$$\text{m s}^{-1}$. The resistance to motion from non-gravitational forces is $R$ N and acts parallel to the slope.

Justifying your answer, show that

$R = \frac{12100}{v} - 170$
parts.solutionMd:
Let the driving force be $F$ N and draw the forces on the car

![Force diagram for a car, drawn as a particle, on a slope inclined at angle theta to the horizontal and moving up the slope with speed v m s to the power minus 1. The driving force F N acts up the slope, the resistance R N acts down the slope, the normal contact force acts perpendicular to the slope and the weight 8500 N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/power/assets/013-force-diagram-for-a-car-drawn-as-a-particle-on-a.png)

Resolve the weight parallel to the slope

$850 \times 10 \times \text{sin}  θ = 8500 \times \frac{1}{50} = 170$

Apply Newton's second law up the slope

*The speed is constant, so the acceleration is zero and the forces along the slope balance*

$F - R - 170 = 0$

**[B1]**

The engine works at 12.1 kW, which is 12100 W, so use $P = F v$ with $F = R + 170$

`12100 = \left(R + 170\right)v`

**[M1]**

Divide both sides by $v$, then subtract 170

$R + 170 = \frac{12100}{v}$

$R = \frac{12100}{v} - 170$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A correct justification that the acceleration is zero because the speed is constant, leading to a three-term equation with the driving force, the resistance and the component of the weight, 170.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $P = F v$ with the power converted to 12100 W and the driving force $R + 170$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct working leading to the given result.

Show that

$R = \frac{1000P}{v} - 130$
parts.solutionMd:

The driving force F N acts down the slope, the resistance (R + 300) N acts up the slope, the normal contact force acts perpendicular to the slope and the weight 8500 N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/power/assets/014-force-diagram-for-a-car-drawn-as-a-particle-on-a.png)

`1000P = \left(R + 130\right)v`

$R = \frac{1000P}{v} - 130$

parts.problemMd: Given that $P = 11 . 4$, find the values of $v$ and $R$.

parts.problemMd:
The engine of a car of mass 800 kg has a maximum power of 45 kW. The car travels along a straight horizontal road, and the resistance to its motion is proportional to its speed. The maximum speed of the car on this road is 36 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Find the acceleration of the car at the instant when its speed is 25 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and its engine is working at maximum power.
parts.solutionMd:
Let the resistance be $k v$ N. At the maximum speed the acceleration is zero, so the driving force equals the resistance

$F = 36 k$

**[M1]**

Use $P = F v$ with the maximum power $P = 45000$ and $v = 36$

$45000 = 36 k \times 36$

**[M1]**

$1296 k = 45000$

$k = \frac{625}{18}$

**[A1]**

At a speed of 25 $\text{m s}^{-1}$, use $P = F v$ again to find the driving force

$45000 = F \times 25$

$F = 1800$

**[B1]**

Apply Newton's second law, with resistance $25 k = 25 \times \frac{625}{18}$

$1800 - 25 \times \frac{625}{18} = 800 a$

**[M1]**

$800 a = 931 . 944 \dots$

$a = 1 . 164930 \dots$

**Final answer:** $a = 1 . 16 \text{m s}^{-2}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of zero acceleration at the maximum speed, so that the driving force equals the resistance $36 k$. This can be implied by later working.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $P = F v$ at the maximum speed, with the power converted to 45000 W.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value of $k = \frac{625}{18}$, or 34.7 or better.
> 
> **B1**: Correct driving force of 1800 at a speed of 25.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law at a speed of 25 with three terms: the driving force, the resistance $25 k$ and the mass times acceleration. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 1.16.

parts.problemMd:
A road train consists of a truck and three trailers joined by light inextensible couplings. When the road train travels with speed $v$$\text{m s}^{-1}$, a resistance to motion of $100 v$ N acts on the truck and a resistance to motion of $20 v$ N acts on each of the three trailers. The maximum speed of the road train on a straight horizontal road is 30 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Find the maximum power of the engine.
parts.solutionMd:
Treat the road train as a single body, so the forces in the couplings cancel out, and add the resistances

$\text{Total resistance} = 100 v + 3 \times 20 v = 160 v$

**[B1]**

At the maximum speed the acceleration is zero, so the driving force equals the total resistance at $v = 30$

$F = 160 \times 30 = 4800$

Use $P = F v$ with $v = 30$

$P = 4800 \times 30$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $P = 144000$** W**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct total resistance of $160 v$ N for the whole road train.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $P = F v$ with the driving force equal to the total resistance at $v = 30$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct maximum power of 144000. An answer of 144 kW is also accepted, with the unit kW stated.

parts.problemMd:
The road train moves up a hill inclined at 5° to the horizontal, along a line of greatest slope, with the resistances to motion unchanged. The greatest speed of the road train up the hill is 20 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Find the total mass of the road train.
parts.solutionMd:
Let the total mass be $m$ kg and draw the forces on the road train as a single body

![Force diagram for the road train, drawn as a single body of mass m kg, on a hill inclined at 5 degrees to the horizontal and moving up the slope. The driving force F N acts up the slope, the resistance 160v N acts down the slope, the normal contact force acts perpendicular to the slope and the weight 10m N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/power/assets/008-force-diagram-for-the-road-train-drawn-as-a-sing.png)

The engine works at its maximum power, so use $P = F v$ with $P = 144000$ and $v = 20$

$144000 = F \times 20$

$F = 7200$

**[B1]**

At the greatest speed the acceleration is zero, so resolve along the slope with the resistance $160 \times 20 = 3200$ N

$7200 - 3200 - 10 m \text{sin}  5 ^{\circ} = 0$

**[M1]**

$10 m \text{sin}  5 ^{\circ} = 4000$

$m = \frac{4000}{10\text{sin}5^{\circ}} = 4589 . 48 \dots$

**Final answer:** $m = 4590$** kg (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct driving force of 7200. Follow through on the power from part (a).
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of zero acceleration along the slope with three terms: the driving force, the resistance of 3200 N and the component of the weight. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.

parts.problemMd:
A skateboarder moves along a straight horizontal road from the point $A$ to the point $B$ at a constant speed of $v$$\text{m s}^{-1}$, working at a constant rate of 150 W. The journey from $A$ to $B$ takes 2 minutes. The skateboarder and skateboard are modelled as a particle of mass 60 kg, and there is a constant resistance to motion of 40 N.

Find

(i) the value of $v$,

(ii) the work done by the skateboarder in moving from $A$ to $B$, and hence the distance $A B$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The speed is constant, so the acceleration is zero and the driving force equals the resistance of 40 N. Use $P = F v$ with $P = 150$

$150 = 40 v$

**[M1]**

$v = 3 . 75$

**[A1]**

(ii)

Rearrange power $= \frac{\text{work done}}{\text{time taken}}$ to give work done $=$ power $\times$ time, with 2 minutes as 120 seconds

$\text{Work done} = 150 \times 120$

**Final answer:** $\text{Work done} = 18000$** J**

**[B1]**

The driving force of 40 N does this work over the distance $A B$, so use work done $=$ force $\times$ distance

$18000 = 40 \times A B$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $A B = 450$** m**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $P = F v$ with the driving force equal to the resistance of 40 N.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value of $v = 3 . 75$.
> 
> **B1**: Correct work done of 18000, with 2 minutes converted to 120 seconds.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of work done $=$ force $\times$ distance with a force of 40 N. Follow through on the work done. Using distance $=$ speed $\times$ time, 3.75 × 120, is also accepted for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct distance of 450.

parts.problemMd:
At $B$ the skateboarder stops working and moves freely for 10 m until reaching the point $C$. The resistance to motion is unchanged.

Find the speed of the skateboarder at $C$.
parts.solutionMd:
**Method 1**

Only the resistance does work between $B$ and $C$, so use the work-energy principle: the loss in kinetic energy equals the work done against the resistance

$\text{KE at} B = \frac{1}{2} \times 60 \times 3 . 75^{2} = 421 . 875$

$\text{Work done against resistance} = 40 \times 10 = 400$

**[M1]**

$\frac{1}{2} \times 60 \times v^{2} = 421 . 875 - 400$

**[M1]**

$30 v^{2} = 21 . 875$

$v = 0 . 853912 \dots$

**Final answer:** $v = 0 . 854 \text{m s}^{-1}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct kinetic energy at $B$ and work done against the resistance over 10 m.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of the work-energy principle with three terms: the kinetic energy at $B$, the work done against the resistance and the kinetic energy at $C$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 0.854.

**Method 2**

With no driving force, the only horizontal force is the resistance. Apply Newton's second law, taking the direction of motion as positive

$- 40 = 60 a$

$a = - \frac{2}{3}$

**[M1]**

The acceleration is constant, so use $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with $u = 3 . 75$ and $s = 10$

`v^{2} = 3.75^{2} + 2 \times \left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right) \times 10`

**[M1]**

$v^{2} = 0 . 729166 \dots$

$v = 0 . 853912 \dots$

**Final answer:** $v = 0 . 854 \text{m s}^{-1}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law with the resistance as the only horizontal force, giving a deceleration of $\frac{2}{3}$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with $u = 3 . 75$, $s = 10$ and the acceleration found. Follow through on the value of $v$ from part (a).
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 0.854.

parts.problemMd:
From $C$ the skateboarder works at a constant rate of 200 W for 50 seconds, reaching the point $D$. The speed of the skateboarder at $D$ is the same as the speed at $B$, and the resistance to motion is unchanged.

Find the distance $C D$.
parts.solutionMd:
The skateboarder works at 200 W for 50 seconds, so use work done $=$ power $\times$ time

$\text{Work done by skateboarder} = 200 \times 50 = 10000$

**[B1]**

Let $C D = x$ m and apply the work-energy principle, with the speed at $D$ equal to 3.75 and the kinetic energy at $C$ equal to 21.875 J from part (b)

$10000 - 40 x = \frac{1}{2} \times 60 \times 3 . 75^{2} - 21 . 875$

**[M1]**

$10000 - 40 x = 400$

$40 x = 9600$

**Final answer:** $C D = 240$** m**

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The power is constant but the speed changes between $C$ and $D$, so the driving force $\frac{P}{v}$ is not constant. That rules out Newton's second law with a single driving force, which is why an energy method is needed here.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct work done by the skateboarder of 10000.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of the work-energy principle with four terms: the work done by the skateboarder, the work done against the resistance, and the kinetic energies at $C$ and $D$. Allow sign errors for this mark. Follow through on the speeds from parts (a) and (b).
> 
> **A1**: Correct distance of 240.

parts.problemMd:
A cyclist and bicycle have a total mass of 120 kg. The resistance to motion is $k v$ N, where $v$$\text{m s}^{-1}$ is the speed of the cyclist and $k$ is a constant. The greatest power that the cyclist can exert is 200 W, and the greatest speed of the cyclist on horizontal ground is 8 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Show that $k = 3 . 125$.
parts.solutionMd:
At the greatest speed the acceleration is zero, so the driving force equals the resistance, $8 k$ N. Use $P = F v$ with $P = 200$ and $v = 8$

$200 = 8 k \times 8$

**[M1]**

$64 k = 200$

$k = \frac{200}{64}$

$k = 3 . 125$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $P = F v$ with the driving force equal to the resistance $8 k$ at the greatest speed of 8.
> 
> **A1**: Correct working leading to the given value of $k$.

parts.problemMd:
The cyclist now rides up a straight path inclined at an angle $α$ to the horizontal, along a line of greatest slope, where $\text{sin}  α = 0 . 1$. The resistance to motion is unchanged.

Find the greatest speed of the cyclist up the path.
parts.solutionMd:
Let the greatest speed be $v$$\text{m s}^{-1}$ and draw the forces on the cyclist

![Force diagram for the cyclist and bicycle, drawn as a particle of mass 120 kg on a slope inclined at angle alpha to the horizontal and moving up the slope. The driving force F N acts up the slope, the resistance 3.125v N acts down the slope, the normal contact force acts perpendicular to the slope and the weight 1200 N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/power/assets/012-force-diagram-for-the-cyclist-and-bicycle-drawn-.png)

At the greatest power use $P = F v$ to write the driving force in terms of $v$

$F = \frac{200}{v}$

**[B1]**

Resolve the weight along the slope

$1200 \text{sin}  α = 1200 \times 0 . 1 = 120$

At the greatest speed the acceleration is zero, so the forces along the slope balance

$\frac{200}{v} - 3 . 125 v - 120 = 0$

**[M1]**

Multiply every term by $8 v$ to clear the fraction and the decimal

$1600 - 25 v^{2} - 960 v = 0$

$25 v^{2} + 960 v - 1600 = 0$

Divide by 5, then factorise

$5 v^{2} + 192 v - 320 = 0$

`\left(5v - 8\right)\left(v + 40\right) = 0`

**[M1]**

A speed cannot be negative, so reject $v = - 40$

$5 v - 8 = 0$

$v = 1 . 6 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct driving force $\frac{200}{v}$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of zero acceleration along the slope with three terms: the driving force, the resistance $3 . 125 v$ and the component of the weight, 120. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method to solve the resulting quadratic equation in $v$, by factorising or by the quadratic formula.
> 
> **A1**: Correct greatest speed of 1.6 only. The negative root must be rejected or ignored.

parts.problemMd:
A runner of mass 65 kg works at a constant rate of $P$ W. Any resistance to motion is ignored. At an instant when the runner is moving at 4 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ on horizontal ground, the acceleration of the runner is twice the acceleration at an instant when the runner is moving at 4 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ up a road inclined at 1.5° to the horizontal, along a line of greatest slope.

Find the value of $P$.
parts.solutionMd:
The power is the same and the speed is 4 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ at both instants, so the driving force $F$ N is the same at both instants. Let the acceleration up the road be $a$$\text{m s}^{-2}$, so the acceleration on the flat is $2 a$$\text{m s}^{-2}$

![Two force diagrams for the runner, drawn as a particle of mass 65 kg. On the left, on horizontal ground, the driving force F N acts forwards. On the right, on a road inclined at 1.5 degrees to the horizontal, the driving force F N acts up the slope, the normal contact force acts perpendicular to the slope and the weight 650 N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/power/assets/016-two-force-diagrams-for-the-runner-drawn-as-a-par.png)

Apply Newton's second law on the horizontal ground

$F = 65 \times 2 a = 130 a$

**[M1]**

Apply Newton's second law up the road

$F - 650 \text{sin}  1 . 5 ^{\circ} = 65 a$

**[M1]**

Substitute $F = 130 a$ to find $a$

$130 a - 650 \text{sin}  1 . 5 ^{\circ} = 65 a$

$65 a = 650 \text{sin}  1 . 5 ^{\circ}$

$a = 10 \text{sin}  1 . 5 ^{\circ}$

Substitute back to find the driving force

$F = 130 \times 10 \text{sin}  1 . 5 ^{\circ} = 1300 \text{sin}  1 . 5 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

Use $P = F v$ with $v = 4$

$P = 4 \times 1300 \text{sin}  1 . 5 ^{\circ} = 5200 \text{sin}  1 . 5 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

$P = 136 . 120 \dots$

**Final answer:** $P = 136$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law on the horizontal ground, with an acceleration of $2 a$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law up the road with three terms: the driving force, the component of the weight and the mass times acceleration. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Correct driving force $1300 \text{sin}  1 . 5 ^{\circ}$, or 34.0 or better.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $P = F v$ with $v = 4$ and the driving force found.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 136.

parts.problemMd:

Find the acceleration of the runner at the instant when the speed is 2 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
parts.solutionMd:
![Force diagram for the runner, drawn as a particle of mass 65 kg on a road inclined at 8 degrees to the horizontal and moving up the slope with speed 2 m s to the power minus 1. The driving force F N acts up the slope, the normal contact force acts perpendicular to the slope and the weight 650 N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/power/assets/017-force-diagram-for-the-runner-drawn-as-a-particle.png)

Use $P = F v$ with the exact power from part (a), $P = 5200 \text{sin}  1 . 5 ^{\circ}$, and $v = 2$

$F = \frac{5200\text{sin}1.5^{\circ}}{2} = 2600 \text{sin}  1 . 5 ^{\circ}$

**[B1]**

Apply Newton's second law up the road

$2600 \text{sin}  1 . 5 ^{\circ} - 650 \text{sin}  8 ^{\circ} = 65 a$

**[M1]**

$a = 40 \text{sin}  1 . 5 ^{\circ} - 10 \text{sin}  8 ^{\circ}$

$a = - 0 . 344653 \dots$

**Final answer:** $a = - 0 . 345 \text{m s}^{-2}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct driving force at a speed of 2, $2600 \text{sin}  1 . 5 ^{\circ}$ or 68.1 or better. Follow through on the power from part (a).

parts.problemMd:
An ambulance of mass 4500 kg travels at a constant speed of 20 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ along the route shown in the diagram. It moves down a straight road $A B$ inclined at 5° to the horizontal, then along a straight horizontal road $B C$, then up a straight road $C D$ inclined at 1° to the horizontal. On the sloping roads it moves along a line of greatest slope. The resistance to motion is $0 . 2 R$ N, where $R$ N is the normal contact force between the ambulance and the road.

![Diagram of the route of the ambulance. From A the road slopes down at 5 degrees to the horizontal to B, runs horizontally from B to C, then slopes up at 1 degree to the horizontal from C to D. An arrow near A shows the ambulance moving down the first slope](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/power/assets/001-diagram-of-the-route-of-the-ambulance-from-a-the.png)

Find the driving force of the engine as the ambulance moves from $A$ to $B$.
parts.solutionMd:
Let the driving force on $A B$ be $F$ N and draw the forces on the ambulance

![Force diagram for the ambulance, drawn as a rectangle, on a road inclined at 5 degrees to the horizontal and moving down the slope. The driving force F N acts down the slope, the resistance 0.2R N acts up the slope, the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the slope and the weight 45000 N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/power/assets/002-force-diagram-for-the-ambulance-drawn-as-a-recta.png)

The resistance depends on the normal contact force, so first resolve perpendicular to the slope

$R = 45000 \text{cos}  5 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

The speed is constant, so the acceleration is zero. Resolve along the slope, taking down the slope as positive

$F + 45000 \text{sin}  5 ^{\circ} - 0 . 2 \times 45000 \text{cos}  5 ^{\circ} = 0$

**[M1]**

$F = 9000 \text{cos}  5 ^{\circ} - 45000 \text{sin}  5 ^{\circ}$

$F = 5043 . 74 \dots$

**Final answer:** $F = 5040$** N (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct resolution perpendicular to the slope to find the normal contact force. Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of zero acceleration along the slope with three terms: the driving force, the component of the weight and the resistance $0 . 2 R$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 5040.

parts.problemMd: Find the power output of the engine as the ambulance moves from $C$ to $D$.
parts.solutionMd:
Let the driving force on $C D$ be $F$ N and draw the forces on the ambulance

![Force diagram for the ambulance, drawn as a rectangle, on a road inclined at 1 degree to the horizontal and moving up the slope. The driving force F N acts up the slope, the resistance 0.2R N acts down the slope, the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the slope and the weight 45000 N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/power/assets/003-force-diagram-for-the-ambulance-drawn-as-a-recta.png)

$R = 45000 \text{cos}  1 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

The speed is constant, so resolve along the slope with zero acceleration, taking up the slope as positive

$F - 0 . 2 \times 45000 \text{cos}  1 ^{\circ} - 45000 \text{sin}  1 ^{\circ} = 0$

**[M1]**

$F = 9000 \text{cos}  1 ^{\circ} + 45000 \text{sin}  1 ^{\circ} = 9783 . 98 \dots$

**[A1]**

Use $P = F v$ with $v = 20$

$P = 9783 . 98 \dots \times 20$

**[M1]**

$P = 195679 . 7 \dots$

**Final answer:** $P = 196000$** W (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct resolution perpendicular to the slope to find the normal contact force on $C D$. Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of zero acceleration along the slope with three terms: the driving force, the resistance $0 . 2 R$ and the component of the weight. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct driving force, 9780 or better.

parts.problemMd:
A car of mass $3 m$ kg tows a trailer of mass $m$ kg along a straight horizontal road, using a light rigid tow-bar parallel to the road. A constant resistance to motion of $R$ N acts on the trailer, and a resistance to motion of `\left(R + kv\right)` N acts on the car, where $v$$\text{m s}^{-1}$ is the speed of the car and $k$ is a constant.

The greatest speed of the car and trailer on this road is 30 $\text{m s}^{-1}$, reached with the engine working at its maximum power of 48.84 kW. When the engine is working at a constant rate of 21 kW, the car and trailer move at a constant speed of 14 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Find

(i) the value of $k$,

(ii) the total resistance to the motion of the car and trailer, in terms of $v$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Treat the car and trailer as a single body, so the force in the tow-bar cancels out

![Diagram of a car and a trailer on a horizontal road, joined by a tow-bar. The driving force F N acts forwards on the car, the resistance (R + kv) N acts backwards on the car and the resistance R N acts backwards on the trailer](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/power/assets/009-diagram-of-a-car-and-a-trailer-on-a-horizontal-r.png)

`\text{Total resistance} = R + \left(R + kv\right) = 2R + kv`

At the greatest speed the acceleration is zero, so the driving force equals the total resistance. Use $P = F v$ with $P = 48840$ and $v = 30$

`48840 = \left(2R + 30k\right) \times 30`

**[M1]**

$2 R + 30 k = 1628$

**[A1]**

The speed of 14 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ is also constant, so use $P = F v$ with $P = 21000$

`21000 = \left(2R + 14k\right) \times 14`

**[M1]**

$2 R + 14 k = 1500$

**[A1]**

Subtract the second equation from the first to eliminate $R$

$16 k = 128$

$k = 8$

**[A1]**

(ii)

Substitute $k = 8$ into $2 R + 14 k = 1500$ to find $R$

$2 R + 112 = 1500$

$R = 694$

**Final answer:** $\text{Total resistance} = 1388 + 8 v$** N**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $P = F v$ at the greatest speed, with the driving force equal to the total resistance $2 R + 30 k$ and the power converted to 48840 W.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation, $2 R + 30 k = 1628$ or equivalent.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $P = F v$ at the constant speed of 14, with the driving force equal to $2 R + 14 k$ and the power converted to 21000 W.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation, $2 R + 14 k = 1500$ or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value of $k = 8$.
> 
> **B1**: Correct total resistance $1388 + 8 v$.

parts.problemMd:
The car now tows the trailer up a straight road inclined at an angle $α$ to the horizontal, along a line of greatest slope, where $\text{sin}  α = \frac{1}{19}$. The resistances to motion on the car and on the trailer are unchanged. The engine is working at a constant rate of 45.3 kW, and at the instant when $v = 12$ the acceleration of the car and trailer is 1.1 $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

Find the mass of the car.
parts.solutionMd:
Treat the car and trailer as a single body of mass $4 m$ kg on the slope

![Force diagram for the car and trailer together, drawn as a single body of mass 4m kg on a road inclined at angle alpha to the horizontal and moving up the slope. The driving force F N acts up the slope, the total resistance (1388 + 8v) N acts down the slope, the normal contact force acts perpendicular to the slope and the weight 40m N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/power/assets/010-force-diagram-for-the-car-and-trailer-together-d.png)

Use $P = F v$ with $P = 45300$ and $v = 12$

$45300 = F \times 12$

$F = 3775$

**[B1]**

Find the total resistance at $v = 12$

$1388 + 8 \times 12 = 1484$

Resolve the weight of the system along the slope

$40 m \text{sin}  α = 40 m \times \frac{1}{19} = \frac{40m}{19}$

Apply Newton's second law up the slope

$3775 - 1484 - \frac{40m}{19} = 4 m \times 1 . 1$

**[M1 A1]**

Collect the terms in $m$

`2291 = m\left(4.4 + \dfrac{40}{19}\right)`

$m = 352 . 176 \dots$

**[M1]**

The mass of the car is $3 m$

$3 m = 1056 . 52 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{Mass of car} = 1060$** kg (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct driving force of 3775.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for the whole system up the slope with four terms: the driving force, the total resistance at $v = 12$, the component of the weight of mass $4 m$ and the mass times acceleration. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only. Follow through on the resistance from part (a).
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method to solve for $m$.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 1060 for the mass of the car. An answer of 352 is the mass of the trailer and does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:
A unicorn of mass 200 kg runs for 10 seconds at a constant speed of 100 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ down a straight canyon inclined at an angle $α$ to the horizontal, along a line of greatest slope from the top to the bottom. The loss in gravitational potential energy of the unicorn is 1200 kJ. The unicorn is working at a constant rate of 2.5 kW.

(i) Show that $\text{sin}  α = 0 . 6$.

(ii) Find the work done by the unicorn against non-gravitational resistances to motion.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The speed is constant, so the distance down the canyon is speed $\times$ time

$\text{Distance} = 100 \times 10 = 1000$

**[B1]**

Use loss in gravitational potential energy $= m g h$ with the loss of 1200000 J to find the vertical drop $h$ m

$200 \times 10 \times h = 1200000$

$h = 600$

**[M1]**

The vertical drop is the side opposite $α$ and the distance along the canyon is the hypotenuse

$\text{sin}  α = \frac{600}{1000}$

$\text{sin}  α = 0 . 6$

**[B1]**

(ii)

![Force diagram for the unicorn, drawn as a particle of mass 200 kg, on a slope inclined at angle alpha to the horizontal and moving down the slope. The driving force acts down the slope, the resistance acts up the slope, the normal contact force acts perpendicular to the slope and the weight 2000 N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/power/assets/004-force-diagram-for-the-unicorn-drawn-as-a-particl.png)

The unicorn works at 2.5 kW, which is 2500 W, for 10 seconds, so use work done $=$ power $\times$ time

$\text{Work done by unicorn} = 2500 \times 10 = 25000$

The speed is constant, so by the work-energy principle the work done against the resistances equals the loss in gravitational potential energy plus the work done by the unicorn

$\text{Work done against resistances} = 1200000 + 25000$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $\text{Work done against resistances} = 1225000$** J**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct distance of 1000 m along the canyon.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of loss in gravitational potential energy $= m g h$ with $g = 10$ and the loss converted to 1200000 J, to find the vertical drop.
> 
> **B1**: Correct working leading to the given result, $\text{sin}  α = 0 . 6$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of the work-energy principle with three terms: the loss in gravitational potential energy, the work done by the unicorn from power $\times$ time, and the work done against the resistances. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value of 1225000. Answers of 1225 kJ, or 1230 kJ with the unit stated, are also accepted.

parts.problemMd:
At the bottom of the canyon, the unicorn collects six children, who sit on its back. The unicorn then runs back up the same line of greatest slope, working at a constant rate of $P$ kW, which is its maximum power. A constant resistance to motion of 500 N acts on the unicorn and the children. At the instant when the unicorn is running with speed 100 $\text{m s}^{-1}$, its acceleration is 6 $\text{m s}^{-2}$. The maximum speed of the unicorn up the canyon is 185 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Find

(i) the combined mass of the children,

(ii) the value of $P$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Let the combined mass of the children be $m$ kg, so the total mass is `\left(200 + m\right)` kg

![Force diagram for the unicorn and the children, drawn as a particle of mass (200 + m) kg, on a slope inclined at angle alpha to the horizontal and moving up the slope. The driving force F N acts up the slope, the resistance 500 N acts down the slope, the normal contact force acts perpendicular to the slope and the weight 10(200 + m) N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/power/assets/005-force-diagram-for-the-unicorn-and-the-children-d.png)

Resolve the weight along the slope, using $\text{sin}  α = 0 . 6$

`10\left(200 + m\right)\text{sin} \; \alpha = 10\left(200 + m\right) \times 0.6 = 1200 + 6m`

At the maximum speed the acceleration is zero, so the driving force balances the resistance and the component of the weight

$F = 500 + 1200 + 6 m$

Use $1000 P = F v$ with $v = 185$

`1000P = \left(500 + 1200 + 6m\right) \times 185`

**[M1]**

$1000 P = 314500 + 1110 m$

**[A1]**

At a speed of 100 $\text{m s}^{-1}$, apply Newton's second law up the slope to find the driving force

`F - \left(1700 + 6m\right) = 6\left(200 + m\right)`

$F = 2900 + 12 m$

Use $1000 P = F v$ with $v = 100$

`1000P = \left(2900 + 12m\right) \times 100`

**[M1]**

$1000 P = 290000 + 1200 m$

**[A1]**

Equate the two expressions for $1000 P$

$314500 + 1110 m = 290000 + 1200 m$

$90 m = 24500$

$m = 272 . 22 \dots$

**Final answer:** $m = 272$** kg (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

Substitute the unrounded value of $m$ into $1000 P = 314500 + 1110 m$

$1000 P = 314500 + 1110 \times 272 . 22 \dots$

$P = 616 . 66 \dots$

**Final answer:** $P = 617$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of zero acceleration at the maximum speed with the driving force equal to $500 + 1200 + 6 m$, and $1000 P = F v$ with $v = 185$. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation, $1000 P = 314500 + 1110 m$ or equivalent.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law at a speed of 100 with four terms, and $1000 P = F v$ with $v = 100$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation, $1000 P = 290000 + 1200 m$ or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 272.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 617. Follow through on the value of $m$.
> 
> The two answers are marked independently.

parts.problemMd:
Two cars move in opposite directions along a line of greatest slope of a straight road inclined at an angle $θ$ to the horizontal, where $\text{cos}  θ = \frac{12}{13}$. Each car can be modelled as a particle of mass 950 kg, and a resistance to motion of magnitude $R$ N acts on each car.

At a particular instant, both cars have an acceleration of 1.2 $\text{m s}^{-2}$ in their own direction of motion. At this instant, the car moving up the road has speed 12 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and its engine is working at a constant rate of $3 P$ W, and the car moving down the road has speed 36 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and its engine is working at a constant rate of $P$ W.

Find the value of $R$.
parts.solutionMd:
Let the driving forces of the cars moving up and down the road be $F_{1}$ N and $F_{2}$ N, and draw the forces on each car

![Force diagram showing two cars, each drawn as a particle of mass 950 kg, on the same road inclined at angle theta to the horizontal. The car moving up the road has driving force F1 N up the slope and resistance R N down the slope. The car moving down the road has driving force F2 N down the slope and resistance R N up the slope. Each car has a normal contact force perpendicular to the slope and a weight of 9500 N acting vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/power/assets/006-force-diagram-showing-two-cars-each-drawn-as-a-p.png)

Since $\text{cos}  θ = \frac{12}{13}$, the triangle has sides 5, 12 and 13, so $\text{sin}  θ = \frac{5}{13}$

$\text{sin}  θ = \frac{5}{13}$

**[B1]**

Resolve the weight of each car along the slope

$9500 \text{sin}  θ = 9500 \times \frac{5}{13} = \frac{47500}{13}$

Use $P = F v$ for each car

$3 P = 12 F_{1}$

$P = 36 F_{2}$

The first gives $P = 4 F_{1}$, so equate the two expressions for $P$

$4 F_{1} = 36 F_{2}$

$F_{1} = 9 F_{2}$

**[B1]**

Apply Newton's second law to the car moving up the road

$F_{1} - R - \frac{47500}{13} = 950 \times 1 . 2$

**[M1 A1]**

Apply Newton's second law to the car moving down the road

$F_{2} + \frac{47500}{13} - R = 950 \times 1 . 2$

**[M1 A1]**

Subtract the second equation from the first to eliminate $R$

$F_{1} - F_{2} - \frac{95000}{13} = 0$

Substitute $F_{1} = 9 F_{2}$

$8 F_{2} = \frac{95000}{13}$

$F_{2} = \frac{11875}{13}$

**[M1]**

Substitute back into the equation for the car moving down the road

$R = \frac{11875}{13} + \frac{47500}{13} - 1140$

$R = 3427 . 307 \dots$

**Final answer:** $R = 3430$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct value of $\text{sin}  θ = \frac{5}{13}$.
> 
> **B1**: Correct relationship between the driving forces, $F_{1} = 9 F_{2}$, or equivalent expressions for both driving forces in terms of $P$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for the car moving up the road with four terms. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation for the car moving up the road.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for the car moving down the road with four terms. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation for the car moving down the road.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method to eliminate $R$ and use the relationship between the driving forces, to find a driving force or $P$.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 3430.

parts.problemMd:
A crate of mass $m$ kg is pulled up a rough ramp inclined at 30° to the horizontal, along a line of greatest slope, by a rope attached to a winch. The rope is parallel to the ramp. The winch works at its maximum power, and a constant frictional force of 3040 N acts on the crate. The crate moves at a constant speed of $v_{1}$$\text{m s}^{-1}$, which is the greatest speed the winch can produce on this ramp.

The same winch then pulls the same crate up a different rough ramp inclined at 45° to the horizontal, along a line of greatest slope, again with the rope parallel to the ramp and the winch working at its maximum power. The constant frictional force on this ramp is 1000 N. The crate moves at a constant speed of $v_{2}$$\text{m s}^{-1}$, which is the greatest speed the winch can produce on this ramp.

There are no other resistances to motion. Given that $v_{2}$ is 5% greater than $v_{1}$, find the value of $m$.
parts.solutionMd:
Let the tension in the rope be $T_{1}$ N on the first ramp and $T_{2}$ N on the second, and draw the forces on the crate on each ramp

![Two force diagrams for a crate of mass m kg. On the left, the crate is on a ramp inclined at 30 degrees with the tension T1 N acting up the ramp, the friction 3040 N acting down the ramp, the normal contact force perpendicular to the ramp and the weight 10m N vertically downwards. On the right, the crate is on a ramp inclined at 45 degrees with the tension T2 N acting up the ramp, the friction 1000 N acting down the ramp, the normal contact force perpendicular to the ramp and the weight 10m N vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/power/assets/007-two-force-diagrams-for-a-crate-of-mass-m-kg-on-t.png)

The speed on the first ramp is constant, so the acceleration is zero and the forces along the ramp balance

$T_{1} = 3040 + 10 m \text{sin}  30 ^{\circ} = 3040 + 5 m$

**[M1]**

The same applies on the second ramp

$T_{2} = 1000 + 10 m \text{sin}  45 ^{\circ} = 1000 + 5 \sqrt{2} m$

**[M1]**

The winch works at the same maximum power on both ramps, so use $P = F v$ for each ramp, where the force is the tension, and equate

$T_{1} v_{1} = T_{2} v_{2}$

Substitute $v_{2} = 1 . 05 v_{1}$ and divide by $v_{1}$

$T_{1} = 1 . 05 T_{2}$

**[B1]**

Substitute the two tensions

`3040 + 5m = 1.05\left(1000 + 5\sqrt{2}m\right)`

**[A1]**

Expand the bracket and collect the terms in $m$

$3040 + 5 m = 1050 + 5 . 25 \sqrt{2} m$

`1990 = \left(5.25\sqrt{2} - 5\right)m`

**[M1]**

$m = 820 . 746 \dots$

**Final answer:** $m = 821$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of zero acceleration on the first ramp with three terms: the tension, the friction and the component of the weight. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of zero acceleration on the second ramp with three terms. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **B1**: Correct use of equal power on both ramps with $v_{2} = 1 . 05 v_{1}$, giving $T_{1} = 1 . 05 T_{2}$ or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation in $m$ only.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method to collect the terms in $m$ and solve.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 821.

parts.problemMd:
A box is pushed along a rough horizontal floor by a horizontal force of magnitude $F$ N. The box moves with constant speed against a frictional force of 5 N. The forces acting on the box are shown in the diagram.

![Force diagram for a box on a horizontal floor, moving to the right with acceleration a m s to the power minus 2. A force of magnitude F N acts horizontally to the right, a frictional force of 5 N acts horizontally to the left, the normal contact force R N acts vertically upwards and the weight mg N acts vertically downwards. The box starts at A and the point B is marked 4 m to the right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/work-and-energy/assets/017-force-diagram-for-a-box-on-a-horizontal-floor-mo.png)

Given that no other forces act on the box, write down the value of $a$ and the value of $F$.
parts.solutionMd:
The box moves with constant speed, so its velocity is not changing

$a = 0$

**[B1]**

There is no acceleration, so the resultant force is zero and the two horizontal forces balance

$F = 5$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct value of the acceleration. Constant speed means the acceleration is zero.
> 
> **B1**: Correct value of $F$. Accept 5 or 5 N.
> 
> The two values are marked independently.

parts.problemMd:
The box moves along the floor from $A$ to the point $B$, 4 metres away.

Find the work done against friction.
parts.solutionMd:
The frictional force is constant and acts along the line of motion, so use work done $=$ force $\times$ distance moved in the direction of the force

$\text{Work done against friction} = 5 \times 4$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $\text{Work done against friction} = 20$** J**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of work done $=$ force $\times$ distance, with the frictional force of 5 N and the distance of 4 m.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value of 20. Units are not required, but if a unit is given it must be the joule.

parts.problemMd:
A child pulls a toy 3 metres along a rough horizontal surface at constant speed, using a force of magnitude 7 N inclined at 40° to the horizontal. The only resistance to motion is the frictional force $F$ N, as shown in the diagram.

![Force diagram for a toy on a rough horizontal surface. A force of 7 N acts at an angle of 40 degrees above the horizontal, a frictional force F N acts horizontally backwards, the normal contact force R N acts vertically upwards and the weight mg N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/work-and-energy/assets/019-force-diagram-for-a-toy-on-a-rough-horizontal-su.png)

Write down the horizontal component of the 7 N force.
parts.solutionMd:
The 7 N force is inclined at 40° to the horizontal, so resolve it along the direction of motion

$7 \text{cos}  40 ^{\circ}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct horizontal component. Accept $7 \text{cos}  40 ^{\circ}$ or 5.36 N, or any answer which rounds to 5.36.

parts.problemMd:
(i) Find an exact expression for the work done by the 7 N force as the toy moves 3 metres.

(ii) The toy is modelled as a particle. Find the work done against friction, giving your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Only the component of the force along the direction of motion does work, so multiply the horizontal component by the distance moved

$\text{Work done} = ( 7 \text{cos}  40 ^{\circ} ) \times 3$

**[M1]**

The question asks for an exact expression, so leave the cosine unevaluated

**Final answer:** $\text{Work done} = 21 \text{cos}  40 ^{\circ}$** J**

**[A1]**

(ii)

The toy moves at constant speed, so the resultant force is zero and the friction balances the horizontal component of the 7 N force

$F = 7 \text{cos}  40 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

The frictional force is constant over the same 3 metres, so the work done against friction takes the same value as the work done by the force

**Final answer:** $\text{Work done against friction} = 16 . 1$** J (1 d.p.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of work done $=$ component of the force along the motion $\times$ distance, with the component of the 7 N force and the distance of 3 m.
> 
> **A1**: Correct exact expression, $21 \text{cos}  40 ^{\circ}$. An unevaluated equivalent such as $3 \times 7 \text{cos}  40 ^{\circ}$ is acceptable. A decimal answer alone does not earn this mark, because an exact expression was asked for.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of constant speed to equate the frictional force to the horizontal component of the 7 N force.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 16.1. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
A light rope is used to lift a bucket of water vertically from rest at the bottom of a well to the surface of the ground. The well is 8 metres deep and the total mass of the bucket of water is 15 kg.

Draw a diagram showing the forces acting on the bucket of water as it moves up the well.
parts.solutionMd:
The rope is the only thing attached to the bucket, so it exerts a tension acting vertically upwards along the rope

The bucket has mass 15 kg, so its weight acts vertically downwards and has magnitude $15 \times 10 = 150$ N

![Force diagram for a bucket of water being raised vertically. The tension T N acts vertically upwards along the rope and the weight of 150 N acts vertically downwards. An arrow beside the bucket shows that it is moving upwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/work-and-energy/assets/016-force-diagram-for-a-bucket-of-water-being-raised.png)

**[B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The tension marked on the diagram, acting vertically upwards along the rope.
> 
> **B1**: The weight marked, acting vertically downwards. Accept 150 N, $15 g$ N or "weight".
>
