> **B1**: One valid assumption which the energy method depends on. Accept air resistance being negligible, or no resistance to motion.
> 
> **B1**: A second, different valid assumption. Accept the balloon being modelled as a particle, the balloon not changing shape or losing water as it falls, or the value of $g$ being constant over the fall. Repeating the first assumption in different words does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:
A skydiver is falling freely under gravity. At 4000 metres above sea level she is falling at a speed of $v \text{m s}^{-1}$. After falling vertically for a further 100 metres, this speed has doubled.

Modelling the skydiver and her equipment as a particle of mass 80 kg, and ignoring the effect of air resistance, use energy principles to find the value of $v$.
parts.solutionMd:
The skydiver falls 100 m, so find the loss in gravitational potential energy using $m g h$

$\text{Loss in GPE} = 80 \times 10 \times 100 = 80000$

**[M1]**

Her speed goes from $v$ to $2 v$, so the gain in kinetic energy is the difference between the two values

`\text{Gain in KE} = \frac{1}{2}(80)\left(2v\right)^2 - \frac{1}{2}(80)v^2 = 120v^2`

**[M1]**

Air resistance is ignored, so mechanical energy is conserved and the two are equal

$120 v^{2} = 80000$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $v = 25 . 8$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $m g h$ with $m = 80$, $g = 10$ and $h = 100$. Using 4000 as the height does not earn this mark.
> 
> **M1**: Correct gain in kinetic energy as the difference between `\frac{1}{2}m\left(2v\right)^2` and $\frac{1}{2} m v^{2}$, giving $120 v^{2}$. Omitting the initial kinetic energy does not earn this mark.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of conservation of mechanical energy, equating the two expressions.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 25.8. A negative value is not accepted, since a speed was asked for.

parts.problemMd: Assuming instead that there is a resistive force, and that the work done against this force during the 100 m fall is $4 v$ kJ, use energy principles to find the value of $v$.
parts.solutionMd:
The work done against the resistance is given in kilojoules, so convert it to joules before combining it with the other terms

$4 v \text{kJ} = 4000 v \text{J}$

**[M1]**

By the work-energy principle, the gain in kinetic energy is the loss in gravitational potential energy less the work done against the resistance

$120 v^{2} = 80000 - 4000 v$

**[M1]**

Collect all the terms on one side and divide through by 40

$3 v^{2} + 100 v - 2000 = 0$

**[M1]**

Solve the quadratic, rejecting the negative root because $v$ is a speed

$v = 14 . 065 \dots$* or *$v = - 47 . 398 \dots$

**Final answer:** $v = 14 . 1$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The resistance is given in kilojoules while everything else is in joules, and that mismatch is the whole difficulty of this part. Convert $4 v$ kJ to $4000 v$ J before you write the energy equation, not afterwards.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct conversion of $4 v$ kJ to $4000 v$ J. Using $4 v$ directly in an equation whose other terms are in joules does not earn this mark.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of the work-energy principle, with the gain in kinetic energy, the loss in gravitational potential energy and the work done against the resistance combined with the correct signs. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **M1**: Correct rearrangement to a three-term quadratic in $v$.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 14.1, with the negative root rejected. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
Jason needs to move a cement mixer of mass 120 kg into the back of his van, which is at a height of 60 cm above the ground. He has a wooden ramp 1.2 metres long and a metal ramp 2.8 metres long, and he knows from experience that the coefficient of friction between the metal ramp and the mixer is exactly half that between the wooden ramp and the mixer.

You may assume that the mixer begins at rest at the bottom of the ramp and finishes at rest at the top.

Show that less energy is needed to push the cement mixer up the wooden ramp than up the metal ramp.
parts.solutionMd:
Sketch the two ramps, which rise through the same height

![Diagram of two ramps drawn as right-angled triangles. The wooden ramp is 1.2 m long and the metal ramp is 2.8 m long, and both rise through a vertical height of 0.6 m, with dashed horizontal and vertical sides](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/work-and-energy/assets/001-diagram-of-two-ramps-drawn-as-right-angled-trian.png)

The mixer starts and finishes at rest, so there is no change in kinetic energy. The energy Jason must supply is the gain in gravitational potential energy plus the work done against friction

Both ramps lift the mixer through the same height of 0.6 m, so the gain in potential energy is the same for each and cannot be what separates them

$\text{Gain in GPE} = 120 \times 10 \times 0 . 6 = 720$

**[B1]**

For a ramp of length $L$ at angle $θ$, friction is $μ \times 120 g \text{cos}  θ$ and it acts over the length $L$, so the work done against it is $μ \times 1200 \times L \text{cos}  θ$

$\text{Work done against friction} = 1200 μ L \text{cos}  θ$

**[M1]**

Now $L \text{cos}  θ$ is the horizontal distance covered by the ramp, which is found from the ramp length and the 0.6 m rise

$L \text{cos}  θ = \sqrt{L^{2}-0.6^{2}}$

**[M1]**

For the wooden ramp, with $L = 1 . 2$ and coefficient $μ$

$\text{Work done against friction} = 1200 μ \sqrt{1.2^{2}-0.6^{2}} = 1247 . 07 \dots μ$

**[A1]**

For the metal ramp, with $L = 2 . 8$ and coefficient $\frac{1}{2} μ$

$\text{Work done against friction} = 1200 \times \frac{1}{2} μ \times \sqrt{2.8^{2}-0.6^{2}} = 1640 . 97 \dots μ$

**[A1]**

Compare the two ramps, remembering that the gain in potential energy is the same for both

*The metal ramp is more than twice as long, and halving the coefficient does not make up for that, so it needs more work against friction*

**Final answer:** **The metal ramp requires more energy, so less energy is needed for the wooden ramp**

**[B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You never need either angle in this question. The combination $L \text{cos}  θ$ that appears in the work done against friction is just the horizontal distance the mixer travels, and you can get that straight from Pythagoras.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct gain in gravitational potential energy of 720 J, identified as the same for both ramps.
> 
> **M1**: Correct expression for the work done against friction on a ramp, with $μ$ times the normal contact force $120 g \text{cos}  θ$ multiplied by the ramp length.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the horizontal distance, either as $\sqrt{L^{2}-0.6^{2}}$ or by finding the angle from $\text{sin}  θ = \frac{0.6}{L}$ and using $L \text{cos}  θ$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct work done against friction on the wooden ramp, $1247 μ$ or better.
> 
> **A1**: Correct work done against friction on the metal ramp, $1641 μ$ or better, with the coefficient halved. Failing to halve the coefficient does not earn this mark.
> 
> **B1**: A clear comparison of the two totals and the correct conclusion. Because the result is given, both friction values must be present and the comparison must be explicit.

parts.problemMd: Given that the work done by the force Jason applies to the cement mixer in pushing it into the van using the wooden ramp is 1850 J, find the coefficient of friction between the cement mixer and the wooden ramp.
parts.solutionMd:
The work Jason does supplies the gain in gravitational potential energy and the work done against friction, with no kinetic energy left over

$1850 = 720 + ( 1247 . 07 \dots ) μ$

**[M1 A1]**

Subtract the potential energy term and divide

$μ = \frac{1130}{1247.07\dots}$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $μ = 0 . 906$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of the work-energy principle, with the work done by Jason equal to the gain in gravitational potential energy plus the work done against friction, and no change in kinetic energy.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation, with 720 and the wooden ramp's friction expression from part (a).
> 
> **M1**: Correct rearrangement to make the coefficient the subject.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 0.906.

parts.problemMd: Hence find the difference between the amounts of energy needed to push the cement mixer up the two different ramps.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the metal ramp's friction expression from part (a) with the coefficient found in part (b), then add the same gain in potential energy

$\text{Energy for the metal ramp} = 720 + 1640 . 97 \dots \times 0 . 906119 \dots = 2206 . 9 \dots$

**[M1]**

Subtract the 1850 J already known for the wooden ramp

**Final answer:** $\text{Difference} = 357$** J (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct total energy for the metal ramp, using the coefficient from part (b) halved and the metal ramp's friction expression, plus the 720 J.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 357. The unrounded coefficient must be used. Follow through on an incorrect coefficient from part (b).

parts.problemMd:
Two loads $A$ and $B$, of masses $m$ kg and $3 m$ kg respectively, are attached to the ends of a light inextensible string passing over a fixed smooth pulley. $A$ is at the bottom of a rough plane inclined at $α$° to the horizontal, where $\text{sin}  α = 0 . 6$, and $B$ hangs freely at a height of 1.3 m above the level of the bottom of the plane, as shown in the diagram.

The system is released from rest, and in the subsequent motion $A$ moves up the plane along the line of greatest slope.

![Diagram showing two loads connected by a string over a fixed smooth pulley. Load A of mass m kg is at the bottom of a rough plane inclined at alpha degrees to the horizontal, and load B of mass 3m kg hangs freely 1.3 m above the level of the bottom of the plane, with a height of 0.3 m also marked](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/work-and-energy/assets/005-diagram-showing-two-loads-connected-by-a-string-.png)

Given that the net loss in gravitational potential energy of the system when $B$ hits the floor is 12.48 J, find the value of $m$.
parts.solutionMd:
The string is inextensible, so when $B$ falls 1.3 m, $A$ moves 1.3 m up the plane. $B$ loses potential energy while $A$ gains it, so the net loss is the difference

$A$ moves along the slope, so its rise is the resolved vertical height

$\text{Rise of} A = 1 . 3 \text{sin}  α = 1 . 3 \times 0 . 6 = 0 . 78$

**[M1]**

Now write the net loss in terms of $m$

$\text{Net loss in GPE} = 3 m ( 10 ) ( 1 . 3 ) - m ( 10 ) ( 0 . 78 )$

**[M1]**

$31 . 2 m = 12 . 48$

**[A1]**

$m = 0 . 4$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct rise of $A$, resolved as $1 . 3 \text{sin}  α$. Using 1.3 as the rise does not earn this mark.
> 
> **M1**: Correct net loss in gravitational potential energy, with the gain by $A$ subtracted from the loss by $B$, using masses $m$ and $3 m$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation $31 . 2 m = 12 . 48$ or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value of 0.4.

parts.problemMd:
The speed of the loads at the point when $B$ hits the ground is exactly 2 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ faster than their speed at the instant when $B$ is 1 m above the ground.

Find

(i) the speed with which $B$ hits the ground,

(ii) the magnitude of the frictional force acting on load $A$.
parts.solutionMd:
![Diagram showing two loads connected by a string over a fixed smooth pulley. Load A of mass m kg is at the bottom of a rough plane inclined at alpha degrees to the horizontal, and load B of mass 3m kg hangs freely 1.3 m above the level of the bottom of the plane, with a height of 0.3 m also marked](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/energy-work-and-power/work-and-energy/assets/005-diagram-showing-two-loads-connected-by-a-string-.png)

(i)

Let $v$ be the speed when $B$ hits the ground and $F$ the frictional force. The string is inextensible, so both loads always move at the same speed and the kinetic energy uses the combined mass $4 m = 1 . 6$ kg

For the whole 1.3 m of motion, the work-energy principle gives

$12 . 48 - \frac{1}{2} ( 1 . 6 ) v^{2} = 1 . 3 F$

**[M1]**

When $B$ is 1 m above the ground the loads have moved 0.3 m, so repeat the calculation over that shorter distance, where the speed is $v - 2$. First find how far $A$ rises as it moves 0.3 m up the slope

$\text{Rise of} A = 0 . 3 \text{sin}  α = 0 . 3 \times 0 . 6 = 0 . 18$

Now find the net loss in gravitational potential energy over the 0.3 m, with $m = 0 . 4$

$\text{Net loss in GPE} = 3 ( 0 . 4 ) ( 10 ) ( 0 . 3 ) - 0 . 4 ( 10 ) ( 0 . 18 ) = 2 . 88$

`2.88 - \frac{1}{2}(1.6)\left(v - 2\right)^2 = 0.3F`

**[M1]**

Eliminate $F$ by scaling the first equation by 3 and the second by 13, then subtracting

`10.4\left(v - 2\right)^2 - 2.4v^2 = 0`

**[M1]**

$8 v^{2} - 41 . 6 v + 41 . 6 = 0$

Solve the quadratic

$v = 3 . 848 \dots$* or *$v = 1 . 351 \dots$

The earlier speed is $v - 2$, which must be positive, so $v$ has to be greater than 2 and the smaller root is rejected

**Final answer:** $v = 3 . 85 \text{m s}^{-1}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

Substitute the unrounded speed back into the equation for the whole 1.3 m

`1.3F = 12.48 - 0.8\left(3.848…\right)^2 = 0.62816…`

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $F = 0 . 483$** N (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Two unknowns need two equations, and the second one comes from applying the same work-energy argument over a shorter stretch of the motion. The friction term scales with the distance travelled, which is what lets you eliminate it.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct work-energy equation over the full 1.3 m, with the net loss in gravitational potential energy of 12.48 J, the gain in kinetic energy using the combined mass of 1.6 kg, and the work done against friction as $1 . 3 F$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **M1**: Correct second work-energy equation over 0.3 m, with the net loss in gravitational potential energy recomputed as 2.88 J and the speed written as $v - 2$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct elimination of $F$ between the two equations, reaching a quadratic in $v$.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 3.85, with the smaller root rejected.
> 
> **M1**: Correct substitution of the speed back into either equation to find the frictional force.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 0.483. The unrounded speed must be used.

parts.problemMd:
A child of mass 40 kg slides down an uneven slide of varying gradients, of length $l$ metres.

On the first run a constant frictional force of 30 N slows the child down. On the second run the child uses a special mat which makes the effect of the frictional force negligible.

On both runs the child starts from rest at the top. The speed at the bottom is $v_{1} \text{m s}^{-1}$ without the mat and $v_{2} \text{m s}^{-1}$ with the mat.

Show that $v_{2}^{2} - v_{1}^{2} = k l$, where $k$ is a constant to be found.
parts.solutionMd:
Let $h$ be the vertical height of the slide. The gradients vary, so consider the overall energy change on each run rather than the forces at any one point

On the first run friction acts along the whole length $l$, so by the work-energy principle

$\frac{1}{2} ( 40 ) v_{1}^{2} = 40 g h - 30 l$

**[M1]**

$20 v_{1}^{2} = 400 h - 30 l$

**[A1]**

On the second run friction is negligible, so mechanical energy is conserved over the same height

$20 v_{2}^{2} = 400 h$

**[M1]**

The height is the same for both runs, so subtracting the first equation from the second removes it

`20\left(v_2^{\,2} - v_1^{\,2}\right) = 30l`

**[M1]**

Divide through by 20

$v_{2}^{2} - v_{1}^{2} = 1 . 5 l$

$k = 1 . 5$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of the work-energy principle for the run with friction, with the gain in kinetic energy, the loss in gravitational potential energy and the work done against friction as $30 l$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation for the first run.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of conservation of mechanical energy for the run with the mat, over the same height.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method subtracting the two equations to eliminate the height.
> 
> **B1**: The printed result reached from correct and complete working, with the value of $k$ stated as 1.5. The value of $k$ is required, since the question asks for it. Because the answer is given, the elimination of $h$ must be visible.

parts.problemMd: Given that the vertical height of the slide is 25 m, and that the value of $v_{2}$ is 25% more than the value of $v_{1}$, find the value of $l$.
parts.solutionMd:
The run with the mat is frictionless, so its speed follows from the height alone

$20 v_{2}^{2} = 400 \times 25$

$v_{2}^{2} = 500$

**[M1]**

A 25% increase means $v_{2} = 1 . 25 v_{1}$, so square both sides to get the relationship between the squared speeds

$v_{2}^{2} = 1 . 5625 v_{1}^{2}   \Rightarrow   v_{1}^{2} = \frac{500}{1.5625} = 320$

**[M1]**

Substitute both squared speeds into the result from part (a)

$500 - 320 = 1 . 5 l$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $l = 120$** m**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct value of $v_{2}^{2}$ from the frictionless run, using the vertical height of 25 m.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $v_{2} = 1 . 25 v_{1}$, squared to give $v_{2}^{2} = 1 . 5625 v_{1}^{2}$. Using $v_{2}^{2} = 1 . 25 v_{1}^{2}$ does not earn this mark.
> 
> **M1**: Correct substitution of both squared speeds into the result from part (a).
> 
> **A1**: Correct value of 120. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:

State, with a reason, the resultant force acting on the avocado.
parts.solutionMd:
The avocado is lying motionless on the table, so it is at rest

**Final answer:** **By Newton's First Law of Motion, an object at rest stays at rest unless a resultant force acts on it**

**[B1]**

The avocado stays at rest on the table, so there can be no resultant force acting on it

**Final answer:** **The resultant force acting on the avocado is 0 N**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1:** Newton's First Law of Motion stated or clearly described: an object at rest remains at rest unless a resultant force acts on it. Any wording carrying that meaning is acceptable, and the law does not have to be named.
> 
> **B1:** The resultant force stated as zero. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
A large maths textbook of weight 25 N is at rest on a horizontal table.

State, with a reason, the magnitude and direction of the normal reaction force acting on the book.
parts.solutionMd:
The book is at rest on the table, so it is not accelerating

**Final answer:** **By Newton's First Law of Motion, the forces acting on the book must be balanced**

**[B1]**

The only downward force on the book is its weight

**Final answer:** **The weight is a force of 25 N acting vertically downwards**

**[B1]**

The normal reaction is the only upward force, so it must balance the weight exactly

**Final answer:** **The normal reaction is a force of 25 N acting vertically upwards**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> **B1:** The weight identified as 25 N acting vertically downwards.

parts.problemMd:
Each of the diagrams below shows the forces acting on a particle. In each case the resultant force on the particle is zero.

![Two force diagrams. In (i) a particle has a force of 12 N acting vertically upwards and a force of P N acting vertically downwards. In (ii) a particle has forces of 7 N vertically upwards, 7 N vertically downwards, P N to the left and 13 N to the right.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/forces/assets/003-two-force-diagrams-in-i-a-particle-has-a-force-o.png)

Find the value of *P* in each case.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The resultant force is zero, so the force acting upwards must equal the force acting downwards

$P = 12$

**[B1]**

(ii)

The two vertical forces are both 7 N, so they already balance and give no information about $P$

The horizontal forces must therefore balance each other

$P = 13$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1:** $P = 12$ in part (i).
> 
> **B1:** $P = 13$ in part (ii). Full credit for the correct value however it is reached, whether by balancing the horizontal forces or by writing an equation such as $P - 13 = 0$ from a chosen positive direction. No credit is lost for not commenting on the vertical forces.

parts.problemMd:
A large steel wrecking ball of weight 24500 N is being lifted by a crane. The tension in the lifting cable is *T* N. Other than the weight of the ball and the tension in the cable, all other forces acting on the ball may be ignored.

![A wrecking ball with the tension T acting vertically upwards and its weight of 24500 N acting vertically downwards, with an arrow showing that the ball moves upwards with constant velocity.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/forces/assets/004-a-wrecking-ball-with-the-tension-t-acting-vertic.png)

The wrecking ball moves vertically upwards with constant velocity.

Find the value of *T*, explaining your reasoning.
parts.solutionMd:
The ball moves with constant velocity, so it is not accelerating

**Final answer:** **By Newton's First Law of Motion, the forces acting on the ball must be balanced**

**[B1]**

The tension acts vertically upwards and the weight vertically downwards, so the two must be equal

$T = 24500$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1:** A statement that the velocity is constant, so there is no acceleration and the forces are balanced. Reference to Newton's First Law is acceptable but not required, and "the resultant force is zero" earns this mark.
> 
> **B1:** $T = 24500$. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
The tension in the cable is now increased by 3000 N.

Describe the resulting motion of the wrecking ball, explaining the physical reasoning behind your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The weight is unchanged, so the upward force is now larger than the downward force

$T = 24500 + 3000 = 27500$

**Final answer:** **There is now a resultant force of 3000 N acting vertically upwards**

**[B1]**

By Newton's First Law of Motion the ball can no longer continue at constant velocity, because the forces on it are no longer balanced

**Final answer:** **The ball continues to move upwards, but its speed increases**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1:** Recognition that the forces are no longer balanced, with a resultant force of 3000 N vertically upwards. Accept "the tension is now greater than the weight" without the value of the resultant.
> 
> **B1:** A description of the motion: the ball continues upwards and speeds up (accelerates upwards). Accept "it accelerates", and accept the reasoning shown as the increase in tension exceeding the weight. A value for the acceleration is not required, as it is not asked for.

parts.problemMd:
A car of weight 12000 N is moving along a horizontal straight road. The car's engine provides a forward driving force of 8500 N. The total resistance to the car's motion is modelled as a constant force of 1000 N. All other forces acting on the car may be ignored.

(i) Write down the magnitude and direction of the normal reaction force exerted on the car by the road.

(ii) The car is modelled as a particle. Draw a diagram showing the forces acting on the car.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The car moves along a horizontal road, so it has no vertical acceleration and the vertical forces balance

The normal reaction must therefore balance the weight

**Final answer:** **The normal reaction is 12000 N acting vertically upwards**

**[B1]**

(ii)

Modelled as a particle, the car has four forces acting on it: its weight, the normal reaction, the driving force and the resistance

![Force diagram for the car modelled as a particle, showing the normal reaction of 12000 N vertically upwards, the weight of 12000 N vertically downwards, the driving force of 8500 N forwards and the resistance of 1000 N backwards, with the direction of motion indicated.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/forces/assets/002-force-diagram-for-the-car-modelled-as-a-particle.png)

**[B1 B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1:** The normal reaction stated as 12000 N vertically upwards.
> 
> **B1:** The weight of 12000 N and the normal reaction of 12000 N shown, both vertical and in opposite directions.
> 
> **B1:** The driving force of 8500 N shown forwards and the resistance of 1000 N shown backwards.
> 
> **B1:** All four forces drawn as labelled arrows, with each label giving either the magnitude or the name of the force.
> 
> The diagram is marked on the force set and the directions, not on neatness, and the arrows need not be drawn to scale. A diagram showing the direction of motion as well is acceptable but not required. Accept the forces labelled by name (weight, normal reaction, driving force, resistance) with or without the magnitudes.

parts.problemMd: Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant force acting on the car.
parts.solutionMd:
The normal reaction and the weight are equal and opposite, so the vertical forces balance and contribute nothing to the resultant

The resultant is therefore horizontal, and is the difference between the driving force and the resistance

$8500 - 1000 = 7500$

**Final answer:** **The resultant force is 7500 N in the direction of the car's motion**

**[M1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1:** Subtracting the resistance from the driving force, with both relevant terms included. Sign errors are condoned for this mark.
> 
> **A1:** 7500 N in the direction of motion. Both the magnitude and the direction are needed, and the direction may be given in words ("forwards", "in the direction of motion") or shown on a diagram. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:

State, with a reason, the resultant force acting on the barbell while it is being held stationary.
parts.solutionMd:
The barbell is held stationary, so it is not accelerating

**[B1]**

Since the forces balance, they have no overall effect on the barbell

**[B1]**

> 
> **B1:** The resultant force stated as zero. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
A truck of total weight 27000 N is moving along a horizontal straight road. The truck's engine provides a forward driving force of 13500 N. The total resistance to the truck's motion is modelled as a constant force of 1700 N. All other forces acting on the truck may be ignored.

The truck is modelled as a particle. Draw a diagram showing the forces acting on the truck.
parts.solutionMd:
The truck moves along a horizontal road, so it has no vertical acceleration and the vertical forces balance

The normal reaction must therefore be equal to the weight, 27000 N

Modelled as a particle, the truck has four forces acting on it: its weight, the normal reaction, the driving force and the resistance

![Force diagram for the truck modelled as a particle, showing the normal reaction of 27000 N vertically upwards, the weight of 27000 N vertically downwards, the driving force of 13500 N forwards and the resistance of 1700 N backwards, with the direction of motion indicated.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/forces/assets/015-force-diagram-for-the-truck-modelled-as-a-partic.png)

**[B1 B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1:** The weight of 27000 N shown acting vertically downwards and the normal reaction shown acting vertically upwards.
> 
> **B1:** The normal reaction given as 27000 N, equal to the weight.
> 
> **B1:** The driving force of 13500 N shown forwards and the resistance of 1700 N shown backwards.
> 
> The diagram is marked on the force set and the directions, not on neatness, and the arrows need not be drawn to scale. Accept the forces labelled by name (weight, normal reaction, driving force, resistance) as well as by magnitude. A diagram showing the direction of motion as well is acceptable but not required.

parts.problemMd: Find the magnitude and direction of the resultant force acting on the truck.
parts.solutionMd:
The normal reaction and the weight are equal and opposite, so the vertical forces balance and contribute nothing to the resultant

The resultant is therefore horizontal, and is the difference between the driving force and the resistance

$13500 - 1700 = 11800$

**Final answer:** **The resultant force is 11800 N in the direction of the truck's motion**

**[M1 A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

parts.problemMd:
As part of an acrobatics display, an acrobat of weight 735 N stands motionless on a horizontal floor. A second acrobat, of weight 495 N, stands motionless on the first acrobat's shoulders.

State, with a reason, the magnitude and direction of the total normal reaction exerted by the floor on the first acrobat.
parts.solutionMd:
Both acrobats are motionless, so neither is accelerating

**Final answer:** **By Newton's First Law of Motion, the forces acting on them must be balanced**

**[B1]**

The floor supports both acrobats, so the total downward force on it is the sum of the two weights

$735 + 495 = 1230$

**Final answer:** **The total weight supported is 1230 N acting vertically downwards**

**[B1]**

The normal reaction is the only upward force, so it must balance this total weight

**Final answer:** **The total normal reaction is 1230 N acting vertically upwards**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1:** A statement that the acrobats are at rest (or not accelerating) and that the forces are therefore balanced.
> 
> **B1:** The total downward force found as $735 + 495 = 1230$. Award this mark for adding both weights, however the sum is described.
> 
> **B1:** The total normal reaction stated as 1230 N acting vertically upwards. Both the magnitude and the direction are needed, and the direction may be stated in words or shown on a diagram. Units are not required.
> 
> A response giving 735 N, using only the lower acrobat's weight, scores the first mark only.

parts.problemMd:
Each of the diagrams below shows the forces acting on a particle. In each case the particle is stationary.

![Two force diagrams. In (i) a particle has forces of 6 N vertically upwards, P N vertically downwards, 13 N to the left and 13 N to the right. In (ii) a particle has forces of 15 N vertically upwards, 15 N vertically downwards, (21 + P) N to the left and (49 − 3P) N to the right.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/forces/assets/014-two-force-diagrams-in-i-a-particle-has-forces-of.png)

Find the value of *P* in each case.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The two horizontal forces are both 13 N, so they already balance and give no information about $P$

The particle is stationary, so the vertical forces must balance each other

$P = 6$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Here the two vertical forces are both 15 N, so this time it is the horizontal forces that determine $P$

Balancing the horizontal forces

$21 + P = 49 - 3 P$

**[M1]**

Collect the terms in $P$ on one side

$4 P = 28$

$P = 7$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1:** $P = 6$ in part (i).
> 
> **M1:** In part (ii), balancing the two horizontal forces to form an equation in $P$, with both relevant terms included. Sign errors are condoned for this mark, and an equation written as $( 21 + P ) - ( 49 - 3 P ) = 0$ from a chosen positive direction is equally acceptable.
> 
> **A1:** $P = 7$.
> 
> Units are not required in either answer.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows the four forces acting on a particle which is in equilibrium.

![A particle with four forces acting on it: (P + Q) N vertically upwards, 7 N vertically downwards, (Q + 7) N to the left and (3Q − 5P) N to the right.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/forces/assets/016-a-particle-with-four-forces-acting-on-it-p-q-n-v.png)

Find the values of *P* and *Q*.
parts.solutionMd:
The particle is in equilibrium, so the forces balance in every direction

Balancing the vertical forces, the force upwards equals the force downwards

$P + Q = 7$

Now balance the horizontal forces

$Q + 7 = 3 Q - 5 P$

Rearrange this second equation so that the unknowns are on the same side

$5 P - 2 Q = - 7$

**[M1 A1]**

Multiply the vertical equation by 2, so that the terms in $Q$ will cancel

$2 P + 2 Q = 14$

Add this to the rearranged horizontal equation

$7 P = 7$

$P = 1$

**[A1]**

Substitute $P = 1$ into the vertical equation

$1 + Q = 7$

$Q = 6$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1:** Balancing the forces in two perpendicular directions to form two equations, with all the relevant terms included in each. Sign errors are condoned for this mark.
> 
> **A1:** Both equations correct: $P + Q = 7$ and $Q + 7 = 3 Q - 5 P$, or equivalent rearrangements.
> 
> **A1:** $P = 1$.
> 
> **A1:** $Q = 6$.
> 
> Any correct method of solving the simultaneous equations is acceptable, whether elimination in either variable or substitution. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
On a building site, a pallet of stone blocks is being raised by a crane. The total weight of the pallet and blocks is 22000 N. To keep the pallet level as it is raised, the tension in each of the two lifting cables is the same, *T* N. Other than the weight of the pallet and blocks and the tension in the cables, all other forces acting on the pallet may be ignored.

![A level pallet held by two vertical cables, each with tension T, and its total weight of 22000 N acting vertically downwards.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/forces/assets/013-a-level-pallet-held-by-two-vertical-cables-each-.png)

The pallet moves vertically upwards with constant speed.

Find the value of *T*.
parts.solutionMd:
The pallet moves with constant speed in a straight line, so it is not accelerating and the forces on it balance

Both cables pull upwards with tension $T$, so the total upward force $2 T$ must balance the weight

$2 T = 22000$

**[M1]**

$T = 11000$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1:** Forming an equation for the vertical equilibrium of the pallet with all three forces included, the tension in each cable and the weight, such as $2 T = 22000$.
> 
> **A1:** $T = 11000$. Units are not required.
> 
> An equation using the tension in only one cable, such as $T = 22000$, does not earn the method mark.

parts.problemMd:
The tension in each cable is now increased by 1000 N.

Describe the resulting motion of the pallet, explaining the physical reasoning behind your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Each of the two cables now pulls 1000 N harder, so the total upward force increases by twice this amount

$2 \times 1000 = 2000$

**Final answer:** **There is now a resultant force of 2000 N acting vertically upwards**

**[B1]**

By Newton's First Law of Motion the pallet can no longer continue at constant speed, because the forces on it are no longer balanced

**Final answer:** **The pallet continues to move upwards, but its speed increases**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1:** Recognition that the total upward force increases by $2 \times 1000 = 2000$, giving a resultant of 2000 N vertically upwards. Accept "the total tension is now greater than the weight" with the doubling shown.
> 
> **B1:** A description of the motion: the pallet continues upwards and speeds up. Accept "it accelerates upwards". A value for the acceleration is not required, as it is not asked for.
> 
> An answer using a resultant of 1000 N, forgetting that both cables change, may still earn the second mark if the description of the motion follows correctly from it.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows the four forces acting on a particle which is in equilibrium.

![A particle with four forces acting on it: (3P − 2Q) N vertically upwards, 11 N vertically downwards, 21 N to the left and (P + 8Q) N to the right.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/forces/assets/001-a-particle-with-four-forces-acting-on-it-3p-2q-n.png)

Find the values of *P* and *Q*.
parts.solutionMd:
The particle is in equilibrium, so the forces balance in every direction

Balancing the horizontal forces, the force to the right equals the force to the left

$P + 8 Q = 21$

Now balance the vertical forces

$3 P - 2 Q = 11$

**[M1 A1]**

Multiply the vertical equation by 4, so that the terms in $Q$ will cancel

$12 P - 8 Q = 44$

Add this to the horizontal equation

$13 P = 65$

$P = 5$

**[A1]**

Substitute $P = 5$ into the horizontal equation

$5 + 8 Q = 21$

$8 Q = 16$

$Q = 2$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1:** Balancing the forces in two perpendicular directions to form two equations, with all the relevant terms included in each. Sign errors are condoned for this mark.
> 
> **A1:** Both equations correct: $P + 8 Q = 21$ and $3 P - 2 Q = 11$, or equivalent rearrangements.
> 
> **A1:** $P = 5$.
> 
> **A1:** $Q = 2$.
> 
> Any correct method of solving the simultaneous equations is acceptable, whether elimination in either variable or substitution. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows the four forces acting on a particle which is moving with constant velocity *v*.

![A particle moving vertically upwards with constant velocity v, with four forces acting on it: (P + 3Q) N vertically upwards, (11Q − 2P) N vertically downwards, (2P + 13) N to the left and (15Q − 2P) N to the right.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/forces/assets/012-a-particle-moving-vertically-upwards-with-consta.png)

Find the values of *P* and *Q*.
parts.solutionMd:
The particle moves with constant velocity, so it is not accelerating and the forces on it balance in every direction, exactly as they would if it were at rest

Balancing the vertical forces

$P + 3 Q = 11 Q - 2 P$

$3 P - 8 Q = 0$

Balancing the horizontal forces

$2 P + 13 = 15 Q - 2 P$

$4 P - 15 Q = - 13$

**[M1 A1]**

Multiply the vertical equation by 4 and the horizontal equation by 3, so that the terms in $P$ will match

$12 P - 32 Q = 0$

$12 P - 45 Q = - 39$

Subtract the second of these from the first

$13 Q = 39$

$Q = 3$

**[A1]**

Substitute $Q = 3$ into $3 P - 8 Q = 0$

$3 P = 24$

$P = 8$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1:** Balancing the forces in two perpendicular directions to form two equations, with all the relevant terms included in each. Sign errors are condoned for this mark.
> 
> **A1:** Both equations correct: $3 P - 8 Q = 0$ and $4 P - 15 Q = - 13$, or equivalent unsimplified forms.
> 
> **A1:** $Q = 3$.
> 
> **A1:** $P = 8$.
> 
> Any correct method of solving the simultaneous equations is acceptable, whether elimination in either variable or substitution. Recognition that constant velocity gives the same condition as rest is implied by forming the equations and is not separately credited. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
A train locomotive is moving along a horizontal straight track. The locomotive's engine provides a forward driving force of 75000 N. The total resistance to the locomotive's motion is modelled as a constant force of *F* N. The locomotive is not pulling any carriages.

The locomotive is modelled as a particle. Draw a diagram showing the forces acting on the locomotive.
parts.solutionMd:
The locomotive moves along a horizontal track, so it has no vertical acceleration and the vertical forces balance

No weight is given, so label the weight $W$ and the normal reaction $R$, which are equal and opposite, even though neither value is known

Modelled as a particle, the locomotive has four forces acting on it: its weight, the normal reaction, the driving force and the resistance

![Force diagram for the locomotive modelled as a particle, showing the normal reaction R vertically upwards, the weight W vertically downwards, the driving force of 75000 N forwards and the resistance of F N backwards, with the direction of motion indicated.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/forces/assets/011-force-diagram-for-the-locomotive-modelled-as-a-p.png)

**[B1 B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1:** The weight shown acting vertically downwards and the normal reaction shown acting vertically upwards. Accept any sensible labels, including $W$ and $R$, or "weight" and "normal reaction".
> 
> **B1:** The driving force of 75000 N shown forwards.
> 
> **B1:** The resistance of $F$ N shown backwards.
> 
> The diagram is marked on the force set and the directions, not on neatness, and the arrows need not be drawn to scale. Full credit is available without numerical values for the vertical forces, since none are given. A diagram showing the direction of motion as well is acceptable but not required. Omitting the vertical forces entirely loses the first mark.

parts.problemMd:
The resultant force acting on the locomotive is 71800 N in the direction of its motion.

Find the value of *F*.
parts.solutionMd:
The weight and the normal reaction are equal and opposite, so the vertical forces contribute nothing to the resultant

The resultant is therefore horizontal, and is the difference between the driving force and the resistance

$75000 - F = 71800$

**[M1]**

Rearrange to find $F$

$F = 75000 - 71800$

$F = 3200$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1:** Forming an equation for the horizontal resultant with both relevant terms included, such as $75000 - F = 71800$. Sign errors are condoned for this mark.
> 
> **A1:** $F = 3200$. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
Each of the diagrams below shows the forces acting on a particle. In each case the particle is moving with constant velocity *v*.

![Two force diagrams. In (i) a particle moving downwards with constant velocity v has forces of (P + 7) N vertically upwards, (1 − 2P) N vertically downwards, 9 N to the left and 9 N to the right. In (ii) a particle moving to the right with constant velocity v has forces of 13 N vertically upwards, 13 N vertically downwards, (16 + P) N to the left, and two forces to the right of 11 N and (2P − 3) N.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/forces/assets/008-two-force-diagrams-in-i-a-particle-moving-downwa.png)

Find the value of *P* in each case.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The particle moves with constant velocity, so the forces balance in every direction

The two horizontal forces are both 9 N, so they already balance and give no information about $P$

Balancing the vertical forces

$P + 7 = 1 - 2 P$

**[M1]**

Collect the terms in $P$ on one side

$3 P = - 6$

$P = - 2$

**[A1]**

(ii)

Here the two vertical forces are both 13 N, so this time it is the horizontal forces that determine $P$

There are two forces acting to the right, so their sum must balance the single force acting to the left

$11 + ( 2 P - 3 ) = 16 + P$

$2 P + 8 = 16 + P$

$P = 8$

**[B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A negative value for $P$ is not a mistake. $P$ is just an unknown number inside a force expression, not a force itself. Substituting $P = - 2$ gives forces of 5 N up and 5 N down, both perfectly sensible. Check your answer by substituting it back into the diagram rather than assuming a negative value means you have gone wrong.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1:** In part (i), balancing the two vertical forces to form an equation in $P$, with both relevant terms included. Sign errors are condoned for this mark, and an equation written as $( P + 7 ) - ( 1 - 2 P ) = 0$ from a chosen positive direction is equally acceptable.
> 
> **A1:** $P = - 2$. The negative value is correct and must not be penalised.
> 
> **B1:** $P = 8$ in part (ii). Both right-hand forces must be included; using only one of them scores zero for this mark.
> 
> Units are not required in either answer.

parts.problemMd:
A pallet of bricks is being raised vertically by a crane at a constant speed of 0.5 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

A student claims that, because the pallet is moving upwards, the resultant force acting on the pallet must also act upwards.

State whether the student is correct, and explain your answer fully.
parts.solutionMd:
The pallet is moving at a constant speed in a straight line, so its velocity is not changing and it is not accelerating

**Final answer:** **The student is not correct**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **By Newton's First Law of Motion, a body moving with constant velocity has no resultant force acting on it, so the resultant force on the pallet is zero**

**[B1]**

The student's error is to assume that motion in a direction requires a force in that direction

**Final answer:** **A resultant force is needed to change a body's velocity, not to keep it moving, so the upward motion does not require an upward resultant force**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1:** A clear statement that the student is not correct.
> 
> **B1:** The resultant force identified as zero, justified by the pallet moving with constant velocity (or not accelerating). Reference to Newton's First Law is acceptable but not required.
> 
> **B1:** An explanation that a resultant force changes a body's velocity rather than maintaining its motion; or, equivalently, that the tension and the weight are balanced even while the pallet moves. Accept any wording carrying this meaning.
> 
> A response which only states that the resultant force is zero, without addressing why the upward motion does not imply an upward force, scores the first two marks.

parts.problemMd:
A yoga practitioner of weight 686 N stands motionless on a horizontal floor with both feet on the ground. He then changes to a new pose in which one leg is lifted into the air, so that he is standing motionless with only one foot on the ground.

State, with a reason, the difference between the total normal reaction exerted by the floor on the practitioner when he has both feet on the ground and the total normal reaction when he has only one foot on the ground.
parts.solutionMd:
In both poses the practitioner is motionless, so he is not accelerating

**Final answer:** **By Newton's First Law of Motion, the forces acting on him must be balanced in both poses**

**[B1]**

His weight is 686 N in both poses, and the total normal reaction is the only upward force, so it must balance that weight each time

**Final answer:** **The total normal reaction is 686 N acting vertically upwards in both poses**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **There is no difference between the two total normal reaction forces**

**[B1]**

Lifting one leg changes only how the total reaction is shared between the feet, not the total itself. With one foot on the ground, that single foot now carries the whole 686 N

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1:** A statement that the practitioner is motionless (or not accelerating) in both poses, so the forces are balanced.
> 
> **B1:** The total normal reaction identified as 686 N, equal to the weight, in both poses.
> 
> **B1:** An explicit statement that there is no difference between the two. Accept "they are the same" or "the difference is zero".
> 
> The final mark requires the comparison to be stated, not merely implied by giving 686 N twice. A response arguing that the reaction halves, or doubles, because of the change in the number of feet scores the first mark only.

parts.problemMd:
The diagrams below show the forces acting on two particles.

![Two force diagrams. Diagram A shows a particle with forces of 5 N vertically upwards, 5 N vertically downwards, (3 + P) N to the left and 8 N to the right. Diagram B shows a particle with forces of 12 N vertically upwards, 7 N vertically downwards, (P + 2) N to the left and (3P − 6) N to the right.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/forces/assets/010-two-force-diagrams-diagram-a-shows-a-particle-wi.png)

(i) The particle in diagram A is in equilibrium. Find the value of *P*.

(ii) Show that the particle in diagram B cannot be in equilibrium, whatever the value of *P*.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The two vertical forces are both 5 N, so they already balance and give no information about $P$

The particle is in equilibrium, so the horizontal forces must balance each other

$3 + P = 8$

$P = 5$

**[B1]**

(ii)

For a particle to be in equilibrium, the forces must balance in every direction, so consider the vertical direction first

The vertical forces in diagram B are 12 N upwards and 7 N downwards, and neither of them depends on $P$

$12 \neq 7$

**[B1]**

So whatever value $P$ takes, the vertical forces leave a resultant

$12 - 7 = 5$

**Final answer:** **There is always a resultant force of 5 N vertically upwards, so the particle cannot be in equilibrium for any value of P**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1:** $P = 5$ in part (i).
> 
> **B1:** In part (ii), identifying that the vertical forces are 12 N and 7 N and that neither involves $P$. Accept this shown as an attempt to balance them vertically, reaching a contradiction.
> 
> **B1:** Concluding that the vertical forces can never balance, so the particle can never be in equilibrium. The conclusion must be stated. Accept the resultant given as 5 N upwards, or simply the observation that $12 \neq 7$ for all $P$.
> 
> Balancing the horizontal forces in diagram B to obtain $P = 4$ is not incorrect, but earns nothing on its own; the marks in part (ii) are for the vertical argument. A response which finds $P = 4$ and concludes that the particle *is* in equilibrium scores no marks in part (ii).

parts.problemMd:
A pallet of large cheeses is being lowered into a cave for storage. The total weight of the pallet and cheeses is 17000 N. To keep the pallet level as it is lowered, the tension in each of the two support ropes is the same, *T* N. Other than the weight of the pallet and cheeses and the tension in the ropes, all other forces acting on the pallet may be ignored.

![A level pallet held by two vertical ropes, each with tension T, and its total weight of 17000 N acting vertically downwards.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/forces/assets/009-a-level-pallet-held-by-two-vertical-ropes-each-w.png)

The pallet moves vertically downwards with constant speed.

Find the value of *T*.
parts.solutionMd:
The pallet moves with constant speed in a straight line, so it is not accelerating and the forces on it balance, even though it is moving downwards

Both ropes pull upwards with tension $T$, so the total upward force $2 T$ must balance the weight

$2 T = 17000$

**[M1]**

$T = 8500$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1:** Forming an equation for the vertical equilibrium of the pallet with all three forces included, the tension in each rope and the weight, such as $2 T = 17000$.
> 
> **A1:** $T = 8500$. Units are not required.
> 
> An equation using the tension in only one rope, such as $T = 17000$, does not earn the method mark.

parts.problemMd:
The tension in each rope is now increased by 500 N.

Describe the resulting motion of the pallet immediately after the change in tension, explaining the physical reasoning behind your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Each of the two ropes now pulls 500 N harder, so the total upward force increases by twice this amount

$2 \times 500 = 1000$

**Final answer:** **There is now a resultant force of 1000 N acting vertically upwards**

**[B1]**

The pallet is moving downwards, so this resultant force acts against the direction of motion

**Final answer:** **The pallet continues to move downwards, but its speed decreases**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1:** Recognition that the total upward force increases by $2 \times 500 = 1000$, giving a resultant of 1000 N vertically upwards.
> 
> **B1:** A description of the motion: the pallet continues downwards but slows down. Accept "it decelerates". A value for the deceleration is not required, as it is not asked for.
> 
> A response stating that the pallet immediately moves upwards scores this second mark only if it is clear that the *acceleration*, not the motion, is upwards. The resultant force is upwards, but the pallet is still travelling downwards immediately after the change.
> 
> An answer using a resultant of 500 N, forgetting that both ropes change, may still earn the second mark if the description of the motion follows correctly from it.

parts.problemMd:
A stack of *n* identical books, each of weight 12 N, rests on a horizontal table. The stack is in equilibrium.

(i) Find, in terms of *n*, the magnitude of the normal reaction exerted by the table on the bottom book of the stack.

(ii) The normal reaction exerted by the table on the bottom book is 96 N. Find the value of *n*.

(iii) State the magnitude and direction of the force exerted on the table by the bottom book, and name the law which justifies your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The whole stack is in equilibrium, so the table must support the total weight of all $n$ books

Each book weighs 12 N, so the total weight of the stack is

$12 n$

The normal reaction is the only upward force on the stack, so it must balance this total weight

$12 n$

**[M1 A1]**

(ii)

Set the expression from part (i) equal to the given normal reaction

$12 n = 96$

$n = 8$

**[B1]**

(iii)

The table pushes up on the bottom book with a force of 96 N, and by Newton's Third Law the book pushes back on the table with a force of equal magnitude in the opposite direction

**Final answer:** **The force exerted on the table by the bottom book is 96 N acting vertically downwards**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **This follows from Newton's Third Law of Motion**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1:** Recognising that the table supports the whole stack, so the total weight is $12 \times n$. Award for the product seen, however it is written.
> 
> **A1:** The normal reaction given as $12 n$ N.
> 
> **B1:** $n = 8$, following correctly from part (i). Follow through from an incorrect expression in part (i).
> 
> **B1:** The force on the table given as 96 N acting vertically downwards. Both the magnitude and the direction are needed. An answer of 96 N upwards scores zero for this mark, as it repeats the force on the book rather than the force on the table.
> 
> **B1:** Newton's Third Law named. Accept "the third law", or a statement of it in words such as "every action has an equal and opposite reaction", provided it is clearly offered as the justifying law.
> 
> Units are not required in parts (i) and (ii).

parts.problemMd:
A tourist of weight 1246 N is riding in a lift to the top of a tall building. He is wearing a backpack, and is standing at rest on the horizontal floor of the lift. The lift is moving vertically upwards at a constant speed of 6.1 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

The total normal reaction exerted on the tourist by the floor of the lift is 1598 N.

(i) Find the weight of the backpack.

(ii) State, with a reason, what difference it would make to your answer if the lift were instead moving vertically downwards at a constant speed of 6.1 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The tourist stands at rest in a lift moving at constant speed, so he is not accelerating and the forces on him balance

The normal reaction therefore balances the combined weight of the tourist and his backpack

$1598 = 1246 + W$

**[M1]**

$W = 1598 - 1246$

$W = 352$

**[A1]**

(ii)

The lift would still be moving at a constant speed in a straight line, so the tourist would still not be accelerating and the forces on him would still balance

**Final answer:** **It would make no difference, and the weight of the backpack would still be 352 N**

**[B1]**

What matters is that the velocity is constant, not the direction in which the lift travels

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1:** Forming an equation for the equilibrium of the tourist and backpack, with all the relevant terms included, for example $1598 = 1246 + W$. Sign errors are condoned for this mark.
> 
> **A1:** The weight of the backpack given as 352 N. Units are not required.
> 
> **B1:** A statement that it would make no difference, with the reason that the speed is still constant so the forces still balance. The verdict alone, without the reason, does not earn this mark.
> 
> A response arguing that the normal reaction would be smaller when travelling downwards scores no marks in part (ii).

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows the four forces acting on a particle which is in equilibrium.

![A particle with four forces acting on it: F₁ N vertically upwards, F₂ N vertically downwards, F₃ N to the left and F₄ N to the right.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/forces/assets/007-a-particle-with-four-forces-acting-on-it-f-n-ver.png)

Given that $5 F_{4} = 9 F_{2}$ and $3 F_{1} + 5 F_{3} = 450$, find the values of $F_{1}$, $F_{2}$, $F_{3}$ and $F_{4}$.
parts.solutionMd:
The particle is in equilibrium, so the forces balance in each of the two perpendicular directions

$F_{1} = F_{2}$

$F_{3} = F_{4}$

**[B1]**

The first given relation connects $F_{4}$ and $F_{2}$, so use the pairings above to rewrite it in terms of $F_{3}$ and $F_{1}$

$5 F_{4} = 9 F_{2}$

$5 F_{3} = 9 F_{1}$

$F_{3} = \frac{9}{5} F_{1}$

**[M1]**

Substitute this into the second given relation, so that only $F_{1}$ remains

`3F_1 + 5\left(\dfrac{9}{5}F_1\right) = 450`

$3 F_{1} + 9 F_{1} = 450$

$12 F_{1} = 450$

**Final answer:** $F_{1} = F_{2} =$** 37.5**

**[A1]**

Now use the relation between $F_{3}$ and $F_{1}$

$F_{3} = \frac{9}{5} \times 37 . 5$

**Final answer:** $F_{3} = F_{4} =$** 67.5**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1:** Both equilibrium relations stated: $F_{1} = F_{2}$ and $F_{3} = F_{4}$.
> 
> **M1:** Using those relations to rewrite one of the given equations so that it connects $F_{3}$ and $F_{1}$ (or $F_{4}$ and $F_{2}$), reducing the problem to a single unknown. Award for the substitution attempted, however it is arranged.
> 
> **A1:** $F_{1} = F_{2} = 37 . 5$.
> 
> **A1:** $F_{3} = F_{4} = 67 . 5$.
> 
> Both members of each pair must be given for the accuracy marks; stating only $F_{1}$ without $F_{2}$, or only $F_{3}$ without $F_{4}$, does not earn the mark. Any equivalent route reaching the same values is acceptable. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
A monorail train is moving along a horizontal straight track. The train's engine provides a forward driving force of *T* N. The total resistance to the train's motion is modelled as a constant force of *F* N.

The train is modelled as a particle. Draw a diagram showing the forces acting on the train.
parts.solutionMd:
The train moves along a horizontal track, so it has no vertical acceleration and the vertical forces balance

No weight is given, so label the weight $W$ and the normal reaction $R$, which are equal and opposite, even though neither value is known

Modelled as a particle, the train has four forces acting on it: its weight, the normal reaction, the driving force and the resistance

![Force diagram for the monorail train modelled as a particle, showing the normal reaction R vertically upwards, the weight W vertically downwards, the driving force of T N forwards and the resistance of F N backwards, with the direction of motion indicated.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/forces/assets/005-force-diagram-for-the-monorail-train-modelled-as.png)

**[B1 B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1:** The weight shown acting vertically downwards and the normal reaction shown acting vertically upwards. Accept any sensible labels, including $W$ and $R$.
> 
> **B1:** The driving force of $T$ N shown forwards.
> 
> **B1:** The resistance of $F$ N shown backwards.
> 
> The diagram is marked on the force set and the directions, not on neatness. Full credit is available without numerical values for the vertical forces, since none are given.

parts.problemMd:
It is given that

- the train's speed is increasing in its direction of motion
- the resultant force acting on the train is 4200 N
- of *T* and *F*, nine times the magnitude of the smaller force is equal to twice the magnitude of the larger force

Find the values of *T* and *F*.
parts.solutionMd:
The train's speed is increasing in the direction of motion, so the resultant force acts forwards

*The driving force is therefore the larger of the two, so T is the larger force and F is the smaller*

**[B1]**

The vertical forces balance, so the resultant is the difference between the two horizontal forces

$T - F = 4200$

Nine times the smaller force equals twice the larger force

$9 F = 2 T$

**[M1]**

Rearrange the second equation to make $T$ the subject

$T = \frac{9}{2} F$

Substitute into the first equation

$\frac{9}{2} F - F = 4200$

$\frac{7}{2} F = 4200$

$F = 1200$

Substitute back to find $T$

$T = \frac{9}{2} \times 1200$

$T = 5400$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1:** Identifying $T$ as the larger force and $F$ as the smaller, justified by the speed increasing in the direction of motion. This must be established before the ratio condition can be used correctly.
> 
> **M1:** Forming both equations: the resultant as the difference of the two forces, such as $T - F = 4200$, and the ratio condition written as nine times one force equal to twice the other. Sign errors are condoned for this mark.
> 
> **A1:** $F = 1200$ and $T = 5400$. Both values are needed.
> 
> A response which takes $F$ as the larger force obtains $9 T = 2 F$ and reaches negative values; it can score the M1, but not the B1 or the A1. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
In a slate quarry, a load of slates is being raised to the surface for processing. The total weight of the slates and the platform on which they rest is 21000 N. To keep the platform level as it is raised, the tension in each of the two lifting cables is the same, *T* N. Other than the weight of the platform and slates and the tension in the cables, all other forces acting on the platform may be ignored.

![A level platform held by two vertical cables, each with tension T, and its total weight of 21000 N acting vertically downwards.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/forces/assets/006-a-level-platform-held-by-two-vertical-cables-eac.png)

The platform moves vertically upwards with a constant speed of 0.25 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Find the value of *T*.
parts.solutionMd:
The platform moves with constant speed in a straight line, so it is not accelerating and the forces on it balance

Both cables pull upwards with tension $T$, so the total upward force $2 T$ must balance the weight

$2 T = 21000$

**[M1]**

$T = 10500$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1:** Forming an equation for the vertical equilibrium of the platform with all three forces included, the tension in each cable and the weight, such as $2 T = 21000$.
> 
> **A1:** $T = 10500$. Units are not required.
> 
> An equation using the tension in only one cable, such as $T = 21000$, does not earn the method mark.

parts.problemMd:
As the platform passes one of the levels in the quarry, two workers of combined weight 1600 N jump onto the centre of the slow-moving platform, hoping to catch a ride to the surface at the end of their shift.

The tension in each cable stays the same, and the platform remains level.

Describe the resulting motion of the platform after the workers jump onto it, considering both the time immediately afterwards and the longer term. Explain the physical reasoning behind your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
The tension is unchanged, so the total upward force is still $2 T = 21000$ N, but the total weight now includes the workers

$21000 + 1600 = 22600$

The downward force now exceeds the upward force

$22600 - 21000 = 1600$

**Final answer:** **There is now a resultant force of 1600 N acting vertically downwards**

**[B1]**

The platform is still travelling upwards at the moment the workers land, so this resultant acts against the direction of motion

**Final answer:** **Immediately afterwards the platform continues to move upwards, but its speed decreases**

**[B1]**

The resultant force does not change, so the platform keeps slowing until its upward velocity reaches zero, and then continues to be pulled downwards

**Final answer:** **The platform then momentarily comes to rest, after which it begins to move downwards with increasing speed**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1:** Recognition that the weight now exceeds the total tension, giving a resultant of 1600 N vertically downwards. Accept the comparison made without the value.
> 
> **B1:** Immediately after the workers land, the platform continues upwards but slows down. Accept "it decelerates".
> 
> **B1:** In the longer term, the upward velocity falls to zero and the platform then moves downwards, speeding up. Both stages are needed for this mark.
> 
> A response stating that the platform moves downwards immediately does not earn the second mark. The resultant force is downwards at once, but the platform's velocity is still upwards. Values for the acceleration and the time taken are not required, as neither is asked for.

parts.problemMd:
Each diagram below shows the forces acting on a block and the direction of its acceleration.

![Three force diagrams, labelled (i), (ii) and (iii). In (i) a block of mass 10 kg has a force of P N acting vertically upwards and its weight 10g N acting vertically downwards, and its acceleration is 7 m s⁻² downwards. In (ii) a block of mass m kg has a force of 40 N acting vertically upwards and its weight mg N acting vertically downwards, and its acceleration is 2 m s⁻² downwards. In (iii) a block of mass 5 kg has a force of 42 N acting vertically upwards and its weight 5g N acting vertically downwards, and its acceleration a m s⁻² is downwards.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/054-three-force-diagrams-labelled-i-ii-and-iii-in-i-.png)

Find the value of the unknown quantity (the force $P$, the mass $m$ or the acceleration $a$) in each case.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Take downwards as positive, the direction of the acceleration, and apply Newton's second law

$10 g - P = 10 \times 7$

**[M1]**

Use $g = 10$

$100 - P = 70$

$P = 30$

**[A1]**

(ii)

Take downwards as positive and apply Newton's second law

$m g - 40 = m \times 2$

**[M1]**

Use $g = 10$

$10 m - 40 = 2 m$

Collect the terms in $m$

$8 m = 40$

$m = 5$

**[A1]**

(iii)

Take downwards as positive and apply Newton's second law

$5 g - 42 = 5 a$

**[M1]**

Use $g = 10$

$50 - 42 = 5 a$

$a = 1 . 6$

**[A1]**

> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for diagram (i), with all three terms: $P$, the weight $10 g$ and $10 \times 7$. Allow sign errors for this mark.

>

parts.problemMd:
A company stores cheeses in a deep cave. Loads are moved in and out of the cave by a lift consisting of a horizontal pallet supported by two vertical ropes, and the tensions in the two ropes are always equal. A full pallet of cheeses has a total mass of 1700 kg.
