parts.solutionMd:
The pallet starts from rest with constant acceleration, so use $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $s = 20$, $u = 0$ and $t = 4$

$20 = 0 \times 4 + \frac{1}{2} \times a \times 4^{2}$

**[M1]**

$20 = 8 a$

$a = 2 . 5 \text{m s}^{-2}$

**[A1]**

Draw a force diagram for the pallet. Each rope has tension $T$ N

![Force diagram for the pallet of mass 1700 kg. Two tensions of T N act vertically upwards, one from each rope, the weight 1700g N acts vertically downwards, and the acceleration of 2.5 m s⁻² is downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/025-force-diagram-for-the-pallet-of-mass-1700-kg-two.png)

Take downwards as positive and apply Newton's second law, $F = m a$

$1700 g - 2 T = 1700 \times 2 . 5$

**[M1 A1]**

Use $g = 10$

$17000 - 2 T = 4250$

$2 T = 12750$

$T = 6375 \text{N}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $s = 20$, $u = 0$ and $t = 4$.
> 
> **A1**: $a = 2 . 5$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for the pallet, with all three terms: the total tension, the weight $1700 g$ and $1700 \times 2 . 5$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation with both ropes included, $1700 g - 2 T = 1700 \times 2 . 5$ or equivalent. Using a single tension $T$ for both ropes does not earn this mark.
> 
> **A1**: 6375. Answers which round to 6380 are also accepted. Follow through on the acceleration. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
Each rope can safely withstand a tension of 10.4 kN.

A new motor is fitted to the lift. With the new motor, a full pallet of mass 1700 kg is raised from rest through a distance of 30 m in 4.9 seconds, with constant acceleration.

Determine whether the ropes can be used safely with the new motor.
parts.solutionMd:
Use $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $s = 30$, $u = 0$ and $t = 4 . 9$ to find the acceleration

$30 = \frac{1}{2} \times a \times 4 . 9^{2}$

$a = 2 . 498958 \dots$

**[M1]**

Draw a force diagram for the pallet, now accelerating upwards

![Force diagram for the pallet of mass 1700 kg. Two tensions of T N act vertically upwards, one from each rope, the weight 1700g N acts vertically downwards, and the acceleration a m s⁻² is upwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/026-force-diagram-for-the-pallet-of-mass-1700-kg-two.png)

Take upwards as positive and apply Newton's second law, using the unrounded acceleration

$2 T - 1700 g = 1700 \times 2 . 498958 \dots$

**[M1]**

Use $g = 10$

$2 T = 17000 + 4248 . 229 \dots$

$T = 10624 . 11 \dots$

**[A1]**

Convert the safe limit to newtons and compare

$10 . 4 \text{kN} = 10400 \text{N}$

$10624 . 11 \dots > 10400$

**Final answer:** **The tension in each rope is more than 10400 N, so the ropes cannot be used safely with the new motor**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $s = 30$, $u = 0$ and $t = 4 . 9$ to find the acceleration.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for the pallet accelerating upwards, with all three terms: the total tension $2 T$, the weight $1700 g$ and $1700 a$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Tension in each rope which rounds to 10600.
> 
> **A1**: Correct comparison with 10400 N, or 10.4 kN, and the conclusion that the ropes cannot be used safely. Comparing a value with 10.4 without converting does not earn this mark.
> 
> An equivalent comparison, such as the total tension 21248 against the combined limit 20800 N, is equally acceptable.

parts.problemMd:
A child pushes two toy wagons along a straight horizontal track. The wagons are connected by a light rigid rod which is parallel to the track, and each wagon has mass 11.2 kg. The resistance to motion of each wagon is a constant force of $P$ N.

The child pushes the rear wagon with a constant horizontal force of 16.6 N, and the wagons move forwards with acceleration 0.25 $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

Find the value of $P$.
parts.solutionMd:
The thrust in the rod cancels when the two wagons are treated as one system of mass 22.4 kg

![Diagram of two wagons, each of mass 11.2 kg, joined by a rod on a horizontal track. A force of 16.6 N acts forwards on the rear wagon, a resistance of P N acts backwards on each wagon, and the acceleration of 0.25 m s⁻² is forwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/028-diagram-of-two-wagons-each-of-mass-11-2-kg-joine.png)

Take the direction of motion as positive and apply Newton's second law, $F = m a$, to the system

$16 . 6 - P - P = 22 . 4 \times 0 . 25$

**[M1 A1]**

$16 . 6 - 2 P = 5 . 6$

$2 P = 11$

$P = 5 . 5$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for the system, with the 16.6 N force, the resistances on both wagons and $22 . 4 \times 0 . 25$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation, $16 . 6 - 2 P = 22 . 4 \times 0 . 25$ or equivalent. Including only one resistance does not earn this mark.
> 
> **A1**: $P = 5 . 5$.
> 
> Applying Newton's second law to each wagon separately and eliminating the thrust is equally acceptable.

parts.problemMd: Find the thrust in the rod.
parts.solutionMd:
Draw a force diagram for the front wagon on its own. The rod pushes it forwards

![Force diagram for the front wagon of mass 11.2 kg. The thrust T N acts forwards, the resistance of 5.5 N acts backwards, the normal contact force R N acts vertically upwards and the weight 11.2g N acts vertically downwards. The acceleration of 0.25 m s⁻² is forwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/029-force-diagram-for-the-front-wagon-of-mass-11-2-k.png)

Take the direction of motion as positive and apply Newton's second law to the front wagon, using $P = 5 . 5$ from part (a)

$T - 5 . 5 = 11 . 2 \times 0 . 25$

**[M1]**

$T - 5 . 5 = 2 . 8$

$T = 8 . 3 \text{N}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for the front wagon, with all three terms: the thrust, the resistance and $11 . 2 \times 0 . 25$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: 8.3. Follow through on the value of $P$ from part (a). Units are not required.
> 
> Applying Newton's second law to the rear wagon instead, $16 . 6 - T - 5 . 5 = 11 . 2 \times 0 . 25$, is equally acceptable.

parts.problemMd:
A hydraulic lift in a warehouse is used to raise a crate of mass 1200 kg, which rests on the horizontal platform of the lift. The platform has mass 300 kg. The lifting force is transmitted to the platform by a light vertical rod, as shown in the diagram.

![A crate of mass 1200 kg resting on a horizontal platform of mass 300 kg, which is supported from below by a vertical rod](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/017-a-crate-of-mass-1200-kg-resting-on-a-horizontal-.png)

The platform and crate start from rest and move vertically upwards with constant acceleration, reaching a speed of 3 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ after 2 seconds.

Find the thrust in the rod.
parts.solutionMd:
The acceleration is constant, so use $v = u + a t$ with $v = 3$, $u = 0$ and $t = 2$

$3 = 0 + 2 a$

**[M1]**

$a = 1 . 5 \text{m s}^{-2}$

**[A1]**

The contact forces between the crate and the platform cancel when they are treated as one system of mass 1500 kg

![Force diagram for the platform and crate treated as a single system of mass 1500 kg. The thrust T N acts vertically upwards, the weight 1500g N acts vertically downwards, and the acceleration of 1.5 m s⁻² is upwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/018-force-diagram-for-the-platform-and-crate-treated.png)

Take upwards as positive and apply Newton's second law, $F = m a$, to the system

$T - 1500 g = 1500 \times 1 . 5$

**[M1]**

Use $g = 10$

$T - 15000 = 2250$

$T = 17250 \text{N}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $v = u + a t$ with $v = 3$, $u = 0$ and $t = 2$.
> 
> **A1**: $a = 1 . 5$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for the system, with all three terms: the thrust, the total weight $1500 g$ and $1500 \times 1 . 5$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: 17250. Answers which round to 17300 are also accepted. Follow through on the acceleration. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd: Find the magnitude and direction of the force exerted by the crate on the platform.
parts.solutionMd:
Draw a force diagram for the crate on its own. The platform pushes up on it with a normal contact force $R$ N

![Force diagram for the crate of mass 1200 kg. The normal contact force R N from the platform acts vertically upwards, the weight 1200g N acts vertically downwards, and the acceleration of 1.5 m s⁻² is upwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/019-force-diagram-for-the-crate-of-mass-1200-kg-the-.png)

Take upwards as positive and apply Newton's second law to the crate

$R - 1200 g = 1200 \times 1 . 5$

**[M1]**

Use $g = 10$

$R - 12000 = 1800$

$R = 13800$

**[A1]**

By Newton's third law, the crate pushes on the platform with a force of the same magnitude in the opposite direction

**Final answer:** **13800 N vertically downwards**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for the crate, with all three terms: the contact force, the weight $1200 g$ and $1200 \times 1 . 5$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: 13800 for the force exerted on the crate by the platform.
> 
> **B1**: 13800 N acting vertically downwards, from Newton's third law. The direction is needed for this mark. Follow through on the magnitude.

parts.problemMd:
Particles $A$ and $B$, of masses 3 kg and $m$ kg respectively, are attached to the ends of a light inextensible string which passes over a fixed smooth pulley. The particles hang vertically, as shown in the diagram.

![A fixed pulley with a string passing over it. Particle A, of mass 3 kg, hangs from one end of the string and particle B, of mass m kg, hangs from the other end](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/020-a-fixed-pulley-with-a-string-passing-over-it-par.png)

The particles are released from rest with the string taut, and $A$ moves downwards with acceleration 6 $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

Find the value of $m$.
parts.solutionMd:
$A$ accelerates downwards and $B$ accelerates upwards, both at 6 $\text{m s}^{-2}$. Draw a force diagram for each particle

![Force diagram for the two particles hanging over a fixed pulley. On A, of mass 3 kg, the tension T N acts upwards, the weight 3g N acts downwards and the acceleration of 6 m s⁻² is downwards. On B, of mass m kg, the tension T N acts upwards, the weight mg N acts downwards and the acceleration of 6 m s⁻² is upwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/021-force-diagram-for-the-two-particles-hanging-over.png)

Everything on $A$ is known except the tension, so start there. Take downwards as positive and apply Newton's second law, $F = m a$

$3 g - T = 3 \times 6$

**[M1]**

Use $g = 10$

$30 - T = 18$

$T = 12$

**[A1]**

For $B$, take upwards as positive and apply Newton's second law

$12 - m g = m \times 6$

**[M1]**

Use $g = 10$

$12 - 10 m = 6 m$

Collect the terms in $m$

$16 m = 12$

$m = 0 . 75$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for $A$, with all three terms: the tension, the weight $3 g$ and $3 \times 6$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: $T = 12$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for $B$, with all three terms: the tension, the weight $m g$ and $6 m$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: $m = 0 . 75$.
> 
> Applying Newton's second law to the whole system, $3 g - m g = ( 3 + m ) \times 6$, is equally acceptable. A correct system equation earns the first three marks.

parts.problemMd:
A block $B$ of mass 4.5 kg rests on a rough horizontal table. It is attached to one end of a light inextensible string, which passes over a small smooth pulley fixed at the edge of the table. A sphere $A$ of mass 3.5 kg is attached to the other end of the string and hangs vertically, 1 m above the ground. The string between $B$ and the pulley is horizontal, as shown in the diagram.

![A block B of mass 4.5 kg on a horizontal table, attached by a horizontal string that passes over a pulley at the edge of the table to a sphere A of mass 3.5 kg hanging vertically](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/030-a-block-b-of-mass-4-5-kg-on-a-horizontal-table-a.png)

The frictional force on $B$ has constant magnitude $F$ N. The system is released from rest with the string taut, and $A$ reaches the ground 0.8 seconds later.

Find the value of $F$.
parts.solutionMd:
$A$ falls 1 m from rest in 0.8 s with constant acceleration, so use $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $s = 1$, $u = 0$ and $t = 0 . 8$

$1 = 0 \times 0 . 8 + \frac{1}{2} \times a \times 0 . 8^{2}$

**[M1]**

$1 = 0 . 32 a$

$a = 3 . 125 \text{m s}^{-2}$

**[A1]**

Draw a force diagram for each object

![Force diagram for the block and sphere. On B, of mass 4.5 kg, the tension T N acts towards the pulley, the friction F N acts away from the pulley, the normal contact force R N acts upwards and the weight 4.5g N acts downwards, with acceleration 3.125 m s⁻² towards the pulley. On A, of mass 3.5 kg, the tension T N acts upwards and the weight 3.5g N acts downwards, with acceleration 3.125 m s⁻² downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/031-force-diagram-for-the-block-and-sphere-on-b-of-m.png)

For $A$, take downwards as positive and apply Newton's second law, $F = m a$, to find the tension

$3 . 5 g - T = 3 . 5 \times 3 . 125$

**[M1]**

Use $g = 10$

$35 - T = 10 . 9375$

$T = 24 . 0625$

**[A1]**

For $B$, the vertical forces balance, so take the direction towards the pulley as positive

$24 . 0625 - F = 4 . 5 \times 3 . 125$

**[M1]**

$24 . 0625 - F = 14 . 0625$

$F = 10$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $s = 1$, $u = 0$ and $t = 0 . 8$.
> 
> **A1**: $a = 3 . 125$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for $A$, with all three terms: the tension, the weight $3 . 5 g$ and $3 . 5 \times 3 . 125$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: $T = 24 . 0625$, or answers which round to 24.1.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for $B$, with all three terms: the tension, the friction and $4 . 5 \times 3 . 125$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: $F = 10$.
> 
> Applying Newton's second law to the whole system, $3 . 5 g - F = 8 \times 3 . 125$, with all three terms, is equally acceptable and earns both Newton's second law M1 marks. A correct system equation also earns the first A1 of that pair.

parts.problemMd:
A crate of mass 4600 kg is pushed in a straight line across horizontal ground by a vehicle, which pushes on the crate through a light horizontal rod. A constant resistance to motion of 3200 N acts on the crate. The rod will break if the thrust in it is greater than 100 kN.

At a certain instant the crate is moving at 1.8 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and is 100 m from a loading bay. The crate is to reach the loading bay within 3 seconds of this instant, with constant acceleration throughout.

Determine whether this is possible without the rod breaking.
parts.solutionMd:
To arrive in exactly 3 seconds, use $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $s = 100$, $u = 1 . 8$ and $t = 3$ to find the acceleration needed

$100 = 1 . 8 \times 3 + \frac{1}{2} \times a \times 3^{2}$

**[M1]**

$100 = 5 . 4 + 4 . 5 a$

$a = 21 . 0222 \dots$

**[A1]**

Draw a force diagram for the crate

![Force diagram for the crate of mass 4600 kg. The thrust T N from the rod acts forwards, the resistance of 3200 N acts backwards, the normal contact force R N acts vertically upwards and the weight 4600g N acts vertically downwards. The acceleration a m s⁻² is forwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/011-force-diagram-for-the-crate-of-mass-4600-kg-the-.png)

Take the direction of motion as positive and apply Newton's second law, $F = m a$, to find the thrust needed for this acceleration

$T - 3200 = 4600 \times 21 . 0222 \dots$

**[M1]**

$T = 99902 . 2 \dots$

**[A1]**

Any greater acceleration needs a greater thrust, so compare this thrust with the limit of 100 kN, which is 100000 N

$99902 . 2 \dots < 100000$

**Final answer:** **The thrust needed is less than 100000 N, so the crate can reach the loading bay within 3 seconds without the rod breaking**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $s = 100$, $u = 1 . 8$ and $t = 3$.
> 
> **A1**: Acceleration which rounds to 21.02.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for the crate, with all three terms: the thrust, the resistance of 3200 N and $4600 a$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Thrust which rounds to 99900.
> 
> **A1**: Correct comparison with 100000 N and the conclusion that it is possible. Enough accuracy must be kept to show the thrust is below the limit.
> 
> Equivalent routes are equally acceptable, for example finding the greatest acceleration the rod allows, $\frac{96800}{4600} = 21 . 04 \dots$, and comparing it with the 21.02 needed, or finding the time to cover 100 m at that greatest acceleration, 2.9985 s, and comparing it with 3 s.

parts.problemMd:
A weather balloon of mass 0.6 kg is attached to a bundle of scientific instruments of mass 2 kg by a light inextensible cable. The balloon is released from rest with the cable taut, and rises vertically with the balloon directly above the bundle. The only forces acting are the weights of the balloon and the bundle, the tension in the cable, and a constant vertical lift force on the balloon.

During the initial period of the ascent the acceleration is constant and the tension in the cable is 29.4 N. Find, for this initial period,

(i) the acceleration of the bundle,

(ii) the magnitude of the lift force on the balloon.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Draw a force diagram for the bundle on its own

![Force diagram for the bundle of mass 2 kg. The tension of 29.4 N acts vertically upwards, the weight 2g N acts vertically downwards, and the acceleration a m s⁻² is upwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/022-force-diagram-for-the-bundle-of-mass-2-kg-the-te.png)

Take upwards as positive and apply Newton's second law, $F = m a$, to the bundle

$29 . 4 - 2 g = 2 a$

**[M1]**

Use $g = 10$

$9 . 4 = 2 a$

$a = 4 . 7 \text{m s}^{-2}$

**[A1]**

(ii)

Treat the balloon and bundle as one system of mass 2.6 kg, since the tension in the cable is internal to it

![Force diagram for the balloon and bundle treated as a single system of mass 2.6 kg. The lift force L N acts vertically upwards, the weight 2.6g N acts vertically downwards, and the acceleration of 4.7 m s⁻² is upwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/023-force-diagram-for-the-balloon-and-bundle-treated.png)

Take upwards as positive and apply Newton's second law to the system

$L - 2 . 6 g = 2 . 6 \times 4 . 7$

**[M1 A1]**

Use $g = 10$

$L - 26 = 12 . 22$

$L = 38 . 22 \text{N}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for the bundle, with all three terms: the tension of 29.4 N, the weight $2 g$ and $2 a$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: $a = 4 . 7$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for the system, with all three terms: the lift, the total weight $2 . 6 g$ and $2 . 6 \times 4 . 7$, or for the balloon alone with all four terms: the lift, the weight $0 . 6 g$, the tension of 29.4 N and $0 . 6 \times 4 . 7$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation, $L - 2 . 6 g = 2 . 6 \times 4 . 7$ or $L - 0 . 6 g - 29 . 4 = 0 . 6 \times 4 . 7$.
> 
> **A1**: 38.22. Answers which round to 38.2 are also accepted. Follow through on the acceleration from part (i). Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
A box $B$ of mass 2 kg rests on a rough horizontal table. It is attached to one end of a light inextensible string, which passes over a small smooth pulley fixed at the edge of the table. A sphere $A$ of mass 1 kg is attached to the other end of the string and hangs vertically. The string between $B$ and the pulley is horizontal, as shown in the diagram.

![A box B of mass 2 kg on a horizontal table, attached by a horizontal string that passes over a pulley at the edge of the table to a sphere A of mass 1 kg hanging vertically](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/043-a-box-b-of-mass-2-kg-on-a-horizontal-table-attac.png)

The frictional force on $B$ has constant magnitude 7.6 N. The system is released from rest with the string taut, and $A$ moves downwards.

Find the acceleration of the system and the tension in the string.
parts.solutionMd:
Draw a force diagram for each object. $A$ accelerates downwards and $B$ accelerates towards the pulley

![Force diagram for the box and sphere. On B, of mass 2 kg, the tension T N acts towards the pulley, the friction of 7.6 N acts away from the pulley, the normal contact force R N acts upwards and the weight 2g N acts downwards, with acceleration a m s⁻² towards the pulley. On A, of mass 1 kg, the tension T N acts upwards and the weight g N acts downwards, with acceleration a m s⁻² downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/044-force-diagram-for-the-box-and-sphere-on-b-of-mas.png)

For $A$, take downwards as positive and apply Newton's second law, $F = m a$

$g - T = a$

**[M1]**

For $B$, the vertical forces balance, so take the direction towards the pulley as positive

$T - 7 . 6 = 2 a$

**[A1]**

Add the two equations to eliminate $T$

$g - 7 . 6 = 3 a$

Use $g = 10$

$10 - 7 . 6 = 3 a$

$a = 0 . 8 \text{m s}^{-2}$

**[A1]**

Substitute $a = 0 . 8$ into $T - 7 . 6 = 2 a$

$T - 7 . 6 = 1 . 6$

$T = 9 . 2 \text{N}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for either object, with all three of its terms. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Both equations correct, $g - T = a$ and $T - 7 . 6 = 2 a$, or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: $a = 0 . 8$.
> 
> **A1**: $T = 9 . 2$. Follow through on the value of $a$.
> 
> Applying Newton's second law to the whole system, $g - 7 . 6 = 3 a$, is equally acceptable for finding $a$. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
$A$ reaches the ground 1.5 seconds after the system is released, and does not rebound. At this instant $B$ is 14 cm from the pulley.

Determine whether $B$ reaches the pulley.
parts.solutionMd:
Use $v = u + a t$ with $u = 0$, $a = 0 . 8$ and $t = 1 . 5$ to find the speed of $B$ when $A$ reaches the ground

$v = 0 + 0 . 8 \times 1 . 5 = 1 . 2$

**[M1]**

Once $A$ is on the ground the string is slack, so friction is now the only horizontal force on $B$

![Force diagram for box B of mass 2 kg after A has reached the ground. The friction of 7.6 N acts away from the pulley, the normal contact force R N acts upwards and the weight 2g N acts downwards. There is no tension. B is moving towards the pulley at 1.2 m s⁻¹](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/045-force-diagram-for-box-b-of-mass-2-kg-after-a-has.png)

Take the direction towards the pulley as positive and apply Newton's second law to $B$

$- 7 . 6 = 2 a$

$a = - 3 . 8$

**[M1]**

Use $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with $v = 0$, $u = 1 . 2$ and $a = - 3 . 8$ to find the distance $B$ would travel before stopping

$0 = 1 . 2^{2} - 2 \times 3 . 8 \times s$

$s = 0 . 18947 \dots \text{m}$

**[M1]**

The distance to the pulley is 14 cm, which is 0.14 m

$0 . 189 \dots > 0 . 14$

**Final answer:** **B reaches the pulley before it comes to rest**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of a constant acceleration formula to find the speed of $B$ when $A$ reaches the ground, with the acceleration from part (a).
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for $B$ with the tension zero, giving a deceleration of 3.8. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with a final speed of zero, to find the stopping distance.
> 
> **A1**: Stopping distance 0.189 m, or 18.9 cm, compared with 0.14 m or 14 cm, and the conclusion that $B$ reaches the pulley.
> 
> Using the work-energy principle, $\frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times 1 . 2^{2} = 7 . 6 s$, to find the stopping distance is equally acceptable for the second and third M1 marks. Comparing the speed of $B$ after 14 cm with zero is also acceptable.

parts.problemMd:
A rock of mass 230 kg is attached to a buoy of mass 10 kg by a light inextensible rope. The rock sinks vertically through water, pulling the buoy vertically downwards behind it with the rope taut.

As the rock sinks, a constant resistance of 150 N acts on it. The combined effect of the buoyancy of the buoy and the water resistance on the buoy is modelled as a constant upward force of $P$ N.

Given that the tension in the rope is 655 N, find the value of $P$.
parts.solutionMd:
Draw a force diagram for each body. Both accelerate downwards at the same rate $a$$\text{m s}^{-2}$

![Force diagram for the buoy and the rock connected by a vertical rope, with the buoy above. On the buoy, of mass 10 kg, the force P N acts upwards, the weight 10g N acts downwards and the tension of 655 N acts downwards along the rope. On the rock, of mass 230 kg, the tension of 655 N acts upwards along the rope, the resistance of 150 N acts upwards and the weight 230g N acts downwards. Both accelerate downwards at a m s⁻²](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/010-force-diagram-for-the-buoy-and-the-rock-connecte.png)

Everything on the rock is known except its acceleration, so start there. Take downwards as positive and apply Newton's second law, $F = m a$

$230 g - 150 - 655 = 230 a$

**[M1]**

Use $g = 10$

$1495 = 230 a$

$a = 6 . 5$

**[A1]**

The buoy also accelerates downwards at 6.5 $\text{m s}^{-2}$, and the rope pulls it downwards. Apply Newton's second law to the buoy, with downwards positive

$10 g + 655 - P = 10 \times 6 . 5$

**[M1 A1]**

$755 - P = 65$

$P = 690$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for the rock, with all four terms: the weight $230 g$, the resistance of 150 N, the tension of 655 N and $230 a$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: $a = 6 . 5$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for the buoy, with all four terms: the weight $10 g$, the tension of 655 N, $P$ and $10 a$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation for the buoy, with the tension acting downwards on it.
> 
> **A1**: $P = 690$.
> 
> Applying Newton's second law to the whole system, $240 g - 150 - P = 240 a$, in place of either equation is equally acceptable.

parts.problemMd:
A lift car of mass 250 kg is raised vertically by a light inextensible cable attached to its top. Inside the lift car, a horizontal tabletop $B$ of mass 3 kg is supported by a light vertical rod fixed to the floor of the lift car. A light wire frame stands on $B$, and a small sphere $A$ of mass 0.05 kg hangs from the top of the frame by a light vertical string, as shown in the diagram.

![A lift car of mass 250 kg hanging from a vertical cable. Inside, a tabletop B of mass 3 kg is supported by a vertical rod from the floor of the car. A triangular wire frame stands on B, and a sphere A of mass 0.05 kg hangs from the top of the frame on a vertical string. An arrow labelled a shows the lift car accelerating upwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/013-a-lift-car-of-mass-250-kg-hanging-from-a-vertica.png)

The lift car starts from rest and moves upwards with constant acceleration $a$$\text{m s}^{-2}$. The thrust in the rod supporting $B$ is 35.38 N.

Find the tension in the string supporting $A$.
parts.solutionMd:
The rod supports $B$, the light frame and $A$ together, so add their masses

$3 + 0 . 05 = 3 . 05 \text{kg}$

![Force diagram for B, the frame and A treated as a single system of mass 3.05 kg. The thrust of 35.38 N acts vertically upwards, the weight 3.05g N acts vertically downwards, and the acceleration a m s⁻² is upwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/014-force-diagram-for-b-the-frame-and-a-treated-as-a.png)

$35 . 38 - 3 . 05 g = 3 . 05 a$

**[M1]**

Use $g = 10$

$4 . 88 = 3 . 05 a$

$a = 1 . 6$

**[A1]**

Now draw a force diagram for $A$ on its own

![Force diagram for sphere A of mass 0.05 kg. The tension T N in the string acts vertically upwards, the weight 0.05g N acts vertically downwards, and the acceleration of 1.6 m s⁻² is upwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/015-force-diagram-for-sphere-a-of-mass-0-05-kg-the-t.png)

Apply Newton's second law to $A$

$T - 0 . 05 g = 0 . 05 \times 1 . 6$

**[M1]**

$T - 0 . 5 = 0 . 08$

$T = 0 . 58 \text{N}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for $B$, the frame and $A$ together, with all three terms: the thrust of 35.38 N, the weight $3 . 05 g$ and $3 . 05 a$. Allow sign errors for this mark. Using 3 kg alone does not earn this mark.
> 
> **A1**: $a = 1 . 6$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for $A$, with all three terms: the tension, the weight $0 . 05 g$ and $0 . 05 a$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: 0.58. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd: Find the tension in the cable.
parts.solutionMd:
The cable supports the lift car and everything inside it, so add all the masses

$250 + 3 . 05 = 253 . 05 \text{kg}$

![Force diagram for the lift car and its contents treated as a single system of mass 253.05 kg. The tension in the cable T N acts vertically upwards, the weight 253.05g N acts vertically downwards, and the acceleration of 1.6 m s⁻² is upwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/016-force-diagram-for-the-lift-car-and-its-contents-.png)

$T - 253 . 05 g = 253 . 05 \times 1 . 6$

**[M1]**

$T = 2530 . 5 + 404 . 88$

$T = 2935 . 38 \text{N}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> **A1**: 2935.38. Answers which round to 2940 are also accepted. Follow through on the acceleration from part (a). Units are not required.

parts.problemMd: Find the distance the lift car rises in the first 3 seconds of its motion.
parts.solutionMd:
The lift car starts from rest with constant acceleration, so use $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $u = 0$, $a = 1 . 6$ and $t = 3$

$s = 0 \times 3 + \frac{1}{2} \times 1 . 6 \times 3^{2}$

**[M1]**

$s = 7 . 2 \text{m}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $u = 0$, $t = 3$ and the acceleration from part (a).

> **A1**: 7.2. Follow through on the acceleration from part (a). Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
Particles $A$ and $B$, of masses $m$ kg and 12 kg respectively, are attached to the ends of a light inextensible string which passes over a fixed smooth pulley. The particles hang vertically, as shown in the diagram.

![A fixed pulley with a string passing over it. Particle A, of mass m kg, hangs from one end of the string and particle B, of mass 12 kg, hangs from the other end](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/004-a-fixed-pulley-with-a-string-passing-over-it-par.png)

The particles are released from rest with the string taut, and each particle then moves with acceleration of magnitude 2 $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

Find the two possible values of $m$.
parts.solutionMd:
The question does not say which particle moves downwards, so consider each case

Case 1: $B$ moves downwards and $A$ moves upwards

![Force diagram for case 1, with the two particles hanging over a fixed pulley. On A, of mass m kg, the tension T N acts upwards, the weight mg N acts downwards and the acceleration of 2 m s⁻² is upwards. On B, of mass 12 kg, the tension T N acts upwards, the weight 12g N acts downwards and the acceleration of 2 m s⁻² is downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/005-force-diagram-for-case-1-with-the-two-particles-.png)

For $B$, take downwards as positive and apply Newton's second law, $F = m a$

$12 g - T = 12 \times 2$

**[M1]**

$T = 120 - 24 = 96$

**[A1]**

For $A$, take upwards as positive

$96 - m g = m \times 2$

**[M1]**

Use $g = 10$ and collect the terms in $m$

$12 m = 96$

$m = 8$

**[A1]**

Case 2: $A$ moves downwards and $B$ moves upwards

![Force diagram for case 2, with the two particles hanging over a fixed pulley. On A, of mass m kg, the tension T N acts upwards, the weight mg N acts downwards and the acceleration of 2 m s⁻² is downwards. On B, of mass 12 kg, the tension T N acts upwards, the weight 12g N acts downwards and the acceleration of 2 m s⁻² is upwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/006-force-diagram-for-case-2-with-the-two-particles-.png)

For $B$, take upwards as positive

$T - 12 g = 12 \times 2$

$T = 120 + 24 = 144$

For $A$, take downwards as positive

$m g - 144 = m \times 2$

**[M1]**

Use $g = 10$ and collect the terms in $m$

$8 m = 144$

$m = 18$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for $B$ in either case, with all three terms: the tension, the weight $12 g$ and $12 \times 2$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct tension for that case, 96 or 144.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for $A$ in the same case, with all three terms: the tension, the weight $m g$ and $2 m$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: The correct value of $m$ for that case, 8 or 18.
> 
> **M1**: Correct equations for both particles in the other case.
> 
> **A1**: The second value of $m$.
> 
> Applying Newton's second law to the whole system in each case, $12 g - m g = ( 12 + m ) \times 2$ and $m g - 12 g = ( m + 12 ) \times 2$, is equally acceptable. A correct system equation earns the M1 and A1 for that case's value of $m$.

parts.problemMd: Given that the tension in the string is 144 N, find the value of $m$.
parts.solutionMd:
From part (a), the tension is 96 N when $B$ moves downwards and 144 N when $A$ moves downwards, so this is case 2

$T = 144$*, so A moves downwards*

**[M1]**

$m = 18$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct identification of the case with a tension of 144 N, from the tensions found in part (a) or by forming the equation for $B$ with $T = 144$.
> 
> **A1**: $m = 18$. Follow through on the values from part (a).

parts.problemMd:
A bucket is raised from the bottom of a vertical well of depth $h$ m by a light rope, which remains vertical. The bucket is modelled as a particle.

![A vertical line representing a well, with the bottom of the well at the lower end, the top of the well at the upper end, and the depth marked as h m](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/007-a-vertical-line-representing-a-well-with-the-bot.png)

The bucket starts from rest at the bottom of the well. For the first part of the motion the rope is taut, and the bucket moves upwards with constant acceleration $a$$\text{m s}^{-2}$. The rope then becomes slack, and the bucket moves freely under gravity until it comes to instantaneous rest exactly at the top of the well.

Show that the total time taken for the bucket to move from the bottom to the top of the well is $T$ seconds, where

$T = \sqrt{\frac{2h(a+g)}{ag}}$
parts.solutionMd:
Let the rope become slack after the bucket has risen $x$ m, when its speed is $V$$\text{m s}^{-1}$. Take upwards as positive

![The well as a vertical line from bottom to top, split at the point where the rope becomes slack. The lower section has length x m, where the bucket accelerates at a m s⁻² from rest to speed V m s⁻¹. The upper section has length (h − x) m, where the bucket moves freely under gravity from speed V to rest](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/008-the-well-as-a-vertical-line-from-bottom-to-top-s.png)

For the first stage, use $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ from rest over $x$ m

$V^{2} = 2 a x$

**[M1]**

For the second stage the acceleration is $- g$, and the bucket comes to rest after a further $( h - x )$ m

$0 = V^{2} - 2 g ( h - x )$

**[M1]**

Both expressions equal $V^{2}$, so equate them to find $x$

$2 a x = 2 g ( h - x )$

$( a + g ) x = g h$

$x = \frac{gh}{a+g}$

Substitute back into $V^{2} = 2 a x$

$V^{2} = \frac{2agh}{a+g}$

**[A1]**

Use $v = u + a t$ for each stage to find the times

$t_{1} = \frac{V}{a}$

$t_{2} = \frac{V}{g}$

**[M1]**

Add the two times

$T = \frac{V}{a} + \frac{V}{g} = \frac{V(a+g)}{ag}$

**[A1]**

Substitute $V = \sqrt{\frac{2agh}{a+g}}$

$T = \sqrt{\frac{2agh}{a+g}} \times \frac{a+g}{ag}$

**[M1]**

Write the factor $\frac{a+g}{ag}$ inside the square root as its square

$T = \sqrt{\frac{2agh}{a+g}\times\frac{(a+g)^{2}}{a^{2}g^{2}}}$

Cancel the common factors of $a$, $g$ and $( a + g )$

$T = \sqrt{\frac{2h(a+g)}{ag}}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of a constant acceleration formula for the first stage, linking the speed when the rope becomes slack to $a$ and the distance.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of a constant acceleration formula for the second stage, with acceleration $- g$ (or deceleration $g$), final speed zero and the remaining distance.
> 
> **A1**: Correct expression for $V^{2}$ in terms of $a$, $g$ and $h$, or for $x$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the time of each stage.
> 
> **A1**: Correct total time in terms of $V$, $a$ and $g$.
> 
> **M1**: Substitution of the expression for $V$ into the total time.
> 
> **B1**: The given result, reached from correct working with every step shown.
> 
> Other valid routes, such as using $s = \frac{1}{2} ( u + v ) t$ for each stage, earn the corresponding marks.

parts.problemMd:
The rope can withstand a maximum tension of $P$ N. When the rope is used at this maximum tension to raise a bucket of mass 10 kg in the way described, from the bottom of a well of depth 30 m, the bucket reaches the top of the well 4.20 seconds after it starts to move.

Hence find the value of $P$.
parts.solutionMd:
Substitute $T = 4 . 2$, $h = 30$ and $g = 10$ into the result from part (a), $T = \sqrt{\frac{2h(a+g)}{ag}}$

$4 . 2 = \sqrt{\frac{60(a+10)}{10a}}$

**[M1]**

Square both sides

$17 . 64 = \frac{6(a+10)}{a}$

Multiply by $a$ and collect the terms in $a$

$11 . 64 a = 60$

$a = 5 . 154639 \dots$

**[A1]**

Draw a force diagram for the bucket while the rope is taut

![Force diagram for the bucket of mass 10 kg while it is being raised. The tension P N acts vertically upwards, the weight 10g N acts vertically downwards, and the acceleration a m s⁻² is upwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/009-force-diagram-for-the-bucket-of-mass-10-kg-while.png)

Take upwards as positive and apply Newton's second law, $F = m a$, using the unrounded acceleration

$P - 10 g = 10 \times 5 . 154639 \dots$

**[M1]**

$P = 100 + 51 . 546 \dots$

**Final answer:** $P = 152$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Substitution of $T = 4 . 2$, $h = 30$ and $g = 10$ into the given formula.
> 
> **A1**: $a = 5 . 15$, or better. The exact value is $\frac{500}{97}$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for the bucket, with all three terms: the tension, the weight $10 g$ and $10 a$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 152. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
A locomotive of mass 10000 kg pulls a number of identical carriages along a straight horizontal track. The locomotive and the carriages are connected in a line by light rigid rods, which are parallel to the track. The locomotive's engine produces a driving force of 20000 N, and the resistance to motion of the locomotive is a constant 3000 N. Each carriage has mass $M$ kg, and the resistance to motion of each carriage is a constant 1000 N.

When three carriages are attached, the tension in the rod connecting the last carriage to the carriage in front of it is 437.8 N greater than the tension in the corresponding rod when four carriages are attached.

Find the value of $M$.
parts.solutionMd:
With $n$ carriages attached, the tensions in the rods cancel when the whole train is treated as one system. Take the direction of motion as positive and apply Newton's second law, $F = m a$

$20000 - 3000 - 1000 n = ( 10000 + n M ) a$

**[M1]**

Substitute $n = 3$ for the acceleration $a_{3}$ with three carriages

$a_{3} = \frac{14000}{10000+3M}$

**[A1]**

Substitute $n = 4$ for the acceleration $a_{4}$ with four carriages

$a_{4} = \frac{13000}{10000+4M}$

**[A1]**

The rod to the last carriage is the only force pulling that carriage forwards. Draw a force diagram for the last carriage

![Force diagram for the last carriage of mass M kg. The tension T N in the rod acts forwards, the resistance of 1000 N acts backwards, the normal contact force R N acts vertically upwards and the weight Mg N acts vertically downwards. The acceleration a m s⁻² is forwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/012-force-diagram-for-the-last-carriage-of-mass-m-kg.png)

Apply Newton's second law to the last carriage

$T - 1000 = M a$

$T = 1000 + M a$

**[M1]**

The difference between the two tensions is 437.8 N, and the 1000 N cancels

$M ( a_{3} - a_{4} ) = 437 . 8$

**[M1]**

Substitute the two accelerations

`M\left(\dfrac{14000}{10000 + 3M} - \dfrac{13000}{10000 + 4M}\right) = 437.8`

Multiply both sides by $( 10000 + 3 M ) ( 10000 + 4 M )$

$M ( 14000 ( 10000 + 4 M ) - 13000 ( 10000 + 3 M ) ) = 437 . 8 ( 10000 + 3 M ) ( 10000 + 4 M )$

**[M1]**

Expand both sides

$17000 M^{2} + 10000000 M = 5253 . 6 M^{2} + 30646000 M + 43780000000$

Collect all the terms on one side and divide by 1000

$11 . 7464 M^{2} - 20646 M - 43780000 = 0$

**[A1]**

Solve the quadratic. The mass must be positive, so reject the negative root

$M = 3000 . 008 \dots$

**Final answer:** $M = 3000$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for the whole train with a general number of carriages, or for three or four carriages directly, with the driving force, all the resistances and the total mass.
> 
> **A1**: Correct acceleration with three carriages, $\frac{14000}{10000+3M}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct acceleration with four carriages, $\frac{13000}{10000+4M}$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for the last carriage alone, giving the tension as $1000 + M a$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of the difference in tensions to form an equation in $M$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method to clear the fractions and form a polynomial equation.
> 
> **A1**: Correct quadratic equation, in any equivalent form.
> 
> **A1**: $M = 3000$, with the negative root rejected. Answers which round to 3000 are accepted.

parts.problemMd:
A block $B$ of mass $m_{B}$ kg rests on a rough horizontal table. It is attached to one end of a light inextensible string, which passes over a small smooth pulley fixed at the edge of the table. A sphere $A$ of mass $m_{A}$ kg is attached to the other end of the string and hangs vertically. The string between $B$ and the pulley is horizontal, as shown in the diagram.

![A block B of mass m_B kg on a horizontal table, attached by a horizontal string that passes over a pulley at the edge of the table to a sphere A of mass m_A kg hanging vertically](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/001-a-block-b-of-mass-m-b-kg-on-a-horizontal-table-a.png)

The frictional force on $B$ has constant magnitude $F$ N. The system is released from rest with the string taut.

Given that $A$ moves downwards, show that the tension in the string is $T$ N, where

$T = \frac{m_{A}}{m_{A}+m_{B}} ( m_{B} g + F )$
parts.solutionMd:
Draw a force diagram for each object, with the common acceleration $a$$\text{m s}^{-2}$

![Force diagram for the block and sphere. On B, of mass m_B kg, the tension T N acts towards the pulley, the friction F N acts away from the pulley, the normal contact force R N acts upwards and the weight m_B g N acts downwards, with acceleration a m s⁻² towards the pulley. On A, of mass m_A kg, the tension T N acts upwards and the weight m_A g N acts downwards, with acceleration a m s⁻² downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/002-force-diagram-for-the-block-and-sphere-on-b-of-m.png)

For $A$, take downwards as positive and apply Newton's second law, $F = m a$

$m_{A} g - T = m_{A} a$

**[M1]**

For $B$, the vertical forces balance, so take the direction towards the pulley as positive

$T - F = m_{B} a$

**[M1 A1]**

Rearrange the equation for $B$ to make $a$ the subject

$a = \frac{T-F}{m_{B}}$

Substitute into the equation for $A$

$m_{A} g - T = \frac{m_{A}(T-F)}{m_{B}}$

**[M1]**

Multiply both sides by $m_{B}$

$m_{A} m_{B} g - m_{B} T = m_{A} T - m_{A} F$

Collect the terms in $T$ on one side

$m_{A} m_{B} g + m_{A} F = ( m_{A} + m_{B} ) T$

Factorise the left-hand side and divide by $( m_{A} + m_{B} )$

$T = \frac{m_{A}}{m_{A}+m_{B}} ( m_{B} g + F )$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for $A$, with all three terms: the weight $m_{A} g$, the tension and $m_{A} a$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for $B$, with all three terms: the tension, the friction and $m_{B} a$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Both equations correct.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method to eliminate $a$ from the two equations.
> 
> **B1**: The given result, reached from correct working with every step shown.
> 
> Adding the two equations to find $a = \frac{m_{A}g-F}{m_{A}+m_{B}}$ first and substituting into either equation is equally acceptable.

parts.problemMd: Given instead that the system remains at rest after it is released, find $F$ in terms of $m_{A}$ and $g$, and verify that the expression for $T$ in part (a) gives the correct tension in this case.
parts.solutionMd:
The system is at rest, so the forces on each object balance

![Force diagram for the block and sphere at rest. On B, the tension T N acts towards the pulley, the friction F N acts away from the pulley, the normal contact force R N acts upwards and the weight m_B g N acts downwards. On A, the tension T N acts upwards and the weight m_A g N acts downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/newtons-second-law/assets/003-force-diagram-for-the-block-and-sphere-at-rest-o.png)

For $A$, the tension balances the weight

$T = m_{A} g$

For $B$, the friction balances the tension

$F = T$

**[M1]**

$F = m_{A} g$

**[A1]**

Substitute $F = m_{A} g$ into the expression from part (a)

$T = \frac{m_{A}}{m_{A}+m_{B}} ( m_{B} g + m_{A} g )$

Take out the common factor of $g$ from the bracket

$T = \frac{m_{A}g(m_{A}+m_{B})}{m_{A}+m_{B}} = m_{A} g$

**Final answer:** **This is the same as the tension found from the forces on A, so the expression gives the correct tension**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of equilibrium for both objects, with the tension equal to the weight of $A$ and the friction equal to the tension.
> 
> **A1**: $F = m_{A} g$.
> 
> **B1**: Correct substitution into the expression from part (a), simplified to $m_{A} g$, with the conclusion that this matches the tension at rest.
> 
> Using the equations from part (a) with $a = 0$ is equally acceptable for the first two marks.

parts.problemMd:

Find the horizontal and vertical components of the force.
parts.solutionMd:
The horizontal component is adjacent to the 30° angle, so use cosine

$\text{Horizontal component} = 16 \text{cos}  30 ^{\circ}$

**Final answer:** $\text{Horizontal component} = 13 . 9$** N (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

The vertical component is opposite the 30° angle, so use sine

$\text{Vertical component} = 16 \text{sin}  30 ^{\circ}$

parts.problemMd: Hence find the resultant force on the particle in the horizontal direction and in the vertical direction, stating the direction of each.
parts.solutionMd:
Horizontally, the 14 N force acts to the left and the horizontal component of the 17 N force acts to the right. Take left as positive

parts.problemMd:
A particle of mass 5 kg slides down a line of greatest slope of a smooth plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal.

Find the acceleration of the particle.
parts.solutionMd:
The plane is smooth, so there is no friction. The only forces are the weight and the normal contact force

![Force diagram for a block of mass 5 kg on a smooth plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. The weight 5g N acts vertically downwards and the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the plane, away from it. The acceleration a m s⁻² is down the plane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/060-force-diagram-for-a-block-of-mass-5-kg-on-a-smoo.png)

$a = 5 \text{m s}^{-2}$

**[A1]**

parts.problemMd: Find the normal contact force exerted by the plane on the particle.
parts.solutionMd:
The particle stays on the plane, so the forces perpendicular to the plane balance

$R = 5 g \text{cos}  30 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $R = 43 . 3$** N (3 s.f.)**

parts.problemMd:
In each part of this question, a block is initially at rest on a rough horizontal surface. The diagram in each part shows all the forces acting on the block, where $R$ N is the normal contact force and $F$ N is the frictional force.

In this part, the block has mass 5 kg and the coefficient of friction between the block and the surface is 0.3. A horizontal force of magnitude 13 N acts on the block, as shown in the diagram.

![A block of mass 5 kg on a rough horizontal surface. A force of 13 N acts horizontally to the right, the frictional force F N acts horizontally to the left, the normal contact force R N acts vertically upwards and the weight 5g N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/054-a-block-of-mass-5-kg-on-a-rough-horizontal-surfa.png)

Find the value of $F$ and determine whether the block remains at rest or begins to move.
parts.solutionMd:
The vertical forces balance, so find the normal contact force and then the maximum possible friction

$R = 5 g = 50$

$μ R = 0 . 3 \times 50 = 15$

**[M1 A1]**

The applied force of 13 N is less than the maximum friction of 15 N, so friction is not at its limit and it balances the applied force

$13 < 15$

**Final answer:** **The block remains at rest, with **$F = 13$

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Do not write $F = μ R$ straight away. The value $μ R$ is only the maximum friction the surface can provide, and friction reaches it only when the block is moving or about to move. Compare the applied force with $μ R$ first.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of $F = μ R$ with $R = 5 g$ to find the maximum friction.
> 
> **A1**: Maximum friction 15.
> 
> **A1**: The block remains at rest and $F = 13$, from a comparison of 13 with 15.

**[M1 A1]**

Compare the applied force with the maximum friction

$10 < 12$

**Final answer:** **The block remains at rest, with **$F = 10$

**[A1]**

A force of 16 N acts horizontally to the right, the frictional force F N acts horizontally to the left, the normal contact force R N acts vertically upwards, the weight 7g N acts vertically downwards, and a further force of 12 N pushes vertically downwards on the top of the block](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/056-a-block-of-mass-7-kg-on-a-rough-horizontal-surfa.png)

Find the value of $F$ and determine whether the block remains at rest or begins to move.
parts.solutionMd:
The vertical forces balance, and the 12 N force pushes the block into the surface

$R = 7 g + 12 = 82$

$μ R = 0 . 2 \times 82 = 16 . 4$

**[M1 A1]**

Compare the applied force with the maximum friction

$16 < 16 . 4$

**Final answer:** **The block remains at rest, with **$F = 16$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
