parts.problemMd:
In this part, a block of mass 10 kg is initially at rest, and the coefficient of friction between the block and the surface is 0.25. A force of magnitude 30 N acts on the block at an angle of 30° above the horizontal, as shown in the diagram.

![A block of mass 10 kg on a rough horizontal surface. A force of 30 N acts upwards and to the right at 30° above the horizontal, the frictional force F N acts horizontally to the left, the normal contact force R N acts vertically upwards and the weight 10g N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/057-a-block-of-mass-10-kg-on-a-rough-horizontal-surf.png)

Find the value of $F$ and determine whether the block remains at rest or begins to move.
parts.solutionMd:
The vertical component of the 30 N force, $30 \text{sin}  30 ^{\circ}$, acts upwards, so resolve vertically to find $R$

$R + 30 \text{sin}  30 ^{\circ} = 10 g$

$R = 100 - 15 = 85$

**[M1]**

Find the maximum possible friction

$μ R = 0 . 25 \times 85 = 21 . 25$

**[A1]**

The horizontal component of the 30 N force pulls the block to the right

$30 \text{cos}  30 ^{\circ} = 25 . 980 \dots$

**[B1]**

This is greater than the maximum friction, so friction cannot hold the block and takes its maximum value

$25 . 980 \dots > 21 . 25$

**Final answer:** **The block begins to move, with **$F = 21 . 25$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Resolving vertically with all three forces to find $R$. Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Maximum friction 21.25, or an answer which rounds to 21.3.
> 
> **B1**: Horizontal component $30 \text{cos}  30 ^{\circ}$, or answers which round to 26.0.
> 
> **A1**: The block begins to move and $F = 21 . 25$, from a comparison of the horizontal component with the maximum friction. An answer which rounds to 21.3 is accepted.

parts.problemMd:
A particle of mass 5 kg is projected up a line of greatest slope of a rough plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction between the particle and the plane is 0.3. The particle comes to instantaneous rest and then slides back down the plane.

Find the magnitude of the frictional force acting on the particle while it moves up the plane, and state its direction.
parts.solutionMd:
While the particle moves up the plane, friction acts down the plane, opposing the motion

![Force diagram for a block of mass 5 kg moving up a rough plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. The weight 5g N acts vertically downwards, the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the plane, and the frictional force F N acts down the plane. The direction of motion is up the plane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/050-force-diagram-for-a-block-of-mass-5-kg-moving-up.png)

The particle does not move perpendicular to the plane, so resolve in that direction

$R = 5 g \text{cos}  30 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

The particle is moving, so friction takes its maximum value, $F = μ R$

$F = 0 . 3 \times 50 \text{cos}  30 ^{\circ} = 12 . 990 \dots$

**Final answer:** $F = 13 . 0$** N (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

**Final answer:** **Friction acts down the plane**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Resolving perpendicular to the plane to find $R$, which must be a component of $5 g$ (using $R = 5 g$ does not earn this mark). Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Any answer which rounds to 13.0. The exact value $\frac{15\sqrt{3}}{2}$ is also accepted.
> 
> **B1**: Direction stated as down the plane, or shown on a diagram.

parts.problemMd: Find the deceleration of the particle while it moves up the plane.
parts.solutionMd:
Take up the plane as positive. Both friction and the component of the weight along the plane act down the plane. Apply Newton's second law

$- F - 5 g \text{sin}  30 ^{\circ} = 5 a$

**[M1]**

Substitute $F = 12 . 990 \dots$ and $g = 10$

$- 12 . 990 \dots - 25 = 5 a$

**[A1]**

$a = - 7 . 5980 \dots$

The negative sign shows the acceleration is down the plane, so the particle is slowing down

**Final answer:** $\text{Deceleration} = 7 . 60 \text{m s}^{-2}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law along the plane, with all three relevant terms (friction, the component of the weight and $5 a$). Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation, for example $- 12 . 99 - 25 = 5 a$.
> 
> **A1**: Deceleration 7.60, or any answer which rounds to 7.60. An acceleration of $- 7 . 60$ with up the plane stated as positive is also accepted.

parts.problemMd: State the magnitude and direction of the frictional force acting on the particle while it slides back down the plane.
parts.solutionMd:
The normal contact force is unchanged, so the magnitude of the friction is unchanged. It now opposes motion down the plane

![Force diagram for a block of mass 5 kg sliding down a rough plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. The weight 5g N acts vertically downwards, the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the plane, and the frictional force F N acts up the plane. The direction of motion is down the plane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/051-force-diagram-for-a-block-of-mass-5-kg-sliding-d.png)

**Final answer:** $F = 13 . 0$** N (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **Friction acts up the plane**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Magnitude 13.0, or the same value as found in part (a).
> 
> **B1**: Direction stated as up the plane, or shown on a diagram.
> 
> The two answers are marked independently.

parts.problemMd: Find the acceleration of the particle while it slides down the plane.
parts.solutionMd:
Take down the plane as positive. The component of the weight acts down the plane and friction acts up it. Apply Newton's second law

$5 g \text{sin}  30 ^{\circ} - F = 5 a$

**[M1]**

Substitute $F = 12 . 990 \dots$ and $g = 10$

$25 - 12 . 990 \dots = 5 a$

**[A1]**

**Final answer:** $a = 2 . 40 \text{m s}^{-2}$** down the plane (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law along the plane, with all three relevant terms. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation, for example $25 - 12 . 99 = 5 a$.
> 
> **A1**: Any answer which rounds to 2.40. The direction does not need to be stated.

parts.problemMd:
A particle of mass 10 kg slides down a line of greatest slope of a smooth plane inclined at 15° to the horizontal.

Find the acceleration of the particle.
parts.solutionMd:
The plane is smooth, so the only forces are the weight and the normal contact force

![Force diagram for a block of mass 10 kg on a smooth plane inclined at 15° to the horizontal. The weight 10g N acts vertically downwards and the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the plane. The acceleration a m s⁻² is down the plane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/044-force-diagram-for-a-block-of-mass-10-kg-on-a-smo.png)

Take down the plane as positive and apply Newton's second law

$10 g \text{sin}  15 ^{\circ} = 10 a$

**[M1]**

Use $g = 10$

$a = 10 \text{sin}  15 ^{\circ}$

**Final answer:** $a = 2 . 59 \text{m s}^{-2}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law along the plane, with the weight resolved along the plane. Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Any answer which rounds to 2.59.

parts.problemMd: Find the normal contact force exerted by the plane on the particle.
parts.solutionMd:
The forces perpendicular to the plane balance

$R = 10 g \text{cos}  15 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

Use $g = 10$

$R = 100 \text{cos}  15 ^{\circ}$

**Final answer:** $R = 96 . 6$** N (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Resolving perpendicular to the plane, with $R$ equal to the component of the weight perpendicular to the plane. Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Any answer which rounds to 96.6.

parts.problemMd:
Three forces, of magnitudes 20 N, 19 N and 10 N, act on a particle, as shown in the diagram.

![Three forces acting on a particle. A force of 20 N acts upwards and to the left at an angle of 50° above the horizontal, a force of 19 N acts horizontally to the right, and a force of 10 N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/037-three-forces-acting-on-a-particle-a-force-of-20-.png)

Find the resultant force on the particle in the horizontal direction and in the vertical direction, stating the direction of each.
parts.solutionMd:
Take right as positive. The horizontal component of the 20 N force, $20 \text{cos}  50 ^{\circ}$, acts to the left

$19 - 20 \text{cos}  50 ^{\circ} = 19 - 12 . 855 \dots$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $\text{Horizontal resultant} = 6 . 14$** N to the right (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

Take up as positive. The vertical component of the 20 N force, $20 \text{sin}  50 ^{\circ}$, acts upwards

$20 \text{sin}  50 ^{\circ} - 10 = 15 . 320 \dots - 10$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $\text{Vertical resultant} = 5 . 32$** N upwards (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Resolving horizontally, with both horizontal forces. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: 6.14 N to the right, or any answer which rounds to 6.14 with its direction stated.
> 
> **M1**: Resolving vertically, with both vertical forces. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: 5.32 N upwards, or any answer which rounds to 5.32 with its direction stated.
> 
> A signed answer is accepted in place of a direction in words, provided the positive direction is stated. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
Three forces, of magnitudes $20 \sqrt{3}$ N, 20 N and $F$ N, act on a particle, as shown in the diagram.

![Three forces acting on a particle. A force of 20√3 N acts upwards and to the right at an angle of 60° above the horizontal, a force of 20 N acts upwards and to the left at an angle of 30° above the horizontal, and a force of F N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/034-three-forces-acting-on-a-particle-a-force-of-20-.png)

Show that the resultant force on the particle in the horizontal direction is zero.
parts.solutionMd:
Find the horizontal component of the $20 \sqrt{3}$ N force, which acts to the right

$20 \sqrt{3} \text{cos}  60 ^{\circ} = 20 \sqrt{3} \times \frac{1}{2} = 10 \sqrt{3}$

Find the horizontal component of the 20 N force, which acts to the left

$20 \text{cos}  30 ^{\circ} = 20 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 10 \sqrt{3}$

**[M1 A1]**

The $F$ N force has no horizontal component. Take right as positive

$10 \sqrt{3} - 10 \sqrt{3} = 0$

**Final answer:** **The resultant force in the horizontal direction is zero**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Resolving both angled forces horizontally. Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Both horizontal components correct, each $10 \sqrt{3}$ or equivalent.
> 
> **B1**: The two components shown to cancel, with a conclusion. Because the result is given, exact values must be seen: a decimal comparison such as $17 . 3 - 17 . 3$ alone does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd: Given that the particle is in equilibrium, find the value of $F$.
parts.solutionMd:
The particle is in equilibrium, so the vertical forces balance. Both angled forces have upward components

$F = 20 \sqrt{3} \text{sin}  60 ^{\circ} + 20 \text{sin}  30 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

Use the exact values $\text{sin}  60 ^{\circ} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ and $\text{sin}  30 ^{\circ} = \frac{1}{2}$

$F = 20 \sqrt{3} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + 20 \times \frac{1}{2} = 30 + 10$

**[A1]**

$F = 40$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Resolving vertically with all three forces. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Correct vertical components, 30 and 10, or a correct unsimplified equation.
> 
> **A1**: $F = 40$.

parts.problemMd:
A particle of mass $m$ kg is attached to one end of a light inextensible string. The other end of the string is attached to a fixed point $P$. A horizontal force of magnitude 12 N acts on the particle, which is in equilibrium with the string inclined at 40° to the vertical, as shown in the diagram.

![A particle of mass m kg hanging from a fixed point P by a string inclined at 40° to a dashed vertical line through P. A horizontal force of 12 N acts on the particle to the left, away from the vertical line](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/032-a-particle-of-mass-m-kg-hanging-from-a-fixed-poi.png)

Find the tension in the string and the value of $m$.
parts.solutionMd:
Three forces act on the particle: the tension along the string towards $P$, the 12 N force and the weight

![Force diagram for the particle. The tension T N acts along the string towards P, at 40° to the vertical. A force of 12 N acts horizontally to the left and the weight mg N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/033-force-diagram-for-the-particle-the-tension-t-n-a.png)

The particle is in equilibrium, so the horizontal forces balance. The horizontal component of the tension is opposite the 40° angle

$T \text{sin}  40 ^{\circ} = 12$

**[M1]**

$T = \frac{12}{\text{sin}40^{\circ}} = 18 . 668 \dots$

**Final answer:** $T = 18 . 7$** N (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

The vertical forces also balance

$T \text{cos}  40 ^{\circ} = m g$

**[M1]**

Use $g = 10$ and the unrounded value of $T$

$10 m = 18 . 668 \dots \times \text{cos}  40 ^{\circ} = 14 . 301 \dots$

**[A1]**

**Final answer:** $m = 1 . 43$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Resolving horizontally, with the component of the tension and the 12 N force. Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Any answer which rounds to 18.7.
> 
> **M1**: Resolving vertically, with the component of the tension and the weight. Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Correct vertical equation with $g = 10$, for example $10 m = 18 . 67 \text{cos}  40 ^{\circ}$.
> 
> **A1**: Any answer which rounds to 1.43.
> 
> Dividing the two equations to give $\text{tan}  40 ^{\circ} = \frac{12}{10m}$ is an equally valid way to find $m$, and earns the same marks for the vertical equation and $m$.

parts.problemMd:
A particle of mass 7 kg is pulled along a rough horizontal plane by a force of magnitude 45 N acting at an angle of 20° above the horizontal, as shown in the diagram. The coefficient of friction between the particle and the plane is 0.4. The particle moves to the right.

![A particle of mass 7 kg on a rough horizontal plane, pulled by a force of 45 N acting upwards and to the right at 20° above the horizontal](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/030-a-particle-of-mass-7-kg-on-a-rough-horizontal-pl.png)

Find the magnitude of the frictional force acting on the particle.
parts.solutionMd:
The upward component of the 45 N force, $45 \text{sin}  20 ^{\circ}$, reduces the normal contact force

![Force diagram for the particle of mass 7 kg. The force of 45 N acts at 20° above the horizontal to the right, the frictional force F N acts horizontally to the left, the normal contact force R N acts vertically upwards and the weight 7g N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/031-force-diagram-for-the-particle-of-mass-7-kg-the-.png)

The particle does not move vertically, so resolve vertically

$R + 45 \text{sin}  20 ^{\circ} = 7 g$

**[M1]**

Use $g = 10$

$R = 70 - 45 \text{sin}  20 ^{\circ} = 54 . 609 \dots$

**[A1]**

The particle is moving, so friction takes its maximum value

$F = μ R = 0 . 4 \times 54 . 609 \dots$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $F = 21 . 8$** N (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Resolving vertically with all three forces. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: $R = 70 - 45 \text{sin}  20 ^{\circ}$, or any value which rounds to 54.6.
> 
> **M1**: Use of $F = μ R$ with the normal contact force from resolving, which must include a component of the 45 N force.
> 
> **A1**: Any answer which rounds to 21.8.

parts.problemMd: Hence find the acceleration of the particle.
parts.solutionMd:
Take the direction of motion as positive and apply Newton's second law horizontally

$45 \text{cos}  20 ^{\circ} - F = 7 a$

**[M1]**

Substitute the unrounded friction

$42 . 286 \dots - 21 . 843 \dots = 7 a$

**[A1]**

**Final answer:** $a = 2 . 92 \text{m s}^{-2}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law horizontally, with all three relevant terms (the horizontal component of the 45 N force, the friction and $7 a$). Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation, following through from the friction found in part (a).
> 
> **A1**: Any answer which rounds to 2.92.

parts.problemMd:
A particle of mass 0.7 kg is on a rough plane inclined at 35° to the horizontal. The particle is held in equilibrium by a force of magnitude $P$ N acting up a line of greatest slope of the plane, as shown in the diagram. The coefficient of friction between the particle and the plane is 0.35, and the particle is about to slip up the plane.

![A particle on a rough plane inclined at 35° to the horizontal. A force of P N acts on the particle up the plane, parallel to a line of greatest slope](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/035-a-particle-on-a-rough-plane-inclined-at-35-to-th.png)

Find the value of $P$.
parts.solutionMd:
The particle is about to slip up the plane, so friction acts down the plane, and it is limiting

![Force diagram for a block of mass 0.7 kg on a rough plane inclined at 35° to the horizontal. The force P N acts up the plane, the frictional force F N acts down the plane, the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the plane and the weight 0.7g N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/036-force-diagram-for-a-block-of-mass-0-7-kg-on-a-ro.png)

Resolve perpendicular to the plane

$R = 0 . 7 g \text{cos}  35 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

Use $g = 10$

$R = 7 \text{cos}  35 ^{\circ} = 5 . 7340 \dots$

**[A1]**

Friction is limiting, so $F = μ R$

$F = 0 . 35 \times 5 . 7340 \dots = 2 . 0069 \dots$

**[M1]**

Resolve along the plane. Friction and the component of the weight both act down the plane

$P = F + 0 . 7 g \text{sin}  35 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

$P = 2 . 0069 \dots + 7 \text{sin}  35 ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

**Final answer:** $P = 6 . 02$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Resolving perpendicular to the plane, with $R$ a component of $0 . 7 g$. Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: $R = 7 \text{cos}  35 ^{\circ}$, or any value which rounds to 5.73.
> 
> **M1**: Use of $F = μ R$ with the normal contact force from resolving.
> 
> **M1**: Resolving along the plane, with all three relevant terms ($P$, the friction and the component of the weight). Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation, with friction acting down the plane.
> 
> **A1**: Any answer which rounds to 6.02.

parts.problemMd:
A particle of mass 3 kg is released from rest on a rough plane inclined at 15° to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction between the particle and the plane is 0.2.

Find the distance the particle travels in the first 3 s after it is released.
parts.solutionMd:
The particle slides down the plane, so friction acts up the plane

![Force diagram for a block of mass 3 kg on a rough plane inclined at 15° to the horizontal. The weight 3g N acts vertically downwards, the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the plane and the frictional force F N acts up the plane. The acceleration a m s⁻² is down the plane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/041-force-diagram-for-a-block-of-mass-3-kg-on-a-roug.png)

Resolve perpendicular to the plane, then use $F = μ R$ since the particle is moving

$R = 3 g \text{cos}  15 ^{\circ} = 30 \text{cos}  15 ^{\circ}$

$F = 0 . 2 \times 30 \text{cos}  15 ^{\circ} = 5 . 7955 \dots$

**[M1]**

Take down the plane as positive and apply Newton's second law

$3 g \text{sin}  15 ^{\circ} - F = 3 a$

**[M1]**

$30 \text{sin}  15 ^{\circ} - 5 . 7955 \dots = 3 a$

$a = 0 . 65633 \dots$

**[A1]**

Use $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $u = 0$ and $t = 3$

$s = 0 + \frac{1}{2} \times 0 . 65633 \dots \times 3^{2}$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $s = 2 . 95 \text{m}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> If your acceleration had come out negative, the particle would not slide at all, because friction would be strong enough to hold it. A positive value here confirms that the component of the weight down the plane is greater than the maximum friction.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of $F = μ R$ with $R$ a component of $3 g$ ($R = 3 g$ does not earn this mark). Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law along the plane, with all three relevant terms. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Acceleration, or any value which rounds to 0.656.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $u = 0$, $t = 3$ and the acceleration found.
> 
> **A1**: Any answer which rounds to 2.95.

parts.problemMd:
A particle of mass 3 kg is projected with speed $u$$\text{m s}^{-1}$ up a line of greatest slope of a rough plane inclined at 25° to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction between the particle and the plane is 0.27. The particle comes to instantaneous rest after moving 1.91 m up the plane.

Show that the deceleration of the particle while it moves up the plane is $( \text{sin}  25 ^{\circ} + 0 . 27 \text{cos}  25 ^{\circ} ) g$$\text{m s}^{-2}$.
parts.solutionMd:
The particle moves up the plane, so friction acts down the plane

![Force diagram for a block of mass 3 kg moving up a rough plane inclined at 25° to the horizontal. The weight 3g N acts vertically downwards, the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the plane and the frictional force F N acts down the plane. The direction of motion is up the plane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/045-force-diagram-for-a-block-of-mass-3-kg-moving-up.png)

Resolve perpendicular to the plane

$R = 3 g \text{cos}  25 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

The particle is moving, so friction takes its maximum value

$F = 0 . 27 \times 3 g \text{cos}  25 ^{\circ}$

Take up the plane as positive and apply Newton's second law

$- 0 . 27 \times 3 g \text{cos}  25 ^{\circ} - 3 g \text{sin}  25 ^{\circ} = 3 a$

**[M1 A1]**

Divide through by 3

$a = - ( \text{sin}  25 ^{\circ} + 0 . 27 \text{cos}  25 ^{\circ} ) g$

The acceleration is negative, so the particle slows down at this rate

$\text{Deceleration} = ( \text{sin}  25 ^{\circ} + 0 . 27 \text{cos}  25 ^{\circ} ) g \text{m s}^{-2}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Resolving perpendicular to the plane, with $R$ a component of $3 g$. Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law along the plane, with all three relevant terms and $F = 0 . 27 R$. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation.
> 
> **B1**: The printed deceleration, reached from correct working with g kept as a letter. Because the result is given, every step must be seen and no decimal approximation may be used.

parts.problemMd: Hence find the value of $u$.
parts.solutionMd:
Use $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with $v = 0$, $s = 1 . 91$ and the acceleration from part (a), which is negative because the particle is slowing down

$0 = u^{2} - 2 ( \text{sin}  25 ^{\circ} + 0 . 27 \text{cos}  25 ^{\circ} ) g \times 1 . 91$

**[M1]**

Use $g = 10$

$u^{2} = 2 \times 6 . 6732 \dots \times 1 . 91 = 25 . 491 \dots$

**[A1]**

**Final answer:** $u = 5 . 05$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with $v = 0$, $s = 1 . 91$ and the deceleration from part (a).
> 
> **A1**: Correct value of $u^{2}$, or a correct equation with $g = 10$.
> 
> **A1**: Any answer which rounds to 5.05.
> 
> A work-energy equation, with the loss of kinetic energy equal to the gain in potential energy plus the work done against friction over 1.91 m, reaching the same value is equally acceptable.

parts.problemMd:
A block $B$ of mass 5 kg rests on a rough horizontal table. It is attached to one end of a light inextensible string, which passes over a small smooth pulley fixed at the edge of the table. A particle $A$ of mass 4 kg is attached to the other end of the string and hangs vertically, as shown in the diagram. The string between $B$ and the pulley is horizontal, and the coefficient of friction between $B$ and the table is 0.35.

![A block B of mass 5 kg on a horizontal table, attached by a horizontal string that passes over a pulley at the edge of the table to a particle A of mass 4 kg hanging vertically](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/042-a-block-b-of-mass-5-kg-on-a-horizontal-table-att.png)

The system is released from rest with the string taut.

Find the acceleration of the system and the tension in the string.
parts.solutionMd:
Draw a force diagram for each object. $A$ accelerates downwards and $B$ accelerates towards the pulley

![Force diagram for the block and particle. On B, of mass 5 kg, the tension T N acts towards the pulley, the friction F N acts away from the pulley, the normal contact force R N acts upwards and the weight 5g N acts downwards, with acceleration a m s⁻² towards the pulley. On A, of mass 4 kg, the tension T N acts upwards and the weight 4g N acts downwards, with acceleration a m s⁻² downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/043-force-diagram-for-the-block-and-particle-on-b-of.png)

$B$ does not move vertically, so $R = 5 g = 50$. $B$ is moving, so friction takes its maximum value

$F = 0 . 35 \times 50 = 17 . 5$

**[B1]**

For $B$, take the direction towards the pulley as positive and apply Newton's second law

$T - 17 . 5 = 5 a$

**[M1]**

For $A$, take downwards as positive

$4 g - T = 4 a$

**[A1]**

Add the two equations to eliminate $T$, and use $g = 10$

$40 - 17 . 5 = 9 a$

**[M1]**

$a = 2 . 5 \text{m s}^{-2}$

**[A1]**

Substitute $a = 2 . 5$ into $4 g - T = 4 a$

$T = 40 - 4 \times 2 . 5$

**Final answer:** $T = 30$** N**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Friction 17.5, from $F = 0 . 35 \times 5 g$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for either object, with all three of its terms. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Both equations correct, $T - 17 . 5 = 5 a$ and $4 g - T = 4 a$, or equivalent.
> 
> **M1**: Solving the two equations to find $a$ (for example by adding them).
> 
> **A1**: $a = 2 . 5$.
> 
> **A1**: $T = 30$. Follow through on the value of $a$.
> 
> Applying Newton's second law to the whole system, $4 g - 17 . 5 = 9 a$, is equally acceptable for finding $a$. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
In each part of this question, a block rests on a rough horizontal surface and is on the point of moving under the action of a force of magnitude $P$ N.

In this part, the block has mass 2 kg, the force acts horizontally, and the coefficient of friction between the block and the surface is 0.4.

![A block of mass 2 kg on a rough horizontal surface, with a force of P N acting on it horizontally to the right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/046-a-block-of-mass-2-kg-on-a-rough-horizontal-surfa.png)

Find the value of $P$.
parts.solutionMd:
Friction acts against the direction the block is about to move in

![Force diagram for the block of mass 2 kg. The force P N acts horizontally to the right, the frictional force F N acts horizontally to the left, the normal contact force R N acts vertically upwards and the weight 2g N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/047-force-diagram-for-the-block-of-mass-2-kg-the-for.png)

The vertical forces balance

$R = 2 g = 20$

The block is on the point of moving, so friction is limiting

$F = μ R = 0 . 4 \times 20 = 8$

**[M1]**

The horizontal forces balance

$P = F$

**[M1]**

$P = 8$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> **M1**: Resolving horizontally, with $P$ equal to the friction.

> **A1**: $P = 8$.

parts.problemMd:
In this part, the block has mass 6 kg and the coefficient of friction between the block and the surface is 0.3. The force of magnitude $P$ N pushes on the block at an angle of 40° below the horizontal, as shown in the diagram, and the block is on the point of moving.

![A block of mass 6 kg on a rough horizontal surface. A force of P N pushes down on the block from the upper left, at an angle of 40° below the horizontal](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/048-a-block-of-mass-6-kg-on-a-rough-horizontal-surfa.png)

parts.solutionMd:
The force pushes the block into the surface, so its vertical component adds to the normal contact force

![Force diagram for the block of mass 6 kg. The force P N pushes down on the block at 40° below the horizontal, the frictional force F N acts horizontally to the left, the normal contact force R N acts vertically upwards and the weight 6g N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/049-force-diagram-for-the-block-of-mass-6-kg-the-for.png)

Resolve vertically

$R = 6 g + P \text{sin}  40 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

The block is on the point of moving, so friction is limiting

$F = 0 . 3 ( 6 g + P \text{sin}  40 ^{\circ} )$

**[M1]**

Resolve horizontally

$P \text{cos}  40 ^{\circ} = 0 . 3 ( 60 + P \text{sin}  40 ^{\circ} )$

**[M1]**

Collect the terms in $P$

$P ( \text{cos}  40 ^{\circ} - 0 . 3 \text{sin}  40 ^{\circ} ) = 18$

**Final answer:** $P = 31 . 4$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Resolving vertically with all three forces to find $R$. Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **M1**: Use of $F = μ R$ with the normal contact force from resolving vertically, which must include a component of $P$.
> 
> **M1**: Resolving horizontally, with the horizontal component of $P$ equal to the friction. Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.

parts.problemMd:
Three forces, of magnitudes 35 N, 17 N and 25 N, act on a particle, as shown in the diagram.

Find the resultant force on the particle in the horizontal direction and in the vertical direction, stating the direction of each.
parts.solutionMd:
Both angled forces are measured from the vertical, so their horizontal components use sine. Take right as positive

$= 28 . 670 \dots + 10 . 565 \dots - 17 = 22 . 235 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{Horizontal resultant} = 22 . 2$** N to the right (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

$35 \text{cos}  55 ^{\circ} - 25 \text{cos}  25 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

$= 20 . 075 \dots - 22 . 657 \dots = - 2 . 5825 \dots$

The negative sign shows the vertical resultant acts downwards

**Final answer:** $\text{Vertical resultant} = 2 . 58$** N downwards (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

parts.problemMd: Hence find the acceleration of the particle.

parts.problemMd:
A particle of mass $m$ kg is released from rest on a rough plane inclined at $θ ^{\circ}$ to the horizontal, where $45 < θ < 90$. The coefficient of friction between the particle and the plane is $μ$.

Given that the particle remains at rest, show that $μ > 1$.
parts.solutionMd:
The particle would slide down the plane without friction, so friction acts up the plane

![Force diagram for a block of mass m kg at rest on a rough plane inclined at θ° to the horizontal. The weight mg N acts vertically downwards, the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the plane and the frictional force F N acts up the plane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/018-force-diagram-for-a-block-of-mass-m-kg-at-rest-o.png)

Resolve perpendicular to the plane

$R = m g \text{cos}  θ ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

The particle is at rest, so the forces along the plane balance

$F = m g \text{sin}  θ ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

Friction can be at most $μ R$, so `F \leqslant \mu R`

`mg\text{sin} \; \theta° \leqslant \mu mg\text{cos} \; \theta°`

**[M1]**

Divide both sides by $m g \text{cos}  θ ^{\circ}$, which is positive because $θ < 90$

`\mu \geqslant \text{tan} \; \theta°`

**[A1]**

For $45 < θ < 90$, $\text{tan}  θ ^{\circ} > \text{tan}  45 ^{\circ} = 1$

`\mu \geqslant \text{tan} \; \theta° > 1`

$μ > 1$

**[B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The particle is at rest, not necessarily on the point of slipping, so friction satisfies `F \leqslant \mu R` rather than $F = μ R$. Writing $F = μ R$ would only show that $μ = \text{tan}  θ ^{\circ}$ in the limiting case, and the question needs the result for every angle in the range.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Resolving perpendicular to the plane, with $R$ a component of $m g$. Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **M1**: Resolving along the plane, with friction equal to the component of the weight along the plane.
> 
> **M1**: Use of `F \leqslant \mu R`. Using $F = μ R$ in place of the inequality does not earn this mark.
> 
> **A1**: `\mu \geqslant \text{tan} \; \theta°`, or equivalent.
> 
> **B1**: The printed result, from $\text{tan}  θ ^{\circ} > 1$ for $45 < θ < 90$. Because the result is given, this step must be stated.

parts.problemMd:
A particle of mass 2 kg is projected with speed $u$$\text{m s}^{-1}$ up a line of greatest slope of a rough plane inclined at 20° to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction between the particle and the plane is 0.2. The particle comes to instantaneous rest after moving 4.85 m up the plane.

Find the value of $u$.
parts.solutionMd:
The particle moves up the plane, so friction acts down the plane

![Force diagram for a block of mass 2 kg moving up a rough plane inclined at 20° to the horizontal. The weight 2g N acts vertically downwards, the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the plane and the frictional force F N acts down the plane. The direction of motion is up the plane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/024-force-diagram-for-a-block-of-mass-2-kg-moving-up.png)

**Method 1**

Resolve perpendicular to the plane, then use $F = μ R$ since the particle is moving

$R = 2 g \text{cos}  20 ^{\circ}$

$F = 0 . 2 \times 20 \text{cos}  20 ^{\circ} = 3 . 7587 \dots$

**[M1]**

Take up the plane as positive and apply Newton's second law

$- F - 2 g \text{sin}  20 ^{\circ} = 2 a$

**[M1 A1]**

$a = - \frac{3.7587\dots+6.8404\dots}{2} = - 5 . 2995 \dots$

**[A1]**

Use $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with $v = 0$ and $s = 4 . 85$

$0 = u^{2} - 2 \times 5 . 2995 \dots \times 4 . 85$

**[M1]**

$u^{2} = 51 . 405 \dots$

**[A1]**

**Final answer:** $u = 7 . 17$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of $F = μ R$ with $R$ a component of $2 g$ ($R = 2 g$ does not earn this mark). Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law along the plane, with all three relevant terms. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation.
> 
> **A1**: Acceleration $- 5 . 30$, or a deceleration of 5.30, or any value which rounds to these.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with $v = 0$, $s = 4 . 85$ and the acceleration found.
> 
> **A1**: $u^{2}$, or any value which rounds to 51.4.
> 
> **A1**: Any answer which rounds to 7.17.

**Method 2**

Resolve perpendicular to the plane, then use $F = μ R$ since the particle is moving

$R = 2 g \text{cos}  20 ^{\circ}$

$F = 0 . 2 \times 20 \text{cos}  20 ^{\circ} = 3 . 7587 \dots$

**[M1]**

Find the work done against friction over the 4.85 m

$\text{Work done against friction} = 3 . 7587 \dots \times 4 . 85 = 18 . 230 \dots$

**[A1]**

The particle rises a vertical height of $4 . 85 \text{sin}  20 ^{\circ}$, so find the gain in potential energy

$\text{Gain in potential energy} = 2 \times 10 \times 4 . 85 \text{sin}  20 ^{\circ} = 33 . 175 \dots$

**[M1 A1]**

By the work-energy principle, the loss in kinetic energy equals the gain in potential energy plus the work done against friction

$\frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times u^{2} = 33 . 175 \dots + 18 . 230 \dots$

**[M1 A1]**

**Final answer:** $u = 7 . 17$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of $F = μ R$ with $R$ a component of $2 g$ ($R = 2 g$ does not earn this mark). Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Work done against friction, or any value which rounds to 18.2.
> 
> **M1**: Use of $m g h$ for the gain in potential energy, with $h = 4 . 85 \text{sin}  20 ^{\circ}$. Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Gain in potential energy, or any value which rounds to 33.2.
> 
> **M1**: Work-energy equation with all three relevant terms (kinetic energy, potential energy and work done against friction). Allow sign errors for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation.
> 
> **A1**: Any answer which rounds to 7.17.

parts.problemMd:
Two particles $A$ and $B$, of masses 2.7 kg and 2.2 kg respectively, are attached to the ends of a light inextensible string. Particle $A$ is held at rest on a rough plane inclined at 25° to the horizontal. The string passes over a small smooth pulley fixed at the top of the plane, and $B$ hangs vertically below the pulley, as shown in the diagram. The part of the string between $A$ and the pulley is parallel to a line of greatest slope of the plane. The coefficient of friction between $A$ and the plane is $μ$.

![Particle A on a rough plane inclined at 25° to the horizontal, attached by a string parallel to the plane that passes over a pulley at the top of the plane to particle B, which hangs vertically](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/015-particle-a-on-a-rough-plane-inclined-at-25-to-th.png)

The system is released from rest with the string taut. Given that $B$ descends 1.82 m in the first 3 s after it is released, find the value of $μ$.
parts.solutionMd:
Find the acceleration from the motion of $B$. Use $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $u = 0$, $s = 1 . 82$ and $t = 3$

$1 . 82 = \frac{1}{2} a \times 3^{2}$

**[M1]**

$a = \frac{91}{225} = 0 . 40444 \dots$

**[A1]**

$A$ moves up the plane, so friction on $A$ acts down the plane

![Force diagram for particles A and B. On A, on the plane inclined at 25°, the tension T N acts up the plane, the frictional force F N acts down the plane, the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the plane and the weight 2.7g N acts vertically downwards, with acceleration a m s⁻² up the plane. On B, the tension T N acts upwards and the weight 2.2g N acts downwards, with acceleration a m s⁻² downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/016-force-diagram-for-particles-a-and-b-on-a-on-the-.png)

Resolve perpendicular to the plane for $A$, then use $F = μ R$ since $A$ is moving

$F = μ \times 2 . 7 g \text{cos}  25 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

For $A$, take up the plane as positive and apply Newton's second law

$T - 2 . 7 g \text{sin}  25 ^{\circ} - 2 . 7 μ g \text{cos}  25 ^{\circ} = 2 . 7 a$

**[M1 A1]**

For $B$, take downwards as positive

$2 . 2 g - T = 2 . 2 a$

**[M1 A1]**

Add the two equations to eliminate $T$, and use $g = 10$ and the exact value of $a$

$22 - 27 \text{sin}  25 ^{\circ} - 27 μ \text{cos}  25 ^{\circ} = 4 . 9 \times \frac{91}{225}$

$24 . 470 \dots μ = 8 . 6075 \dots$

**Final answer:** $μ = 0 . 352$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $u = 0$, $s = 1 . 82$ and $t = 3$.
> 
> **A1**: $a = \frac{91}{225}$, or any value which rounds to 0.404.
> 
> **M1**: Use of $F = μ R$ with $R$ a component of $2 . 7 g$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for $A$ along the plane, with all four relevant terms. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation for $A$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for $B$, with all three relevant terms. Allow sign errors for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation for $B$.
> 
> **A1**: Any answer which rounds to 0.352.
> 
> Applying Newton's second law to the whole system in place of either single-particle equation is equally acceptable. A value of $a$ rounded to 0.404 before substitution still leads to 0.352.

parts.problemMd:
Two particles $A$ and $B$, of masses 4 kg and 3 kg respectively, are attached to the ends of a light inextensible string. Particle $A$ is held at rest on a rough plane inclined at 35° to the horizontal. The string passes over a small smooth pulley fixed at the top of the plane, and $B$ hangs vertically below the pulley, as shown in the diagram. The part of the string between $A$ and the pulley is parallel to a line of greatest slope of the plane. The coefficient of friction between $A$ and the plane is 0.15.

The system is released from rest with the string taut, and $B$ moves downwards.

Find the acceleration of the system and the tension in the string.
parts.solutionMd:
$A$ moves up the plane, so friction on $A$ acts down the plane

![Force diagram for particles A and B. On A, on the plane inclined at 35°, the tension T N acts up the plane, the frictional force F N acts down the plane, the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the plane and the weight 4g N acts vertically downwards, with acceleration a m s⁻² up the plane. On B, the tension T N acts upwards and the weight 3g N acts downwards, with acceleration a m s⁻² downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/039-force-diagram-for-particles-a-and-b-on-a-on-the-.png)

Resolve perpendicular to the plane for $A$, then use $F = μ R$ since $A$ is moving

$R = 4 g \text{cos}  35 ^{\circ}$

$F = 0 . 15 \times 40 \text{cos}  35 ^{\circ} = 4 . 9149 \dots$

**[M1]**

For $A$, take up the plane as positive and apply Newton's second law

$T - 4 g \text{sin}  35 ^{\circ} - F = 4 a$

**[M1 A1]**

For $B$, take downwards as positive

$3 g - T = 3 a$

**[M1 A1]**

Add the two equations to eliminate $T$, and use $g = 10$

$30 - 40 \text{sin}  35 ^{\circ} - 4 . 9149 \dots = 7 a$

**Final answer:** $a = 0 . 306 \text{m s}^{-2}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

Substitute the unrounded $a = 0 . 30600 \dots$ into $3 g - T = 3 a$

$T = 30 - 3 \times 0 . 30600 \dots$

**Final answer:** $T = 29 . 1$** N (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of $F = μ R$ with $R$ a component of $4 g$. Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for $A$ along the plane, with all four relevant terms. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.

> **A1**: Correct equation for $A$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for $B$, with all three relevant terms. Allow sign errors for this mark only.

> **A1**: Correct equation for $B$.
> 
> **A1**: Any answer which rounds to 0.306.
> 
> **A1**: Any answer which rounds to 29.1. Follow through on the value of $a$.

> Applying Newton's second law to the whole system in place of either single-particle equation is equally acceptable. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
$B$ reaches the ground 3.2 s after the system is released, and does not rebound. Particle $A$ does not reach the pulley.

Find the total distance travelled by $A$ from the instant the system is released until $A$ first comes to instantaneous rest.
parts.solutionMd:
While $B$ falls, $A$ moves up the plane from rest with $a = 0 . 30600 \dots$ for 3.2 s. Use $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$

$s_{1} = \frac{1}{2} \times 0 . 30600 \dots \times 3 . 2^{2} = 1 . 5667 \dots$

**[M1]**

Use $v = u + a t$ to find the speed of $B$ as it reaches the ground

$v = 0 . 30600 \dots \times 3 . 2 = 0 . 97921 \dots$

**[M1]**

The string is inextensible, so $A$ and $B$ always move with the same speed. At the instant $B$ reaches the ground, $A$ is moving up the plane at this same speed

$v_{A} = 0 . 97921 \dots \text{m s}^{-1}$

Once $B$ is on the ground the string is slack, so there is no tension. $A$ is still moving up the plane, so friction still acts down the plane

![Force diagram for particle A after B reaches the ground. On the plane inclined at 35°, the frictional force F N acts down the plane, the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the plane and the weight 4g N acts vertically downwards. There is no tension. A is moving up the plane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/040-force-diagram-for-particle-a-after-b-reaches-the.png)

Take up the plane as positive and apply Newton's second law to $A$

$- 4 g \text{sin}  35 ^{\circ} - 0 . 15 \times 4 g \text{cos}  35 ^{\circ} = 4 a$

**[M1]**

$a = - 10 ( \text{sin}  35 ^{\circ} + 0 . 15 \text{cos}  35 ^{\circ} ) = - 6 . 9644 \dots$

**[A1]**

Use $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with $v = 0$ and $u = 0 . 97921 \dots$ to find how much further $A$ travels

$0 = 0 . 97921 \dots^{2} - 2 \times 6 . 9644 \dots \times s_{2}$

$s_{2} = 0 . 068839 \dots$

**[M1]**

Add the two distances

$s_{1} + s_{2} = 1 . 5667 \dots + 0 . 068839 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{Total distance} = 1 . 64 \text{m}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $u = 0$, $t = 3 . 2$ and the acceleration from part (a).
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $v = u + a t$ to find the speed of $B$ as it reaches the ground, which is also the speed of $A$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for $A$ with no tension, with the weight component and friction. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Deceleration, or any value which rounds to 6.96.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with a final speed of zero, to find the further distance.
> 
> **A1**: Any answer which rounds to 1.64.
> 
> Finding the further distance with a work-energy equation, with the loss of kinetic energy of $A$ equal to its gain in potential energy plus the work done against friction, is equally acceptable for the third and fifth marks.

parts.problemMd:
In a warehouse, a load of weight $W$ N is lifted by two light cables. The tension in each cable is $T$ N, and each cable makes an angle of $θ ^{\circ}$ with the vertical, as shown in the diagram. The only forces acting on the load are its weight and the tensions in the two cables.

![A load hanging from two cables. Each cable has tension T N and makes an angle θ° with a dashed vertical line through the load, one on each side. The weight W N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/001-a-load-hanging-from-two-cables-each-cable-has-te.png)

The load is initially at rest. Find an inequality in terms of $T$ and $θ$ that $W$ must satisfy if the load is to be lifted.
parts.solutionMd:
The horizontal components of the two tensions cancel. Each tension has an upward component $T \text{cos}  θ ^{\circ}$

$\text{Resultant upward force} = 2 T \text{cos}  θ ^{\circ} - W$

**[M1 A1]**

The load starts to rise from rest only if the resultant upward force is positive

$2 T \text{cos}  θ ^{\circ} - W > 0$

$W < 2 T \text{cos}  θ ^{\circ}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Resolving vertically, with the vertical components of both tensions and the weight. Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Resultant upward force $2 T \text{cos}  θ ^{\circ} - W$, or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: $W < 2 T \text{cos}  θ ^{\circ}$, or equivalent. The inequality must be strict.

parts.problemMd: Given that the load is still accelerating upwards when $θ = 45$, find an inequality in terms of $W$ that $T$ must satisfy.
parts.solutionMd:
Substitute $θ = 45$ into the condition from part (a), using $\text{cos}  45 ^{\circ} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}$

$W < 2 T \times \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \sqrt{2} T$

**[M1]**

Divide by $\sqrt{2}$

$T > \frac{W}{\sqrt{2}}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Substituting $θ = 45$ into the condition from part (a), or into a fresh vertical resolution.
> 
> **A1**: $T > \frac{W}{\sqrt{2}}$. Equivalent forms such as $T > \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} W$ or $T > 0 . 707 W$ are accepted. The inequality must be strict.

parts.problemMd:
A small smooth ring $B$ of mass $m$ kg is threaded on a light inextensible string. The ends of the string are attached to fixed points $A$ and $C$, where $A$ is vertically above $C$. The ring is held in equilibrium by a horizontal force of magnitude 3 N, with the parts $A B$ and $B C$ of the string making angles of 35° and 55° respectively with the vertical, as shown in the diagram.

![A ring B on a string whose ends are attached to point A and point C, with A vertically above C on a dashed vertical line. The part AB makes an angle of 35° with the vertical and the part BC makes an angle of 55° with the vertical. A horizontal force of 3 N acts on B, away from the line AC](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/002-a-ring-b-on-a-string-whose-ends-are-attached-to-.png)

Find the value of $m$.
parts.solutionMd:
The ring is smooth, so the tension $T$ N is the same in both parts of the string

![Force diagram for the ring B. The tension T N acts along BA, at 35° to the vertical, upwards and to the right. The tension T N acts along BC, at 55° to the vertical, downwards and to the right. A force of 3 N acts horizontally to the left and the weight mg N acts vertically downwards. A dashed vertical line and a dashed horizontal line are drawn through the ring, with the angle between BA and the upward vertical marked 35° and the angle between BC and the downward vertical marked 55°](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/003-force-diagram-for-the-ring-b-the-tension-t-n-act.png)

Each part of the string makes the same angle with the vertical at the ring as it does at its fixed point, because the dashed vertical through the ring is parallel to $A C$

Resolve horizontally. Both tensions have components towards the line $A C$

$T \text{sin}  35 ^{\circ} + T \text{sin}  55 ^{\circ} = 3$

**[M1]**

$T = \frac{3}{\text{sin}35^{\circ}+\text{sin}55^{\circ}} = 2 . 1540 \dots$

**[A1]**

Resolve vertically. The tension in $A B$ pulls upwards; the tension in $B C$ and the weight pull downwards

$T \text{cos}  35 ^{\circ} = T \text{cos}  55 ^{\circ} + m g$

**[M1 A1]**

Use $g = 10$ and the unrounded value of $T$

$10 m = 2 . 1540 \dots ( \text{cos}  35 ^{\circ} - \text{cos}  55 ^{\circ} ) = 0 . 52898 \dots$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $m = 0 . 0529$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Resolving horizontally, with the same tension in both parts of the string and all three terms. Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: $T$, or any value which rounds to 2.15.
> 
> **M1**: Resolving vertically, with all three terms. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Correct vertical equation.
> 
> **M1**: Substituting the value of $T$ to find $m$.
> 
> **A1**: Any answer which rounds to 0.0529.
> 
> Treating the two tensions as different unknowns does not earn the first M1, because the ring is smooth.

parts.problemMd:
A particle of mass $m$ kg is pulled up a line of greatest slope of a smooth plane inclined at 25° to the horizontal by a force of magnitude 60 N. The force acts at an angle of 15° above the line of greatest slope, in the vertical plane containing it, as shown in the diagram. The particle accelerates up the plane at 0.3 $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

![A particle on a smooth plane inclined at 25° to the horizontal. A force of 60 N acts on the particle upwards and up the plane, at an angle of 15° above the line of greatest slope](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/004-a-particle-on-a-smooth-plane-inclined-at-25-to-t.png)

Find the value of $m$.

The component of the 60 N force along the plane is $60 \text{cos}  15 ^{\circ}$

A force of 60 N acts at 15° above the plane, the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the plane and the weight mg N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/005-force-diagram-for-a-block-of-mass-m-kg-on-a-smoo.png)

$60 \text{cos}  15 ^{\circ} - m g \text{sin}  25 ^{\circ} = 0 . 3 m$

$m ( 0 . 3 + 10 \text{sin}  25 ^{\circ} ) = 60 \text{cos}  15 ^{\circ}$

$m = \frac{57.955\dots}{4.5261\dots}$

**[A1]**

parts.problemMd: Find the magnitude of the normal contact force exerted by the plane on the particle.
parts.solutionMd:
The particle does not move perpendicular to the plane. The 60 N force has a component $60 \text{sin}  15 ^{\circ}$ away from the plane

$R + 60 \text{sin}  15 ^{\circ} = m g \text{cos}  25 ^{\circ}$

**[M1 A1]**

Use $g = 10$ and the unrounded mass

$R = 12 . 804 \dots \times 10 \text{cos}  25 ^{\circ} - 60 \text{sin}  15 ^{\circ} = 116 . 04 \dots - 15 . 529 \dots$

**Final answer:** $R = 101$** N (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Resolving perpendicular to the plane, with all three relevant terms. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation, following through from the mass found in part (a).
