parts.problemMd:
A particle of mass 0.8 kg is released from rest on a rough plane inclined at an angle $θ$ to the horizontal, where $\text{tan}  θ = \frac{2}{7}$. The particle slides down a line of greatest slope, and 4 s after it is released its speed is 1.35 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Find the coefficient of friction between the particle and the plane.
parts.solutionMd:
From a right-angled triangle with opposite 2 and adjacent 7, the hypotenuse is $\sqrt{2^{2}+7^{2}} = \sqrt{53}$

$\text{sin}  θ = \frac{2}{\sqrt{53}}$

$\text{cos}  θ = \frac{7}{\sqrt{53}}$

**[B1]**

Find the acceleration using $v = u + a t$ with $u = 0$, $v = 1 . 35$ and $t = 4$

$1 . 35 = 0 + 4 a$

**[M1]**

$a = 0 . 3375$

**[A1]**

The particle slides down the plane, so friction acts up the plane

![Force diagram for a block of mass 0.8 kg on a rough plane inclined at θ to the horizontal. The weight 0.8g N acts vertically downwards, the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the plane and the frictional force F N acts up the plane. The acceleration a m s⁻² is down the plane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/006-force-diagram-for-a-block-of-mass-0-8-kg-on-a-ro.png)

Resolve perpendicular to the plane, then use $F = μ R$ since the particle is moving

$F = μ \times 0 . 8 g \text{cos}  θ = μ \times 8 \times \frac{7}{\sqrt{53}}$

**[M1]**

Take down the plane as positive and apply Newton's second law

$0 . 8 g \text{sin}  θ - F = 0 . 8 a$

**[M1]**

Substitute $g = 10$, the exact trigonometric values and $a = 0 . 3375$

$8 \times \frac{2}{\sqrt{53}} - μ \times 8 \times \frac{7}{\sqrt{53}} = 0 . 8 \times 0 . 3375$

**[A1]**

$μ = \frac{16/\sqrt{53}-0.27}{56/\sqrt{53}}$

**Final answer:** $μ = 0 . 251$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Both $\text{sin}  θ = \frac{2}{\sqrt{53}}$ and $\text{cos}  θ = \frac{7}{\sqrt{53}}$, or the angle used to full accuracy ($θ = 15 . 945 \dots ^{\circ}$).
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $v = u + a t$ with $u = 0$, $v = 1 . 35$ and $t = 4$.
> 
> **A1**: $a = 0 . 3375$.
> 
> **M1**: Use of $F = μ R$ with $R$ a component of $0 . 8 g$. Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law along the plane, with all three relevant terms. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation.
> 
> **A1**: Any answer which rounds to 0.251.

parts.problemMd:
A small object is placed on a rough plane whose angle of inclination to the horizontal can be adjusted. The coefficient of friction between the object and the plane is $μ$.

When the plane is inclined at an angle $θ_{1}$ to the horizontal, the object is released from rest and remains at rest. When the plane is inclined at a larger angle $θ_{2}$ to the horizontal, where $θ_{2} < 90 ^{\circ}$, the object is released from rest and slides down the plane.

Show that `\text{tan} \; \theta_{1} \leqslant \mu < \text{tan} \; \theta_{2}`.
parts.solutionMd:
In both cases the object would slide down the plane without friction, so friction acts up the plane. Let the mass of the object be $m$ kg

![Force diagram for a block of mass m kg on a rough plane inclined at angle θ to the horizontal. The weight mg N acts vertically downwards, the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the plane and the frictional force F N acts up the plane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/007-force-diagram-for-a-block-of-mass-m-kg-on-a-roug.png)

When the angle is $θ_{1}$, resolve perpendicular to and along the plane

$R = m g \text{cos}  θ_{1}$

$F = m g \text{sin}  θ_{1}$

**[M1]**

The object is at rest, so friction can be at most $μ R$

`mg\text{sin} \; \theta_{1} \leqslant \mu mg\text{cos} \; \theta_{1}`

**[M1]**

Divide by $m g \text{cos}  θ_{1}$, which is positive

`\text{tan} \; \theta_{1} \leqslant \mu`

**[A1]**

When the angle is $θ_{2}$, the object slides, so friction takes its maximum value $μ m g \text{cos}  θ_{2}$. It accelerates down the plane, so the component of the weight down the plane is greater than the friction

$m g \text{sin}  θ_{2} > μ m g \text{cos}  θ_{2}$

**[M1]**

Divide by $m g \text{cos}  θ_{2}$, which is positive because $θ_{2} < 90 ^{\circ}$

$μ < \text{tan}  θ_{2}$

**[A1]**

Combine the two results

`\text{tan} \; \theta_{1} \leqslant \mu < \text{tan} \; \theta_{2}`

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Resolving perpendicular to and along the plane for the first case. Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **M1**: Use of `F \leqslant \mu R` in the first case. Using $F = μ R$ here does not earn this mark.
> 
> **A1**: `\text{tan} \; \theta_{1} \leqslant \mu`, with a non-strict inequality.
> 
> **M1**: Correct condition for sliding in the second case: the component of the weight down the plane greater than $μ R$, or a positive acceleration from Newton's second law with $F = μ R$.
> 
> **A1**: $μ < \text{tan}  θ_{2}$, with a strict inequality.
> 
> **B1**: The printed result, combining both cases. Because the result is given, both inequalities must be correct.

parts.problemMd:
A particle of mass 0.5 kg is on a rough plane inclined at 35° to the horizontal. A force of magnitude 6 N acts on the particle, towards the plane, at an angle of $θ ^{\circ}$ to a line of greatest slope, as shown in the diagram. The force acts in the vertical plane containing the line of greatest slope. The coefficient of friction between the particle and the plane is 0.4, and the particle is about to slip up the plane.

![A particle on a rough plane inclined at 35° to the horizontal. A force of 6 N pushes on the particle up the plane and towards it, at an angle of θ° to a dashed line along the line of greatest slope](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/010-a-particle-on-a-rough-plane-inclined-at-35-to-th.png)

You may use without proof the identity:

$6 \text{cos}  θ ^{\circ} - 2 . 4 \text{sin}  θ ^{\circ} \equiv \frac{6\sqrt{29}}{5} \text{cos} ( θ ^{\circ} + \text{tan}^{-1}  0 . 4 )$

Find the value of $θ$.
parts.solutionMd:
The particle is about to slip up the plane, so friction acts down the plane and is limiting

![Force diagram for a block of mass 0.5 kg on a rough plane inclined at 35° to the horizontal. A force of 6 N pushes on the block at θ° to the plane, up the plane and towards it. The frictional force F N acts down the plane, the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the plane and the weight 0.5g N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/011-force-diagram-for-a-block-of-mass-0-5-kg-on-a-ro.png)

Resolve perpendicular to the plane. The 6 N force pushes into the plane, so its component adds to the normal contact force

$R = 0 . 5 g \text{cos}  35 ^{\circ} + 6 \text{sin}  θ ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

Friction is limiting

$F = 0 . 4 ( 0 . 5 g \text{cos}  35 ^{\circ} + 6 \text{sin}  θ ^{\circ} )$

**[M1]**

Resolve along the plane. Friction and the component of the weight act down the plane

$6 \text{cos}  θ ^{\circ} = 0 . 4 ( 0 . 5 g \text{cos}  35 ^{\circ} + 6 \text{sin}  θ ^{\circ} ) + 0 . 5 g \text{sin}  35 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

Use $g = 10$ and collect the terms in $θ$ on the left-hand side

$6 \text{cos}  θ ^{\circ} - 2 . 4 \text{sin}  θ ^{\circ} = 2 \text{cos}  35 ^{\circ} + 5 \text{sin}  35 ^{\circ} = 4 . 5061 \dots$

**[A1]**

Use the given identity

$\frac{6\sqrt{29}}{5} \text{cos} ( θ ^{\circ} + \text{tan}^{-1}  0 . 4 ) = 4 . 5061 \dots$

$\text{cos} ( θ ^{\circ} + 21 . 801 \dots ^{\circ} ) = 0 . 69731 \dots$

**[M1]**

$θ + 21 . 801 \dots = 45 . 788 \dots$

**Final answer:** $θ = 24 . 0$** (1 d.p.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Resolving perpendicular to the plane, with all three relevant terms. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **M1**: Use of $F = μ R$ with the normal contact force from resolving, including the component of the 6 N force.
> 
> **M1**: Resolving along the plane, with all three relevant terms. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation in the form $6 \text{cos}  θ ^{\circ} - 2 . 4 \text{sin}  θ ^{\circ} = 4 . 506$, or equivalent.
> 
> **M1**: Use of the given identity to reach an equation in $\text{cos} ( θ ^{\circ} + \text{tan}^{-1}  0 . 4 )$ and use of inverse cosine.
> 
> **A1**: Any answer which rounds to 24.0.

parts.problemMd:
A particle of mass $m$ kg is projected with speed $u$$\text{m s}^{-1}$ up a line of greatest slope of a rough plane inclined at an angle $θ$ to the horizontal. The coefficient of friction between the particle and the plane is $μ$. The particle comes to instantaneous rest after $t_{1}$ seconds, having moved a distance $s$ metres up the plane.

Show that

(i) $t_{1} = \frac{u}{g(\text{sin}θ+μ\text{cos}θ)}$

(ii) $s = \frac{u^{2}}{2g(\text{sin}θ+μ\text{cos}θ)}$
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The particle moves up the plane, so friction acts down the plane

![Force diagram for a block of mass m kg moving up a rough plane inclined at θ to the horizontal. The weight mg N acts vertically downwards, the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the plane and the frictional force F N acts down the plane. The direction of motion is up the plane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/008-force-diagram-for-a-block-of-mass-m-kg-moving-up.png)

Resolve perpendicular to the plane, then use $F = μ R$ since the particle is moving

$R = m g \text{cos}  θ$

$F = μ m g \text{cos}  θ$

**[M1]**

Take up the plane as positive and apply Newton's second law

$- μ m g \text{cos}  θ - m g \text{sin}  θ = m a$

**[M1]**

Divide through by $m$

$a = - g ( \text{sin}  θ + μ \text{cos}  θ )$

**[A1]**

Use $v = u + a t$ with $v = 0$ at time $t_{1}$

$0 = u - g ( \text{sin}  θ + μ \text{cos}  θ ) t_{1}$

**[M1]**

$t_{1} = \frac{u}{g(\text{sin}θ+μ\text{cos}θ)}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Use $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with $v = 0$

$0 = u^{2} - 2 g ( \text{sin}  θ + μ \text{cos}  θ ) s$

**[M1]**

$s = \frac{u^{2}}{2g(\text{sin}θ+μ\text{cos}θ)}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Resolving perpendicular to the plane and use of $F = μ R$, with $R$ a component of $m g$. Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law along the plane, with all three relevant terms. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: $a = - g ( \text{sin}  θ + μ \text{cos}  θ )$, or a deceleration of $g ( \text{sin}  θ + μ \text{cos}  θ )$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $v = u + a t$ with $v = 0$ and the acceleration found.
> 
> **B1**: The printed expression for $t_{1}$, from correct working.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with $v = 0$ and the acceleration found. Using $s = \frac{1}{2} ( u + v ) t$ with $t_{1}$ is equally acceptable.
> 
> **B1**: The printed expression for $s$, from correct working.
> 
> Because the results are given, every step must be seen.

parts.problemMd:
After coming to instantaneous rest, the particle slides back down the plane and returns to its starting point $t_{2}$ seconds later.

Find an expression for $t_{2}$ in terms of $u$, $g$, $μ$ and $θ$.
parts.solutionMd:
The particle now moves down the plane, so friction acts up the plane

![Force diagram for a block of mass m kg sliding down a rough plane inclined at θ to the horizontal. The weight mg N acts vertically downwards, the normal contact force R N acts perpendicular to the plane and the frictional force F N acts up the plane. The direction of motion is down the plane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/009-force-diagram-for-a-block-of-mass-m-kg-sliding-d.png)

Take down the plane as positive and apply Newton's second law. The normal contact force is unchanged, so friction is still $μ m g \text{cos}  θ$

$m g \text{sin}  θ - μ m g \text{cos}  θ = m a_{2}$

**[M1]**

$a_{2} = g ( \text{sin}  θ - μ \text{cos}  θ )$

**[A1]**

The particle starts from rest and travels the same distance $s$ back down. Use $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $u = 0$

$s = \frac{1}{2} a_{2} t_{2}^{2}$

**[M1]**

Substitute the expression for $s$ from part (a) and $a_{2}$, then make $t_{2}$ the subject

$t_{2}^{2} = \frac{2s}{a_{2}} = \frac{u^{2}}{g^{2}(\text{sin}θ+μ\text{cos}θ)(\text{sin}θ-μ\text{cos}θ)}$

Multiply out the brackets in the denominator, which are a difference of two squares

$( \text{sin}  θ + μ \text{cos}  θ ) ( \text{sin}  θ - μ \text{cos}  θ ) = \text{sin}^{2}  θ - μ^{2} \text{cos}^{2}  θ$

Take the positive square root

$t_{2} = \frac{u}{g\sqrt{\text{sin}^{2}θ-μ^{2}\text{cos}^{2}θ}}$

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The particle only slides back down if the component of the weight down the plane is greater than the maximum friction, that is if $μ < \text{tan}  θ$. That is exactly the condition for $\text{sin}^{2}  θ - μ^{2} \text{cos}^{2}  θ$ to be positive, so the square root in your answer is only defined when the question makes sense.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law down the plane, with friction now acting up the plane and all three relevant terms. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: $a_{2} = g ( \text{sin}  θ - μ \text{cos}  θ )$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $s = \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ from rest, with the expression for $s$ from part (a).
> 
> **A1**: A correct expression for $t_{2}$ in terms of $u$, $g$, $μ$ and $θ$ only. The unsimplified $\sqrt{\frac{u^{2}}{g^{2}(\text{sin}θ+μ\text{cos}θ)(\text{sin}θ-μ\text{cos}θ)}}$ is accepted.

parts.problemMd:
Two particles $A$ and $B$, each of mass $m$ kg, are attached to the ends of a light inextensible string. $A$ rests on a rough plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal and $B$ rests on a rough plane inclined at 70° to the horizontal. The planes meet at a ridge, where a small smooth pulley is fixed. The string passes over the pulley, and each part of the string lies along a line of greatest slope of its plane, as shown in the diagram. The coefficient of friction between each particle and its plane is 0.15.

![Two rough planes meeting at a ridge with a pulley at the top. The left plane is inclined at 30° to the horizontal and particle A rests on it. The right plane is inclined at 70° to the horizontal and particle B rests on it, at a height of 0.75 m above the ground. A string along each plane passes over the pulley and connects A and B](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/020-two-rough-planes-meeting-at-a-ridge-with-a-pulle.png)

The system is released from rest with the string taut and with $B$ at a height of 0.75 m above the ground. $B$ moves down its plane.

Find the acceleration of the particles while $B$ is moving.
parts.solutionMd:
$A$ moves up its plane, so $F_{1}$ acts down the 30° plane. $B$ moves down its plane, so $F_{2}$ acts up the 70° plane

![Force diagram for particle A on the plane inclined at 30°. The tension T N acts up the plane, the frictional force F₁ N acts down the plane, the normal contact force R₁ N acts perpendicular to the plane and the weight mg N acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/021-force-diagram-for-particle-a-on-the-plane-inclin.png)

![Force diagram for particle B on the plane inclined at 70°. The tension T N and the frictional force F₂ N both act up the plane, the normal contact force R₂ N acts perpendicular to the plane and the weight mg N acts vertically downwards. The acceleration a m s⁻² is down the plane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/022-force-diagram-for-particle-b-on-the-plane-inclin.png)

Each particle is moving, so friction takes its maximum value on each

$F_{1} = 0 . 15 m g \text{cos}  30 ^{\circ}$

$F_{2} = 0 . 15 m g \text{cos}  70 ^{\circ}$

**[M1]**

For $A$, take up its plane as positive and apply Newton's second law

$T - m g \text{sin}  30 ^{\circ} - 0 . 15 m g \text{cos}  30 ^{\circ} = m a$

**[M1 A1]**

For $B$, take down its plane as positive

$m g \text{sin}  70 ^{\circ} - T - 0 . 15 m g \text{cos}  70 ^{\circ} = m a$

**[M1 A1]**

Add the two equations to eliminate $T$, then divide by $m$ and use $g = 10$

$10 ( \text{sin}  70 ^{\circ} - \text{sin}  30 ^{\circ} - 0 . 15 \text{cos}  30 ^{\circ} - 0 . 15 \text{cos}  70 ^{\circ} ) = 2 a$

**Final answer:** $a = 1 . 29 \text{m s}^{-2}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of $F = μ R$ for either particle, with $R$ a component of $m g$. Allow a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for $A$ along its plane, with all four relevant terms. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation for $A$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for $B$ along its plane, with all four relevant terms. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation for $B$.
> 
> **A1**: Any answer which rounds to 1.29.
> 
> Applying Newton's second law to the whole system in place of either single-particle equation is equally acceptable. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
When $B$ reaches the ground it does not rebound. $A$ does not reach the pulley.

Find the total distance travelled by $A$ from the instant the system is released until $A$ first comes to instantaneous rest.
parts.solutionMd:
$B$ falls a vertical height of 0.75 m down the 70° plane, so find the distance it moves along the plane. $A$ moves the same distance up its plane

$s_{1} = \frac{0.75}{\text{sin}70^{\circ}} = 0 . 79813 \dots$

**[M1 A1]**

Use $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with $u = 0$ and $a = 1 . 2924 \dots$ to find the speed of $B$ as it reaches the ground

$v^{2} = 2 \times 1 . 2924 \dots \times 0 . 79813 \dots = 2 . 0630 \dots$

**[M1]**

The string is inextensible, so $A$ and $B$ always move with the same speed. At the instant $B$ reaches the ground, $A$ is moving up its plane at this same speed

$v_{A}^{2} = 2 . 0630 \dots$

Once $B$ is on the ground the string is slack, so there is no tension. $A$ is still moving up its plane, so friction still acts down the plane

![Force diagram for particle A after B reaches the ground. On the plane inclined at 30°, the frictional force F₁ N acts down the plane, the normal contact force R₁ N acts perpendicular to the plane and the weight mg N acts vertically downwards. There is no tension. A is moving up the plane](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/forces-and-equilibrium/resolving-forces-inclined-planes-and-friction/assets/023-force-diagram-for-particle-a-after-b-reaches-the.png)

Take up the plane as positive and apply Newton's second law to $A$

$- m g \text{sin}  30 ^{\circ} - 0 . 15 m g \text{cos}  30 ^{\circ} = m a$

**[M1]**

$a = - 10 ( \text{sin}  30 ^{\circ} + 0 . 15 \text{cos}  30 ^{\circ} ) = - 6 . 2990 \dots$

**[A1]**

Use $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with $v = 0$ and $u^{2} = 2 . 0630 \dots$ to find how much further $A$ travels

$0 = 2 . 0630 \dots - 2 \times 6 . 2990 \dots \times s_{2}$

$s_{2} = 0 . 16376 \dots$

**[M1]**

Add the two distances

$s_{1} + s_{2} = 0 . 79813 \dots + 0 . 16376 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{Total distance} = 0 . 962 \text{m}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of trigonometry to convert the vertical height of 0.75 m into a distance along the 70° plane.
> 
> **A1**: $s_{1}$, or any value which rounds to 0.798.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with $u = 0$, the acceleration from part (a) and $s_{1}$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of Newton's second law for $A$ with no tension, with the weight component and friction. Allow sign errors and a sine and cosine mix for this mark only.
> 
> **A1**: Deceleration, or any value which rounds to 6.30.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with a final speed of zero, to find the further distance.
> 
> **A1**: Any answer which rounds to 0.962.
> 
> Finding the further distance with a work-energy equation for $A$ is equally acceptable for the fourth and sixth marks.

parts.problemMd:
A particle *P* moves in a straight line with constant acceleration. *P* starts from rest, and 4.5 seconds later its velocity is 10.35 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Find the acceleration of *P*.
parts.solutionMd:
The particle starts from rest, so use $v = u + a t$ with $u = 0$, $v = 10 . 35$ and $t = 4 . 5$

$10 . 35 = 0 + 4 . 5 a$

**[M1]**

$a = 2 . 3 \text{m s}^{-2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $v = u + a t$ with $u = 0$, $v = 10 . 35$ and $t = 4 . 5$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct acceleration of 2.3.

parts.problemMd:
A particle moves in a straight line with constant acceleration 0.8 $\text{m s}^{-2}$. In 8 seconds the particle travels 30 m.

Find the velocity of the particle at the end of the 8 seconds.
parts.solutionMd:
To find the initial velocity first, use $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $s = 30$, $t = 8$ and $a = 0 . 8$

$30 = 8 u + \frac{1}{2} \times 0 . 8 \times 8^{2}$

**[M1]**

$30 = 8 u + 25 . 6$

$u = 0 . 55$

Use $v = u + a t$ to find the final velocity

$v = 0 . 55 + 0 . 8 \times 8$

**[M1]**

$v = 6 . 95 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> You can reach the final velocity in one step with $s = v t - \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$, which links $s$, $v$, $a$ and $t$ without $u$: $30 = 8 v - 25 . 6$ gives $v = 6 . 95$ straight away.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $s = 30$, $t = 8$ and $a = 0 . 8$ to find the initial velocity.
>

parts.problemMd:
A particle moves in a straight line. The diagram shows the velocity-time graph for the particle from time 0 to time *t* seconds. The velocity of the particle is *u* $\text{m s}^{-1}$ at time 0 and *v* $\text{m s}^{-1}$ at time *t* seconds.

![Velocity-time graph: a straight line rising from velocity u on the vertical axis at time 0 to velocity v at time t, with dashed lines from the end point to both axes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/constant-acceleration/assets/015-velocity-time-graph-a-straight-line-rising-from-.png)

(i) Explain how the graph shows that the acceleration of the particle is constant.

(ii) Show that the displacement of the particle from its position at time 0 is given by

$s = \frac{1}{2} t ( u + v )$
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The acceleration is the gradient of the velocity-time graph

*The graph is a straight line, so its gradient is constant*

**Final answer:** **The acceleration is equal to this gradient, so the acceleration is constant**

**[B1]**

(ii)

The displacement is the area under the velocity-time graph, which is a trapezium with parallel sides $u$ and $v$ and width $t$

$s = \frac{1}{2} ( u + v ) \times t$

**[M1]**

$s = \frac{1}{2} t ( u + v )$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A straight line has a constant gradient, and the gradient of a velocity-time graph is the acceleration. Both points are needed.
> 
> **M1**: Use of the area under the graph as the displacement, with the area found as a trapezium, or as a rectangle of height $u$ plus a triangle of height $v - u$.
> 
> **B1**: The given result reached with the area method seen.

parts.problemMd:
Use the constant acceleration equations

$v = u + a t$ and $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$

to show that

$v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$
parts.solutionMd:
The required result does not involve $t$, so make $t$ the subject of $v = u + a t$

$t = \frac{v-u}{a}$

Substitute this into $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$

`s = u\left(\dfrac{v - u}{a}\right) + \dfrac{1}{2}a\left(\dfrac{v - u}{a}\right)^{2}`

**[M1]**

Expand each term

$s = \frac{uv-u^{2}}{a} + \frac{v^{2}-2uv+u^{2}}{2a}$

**[A1]**

Multiply through by $2 a$ to clear the fractions

$2 a s = 2 u v - 2 u^{2} + v^{2} - 2 u v + u^{2}$

**[M1]**

Collect like terms

$2 a s = v^{2} - u^{2}$

$v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Elimination of $t$ by substituting an expression for $t$ from $v = u + a t$ into $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct expanded expression for $s$ in terms of $u$, $v$ and $a$.
> 
> **M1**: Clearing the fractions, e.g. by multiplying by $2 a$.
> 
> **B1**: The given result reached from correct working with no errors. As the result is given, every step must be shown.

parts.problemMd:
A train leaves station *O* from rest and moves along a straight track with constant acceleration 0.12 $\text{m s}^{-2}$. After 190 seconds the train passes a signal. The train then decelerates uniformly at 0.18 $\text{m s}^{-2}$ until it comes to rest at station *X*.

Find the distance *OX*.
parts.solutionMd:
For the first stage, from $O$ to the signal, use $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $u = 0$, $a = 0 . 12$ and $t = 190$

$s_{1} = 0 + \frac{1}{2} \times 0 . 12 \times 190^{2}$

**[M1]**

$s_{1} = 2166$

**[A1]**

The speed at the signal is the initial speed for the second stage, so use $v = u + a t$ for the first stage

$v = 0 + 0 . 12 \times 190 = 22 . 8$

**[B1]**

For the second stage, use $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with $u = 22 . 8$, $v = 0$ and $a = - 0 . 18$

$0 = 22 . 8^{2} + 2 \times ( - 0 . 18 ) \times s_{2}$

**[M1]**

$0 . 36 s_{2} = 519 . 84$

$s_{2} = 1444$

Add the two distances

$O X = 2166 + 1444$

$O X = 3610 \text{m}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ for the first stage with $u = 0$, $a = 0 . 12$ and $t = 190$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct first-stage distance of 2166.
> 
> **B1**: Correct speed of 22.8 at the signal.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of a constant acceleration equation for the second stage with the speed at the signal found, $v = 0$ and $a = - 0 . 18$. Allow a sign error in the acceleration.
> 
> **A1**: Correct distance of 3610 m. Accept 3.61 km with the unit stated.

parts.problemMd:
A particle moves in a straight line with constant acceleration 1.5 $\text{m s}^{-2}$ and does not change its direction of motion. After travelling 52.44 m, the particle has velocity 12.6 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Find the time taken for the particle to travel this distance.
parts.solutionMd:
The initial velocity is not given, so use $s = v t - \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $s = 52 . 44$, $v = 12 . 6$ and $a = 1 . 5$

$52 . 44 = 12 . 6 t - \frac{1}{2} \times 1 . 5 \times t^{2}$

**[M1]**

$0 . 75 t^{2} - 12 . 6 t + 52 . 44 = 0$

Solve the quadratic using the quadratic formula

$t = \frac{12.6\pm\sqrt{12.6^{2}-4\times0.75\times52.44}}{2\times0.75}$

$t = \frac{12.6\pm1.2}{1.5}$

$t = 7 . 6 \text{or} t = 9 . 2$

**[A1]**

To decide which time is valid, find the initial velocity for each using $u = v - a t$

$t = 9 . 2 \text{:} u = 12 . 6 - 1 . 5 \times 9 . 2 = - 1 . 2$

**[M1]**

$t = 7 . 6 \text{:} u = 12 . 6 - 1 . 5 \times 7 . 6 = 1 . 2$

A negative initial velocity means the particle would start by moving the other way and then turn round, so reject $t = 9 . 2$

$t = 7 . 6 \text{s}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $s = v t - \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $s = 52 . 44$, $v = 12 . 6$ and $a = 1 . 5$.
> 
> **A1**: Both roots, 7.6 and 9.2.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method to test which root is valid, e.g. finding the initial velocity for a root, or reasoning that the particle must not change direction.
> 
> **A1**: $t = 7 . 6$ with $t = 9 . 2$ rejected.
> 
> Alternative method: $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ gives $u^{2} = 1 . 44$ (M1), $u = 1 . 2$ because the particle does not change direction (A1), then $v = u + a t$ with $u = 1 . 2$ (M1) gives $t = 7 . 6$ (A1).

parts.problemMd:
A car travels along a straight horizontal road. The car passes a point *A* with speed 21 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and accelerates uniformly at 0.2 $\text{m s}^{-2}$ until it reaches a point *B*, where *AB* = 1.5 km. At *B* the car begins to decelerate uniformly at 3.1 $\text{m s}^{-2}$ until it comes to rest.

Find the distance the car travels while it is decelerating.
parts.solutionMd:
The speed at $B$ links the two stages. For $A$ to $B$, use $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with $u = 21$, $a = 0 . 2$ and $s = 1500$

$v^{2} = 21^{2} + 2 \times 0 . 2 \times 1500$

**[M1]**

$v^{2} = 1041$

**[A1]**

For the deceleration, use $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ again with $u^{2} = 1041$, $v = 0$ and $a = - 3 . 1$

$0 = 1041 + 2 \times ( - 3 . 1 ) \times s$

**[M1]**

$s = \frac{1041}{6.2} = 167 . 903 . . .$

**Final answer:** $s = 168 \text{m}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ from $A$ to $B$ with $u = 21$, $a = 0 . 2$ and $s = 1500$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value of $v^{2} = 1041$, or a speed at $B$ of 32.264... Premature rounding of the speed may lose the final mark.
> 
> **M1**: Use of a constant acceleration equation for the deceleration with the speed at $B$ found, $v = 0$ and $a = - 3 . 1$. Allow a sign error in the acceleration.
> 
> **A1**: Correct distance, or answers which round to 168.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows the velocity-time graph for a particle moving in a straight line. Velocity is measured in metres per second and time in seconds.

![Velocity-time graph: a straight line from velocity 4 at time 0 up to 9 at time 6, horizontal at 9 until time 9, a straight line up to V at time 13, horizontal at V until time T, then a straight line down to zero at time 36](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/constant-acceleration/assets/009-velocity-time-graph-a-straight-line-from-velocit.png)

The particle travels 150 m from time *T* to time 36, and 309 m in total.

Find the values of *T* and *V*.
parts.solutionMd:
The velocity is never negative, so each distance is the area under the graph. Split the area into five sections

![Velocity-time graph from the question with dashed vertical lines at times 6, 9, 13 and T dividing the area under the graph into five numbered sections](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/constant-acceleration/assets/010-velocity-time-graph-from-the-question-with-dashe.png)

The final section, from $T$ to 36, is a triangle of height $V$

$\frac{1}{2} V ( 36 - T ) = 150$

**[M1 A1]**

Add the areas of all five sections for the total distance

$\frac{1}{2} ( 4 + 9 ) \times 6 + 9 \times 3 + \frac{1}{2} ( 9 + V ) \times 4 + V ( T - 13 ) + 150 = 309$

**[M1 A1]**

$39 + 27 + 18 + 2 V + V T - 13 V + 150 = 309$

$V T - 11 V = 75$

Rearrange the first equation to the same form

$36 V - V T = 300$

Add the two equations to eliminate $V T$

$25 V = 375$

**[M1]**

$V = 15$

Substitute into $36 V - V T = 300$

$540 - 15 T = 300$

$T = 16 ,  V = 15$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of the area of the final triangle to form an equation in $T$ and $V$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation, e.g. $\frac{1}{2} V ( 36 - T ) = 150$.
> 
> **M1**: Use of the total area under the graph, including all five sections, to form a second equation.
> 
> **A1**: Correct second equation in any form.
> 
> **M1**: Solving the two equations simultaneously by any valid method.
> 
> **A1**: Both $T = 16$ and $V = 15$.

parts.problemMd:
A train leaves station *O* from rest and moves along a straight track with constant acceleration 0.2 $\text{m s}^{-2}$. After 125 seconds the train passes a signal. The train then decelerates uniformly and comes to rest at station *X* 75 seconds later.

Find the distance *OX*.
parts.solutionMd:
The journey has two stages, linked by the speed at the signal

![Journey diagram: a straight line with O, the signal and X marked in order; the train moves from rest at O for 125 seconds with acceleration 0.2 metres per second squared to the signal, then decelerates for 75 seconds to rest at X](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/constant-acceleration/assets/011-journey-diagram-a-straight-line-with-o-the-signa.png)

Use $v = u + a t$ for the first stage to find the speed at the signal

$v = 0 + 0 . 2 \times 125 = 25$

**[B1]**

For the first stage, use $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $u = 0$, $a = 0 . 2$ and $t = 125$

$s_{1} = 0 + \frac{1}{2} \times 0 . 2 \times 125^{2}$

**[M1]**

$s_{1} = 1562 . 5$

**[A1]**

The deceleration is not given, so for the second stage use $s = \frac{1}{2} ( u + v ) t$ with $u = 25$, $v = 0$ and $t = 75$

$s_{2} = \frac{1}{2} \times ( 25 + 0 ) \times 75$

**[M1]**

$s_{2} = 937 . 5$

Add the two distances

$O X = 1562 . 5 + 937 . 5$

$O X = 2500 \text{m}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ for the first stage with $u = 0$, $a = 0 . 2$ and $t = 125$.

> **A1**: Correct first-stage distance of 1562.5.

> **M1**: Correct method for the second-stage distance with the speed at the signal found, $v = 0$ and $t = 75$, e.g. $s = \frac{1}{2} ( u + v ) t$, or finding the deceleration first.

> **A1**: Correct distance of 2500 m. Accept 2.5 km with the unit stated.

parts.problemMd:
The train then leaves *X* from rest and moves back along the same track, in the opposite direction, with constant acceleration 0.1 $\text{m s}^{-2}$. The train passes through *O* without stopping. 300 seconds after leaving *X*, the train passes a signal 850 m before station *Y*. The train then decelerates uniformly and comes to rest at *Y*.

parts.solutionMd:

**[M1]**

The signal is 4500 m from $X$ and $O$ is 2500 m from $X$, and $Y$ is a further 850 m on

parts.problemMd:
In a crash test, a car starts from rest and moves along a straight horizontal track with constant acceleration until it hits a wall. The length of track available is 0.8 km.

In one test the car has constant acceleration 1.6 $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

Find the greatest possible speed, in $\text{km h}^{-1}$, with which the car can hit the wall.
parts.solutionMd:
The speed is greatest when the car uses the whole track, 800 m. Use $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with $u = 0$, $a = 1 . 6$ and $s = 800$

$v^{2} = 0 + 2 \times 1 . 6 \times 800$

**[M1]**

$v = \sqrt{2560} = 50 . 596 . . . \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

Convert to kilometres per hour by multiplying by 3600 and dividing by 1000

$50 . 596 . . . \times \frac{3600}{1000} = 182 . 147 . . .$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $182 \text{km h}^{-1}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with $u = 0$, $a = 1 . 6$ and $s = 800$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct speed of 50.6 m s⁻¹, or an exact form such as $16 \sqrt{10}$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct conversion of the speed found from m s⁻¹ to km h⁻¹.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 182, in km h⁻¹.

parts.problemMd:
The acceleration used in a test is normally 1.2 $\text{m s}^{-2}$, but it can be increased or decreased by up to 40%.

Determine whether it is possible to crash test a car at a speed of 200 $\text{km h}^{-1}$.
parts.solutionMd:
The greatest possible speed comes from the greatest acceleration over the whole 800 m

$a_{\text{max}} = 1 . 2 \times 1 . 4 = 1 . 68$

**[B1]**

Use $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with $u = 0$, $a = 1 . 68$ and $s = 800$

$v^{2} = 0 + 2 \times 1 . 68 \times 800$

$v = \sqrt{2688} = 51 . 845 . . . \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[M1]**

Convert 200 km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹ to compare

$200 \times \frac{1000}{3600} = 55 . 555 . . . \text{m s}^{-1}$

$51 . 845 . . . < 55 . 555 . . .$

**Final answer:** **The greatest possible speed is less than 200 km h⁻¹, so it is not possible**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct greatest acceleration of 1.68.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with $u = 0$, $s = 800$ and the greatest acceleration found.
> 
> **A1**: Correct comparison of 51.8 m s⁻¹ with 55.6 m s⁻¹, or of 187 km h⁻¹ with 200 km h⁻¹, and the conclusion that it is not possible.

At *B* the car begins to decelerate uniformly at 2.75 $\text{m s}^{-2}$ until it comes to rest.

parts.solutionMd:
The speed at $B$ links the two stages. For $A$ to $B$, use $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with $u = 17 . 2$, $a = 0 . 4$ and $s = 800$

Add the two times

parts.problemMd:
Two stations, *A* and *B*, are 8.2 km apart on a straight track. A train leaves *A* from rest and moves towards *B* with constant acceleration 0.2 $\text{m s}^{-2}$. At the same instant, a second train leaves *B* from rest and moves towards *A* along a parallel track with constant acceleration 0.16 $\text{m s}^{-2}$. The trains are modelled as particles.

Find the distance from *A* at which the trains pass each other.
parts.solutionMd:
Both trains have been moving for the same time, $T$ seconds, when they pass, and together they have covered the whole 8200 m

![Position diagram: a straight line from A to B, 8200 m apart; one train moves from rest at A towards B with acceleration 0.2 metres per second squared, the other from rest at B towards A with acceleration 0.16 metres per second squared, and they meet at a point between, a distance s1 from A and s2 from B](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/constant-acceleration/assets/005-position-diagram-a-straight-line-from-a-to-b-820.png)

$s_{2} = \frac{1}{2} \times 0 . 16 \times T^{2} = 0 . 08 T^{2}$

**[M1 A1]**

The two distances add up to 8200 m

$0 . 1 T^{2} + 0 . 08 T^{2} = 8200$

**[M1]**

$T^{2} = 45555 . 555 . . .$

**[A1]**

The distance from $A$ is the first train's distance

$s_{1} = 0 . 1 \times 45555 . 555 . . . = 4555 . 555 . . .$

**Final answer:** $4560 \text{m}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> **A1**: Both expressions correct.
>

parts.problemMd:
Two particles, *A* and *B*, move along parallel straight lines. The diagram shows the velocity-time graphs for their motion, with *A* shown by the solid line and *B* by the dotted line. Velocity is measured in metres per second and time in seconds.

![Velocity-time graphs for two particles. Particle A, solid line: from 0 at time 0 up to 5 at time 4, horizontal at 5 until time 12, up to 10 at time 21, then horizontal at 10. Particle B, dotted line: from 0 at time 0 up to 8 at time 15, then down to 0 at time 25. The lines cross at times T1, between 4 and 12, and T2, between 15 and 21](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/constant-acceleration/assets/003-velocity-time-graphs-for-two-particles-particle-.png)

The particles have equal velocities at times $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ seconds, where $4 < T_{1} < 12$ and $15 < T_{2} < 21$.

Find $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$, giving your answers correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Between 4 and 12 seconds, $A$ has constant velocity 5. For the first 15 seconds, $B$ accelerates from rest to 8, so its acceleration is the gradient

$a_{B} = \frac{8}{15}$

$T_{1}$ is when $B$ reaches a velocity of 5, so use $v = u + a t$

$5 = 0 + \frac{8}{15} T_{1}$

**[M1]**

$T_{1} = \frac{75}{8} = 9 . 375$

**Final answer:** $T_{1} = 9 . 38$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

Between 15 and 21 seconds, $A$ accelerates from 5 at 12 seconds to 10 at 21 seconds

$v_{A} = 5 + \frac{5}{9} ( t - 12 )$

**[M1]**

$B$ decelerates from 8 at 15 seconds to 0 at 25 seconds

$v_{B} = 8 - 0 . 8 ( t - 15 )$

**[M1 A1]**

Set the velocities equal at $t = T_{2}$

$5 + \frac{5}{9} ( T_{2} - 12 ) = 8 - 0 . 8 ( T_{2} - 15 )$

**[M1]**

Multiply through by 45

$225 + 25 ( T_{2} - 12 ) = 360 - 36 ( T_{2} - 15 )$

$25 T_{2} - 75 = 900 - 36 T_{2}$

$61 T_{2} = 975$

$T_{2} = 15 . 983606 . . .$

**Final answer:** $T_{2} = 16 . 0$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for $T_{1}$ using the acceleration of $B$ as a gradient, e.g. $\frac{8}{15} T_{1} = 5$.
> 
> **A1**: $T_{1} = 9 . 375$, or answers which round to 9.38.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the velocity of $A$ between 12 and 21 seconds, using its acceleration of $\frac{5}{9}$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the velocity of $B$ between 15 and 25 seconds, using its deceleration of 0.8.
> 
> **A1**: Both velocity expressions correct.
> 
> **M1**: Setting the two velocities equal and solving for $T_{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: $T_{2} = 15 . 98 . . .$, or answers which round to 16.0.
> 
> The two answers are marked independently.

parts.problemMd:
A particle is projected vertically upwards from horizontal ground with speed 35.6 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Find the length of time for which the particle is at least 15 m above the ground.
parts.solutionMd:
Take upwards as positive, so the acceleration is $- 10 \text{m s}^{-2}$. The particle passes the 15 m level twice, once on the way up and once on the way down

![Vertical motion sketch: the particle leaves the ground moving upwards with speed 35.6 metres per second, with a dashed horizontal line at a height of 15 m above the ground, and upwards marked as the positive direction](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/constant-acceleration/assets/008-vertical-motion-sketch-the-particle-leaves-the-g.png)

Use $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $s = 15$, $u = 35 . 6$ and $a = - 10$

$15 = 35 . 6 t + \frac{1}{2} \times ( - 10 ) \times t^{2}$

**[M1]**

$5 t^{2} - 35 . 6 t + 15 = 0$

**[A1]**

Solve using the quadratic formula to find the two times at which the particle is 15 m above the ground

$t = \frac{35.6\pm\sqrt{35.6^{2}-4\times5\times15}}{2\times5}$

$t = 0 . 449758 . . . \text{or} t = 6 . 670241 . . .$

The particle is at least 15 m above the ground between these two times

$6 . 670241 . . . - 0 . 449758 . . . = 6 . 220482 . . .$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $6 . 22 \text{s}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $s = 15$, $u = 35 . 6$ and $a = \pm 10$. Allow sign errors.
> 
> **A1**: Correct three-term quadratic, e.g. $5 t^{2} - 35 . 6 t + 15 = 0$.
> 
> **M1**: Solving the quadratic and subtracting the smaller time from the larger.
> 
> **A1**: Correct length of time, or answers which round to 6.22.
> 
> The symmetry method (speed at 15 m, time from 15 m to the highest point, doubled) earns full marks.

parts.problemMd:
A train leaves a station from rest and moves along a straight track with constant acceleration 0.12 $\text{m s}^{-2}$. 40 seconds later, a second train leaves the same station from rest and moves along the same track in the same direction with constant acceleration 0.2 $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

Find the time after the second train leaves the station at which it catches up with the first train. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
When the second train catches up, both trains are the same distance from the station. Let $T$ seconds be the time since the first train left, so the second train has been moving for $T - 40$ seconds

![Position diagram: a straight line starting at the station, with both trains level at the same point, the first train having moved from rest for T seconds and the second train from rest for T minus 40 seconds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/constant-acceleration/assets/007-position-diagram-a-straight-line-starting-at-the.png)

For the first train, use $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $u = 0$, $a = 0 . 12$ and time $T$

$s = \frac{1}{2} \times 0 . 12 \times T^{2}$

For the second train, use the same equation with $a = 0 . 2$ and time $T - 40$

$s = \frac{1}{2} \times 0 . 2 \times ( T - 40 )^{2}$

**[M1 A1]**

Equate the distances

$0 . 06 T^{2} = 0 . 1 ( T - 40 )^{2}$

**[M1]**

$0 . 06 T^{2} = 0 . 1 T^{2} - 8 T + 160$

$T^{2} - 200 T + 4000 = 0$

Solve using the quadratic formula

$T = \frac{200\pm\sqrt{200^{2}-4\times4000}}{2}$

$T = 177 . 459 . . . \text{or} T = 22 . 540 . . .$

The second train has not left the station until $T = 40$, so reject $T = 22 . 540 . . .$

$T = 177 . 459 . . .$

**[A1]**

The time after the second train leaves is 40 seconds less

$T - 40 = 137 . 459 . . .$

**Final answer:** $137 \text{s}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $u = 0$ for both trains, with times differing by 40 seconds.
> 
> **A1**: Both expressions correct.
> 
> **M1**: Equating the two distances and forming a quadratic equation.
> 
> **A1**: $T = 177 . 459 . . .$ with $T = 22 . 540 . . .$ rejected.
> 
> **A1**: Correct time, or answers which round to 137.
> 
> Taking $t$ as the time since the second train left is equally acceptable: $0 . 06 ( t + 40 )^{2} = 0 . 1 t^{2}$ gives $t = 137 . 459 . . .$, with the negative root rejected.

parts.problemMd: Find the distance, in kilometres, that each train has travelled when the second train catches up with the first. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Use the first train's distance with $T = 177 . 459 . . .$

$s = \frac{1}{2} \times 0 . 12 \times 177 . 459 . . .^{2}$

**[M1]**

$s = 1889 . 516 . . . \text{m}$

**Final answer:** $s = 1 . 89 \text{km}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ for either train with the time from part (a).
> 
> **A1**: Correct distance in kilometres, or answers which round to 1.89. Follow through on the time from part (a).

parts.problemMd:
A ball is projected vertically upwards from horizontal ground. The ball hits the ground 1.6 seconds after reaching its greatest height.

Find the greatest height reached by the ball and the speed of projection.
parts.solutionMd:
Little is known about the upward motion, so start with the fall from the greatest height, where the ball is momentarily at rest

![Vertical motion sketch: the ball at its greatest height H with velocity 0, falling back to the ground in 1.6 seconds, with downwards marked as the positive direction for the fall](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/constant-acceleration/assets/013-vertical-motion-sketch-the-ball-at-its-greatest-.png)

Take downwards as positive for the fall, so the acceleration is $10 \text{m s}^{-2}$, and use $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $u = 0$ and $t = 1 . 6$

$s = 0 + \frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 1 . 6^{2}$

**[M1]**

$\text{Greatest height} = 12 . 8 \text{m}$

**[A1]**

The motion is symmetrical, so the ball also takes 1.6 seconds to rise to its greatest height. Take upwards as positive and use $v = u + a t$ with $v = 0$, $a = - 10$ and $t = 1 . 6$

$0 = u - 10 \times 1 . 6$

**[M1]**

$u = 16 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ for the fall with $u = 0$, $t = 1 . 6$ and $a = \pm 10$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct greatest height of 12.8.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the speed of projection, e.g. $v = u + a t$ with $v = 0$ and $t = 1 . 6$ for the rise, or $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with the height found.
> 
> **A1**: Correct speed of 16.
> 
> The two answers are marked independently.

parts.problemMd:
A firework is projected vertically upwards with speed 38.5 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ from the top of a building of height 135 m.

Find the length of time for which the firework is more than 150 m above the ground.
parts.solutionMd:
Take upwards as positive from the top of the building, so the acceleration is $- 10 \text{m s}^{-2}$. A height of 150 m above the ground is 15 m above the point of projection

![Vertical motion sketch: a building 135 m tall with the firework projected upwards from its top at 38.5 metres per second, a dashed horizontal line at 150 m above the ground, and upwards marked as the positive direction](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/constant-acceleration/assets/001-vertical-motion-sketch-a-building-135-m-tall-wit.png)

Use $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $s = 15$, $u = 38 . 5$ and $a = - 10$

$15 = 38 . 5 t + \frac{1}{2} \times ( - 10 ) \times t^{2}$

**[M1]**

$5 t^{2} - 38 . 5 t + 15 = 0$

**[A1]**

Solve using the quadratic formula to find the two times at which the firework is 150 m above the ground

$t = \frac{38.5\pm\sqrt{38.5^{2}-4\times5\times15}}{2\times5}$

$t = 0 . 411613 . . . \text{or} t = 7 . 288386 . . .$

The firework is above 150 m between these two times

$7 . 288386 . . . - 0 . 411613 . . . = 6 . 876772 . . .$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $6 . 88 \text{s}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $s = 15$, $u = 38 . 5$ and $a = \pm 10$, or an equivalent equation measured from the ground. Allow sign errors.
> 
> **A1**: Correct three-term quadratic, e.g. $5 t^{2} - 38 . 5 t + 15 = 0$.
> 
> **M1**: Solving the quadratic and subtracting the smaller time from the larger.
> 
> **A1**: Correct length of time, or answers which round to 6.88.
> 
> A symmetry method (speed at 150 m, time from there to the greatest height, doubled) earns full marks.

parts.problemMd:
The firework explodes 2 seconds after reaching its greatest height.

Find the height above the ground at which the firework explodes.
parts.solutionMd:
First find the greatest height above the top of the building, where the velocity is zero

![Vertical motion sketch: the building with the firework projected upwards from its top, rising to its greatest height where its velocity is 0, then falling for 2 seconds to the point where it explodes, above the building](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/constant-acceleration/assets/002-vertical-motion-sketch-the-building-with-the-fir.png)

Use $v^{2} = u^{2} + 2 a s$ with $u = 38 . 5$, $v = 0$ and $a = - 10$

$0 = 38 . 5^{2} + 2 \times ( - 10 ) \times s$

$s = \frac{1482.25}{20} = 74 . 1125$

**[M1]**

For the fall, take downwards as positive and use $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $u = 0$, $a = 10$ and $t = 2$

$s = 0 + \frac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 2^{2} = 20$

**[M1]**

Add the height of the building and the rise, then subtract the fall

$135 + 74 . 1125 - 20 = 189 . 1125$

**Final answer:** $189 \text{m}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the greatest height reached above the top of the building, or above the ground.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the distance fallen in 2 seconds from rest.
> 
> **A1**: Correct height above the ground, or answers which round to 189.
> 
> Finding the time to the greatest height (3.85 s) and using $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $t = 5 . 85$ from the point of projection is equally acceptable.

parts.problemMd:
Two trains leave station *O* from rest at the same instant and move in opposite directions along a straight track.

The first train moves with constant acceleration 0.15 $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

The second train moves with constant acceleration 0.24 $\text{m s}^{-2}$ for 210 seconds until it passes a signal. It then decelerates uniformly and comes to rest at station *X* 60 seconds later. After waiting at *X* for 2 minutes, the second train leaves *X* from rest and moves back towards *O* with constant acceleration 0.08 $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

Find the distance between the two trains 10 minutes after they leave *O*.
parts.solutionMd:
Work in seconds, so the trains are compared after 600 seconds. Measure distances from $O$, with each train's direction shown

![Position diagram: a straight line with O in the middle; the first train moves left from rest at O with acceleration 0.15 metres per second squared; to the right of O are the signal and then X; the second train moves right from O for 210 seconds with acceleration 0.24 metres per second squared to the signal, decelerates for 60 seconds to rest at X, waits 2 minutes, then moves left from X with acceleration 0.08 metres per second squared](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/constant-acceleration/assets/004-position-diagram-a-straight-line-with-o-in-the-m.png)

For the first train, use $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $u = 0$, $a = 0 . 15$ and $t = 600$

$s = \frac{1}{2} \times 0 . 15 \times 600^{2}$

**[M1]**

$s = 27000 \text{m}$

**[A1]**

For the second train from $O$ to the signal, use $v = u + a t$ for the speed at the signal

$v = 0 . 24 \times 210 = 50 . 4$

**[B1]**

Find the distance from $O$ to the signal and from the signal to $X$

$\frac{1}{2} \times 0 . 24 \times 210^{2} = 5292$

$\frac{1}{2} \times ( 50 . 4 + 0 ) \times 60 = 1512$

**[M1]**

$O X = 5292 + 1512 = 6804$

**[A1]**

The second train reaches $X$ after 270 seconds and waits 120 seconds, so it moves back towards $O$ for

$600 - 270 - 120 = 210 \text{s}$

Use $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ with $u = 0$, $a = 0 . 08$ and $t = 210$

$s = \frac{1}{2} \times 0 . 08 \times 210^{2} = 1764$

**[M1]**

The second train is still on the $X$ side of $O$, at a distance

$6804 - 1764 = 5040 \text{m}$

The trains are on opposite sides of $O$, so add the distances

$27000 + 5040$

$32040 \text{m}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct use of $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ for the first train with $t = 600$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct distance of 27000 for the first train.
> 
> **B1**: Correct speed of 50.4 at the signal.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for both stages of the second train's journey from $O$ to $X$, using the speed at the signal found.
> 
> **A1**: Correct distance $O X = 6804$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ for the return journey from $X$ with $t = 210$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct distance of 32040 m. Accept 32.0 km or 32.04 km with the unit stated.

parts.problemMd:
A ball is projected vertically upwards from horizontal ground with speed 29.3 $\text{m s}^{-1}$. At the same instant, a second ball is projected vertically downwards with speed 8.2 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ from a point 150 m directly above the first ball. The balls collide.

Find the time at which the balls collide and the height above the ground at which the collision occurs.
parts.solutionMd:
When the balls collide, they have been moving for the same time, $T$ seconds, and together they have covered the 150 m between them

![Vertical motion sketch: a vertical line from the ground to a point 150 m above it; the first ball moves upwards from the ground at 29.3 metres per second a distance s1, the second ball moves downwards from 150 m at 8.2 metres per second a distance s2, and they meet; upwards is positive for the first ball and downwards is positive for the second](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/constant-acceleration/assets/006-vertical-motion-sketch-a-vertical-line-from-the-.png)

For the first ball, take upwards as positive, so $a = - 10$, and use $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$

$s_{1} = 29 . 3 T - 5 T^{2}$

For the second ball, take downwards as positive, so $a = 10$

$s_{2} = 8 . 2 T + 5 T^{2}$

**[M1 A1]**

The distances add up to 150 m

$29 . 3 T - 5 T^{2} + 8 . 2 T + 5 T^{2} = 150$

**[M1]**

$37 . 5 T = 150$

$T = 4 \text{s}$

**[A1]**

The height of the collision is the first ball's displacement at $T = 4$

$s_{1} = 29 . 3 \times 4 - 5 \times 4^{2}$

**[M1]**

$s_{1} = 117 . 2 - 80$

$\text{Height} = 37 . 2 \text{m}$

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The $T^{2}$ terms cancel because both balls have the same acceleration. Relative to each other the balls move as if gravity were switched off, closing the 150 m gap at a constant $29 . 3 + 8 . 2 = 37 . 5 \text{m s}^{-1}$, so the time is simply $150 \div 37 . 5$.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of $s = u t + \frac{1}{2} a t^{2}$ for either ball with $a = \pm 10$ and the same time for both. Allow sign errors.
> 
> **A1**: Both displacement expressions correct.
> 
> **M1**: Setting the sum of the two distances equal to 150, or an equivalent equation using heights above the ground.
> 
> **A1**: Correct time of 4.
> 
> **M1**: Substitution of the time found into the first ball's displacement, or into $150 - s_{2}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct height of 37.2.
> 
> The two answers are marked independently.

parts.problemMd:
(i) Find the speed of each ball when they collide.

(ii) Show that both balls are moving downwards when they collide.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Use $v = u + a t$ with $t = 4$ for each ball, keeping each ball's positive direction from part (a)

$v_{1} = 29 . 3 - 10 \times 4 = - 10 . 7$

$\text{Speed of the first ball} = 10 . 7 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[B1]**

$v_{2} = 8 . 2 + 10 \times 4 = 48 . 2$

$\text{Speed of the second ball} = 48 . 2 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

*Upwards is positive for the first ball and its velocity is negative, so it is moving downwards*

**[B1]**

*Downwards is positive for the second ball and its velocity is positive, so it is moving downwards*

**Final answer:** **Both balls are moving downwards when they collide**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct speed of 10.7 for the first ball. The speed must be positive.
> 
> **B1**: Correct speed of 48.2 for the second ball.
> 
> **B1**: A correct reason why the first ball is moving downwards, e.g. its velocity is negative when upwards is positive, or it reaches its greatest height at 2.93 seconds, before the collision at 4 seconds.
> 
> **B1**: A complete conclusion that both balls are moving downwards, with the second ball's direction justified.

parts.problemMd:
The displacement of a particle is shown in the displacement-time graph below. Displacement is measured in metres from its starting position and time is measured in seconds.

![Displacement-time graph on a labelled grid, rising in a straight line from the origin, then horizontal, then falling in a straight line back to zero displacement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/002-displacement-time-graph-on-a-labelled-grid-risin.png)

(i) Find the displacement of the particle from its starting position after 3 seconds.

(ii) For how long was the particle stationary?

(iii) Find the velocity of the particle for the last 5 seconds of its motion.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

To find the displacement after 3 seconds, read up from $t = 3$ to the graph and across to the displacement axis

![Displacement-time graph with dashed construction lines drawn up from 3 seconds to the graph and across to the displacement axis](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/003-displacement-time-graph-with-dashed-construction.png)

$15 \text{m}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

The particle is stationary while its displacement is not changing, which is where the graph is horizontal

$7 - 4 = 3$

$3 \text{seconds}$

**[B1]**

(iii)

The velocity is the gradient of a displacement-time graph, so use $\text{velocity} = \frac{\text{change in displacement}}{\text{change in time}}$ over the last 5 seconds

$v = \frac{0-20}{12-7}$

**[M1]**

$v = - 4 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct displacement of 15 m, read from the graph at 3 seconds.
> 
> **B1**: Correct duration of 3 seconds, from the horizontal section of the graph between 4 and 7 seconds.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the gradient of the final section, using the change in displacement divided by the change in time. Allow this mark for a correct gradient calculation using any two points on that section.
> 
> **A1**: Correct velocity of −4 m s⁻¹. The negative sign is required, because the question asks for a velocity rather than a speed. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
A particle is set into motion with a constant velocity of $3 \text{m s}^{-1}$. After 5 seconds the particle stops and remains stationary for 6 seconds. The particle then moves with a constant velocity of $- 6 \text{m s}^{-1}$ until it returns to its initial position.

Sketch a displacement-time graph for the motion of the particle.
parts.solutionMd:
Each stage has a constant velocity, so each section is a straight line. To place the first corner, use $\text{displacement} = \text{velocity} \times \text{time}$

$s = 3 \times 5 = 15$

**[B1]**

The particle is stationary for the next 6 seconds, so the graph is horizontal from $t = 5$ to $t = 11$

The particle returns to its initial position, a distance of 15 m, so use $\text{time} = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}$

$\frac{15}{6} = 2 . 5$

**[M1]**

The motion therefore ends at $11 + 2 . 5 = 13 . 5$ seconds

![Displacement-time graph rising in a straight line from the origin to 15 m at 5 seconds, horizontal until 11 seconds, then falling in a straight line to zero at 13.5 seconds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/016-displacement-time-graph-rising-in-a-straight-lin.png)

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct first section, a straight line from the origin reaching a displacement of 15 m at 5 seconds.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the duration of the final section, dividing the displacement to be covered by the speed.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct graph, with the horizontal section from 5 to 11 seconds and a straight line returning to zero displacement at 13.5 seconds. Follow through from an incorrect first section, provided the shape is right.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows the velocity-time graph for a particle moving in a straight line. Time is measured in seconds and velocity is measured in metres per second.

![Velocity-time graph on a labelled grid, rising in a straight line from the origin to a horizontal section, then falling, and finally rising again](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/008-velocity-time-graph-on-a-labelled-grid-rising-in.png)

(i) Write down the velocity of the particle after 3 seconds.

(ii) Write down the speed of the particle after 8.5 seconds.

(iii) State the period of time during which the particle is moving with constant velocity.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Read up from $t = 3$ to the graph and across to the velocity axis

![Velocity-time graph with dashed construction lines drawn from 3 seconds and from 8.5 seconds up to the graph and across to the velocity axis](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/009-velocity-time-graph-with-dashed-construction-lin.png)

$0 . 75 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Read the graph at $t = 8 . 5$ in the same way

$1 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[B1]**

(iii)

The velocity is constant where the graph is horizontal

**Final answer:** **From 6 seconds to 7.5 seconds**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct velocity of 0.75 m s⁻¹ read from the graph at 3 seconds.
> 
> **B1**: Correct speed of 1 m s⁻¹ read from the graph at 8.5 seconds. The velocity is positive here, so the speed and the velocity have the same value.

> **B1**: Correct period from 6 to 7.5 seconds, identified from the horizontal section of the graph. Accept an answer given as a duration of 1.5 seconds provided the two times are stated.

parts.problemMd: Find the displacement of the particle from its starting position after 6 seconds.
parts.solutionMd:
The displacement is the area under the velocity-time graph, which for the first 6 seconds is a triangle of base 6 and height 1.5

![Velocity-time graph with the region under the graph between 0 and 6 seconds shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/010-velocity-time-graph-with-the-region-under-the-gr.png)

$s = \frac{1}{2} \times 6 \times 1 . 5$

**[M1]**

$s = 4 . 5 \text{m}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

parts.problemMd:
A particle moves in a straight line. It starts from rest and moves with constant acceleration $5 \text{m s}^{-2}$ for 4 seconds. It then travels at constant speed for a further 8 seconds. Over the next 3 seconds the velocity of the particle decreases uniformly until the particle comes to rest.

(i) Sketch the velocity-time graph for the motion of the particle.

(ii) Find the total displacement of the particle from its starting position.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The acceleration is the gradient of a velocity-time graph, so use $v = u + a t$ with $u = 0$, $a = 5$ and $t = 4$ to find the velocity reached

$v = 5 \times 4 = 20$

**[B1]**

The particle then holds this velocity for 8 seconds, so the graph is horizontal until $t = 12$, and returns to the time axis at $t = 15$

![Velocity-time graph rising in a straight line from the origin to 20 metres per second at 4 seconds, horizontal until 12 seconds, then falling in a straight line to zero at 15 seconds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/001-velocity-time-graph-rising-in-a-straight-line-fr.png)

**[B1 B1]**

(ii)

The displacement is the area under the velocity-time graph, which is a trapezium with parallel sides 15 and 8, and height 20

$s = \frac{15+8}{2} \times 20$

**[M1]**

$s = \frac{23}{2} \times 20$

$s = 230 \text{m}$

**[A1 A1]**

> **B1**: Correct shape, starting at the origin, rising to a maximum, horizontal, then falling to the time axis.
>

parts.problemMd:

(ii) Write down the time at which the participant is furthest from *O* on their third run.

The greatest distance from *O* is the height of the tallest peak

$20 \text{m}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

The third run is the third peak, so read off the time at its highest point

$16 \text{seconds}$

parts.problemMd: Find the average speed of the participant over the four runs.
parts.solutionMd:
Distance counts the outward and return journeys of every run, so the total distance is twice the sum of the four peak displacements

![Displacement-time graph with dashed construction lines drawn from each of the four peaks across to the displacement axis](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/005-displacement-time-graph-with-dashed-construction.png)

$\text{total distance} = 2 ( 20 + 12 + 6 + 2 )$

**[M1]**

$\text{total distance} = 80$

**[A1]**

The four runs are complete at $t = 20$, so use $\text{average speed} = \frac{\text{total distance}}{\text{total time}}$

$\text{average speed} = \frac{80}{20}$

**[M1]**

$4 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The participant ends where they started, so the total displacement over the four runs is zero and the average velocity is zero. Average speed uses distance, which counts every metre travelled in both directions, so it is the doubling of the four peaks that makes this question work.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the total distance, doubling the sum of the four peak displacements to account for both the outward and the return journey of each run.
> 
> **A1**: Correct total distance of 80 m.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the average speed, dividing the total distance by the total time of 20 seconds.
> 
> **A1**: Correct average speed of 4 m s⁻¹. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
A particle moves in a straight line starting at the origin *O*. Initially at rest, it moves with constant acceleration for 6 seconds until it reaches the point *A*. The displacement of the particle at *A* is 9 m. The particle then decelerates uniformly for 4 seconds until it reaches the point *B* with velocity $2 \text{m s}^{-1}$. The particle then remains in motion at this velocity until it reaches the point *C*, where its displacement from *B* is 12 m.

Draw the velocity-time graph for the motion of the particle on the axes below, and show that the final displacement of the particle from *O* is 31 m.

![Blank axes with time in seconds from 0 to 16 on the horizontal axis and velocity in metres per second from 0 to 4 on the vertical axis](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/014-blank-axes-with-time-in-seconds-from-0-to-16-on-.png)
parts.solutionMd:
The first section is a triangle whose area is the 9 m displacement, so use $\text{area} = \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}$ to find the velocity at *A*

$\frac{1}{2} ( 6 \times v ) = 9$

$v = 3$

**[B1]**

The deceleration lasts 4 seconds and ends at $2 \text{m s}^{-1}$, so *B* is at $t = 6 + 4 = 10$

**[B1]**

The particle then travels 12 m at a constant $2 \text{m s}^{-1}$, so use $\text{time} = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}$ to place *C*

$\frac{12}{2} = 6$

$t = 10 + 6 = 16$

![Velocity-time graph rising from the origin to A at 6 seconds and 3 metres per second, falling to B at 10 seconds and 2 metres per second, then horizontal to C at 16 seconds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/015-velocity-time-graph-rising-from-the-origin-to-a-.png)

**[B1]**

The total displacement is the area under the whole graph, made up of a triangle, a trapezium and a rectangle

$s = 9 + \frac{1}{2} ( 2 + 3 ) \times 4 + 12$

**[M1]**

$s = 9 + 10 + 12$

$s = 31 \text{m}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct velocity of 3 m s⁻¹ at *A*, obtained by equating the area of the first triangle to the given displacement of 9 m.
> 
> **B1**: Correct coordinates for *B*, at 10 seconds and 2 m s⁻¹.
> 
> **B1**: Correct coordinates for *C*, at 16 seconds and 2 m s⁻¹, with a fully correct graph drawn through all three points.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the total area under the graph, using all three sections. Accept any equivalent correct split of the region.
> 
> **B1**: The given result of 31 m is reached from complete working, with the value of each of the three areas visible.

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
The speed is the magnitude of the gradient of a displacement-time graph. For the first section the particle covers 4 m in *T* seconds

![Displacement-time graph with the first sloping section and the final sloping section both highlighted](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/013-displacement-time-graph-with-the-first-sloping-s.png)

**[B1]**

The last 3 seconds run from 11 to 14 seconds, over which the particle covers 4 m back to its starting position

$\text{speed} = \frac{4}{3}$

**[B1]**

The first speed is half the second, so equate the two

$\frac{4}{T} = \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{4}{3}$

**[M1]**

$\frac{4}{T} = \frac{2}{3}$

$T = 6$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**

> 
> **B1**: Correct value $\frac{4}{3}$ for the speed during the last 3 seconds. The value must be positive, since a speed is being compared; using the signed gradient of $- \frac{4}{3}$ leads to a negative value of *T* and does not score the final mark.

parts.solutionMd:
The acceleration is the gradient of a velocity-time graph, so use $v = u + a t$ with $u = 0$ to find the velocity reached

$v = 3 \times 5 = 15$

**[B1]**

The time at constant speed is not given, so find it from $\text{time} = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}$

$\frac{45}{15} = 3$

**[M1]**

The constant-speed stage therefore ends at $t = 8$, and the cable car comes to rest 10 seconds after that, at $t = 18$

**[A1]**

parts.problemMd:
A ferry leaves port (point *O*) and travels directly towards its destination (point *B*). Its journey is shown on the displacement-time graph below, where displacement is measured in metres and time in seconds.

![Displacement-time graph on a labelled grid, rising from the origin in two straight sections through a marked point A to the destination at a marked point B](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/061-displacement-time-graph-on-a-labelled-grid-risin.png)

Use the graph to find

(i) the distance, in km, between the port and the destination,

(ii) the velocity of the ferry, in metres per second, between the points *A* and *B*.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The ferry travels in one direction throughout, so the distance equals the displacement at *B*. Convert from metres to kilometres

$35000 \div 1000$

$35 \text{km}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

The velocity is the gradient of the displacement-time graph between the two points

$v = \frac{35000-15000}{1800-1000} = \frac{20000}{800}$

**[M1]**

$v = 25 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct distance of 35 km. The conversion from metres must be carried out; 35 000 alone does not score, since the answer was asked for in kilometres.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the gradient between *A* and *B*, using the change in displacement divided by the change in time, with values read correctly from the graph.
> 
> **A1**: Correct velocity of 25 m s⁻¹.

parts.problemMd: The ferry company would like the journey to be completed within a maximum time of 25 minutes. Find, correct to 3 significant figures, the average velocity at which the ferry would need to travel in order to achieve this.
parts.solutionMd:
The average velocity is the total displacement divided by the total time, so convert the 25 minutes into seconds first

$\text{average velocity} = \frac{35000}{25\times60} = \frac{35000}{1500}$

**[M1]**

$23 . 3 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the average velocity, dividing the total displacement by the total time, with the time converted to seconds.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value. Accept answers which round to 23.3, or the exact value $\frac{70}{3}$.

parts.problemMd:
A robot lawnmower is tested by running it back and forth along a 20 m horizontal strip of grass. Starting in the middle of the strip, the lawnmower moves with a constant velocity of $- 0 . 2 \text{m s}^{-1}$ for 15 seconds. The velocity is then changed instantly to $0 . 8 \text{m s}^{-1}$, and this is maintained until the lawnmower has displacement 9 m from its starting position. The lawnmower is left in this position for 2 seconds, before the final part of the test, in which it moves with a constant velocity of $- 0 . 5 \text{m s}^{-1}$ for 8 seconds.

Plot the displacement-time graph of the robot lawnmower on the axes below.

![Blank axes with time in seconds from 0 to 40 on the horizontal axis and displacement in metres from −10 to 10 on the vertical axis](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/057-blank-axes-with-time-in-seconds-from-0-to-40-on-.png)
parts.solutionMd:
Each stage has a constant velocity, so every section is a straight line. For the first stage use $\text{displacement} = \text{velocity} \times \text{time}$

$- 0 . 2 \times 15 = - 3$

**[B1]**

The second stage covers a change of 12 m, so find its duration from $\text{time} = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}$

$\frac{12}{0.8} = 15$

**[M1]**

The second stage therefore ends at $t = 30$, and the lawnmower is then stationary until $t = 32$

**[A1]**

For the final stage the displacement changes by $- 0 . 5 \times 8 = - 4$, finishing at $s = 5$ when $t = 40$

![Displacement-time graph falling from the origin to −3 m at 15 seconds, rising to 9 m at 30 seconds, horizontal until 32 seconds, then falling to 5 m at 40 seconds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/058-displacement-time-graph-falling-from-the-origin-.png)

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct first section, a straight line from the origin to −3 m at 15 seconds.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the duration of the second stage, dividing the 12 m change in displacement by the speed of 0.8 m s⁻¹.
> 
> **A1**: Correct second and third sections, a straight line reaching 9 m at 30 seconds followed by a horizontal section to 32 seconds.
> 
> **B1**: Correct final section, a straight line falling to 5 m at 40 seconds.

parts.problemMd:
(i) Write down the time taken to complete the test.

(ii) Write down the final displacement of the robot lawnmower.

(iii) Find the distance travelled by the robot lawnmower during the test.
parts.solutionMd:
