The test ends at the right-hand end of the graph

$40 \text{seconds}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Read the displacement at $t = 40$

$5 \text{m}$

**[B1]**

(iii)

The lawnmower changes direction twice, so add the distance covered on each moving section

$\text{distance} = 3 + 12 + 4$

**[M1]**

$19 \text{m}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct total time of 40 seconds.
> 
> **B1**: Correct final displacement of 5 m.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the distance, adding the magnitude of the displacement change on each of the three moving sections. Follow through from an incorrect graph in part (a).
> 
> **A1**: Correct distance of 19 m.

parts.problemMd:
A cable car crosses a river, running horizontally at a fixed height. It leaves one side of the river from rest with constant acceleration $1 . 2 \text{m s}^{-2}$ for 5 seconds. It then travels at constant speed until it has covered a further 42 m. The cable car then moves with constant acceleration $- 0 . 5 \text{m s}^{-2}$ until its velocity is $1 . 5 \text{m s}^{-1}$. It stays at this velocity for 5 seconds, before taking a further 6 seconds to come to rest with uniform deceleration.

Sketch the velocity-time graph for the journey of the cable car across the river.
parts.solutionMd:
The acceleration is the gradient of a velocity-time graph, so use $v = u + a t$ with $u = 0$ to find the velocity reached

$v = 1 . 2 \times 5 = 6$

**[B1]**

The time at constant speed is not given, so find it from $\text{time} = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}$

$\frac{42}{6} = 7$

**[M1]**

The constant-speed stage therefore ends at $t = 12$

The velocity then falls from 6 to 1.5 at a rate of $0 . 5 \text{m s}^{-2}$, so divide the change in velocity by that rate

$\frac{6-1.5}{0.5} = 9$

**[M1]**

This stage ends at $t = 21$, and the cable car then travels at $1 . 5 \text{m s}^{-1}$ until $t = 26$

It comes to rest 6 seconds later, at $t = 32$

![Velocity-time graph rising in a straight line from the origin to 6 metres per second at 5 seconds, horizontal until 12 seconds, falling to 1.5 metres per second at 21 seconds, horizontal until 26 seconds, then falling to zero at 32 seconds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/041-velocity-time-graph-rising-in-a-straight-line-fr.png)

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct maximum velocity of 6 m s⁻¹, seen on the graph or in working.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the duration of the constant-speed stage, dividing the distance of 42 m by the speed.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the duration of the third stage, dividing the change in velocity by 0.5.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct graph with five straight sections, the velocities 6 and 1.5, and the times 5, 12, 21, 26 and 32 seconds correctly marked. Follow through from an incorrect maximum velocity, provided the shape is right.

parts.problemMd:
A particle moves along a horizontal straight line. Its displacement from a fixed point *O*, in metres, is shown for the first 20 seconds of its motion on the displacement-time graph below.

![Displacement-time graph on a labelled grid made of straight sections, starting above zero displacement, rising, level, falling below the time axis with a short level section, and finally rising back to zero displacement](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/034-displacement-time-graph-on-a-labelled-grid-made-.png)

(i) Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first 10 seconds.

(ii) Find the average speed of the particle over the first 20 seconds.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Distance counts movement in both directions as positive. The particle starts 3 m from *O*, rises to 11 m, and at $t = 10$ is back down to 5 m

![Displacement-time graph with dashed construction lines drawn from 10 seconds up to the falling section and across to the displacement axis](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/035-displacement-time-graph-with-dashed-construction.png)

$\text{distance} = ( 11 - 3 ) + ( 11 - 5 )$

**[M1]**

$14 \text{m}$

**[A1]**

(ii)

Over 20 seconds the particle moves 8 m out to 11 m, 12 m back to −1 m, 4 m further to −5 m, then 5 m back to 0

$\text{total distance} = 8 + 12 + 4 + 5$

$\text{total distance} = 29$

**[M1]**

Divide the total distance by the total time

$\text{average speed} = \frac{29}{20}$

$1 . 45 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the distance in the first 10 seconds, adding the distance up to 11 m and the distance back down to 5 m. The displacement at 10 seconds must be read as 5 m.
> 
> **A1**: Correct distance of 14 m. An answer of 5 or 2, from the displacement alone, does not score.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the total distance over 20 seconds, adding the magnitudes of all four moving sections.
> 
> **A1**: Correct average speed of 1.45 m s⁻¹.

parts.problemMd:
A TV camera runs along a horizontal track beside the pitch at a rugby match. The pitch is 90 m long and the camera is initially positioned at the halfway line.

The camera moves from rest at a constant velocity and after 4 seconds has displacement −38 m. The camera then moves at a constant speed of $5 \text{m s}^{-1}$ to a position 17 m beyond the halfway line on the other side. It remains in this position for 6 seconds, then moves for the next 9 seconds with velocity $- 3 \text{m s}^{-1}$.

Sketch a displacement-time graph to illustrate the motion of the camera.
parts.solutionMd:
Each stage has a constant velocity, so the graph is a series of straight lines. Take the halfway line as zero displacement

The camera reaches −38 m after 4 seconds

**[B1]**

It then moves from −38 m to 17 m, a distance of $38 + 17 = 55$ m, at $5 \text{m s}^{-1}$, so use $\text{time} = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}$

$\frac{55}{5} = 11$

**[M1]**

The camera therefore reaches 17 m at $t = 15$ and stays there until $t = 21$

Over the final 9 seconds its displacement changes by $- 3 \times 9 = - 27$, so it finishes at

$s = 17 - 27 = - 10$

![Displacement-time graph falling in a straight line from the origin to −38 m at 4 seconds, rising through zero to 17 m at 15 seconds, horizontal until 21 seconds, then falling through zero to −10 m at 30 seconds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/021-displacement-time-graph-falling-in-a-straight-li.png)

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct first section, a straight line from the origin down to −38 m at 4 seconds.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the duration of the second section, dividing the distance of 55 m by the speed of 5 m s⁻¹.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct graph with straight sections through 17 m at 15 seconds, horizontal until 21 seconds, and ending at −10 m at 30 seconds.

parts.problemMd: Find the average velocity of the camera during its motion.
parts.solutionMd:
![Displacement-time graph falling in a straight line from the origin to −38 m at 4 seconds, rising through zero to 17 m at 15 seconds, horizontal until 21 seconds, then falling through zero to −10 m at 30 seconds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/021-displacement-time-graph-falling-in-a-straight-li.png)

The average velocity is the total displacement divided by the total time. The camera finishes 10 m on the negative side of the halfway line after 30 seconds

$\text{average velocity} = \frac{-10}{30}$

**[M1]**

$- 0 . 333 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the average velocity, dividing the final displacement by the total time. Follow through from the final displacement and time in part (a).
> 
> **A1**: Correct average velocity. Accept $- \frac{1}{3}$ or answers which round to −0.333, or 0.333 m s⁻¹ with its direction stated as towards the side of the halfway line where the camera finishes. An answer of 0.333 with no sign or direction does not score, because a velocity was asked for.

parts.problemMd:
A snooker ball is struck so that it travels in a straight line up and down a snooker table. The graph shows the velocity of the ball, $v \text{m s}^{-1}$, at time *t* seconds after being struck.

![Velocity-time graph on a labelled grid, falling in a straight line from a positive value, then changing sign instantaneously to a negative value and rising back to the time axis](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/062-velocity-time-graph-on-a-labelled-grid-falling-i.png)

(i) Write down the time at which the snooker ball hits a cushion.

(ii) Find the amount by which the speed of the ball is reduced when it hits the cushion.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The ball reverses direction at the cushion, so the velocity changes sign instantaneously

$0 . 8 \text{seconds}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

The speed is the magnitude of the velocity, so it falls from 2 to 1

$1 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct time of 0.8 seconds, identified from the instantaneous change of sign in the velocity.
> 
> **B1**: Correct reduction of 1 m s⁻¹, from a speed of 2 m s⁻¹ before the cushion to 1 m s⁻¹ after it. A reduction of 3, from 2 to −1, does not score, since a speed rather than a velocity is being compared.

parts.problemMd:
(i) Find the magnitude of the acceleration of the snooker ball before it hits the cushion.

(ii) After the ball hits the cushion its velocity is increasing, but the ball is slowing down. Explain briefly why this is so.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The acceleration is the gradient of the velocity-time graph, and a magnitude is asked for

`|a| = \left|\dfrac{2 - 4}{0.8}\right|`

**[M1]**

`|a| = 2.5\text{ m s}^{-2}`

**[A1]**

(ii)

After the cushion the velocity is negative and rising towards zero, so its magnitude is falling

**Final answer:** **The velocity is negative, so as it increases towards zero the speed of the ball decreases**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the gradient of the section before the cushion, using the change in velocity divided by the change in time.
> 
> **A1**: Correct magnitude of 2.5 m s⁻². Accept −2.5 provided the magnitude is then stated.
> 
> **B1**: A correct explanation making clear that the velocity after the cushion is negative, so that an increase in velocity corresponds to a decrease in speed. Accept any equivalent wording referring to the ball moving in the negative direction and slowing as its velocity rises towards zero.

parts.problemMd:
(i) Find the total distance travelled by the snooker ball.

(ii) Find the final displacement of the ball from its starting position.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The distance is the total area between the graph and the time axis, taking both regions as positive

![Velocity-time graph with the region above the axis before the cushion shaded, and the region below the axis after the cushion shaded in a darker tone](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/063-velocity-time-graph-with-the-region-above-the-ax.png)

$\text{distance} = \frac{1}{2} ( 4 + 2 ) ( 0 . 8 ) + \frac{1}{2} ( 1 . 6 ) ( 1 )$

**[M1]**

$\text{distance} = 2 . 4 + 0 . 8$

$3 . 2 \text{m}$

**[A1]**

(ii)

The displacement is signed, so the area below the time axis counts as negative

$s = 2 . 4 - 0 . 8$

**[M1]**

$s = 1 . 6 \text{m}$

**[A1]**

> 
> **A1**: Correct total distance of 3.2 m.
>

parts.problemMd:
In drag racing, two cars start from rest side by side and accelerate in a straight horizontal line, the first to cross the finish line being declared the winner. Immediately after crossing the finish line each car releases a parachute, enabling it to decelerate to rest as quickly as possible.

The graph shows the velocities, in metres per second, of two cars from the start of a race until they come to rest afterwards.

![Velocity-time graph on a labelled grid showing two cars, drawn as a solid line and a dotted line, each accelerating to a maximum velocity, holding it briefly, then decelerating to rest](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/065-velocity-time-graph-on-a-labelled-grid-showing-t.png)

(i) State which car won the race.

(ii) Write down the top speed achieved by car *A* during the race.

(iii) Find the magnitude of the acceleration of car *B*.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Each car begins to decelerate the moment it crosses the finish line, so the car that turns first is the winner

**Final answer:** **Car B won the race**

**[B1]**

(ii)

Read the height of the horizontal section of car *A*'s graph

$120 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[B1]**

(iii)

The acceleration is the gradient of the velocity-time graph, and car *B* reaches $150 \text{m s}^{-1}$ in 3 seconds

`|a| = \left|\dfrac{150 - 0}{3 - 0}\right|`

**[M1]**

`|a| = 50\text{ m s}^{-2}`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Car *B*, identified because it begins to decelerate first, at 3.5 seconds against 3.75 seconds for car *A*. A bare answer of car *B* scores.
> 
> **B1**: Correct top speed of 120 m s⁻¹ for car *A*.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the gradient of the accelerating section of car *B*'s graph.
>

parts.problemMd: Verify that both cars covered the length of the drag racetrack, 300 m, before decelerating.
parts.solutionMd:
The distance covered before decelerating is the area under each car's graph up to the moment it begins to slow, made up of a triangle and a rectangle

![Velocity-time graph for the two cars with dashed vertical lines marking the start and end of each car's constant-velocity phase](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/066-velocity-time-graph-for-the-two-cars-with-dashed.png)

For car *A*, which reaches $120 \text{m s}^{-1}$ at 2.5 seconds and turns at 3.75 seconds

$\frac{1}{2} ( 2 . 5 ) ( 120 ) + ( 3 . 75 - 2 . 5 ) ( 120 ) = 150 + 150$

**[M1 A1]**

For car *B*, which reaches $150 \text{m s}^{-1}$ at 3 seconds and turns at 3.5 seconds

$\frac{1}{2} ( 3 ) ( 150 ) + ( 3 . 5 - 3 ) ( 150 ) = 225 + 75$

**Final answer:** **Both cars covered 300 m before decelerating**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the area under one car's graph up to the moment it begins to decelerate, using a triangle and a rectangle.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value of 300 m for car *A*, with both areas visible.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value of 300 m for car *B*, with both areas visible, and a conclusion stating that both cars covered the 300 m. Because the result is given, the working for each car must be shown.

parts.problemMd: Explain, without performing any calculations, how it can be seen from the graph that both cars had the same deceleration.
parts.solutionMd:
The deceleration is the gradient of each car's final section, and the two sections are drawn parallel

**Final answer:** **The two deceleration sections are parallel, so they have the same gradient**

**[B1]**

parts.problemMd:

parts.problemMd:
A trainee is practising a take-off manoeuvre by piloting an aircraft along a straight horizontal runway. The velocity-time graph below describes the motion of the aircraft, where velocity is measured in metres per second.

![Velocity-time graph rising from the origin to velocity V at time T, horizontal until time T plus 10, then falling to zero at time 2T](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/064-velocity-time-graph-rising-from-the-origin-to-ve.png)

The aircraft accelerated at $5 \text{m s}^{-2}$, and the trainee pilot used 1.68 km of the runway to complete the manoeuvre.

Show that

(i) $V = 5 T$,

(ii) $V ( T + 5 ) = 1680$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The acceleration is the gradient of the velocity-time graph, and the aircraft starts from rest

$\frac{V}{T} = 5$

$V = 5 T$

**[B1]**

(ii)

The runway used is the area under the graph. Convert the distance to metres first, so that it matches the velocity units

$1 . 68 \text{km} = 1680 \text{m}$

The region is a trapezium with parallel sides $2 T$ and $( T + 10 ) - T = 10$, and height *V*, so use $\text{area} = \frac{1}{2} ( a + b ) h$

`\dfrac{1}{2}\left(2T + 10\right)V = 1680`

**[M1]**

Divide the bracket by 2

$V ( T + 5 ) = 1680$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct derivation of $V = 5 T$ from the gradient of the first section, with the gradient expression seen.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the area of the trapezium, with the two parallel sides identified as $2 T$ and 10, and equated to 1680.
> 
> **B1**: The given result is reached from complete working. The conversion of 1.68 km to 1680 m must be visible, and the simplification from $\frac{1}{2} ( 2 T + 10 ) V$ to $V ( T + 5 )$ must be shown.

parts.problemMd: Hence find the values of *V* and *T*.
parts.solutionMd:
Substitute $V = 5 T$ into the second equation to eliminate *V*

$5 T ( T + 5 ) = 1680$

$T^{2} + 5 T - 336 = 0$

**[M1]**

Factorise

$( T + 21 ) ( T - 16 ) = 0$

Only the positive root is possible, because *T* is a time

$T = 16$

**[A1]**

Substitute back into $V = 5 T$

$V = 5 \times 16$

$V = 80$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for eliminating one unknown between the two equations, leading to a correct three-term quadratic.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value $T = 16$. The negative root must be rejected, since *T* is a time.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value $V = 80$.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows part of the velocity-time graph for a particle moving in a straight line. The particle starts from rest and its acceleration during the first *T* seconds is $4 \text{m s}^{-2}$. After *T* seconds the particle has been displaced from its starting position by 18 m.

![Velocity-time graph rising in a straight line from the origin to velocity V at time T](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/006-velocity-time-graph-rising-in-a-straight-line-fr.png)

Find the values of *V* and *T*.
parts.solutionMd:
The acceleration is the gradient of a velocity-time graph, and the particle starts from rest

$\frac{V}{T} = 4$

$V = 4 T$

**[B1]**

The displacement is the area under the graph, which is a triangle of base *T* and height *V*

![Velocity-time graph with the triangular region under the line shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/007-velocity-time-graph-with-the-triangular-region-u.png)

$\frac{1}{2} V T = 18$

$V T = 36$

**[M1]**

Substitute $V = 4 T$ into the second equation to eliminate *V*

$4 T^{2} = 36$

$T^{2} = 9$

Only the positive root is possible, because *T* is a time

$T = 3$

**[A1]**

Substitute back to find *V*

$V = 4 \times 3$

$V = 12$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct relationship $V = 4 T$, obtained from the gradient of the graph.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the displacement as the area of the triangle, leading to $V T = 36$ or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value $T = 3$. The negative root must be rejected, since *T* is a time.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value $V = 12$.

parts.problemMd:
A ferry leaves a port *O* and travels in a straight line to its destination *C*. Its journey is shown on the displacement-time graph below, where displacement is measured in metres and time in seconds.

![Displacement-time graph on a labelled grid, rising from the origin in three straight sections through marked points A and B to the destination at a marked point C](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/042-displacement-time-graph-on-a-labelled-grid-risin.png)

Find the velocity of the ferry during the fastest part of its journey.
parts.solutionMd:
The velocity is the gradient of the displacement-time graph, so the fastest part of the journey is the steepest section, from *A* to *B*

$v = \frac{26000-6000}{1200-400}$

**[M1]**

$v = \frac{20000}{800}$

$v = 25 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the gradient of the section from *A* to *B*, using the change in displacement divided by the change in time, with values read correctly from the graph. Also award this mark for finding the gradients of all three sections and selecting the greatest.
> 
> **A1**: Correct velocity of 25 m s⁻¹.

parts.problemMd:
The ferry company would like to reduce the total journey time from *O* to *C* by 5 minutes. The velocity of the ferry can be increased only between *A* and *B*.

Find the increase in velocity required.
parts.solutionMd:
The whole saving must come from the section from *A* to *B*, which currently takes 800 seconds. Convert the 5 minutes into seconds and subtract

$800 - 5 \times 60 = 500$

**[M1]**

The distance from *A* to *B* is unchanged, so the new velocity is that distance divided by the new time

$v = \frac{20000}{500} = 40$

**[M1]**

The increase is the difference between the new and the original velocities

$40 - 25$

$15 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the new time for the section from *A* to *B*, subtracting 300 seconds from 800 seconds. The conversion of 5 minutes to seconds must be seen or implied.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the new velocity, dividing the distance of 20 000 m by the new time.
> 
> **A1**: Correct increase of 15 m s⁻¹. Follow through from the velocity found in part (a).

parts.problemMd:
In drag racing, two cars start from rest side by side and accelerate rapidly in a straight horizontal line, the first to cross the finish line being declared the winner. Immediately after crossing the finish line each car releases a parachute, enabling it to decelerate to rest as quickly as possible.

The graph shows the velocities, in metres per second, of two cars from the start of a race until they come to rest afterwards.

![Velocity-time graph for two cars, car A drawn as a solid line and car B as a dotted line, each rising from rest and later returning to rest, with car B holding a constant velocity V for a period](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/043-velocity-time-graph-for-two-cars-car-a-drawn-as-.png)

(i) State which car was still accelerating when it crossed the finish line.

(ii) Find the magnitude of the acceleration of car *A*.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Each car begins to decelerate the moment it crosses the finish line. Car *A*'s velocity rises right up to the moment it starts to fall

**Final answer:** **Car A**

**[B1]**

(ii)

The acceleration is the gradient of car *A*'s first section, which reaches $\frac{500}{3} \text{m s}^{-1}$ at 4.8 seconds

`|a| = \dfrac{500}{3} \div 4.8`

**[M1]**

`|a| = \dfrac{625}{18}`

`|a| = 34.7\text{ m s}^{-2}`

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Car *A*. A bare answer scores.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the gradient of the accelerating section of car *A*'s graph.
> 
> **A1**: Correct magnitude. Accept $\frac{625}{18}$ or answers which round to 34.7.

parts.problemMd: The drag strip is 400 m long. Find the value of *V*.
parts.solutionMd:
Car *B* covers the 400 m before it begins to decelerate at 5.6 seconds, so the area under its graph up to that time is 400

![Velocity-time graph with the trapezium under car B's graph from 0 to 5.6 seconds shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/044-velocity-time-graph-with-the-trapezium-under-car.png)

That area is a trapezium of height *V*, with parallel sides 5.6 and $5 . 6 - 2 . 2 = 3 . 4$

$\frac{1}{2} ( 5 . 6 + 3 . 4 ) V = 400$

**[M1]**

$4 . 5 V = 400$

**[A1]**

$V = 88 . 9$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the area under car *B*'s graph up to 5.6 seconds, equated to 400. Accept a triangle and a rectangle in place of the trapezium.
> 
> **A1**: Correct simplified equation $4 . 5 V = 400$ or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value. Accept $\frac{800}{9}$ or answers which round to 88.9.

parts.problemMd: Hence show that car *B* covered half of its total distance while it was decelerating.
parts.solutionMd:
Car *B* decelerates from *V* to rest between 5.6 and 14.6 seconds, so the distance covered while decelerating is the area of a triangle of height *V*

![Velocity-time graph with the triangle under car B's graph from 5.6 to 14.6 seconds shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/045-velocity-time-graph-with-the-triangle-under-car-.png)

$\text{distance} = \frac{1}{2} ( 14 . 6 - 5 . 6 ) \times \frac{800}{9}$

**[M1]**

$\text{distance} = 400$

**[A1]**

Car *B* covered 400 m before it began to decelerate, so its total distance is

$400 + 400 = 800$

**Final answer:** **Car B covered 400 m of its 800 m while decelerating, which is half of its total distance**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the area of the triangle under car *B*'s graph from 5.6 to 14.6 seconds, using the value of *V* from part (b).
> 
> **A1**: Correct distance of 400 m while decelerating. Accept a value which rounds to 400 from the use of 88.9.
> 
> **B1**: A correct conclusion comparing the 400 m while decelerating with the total distance of 800 m. Because the result is given, the working must be shown.

parts.problemMd:
A particle moves in a vertical line, starting at the top of a cliff and finishing when it reaches the sea below. At time *t* seconds the displacement of the particle above its starting point is *s* metres, where $s = 2 t ( 4 - t )$. The displacement-time graph for the motion is shown below.

![Displacement-time curve rising from the origin to a maximum, falling back through the time axis and continuing below it until the curve ends](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/050-displacement-time-curve-rising-from-the-origin-t.png)

Find the greatest height of the particle above the sea.
parts.solutionMd:
The curve is symmetrical and crosses the time axis at $t = 0$ and $t = 4$, so its maximum is halfway between them

$t = \frac{0+4}{2} = 2$

**[M1]**

Substitute $t = 2$ into the equation for *s*

$s = 2 ( 2 ) ( 4 - 2 ) = 8$

**[A1]**

![Displacement-time curve with dashed construction lines from its maximum point down to the time axis and across to the displacement axis](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/051-displacement-time-curve-with-dashed-construction.png)

The graph ends at $s = - 24$ when the particle reaches the sea, so the sea is 24 m below the starting point

$24 + 8$

$32 \text{m}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the time of the maximum, using the symmetry of the curve between its zeros at 0 and 4. Accept the use of $\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} = 0$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct greatest displacement of 8 m above the starting point.
> 
> **B1**: Correct height of 32 m above the sea, adding the depth of the sea below the starting point. Follow through from an incorrect greatest displacement.

parts.problemMd: Find the average velocity of the particle over the whole motion.
parts.solutionMd:
The average velocity is the total displacement divided by the total time. The particle ends 24 m below its starting point after 6 seconds

$\text{average velocity} = \frac{-24}{6}$

**[M1]**

$- 4 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the average velocity, dividing the final displacement by the total time of 6 seconds.
> 
> **A1**: Correct average velocity of −4 m s⁻¹, or 4 m s⁻¹ with its direction stated as downwards. An answer of 4 with no sign or direction does not score, because a velocity was asked for.

parts.problemMd: Find the average speed of the particle over the whole motion.
parts.solutionMd:
The average speed is the total distance divided by the total time. The particle moves 8 m up to its highest point, 8 m back down to its starting point, then a further 24 m down to the sea

$\text{total distance} = 8 + 8 + 24$

**[M1]**

$\text{total distance} = 40$

**[A1]**

Divide by the total time of 6 seconds

$\text{average speed} = \frac{40}{6}$

**[M1]**

$6 . 67 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the total distance, counting the upward and downward movement separately, using the greatest displacement from part (a).
> 
> **A1**: Correct total distance of 40 m.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the average speed, dividing the total distance by the total time of 6 seconds. Dividing the displacement of 24 m by 6 does not score.
> 
> **A1**: Correct average speed. Accept $\frac{20}{3}$ or answers which round to 6.67.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows the velocity-time graph for a train travelling between two stations, starting at station *X* and finishing at station *Y*. Velocity is measured in kilometres per hour and time in minutes.

![Velocity-time graph on a labelled grid made of straight sections, rising from rest, level, rising again, level, falling, level, then falling to rest](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/026-velocity-time-graph-on-a-labelled-grid-made-of-s.png)

Find the distance between station *X* and station *Y*.
parts.solutionMd:
The distance is the area under the velocity-time graph. The time is in minutes, so divide the area by 60 at the end to convert to hours

![Velocity-time graph with the region under the graph shaded and divided by vertical lines at 10, 12, 20 and 35 minutes](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/027-velocity-time-graph-with-the-region-under-the-gr.png)

Split the area at 10, 12, 20 and 35 minutes into four trapezia and a rectangle

$\text{area} = \frac{1}{2} ( 10 + 7 ) ( 60 ) + \frac{1}{2} ( 60 + 80 ) ( 2 ) + ( 8 ) ( 80 ) + \frac{1}{2} ( 80 + 50 ) ( 15 ) + \frac{1}{2} ( 25 + 15 ) ( 50 )$

**[M1]**

$\text{area} = 510 + 140 + 640 + 975 + 1000$

$\text{area} = 3265$

$\text{distance} = \frac{3265}{60}$

**[M1]**

$54 . 4 \text{km}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the total area under the graph. Accept any correct split into triangles, rectangles and trapezia.
> 
> **M1**: Correct conversion of the time units, dividing an area in km h⁻¹ × minutes by 60, or converting every time to hours before finding the area.
> 
> **A1**: Correct distance. Accept $\frac{653}{12}$ or answers which round to 54.4.

parts.problemMd: Find the greatest magnitude of the acceleration of the train, giving your answer in m s⁻².
parts.solutionMd:
![Velocity-time graph on a labelled grid made of straight sections, rising from rest, level, rising again, level, falling, level, then falling to rest](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/026-velocity-time-graph-on-a-labelled-grid-made-of-s.png)

The magnitude of the acceleration is the steepness of the graph. Compare the four sloping sections, in km h⁻¹ per minute

$\frac{60-0}{3-0} = 20$

$\frac{80-60}{12-10} = 10$

$\frac{50-80}{35-20} = - 2$

$\frac{0-50}{60-50} = - 5$

**[M1]**

The first section is the steepest. Convert its change in velocity to metres per second and its 3 minutes to 180 seconds

$60 \text{km h}^{-1} = \frac{60\times1000}{3600} = \frac{50}{3} \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[M1]**

$a = \frac{50}{3} \div 180$

$0 . 0926 \text{m s}^{-2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method identifying the steepest section as the one from 0 to 3 minutes, by comparing gradients or by clear selection from the graph.
> 
> **M1**: Correct conversion of both units for that section, km h⁻¹ to m s⁻¹ and minutes to seconds.
> 
> **A1**: Correct acceleration. Accept $\frac{5}{54}$ or answers which round to 0.0926.

parts.problemMd:
A cable car crosses a river, running horizontally at a fixed height. It leaves one side of the river from rest with constant acceleration $2 \text{m s}^{-2}$ for 3 seconds. It then travels at constant speed until it has covered a further 24 m. The cable car then moves with constant acceleration $- 1 \text{m s}^{-2}$ until its velocity is $- 2 \text{m s}^{-1}$. It then decelerates uniformly and comes to rest on the other side of the river 5 seconds later.

Sketch the velocity-time graph for the journey of the cable car across the river.
parts.solutionMd:
The acceleration is the gradient of a velocity-time graph, so use $v = u + a t$ with $u = 0$ to find the velocity reached

$v = 2 \times 3 = 6$

**[B1]**

The time at constant speed is not given, so find it from $\text{time} = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}$

$\frac{24}{6} = 4$

**[M1]**

The constant-speed stage ends at $t = 7$

The velocity then falls from 6 to −2 at $1 \text{m s}^{-2}$, so divide the change in velocity by that rate

$\frac{6-(-2)}{1} = 8$

This stage ends at $t = 15$, and the velocity reaches zero 6 seconds into it, at $t = 13$

The cable car then comes to rest 5 seconds later, at $t = 20$

![Velocity-time graph rising from the origin to 6 metres per second at 3 seconds, horizontal until 7 seconds, falling through zero at 13 seconds to −2 metres per second at 15 seconds, then rising back to zero at 20 seconds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/019-velocity-time-graph-rising-from-the-origin-to-6-.png)

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct maximum velocity of 6 m s⁻¹, seen on the graph or in working.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the duration of the constant-speed stage, dividing the distance of 24 m by the speed.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct graph with straight sections, crossing the time axis at 13 seconds, reaching −2 m s⁻¹ at 15 seconds and returning to zero at 20 seconds.

parts.problemMd: Find the total distance travelled by the cable car.
parts.solutionMd:
The distance is the total area between the graph and the time axis, counting the region below the axis as positive

![Velocity-time graph with the trapezium above the time axis shaded, and the triangle below the time axis shaded in a darker tone](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/020-velocity-time-graph-with-the-trapezium-above-the.png)

The region above the axis is a trapezium with parallel sides 13 and 4 and height 6. The region below is a triangle of base 7 and height 2

$\text{distance} = \frac{1}{2} ( 13 + 4 ) ( 6 ) + \frac{1}{2} ( 7 ) ( 2 )$

**[M1]**

$\text{distance} = 51 + 7$

$58 \text{m}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the total distance, adding the area above the time axis and the area below it as positive values. Follow through from the graph in part (a).
> 
> **A1**: Correct total distance of 58 m.

parts.problemMd: Explain why 44 m would be a suitable upper bound for the width of the river where the cable car crosses it.
parts.solutionMd:
The width of the river depends on where the cable car finishes, not on how far it travels. For the displacement, the region below the time axis counts as negative

$s = 51 - 7 = 44$

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **The cable car finishes 44 m from where it started, on the other side of the river, so the river can be at most 44 m wide**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct displacement of 44 m, subtracting the area below the time axis from the area above it.
> 
> **B1**: A correct explanation that 44 m is the straight-line distance between the start and the finish, which lie on either side of the river, so the river can be no wider than this. Accept any equivalent wording. A response based on the total distance of 58 m does not score, because the cable car travels back over part of its route.

parts.problemMd:
The range of a mobility scooter is the distance it can travel on a single charge of its battery. The range is estimated by running the scooter on a machine that is equivalent to driving it along a straight horizontal road.

The scooter starts from rest and moves with constant acceleration $2 \text{m s}^{-2}$ for 4 seconds. It then maintains a constant velocity for the next 16 minutes. Its velocity is then reduced uniformly by a quarter, which takes 5 seconds, and it runs at this new velocity for a further 13.5 minutes. Finally, as the battery runs out, the scooter decelerates uniformly and comes to rest in 25 seconds.

Show that the scooter travels more than 12.6 km on a single charge, and that the battery lasts for approximately half an hour.
parts.solutionMd:
The distance is the area under the velocity-time graph. Start with the two constant velocities, using $v = u + a t$ with $u = 0$

$v = 2 \times 4 = 8$

**[B1]**

Reducing the velocity by a quarter leaves three quarters of it

$\frac{3}{4} \times 8 = 6$

**[B1]**

The times are a mix of seconds and minutes, so convert the minutes into seconds

$16 \times 60 = 960$

$13 . 5 \times 60 = 810$

**[B1]**

![Velocity-time sketch not to scale, rising from rest to 8 metres per second at 4 seconds, horizontal until 964 seconds, falling to 6 metres per second at 969 seconds, horizontal until 1779 seconds, then falling to rest at 1804 seconds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/033-velocity-time-sketch-not-to-scale-rising-from-re.png)

The area splits into a triangle, a rectangle, a trapezium, a rectangle and a triangle

$\text{distance} = \frac{1}{2} ( 4 ) ( 8 ) + ( 960 ) ( 8 ) + \frac{1}{2} ( 8 + 6 ) ( 5 ) + ( 810 ) ( 6 ) + \frac{1}{2} ( 25 ) ( 6 )$

**[M1]**

$\text{distance} = 16 + 7680 + 35 + 4860 + 75$

**[A1]**

$\text{distance} = 12666$

**Final answer:** **The scooter travels 12 666 m, which is 12.666 km, so it travels more than 12.6 km**

**[B1]**

The total time is the sum of the five stages, in seconds

$\text{time} = 4 + 960 + 5 + 810 + 25 = 1804$

**[M1]**

$1804 \text{seconds} = 30 \text{minutes} 4 \text{seconds}$

**Final answer:** **The battery lasts 30 minutes 4 seconds, which is approximately half an hour**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct constant velocity of 8 m s⁻¹.
> 
> **B1**: Correct reduced velocity of 6 m s⁻¹.
> 
> **B1**: Correct conversions of 16 minutes and 13.5 minutes to 960 seconds and 810 seconds.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the total area under the graph, using all five sections with times in seconds.
> 
> **A1**: Correct areas of 16, 7680, 35, 4860 and 75 for the five sections, or a correct equivalent split.
> 
> **B1**: A correct conclusion that 12 666 m is more than 12.6 km.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the total time, adding all five stages in consistent units.
> 
> **B1**: A correct conclusion that 1804 seconds, or 30 minutes 4 seconds, is approximately half an hour.

parts.problemMd:
A TV camera runs along a horizontal track beside the pitch at a football match. The pitch is 100 m long and the camera is initially positioned at the halfway line.

The camera moves from rest at a constant velocity and after 5 seconds has displacement 35 m. It remains in this position for 3 seconds, before moving back to the halfway line at a constant speed of $10 \text{m s}^{-1}$. The camera then moves with constant velocity $- 2 . 5 \text{m s}^{-1}$ until it has travelled a total distance of 80 m.

Sketch a displacement-time graph to illustrate the motion of the camera.
parts.solutionMd:
Each stage has a constant velocity, so the graph is a series of straight lines. Take the halfway line as zero displacement

The camera reaches 35 m after 5 seconds and stays there until $t = 8$

**[B1]**

The camera returns 35 m to the halfway line at $10 \text{m s}^{-1}$, so use $\text{time} = \frac{\text{distance}}{\text{speed}}$

$\frac{35}{10} = 3 . 5$

**[M1]**

The camera is therefore back at the halfway line at $t = 8 + 3 . 5 = 11 . 5$

By then it has travelled 70 m, so the final stage covers the rest of the 80 m

$80 - 70 = 10$

$\frac{10}{2.5} = 4$

**[M1]**

The final stage lasts 4 seconds in the negative direction, so the motion ends at

$t = 11 . 5 + 4 = 15 . 5$

$s = - 2 . 5 \times 4 = - 10$

![Displacement-time graph rising in a straight line from the origin to 35 m at 5 seconds, horizontal until 8 seconds, falling through zero at 11.5 seconds, and continuing down to −10 m at 15.5 seconds](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/046-displacement-time-graph-rising-in-a-straight-lin.png)

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct first two sections, a straight line from the origin to 35 m at 5 seconds, then horizontal until 8 seconds.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the duration of the return to the halfway line, dividing the 35 m by the speed of 10 m s⁻¹.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the duration of the final section, dividing the remaining distance of 10 m by the speed of 2.5 m s⁻¹.
> 
> **A1**: Fully correct graph with straight sections, reaching zero displacement at 11.5 seconds and ending at −10 m at 15.5 seconds.

parts.problemMd: Find the length of time for which the camera is more than 20 m from the halfway line.
parts.solutionMd:
The camera is more than 20 m from the halfway line only around its furthest point of 35 m. On the far side it never gets more than 10 m away

On the first stage the camera moves at $\frac{35}{5} = 7 \text{m s}^{-1}$, so it passes 20 m when

$t = \frac{20}{7}$

**[M1]**

On the return it leaves 35 m at $t = 8$ at $10 \text{m s}^{-1}$, so it is back at 20 m after covering 15 m

$t = 8 + \frac{15}{10} = 9 . 5$

**[M1]**

![Displacement-time graph with a dashed horizontal line at 20 m, and dashed vertical lines where the graph crosses it on the way out and on the way back](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/047-displacement-time-graph-with-a-dashed-horizontal.png)

The length of time is the difference between these two times

$9 . 5 - \frac{20}{7}$

$6 . 64 \text{seconds}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the time at which the camera first reaches 20 m, using its velocity of 7 m s⁻¹ on the first stage.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the time at which the camera passes 20 m on its return, from the 15 m covered at 10 m s⁻¹ after 8 seconds.
> 
> **A1**: Correct length of time. Accept $\frac{93}{14}$ or answers which round to 6.64.

parts.problemMd:
A snooker ball is struck so that it travels in a straight line up and down a snooker table. The graph shows the velocity of the ball, $v \text{m s}^{-1}$, at time *t* seconds after being struck.

![Velocity-time graph falling in a straight line from a positive value, then changing sign instantaneously to a negative value and rising in a straight line to the time axis at time T](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/048-velocity-time-graph-falling-in-a-straight-line-f.png)

(i) Write down the time at which the snooker ball hits the cushion.

(ii) Find the percentage reduction in the speed of the ball when it hits the cushion.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The ball reverses direction at the cushion, so the velocity changes sign instantaneously

$0 . 6 \text{seconds}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

The speed is the magnitude of the velocity, so it falls from 3 to 1.5

$\frac{3-1.5}{3} \times 100$

`50\%`

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct time of 0.6 seconds, identified from the instantaneous change of sign in the velocity.
> 
> **B1**: Correct reduction of 50%. A reduction worked out from a velocity of 3 to a velocity of −1.5 does not score, since the speeds are being compared.

parts.problemMd:
(i) Find the magnitude of the acceleration of the snooker ball before it hits the cushion.

(ii) Show that the magnitude of the acceleration of the snooker ball after it hits the cushion is $\frac{15}{10T-6} \text{m s}^{-2}$.
parts.solutionMd:
![Velocity-time graph falling in a straight line from a positive value, then changing sign instantaneously to a negative value and rising in a straight line to the time axis at time T](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/048-velocity-time-graph-falling-in-a-straight-line-f.png)

(i)

The acceleration is the gradient of the velocity-time graph, and a magnitude is asked for

`|a| = \left|\dfrac{3 - 5}{0.6}\right| = \dfrac{10}{3}`

**[M1]**

`|a| = 3.33\text{ m s}^{-2}`

**[A1]**

(ii)

After the cushion the velocity rises from −1.5 at $t = 0 . 6$ to 0 at $t = T$. This gradient is positive, because *T* is greater than 0.6

$a = \frac{0-(-1.5)}{T-0.6}$

$a = \frac{1.5}{T-0.6}$

Multiply the numerator and the denominator by 10 to clear the decimals

`|a| = \dfrac{15}{10T - 6}\text{ m s}^{-2}`

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the gradient of the section before the cushion, using the change in velocity divided by the change in time.
> 
> **A1**: Correct magnitude. Accept $\frac{10}{3}$ or answers which round to 3.33. Accept −3.33 provided the magnitude is then stated.
> 
> **B1**: The given result reached from the correct gradient $\frac{1.5}{T-0.6}$, with the multiplication by 10 shown.

parts.problemMd:
When the snooker ball comes to rest, its displacement from the point where it was struck is 0.3 m.

Find the value of *T* and the total distance travelled by the ball.
parts.solutionMd:
The displacement is the area above the time axis minus the area below it

![Velocity-time graph with the trapezium above the time axis before the cushion shaded, and the triangle below the time axis after the cushion shaded in a darker tone](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/049-velocity-time-graph-with-the-trapezium-above-the.png)

The area before the cushion is a trapezium with parallel sides 5 and 3 and width 0.6

$\frac{1}{2} ( 5 + 3 ) \times 0 . 6 = 2 . 4$

The area after the cushion is a triangle of base $T - 0 . 6$ and height 1.5, below the axis

$2 . 4 - \frac{1}{2} ( T - 0 . 6 ) ( 1 . 5 ) = 0 . 3$

**[M1]**

$0 . 75 ( T - 0 . 6 ) = 2 . 1$

$T - 0 . 6 = 2 . 8$

$T = 3 . 4$

**[A1]**

The total distance counts both areas as positive

$\text{distance} = 2 . 4 + \frac{1}{2} ( 3 . 4 - 0 . 6 ) ( 1 . 5 )$

**[M1]**

$\text{distance} = 2 . 4 + 2 . 1$

$4 . 5 \text{m}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the displacement, the area of the trapezium minus the area of the triangle, equated to 0.3.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value $T = 3 . 4$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the total distance, adding the two areas as positive values. Accept $2 . 4 + ( 2 . 4 - 0 . 3 )$. Follow through from an incorrect value of *T*.
> 
> **A1**: Correct total distance of 4.5 m.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows the displacement-time graph for a ferry travelling in a straight line between two ports, at the points *O* and *D* on the graph. Displacement is measured in metres and time in seconds. The points *A*, *B* and *C* do not represent ports.

![Displacement-time graph on a fine labelled grid, rising from the origin in four straight sections through marked points A, B and C to the second port at a marked point D](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/036-displacement-time-graph-on-a-fine-labelled-grid-.png)

Find the difference between the velocities of the ferry during the fastest and the slowest parts of its journey.
parts.solutionMd:
The velocity is the gradient of the displacement-time graph. The fastest part is the steepest section, from *A* to *B*, and the slowest is the shallowest, from *C* to *D*

$v_{AB} = \frac{35000-5000}{1250-250} = 30$

**[M1]**

$v_{CD} = \frac{40000-37500}{2000-1500} = 5$

**[A1]**

$30 - 5$

$25 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the gradient of a section, using the change in displacement divided by the change in time, with values read correctly from the graph.
> 
> **A1**: Correct velocities of 30 m s⁻¹ for the fastest section and 5 m s⁻¹ for the slowest. Also award this mark for all four gradients (20, 30, 10 and 5) with the greatest and least selected.
> 
> **A1**: Correct difference of 25 m s⁻¹.

parts.problemMd:
The ferry company would like to reduce the total journey time. The velocity of the ferry can be increased only while it is more than 5 km from both ports, and the maximum speed of the ferry is $45 \text{m s}^{-1}$.

Find, to the nearest second, the greatest possible reduction in the journey time.
parts.solutionMd:
5 km is 5000 m. The ferry is more than 5000 m from *O* once it passes *A*, and more than 5000 m from *D*, at 40 000 m, until it reaches *B* at 35 000 m

![Displacement-time graph with horizontal lines at 5000 m and 35 000 m, marking where the ferry is 5 km from each port](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/037-displacement-time-graph-with-horizontal-lines-at.png)

So only the section from *A* to *B* can be sped up. It covers 30 000 m, which currently takes 1000 seconds, so at the maximum speed it takes

$\text{time} = \frac{30000}{45} = \frac{2000}{3}$

**[M1]**

The reduction is the difference between the current and the new times

$1000 - \frac{2000}{3} = \frac{1000}{3} = 333 . 3 \dots$

**[M1]**

$333 \text{seconds}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct identification of the section from *A* to *B* as the only part more than 5 km from both ports, and a correct method for its time at 45 m s⁻¹.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the reduction, subtracting the new time from the current 1000 seconds.
> 
> **A1**: Correct reduction of 333 seconds, to the nearest second.

parts.problemMd:
A snooker ball is struck so that it travels in a straight line up and down a snooker table. The graph shows the velocity of the ball, $v \text{m s}^{-1}$, at time *t* seconds after it is struck.

![Velocity-time graph on a labelled grid made of three straight sections, each separated by an instantaneous change of sign in the velocity](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/030-velocity-time-graph-on-a-labelled-grid-made-of-t.png)

Write down the times at which the snooker ball hits a cushion, and hence find the length of the snooker table.
parts.solutionMd:
The ball hits a cushion whenever its velocity changes sign instantaneously

$0 . 8 \text{seconds}$

**[B1]**

$3 . 2 \text{seconds}$

**[B1]**

Between the two cushions the ball travels the full length of the table, which is the area between the graph and the time axis from 0.8 to 3.2 seconds

![Velocity-time graph with the trapezium between the graph and the time axis from 0.8 to 3.2 seconds shaded](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/031-velocity-time-graph-with-the-trapezium-between-t.png)

That region is a trapezium with parallel sides 1.75 and 1.25, and width $3 . 2 - 0 . 8 = 2 . 4$

$\text{length} = \frac{1}{2} ( 1 . 75 + 1 . 25 ) ( 2 . 4 )$

**[M1]**

$3 . 6 \text{m}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct time of 0.8 seconds.
> 
> **B1**: Correct time of 3.2 seconds.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for the area between the graph and the time axis from 0.8 to 3.2 seconds, treated as a positive length.
> 
> **A1**: Correct length of 3.6 m. The ball is modelled as a particle, so the distance between the cushions is the length of the table.

parts.problemMd: Show that the snooker ball comes to rest at exactly the point from which it was struck.
parts.solutionMd:
The ball comes to rest where it was struck if its final displacement is zero. Areas above the time axis count as positive and the area below it as negative

![Velocity-time graph with the two regions above the time axis shaded, and the region below the time axis shaded in a darker tone](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/032-velocity-time-graph-with-the-two-regions-above-t.png)

$s = \frac{1}{2} ( 3 . 75 + 2 . 25 ) ( 0 . 8 ) - 3 . 6 + \frac{1}{2} ( 5 . 6 - 3 . 2 ) ( 1 )$

**[M1]**

$s = 2 . 4 - 3 . 6 + 1 . 2$

**[A1]**

$s = 0$

**Final answer:** **The final displacement is zero, so the ball comes to rest at the point from which it was struck**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the final displacement, adding the areas above the time axis and subtracting the area below it.
> 
> **A1**: Correct areas of 2.4 and 1.2 for the two regions above the time axis. Follow through the middle area from part (a).
> 
> **B1**: A correct conclusion from a final displacement of exactly zero. Because the result is given, all three areas must be seen.

parts.problemMd:
Two particles, *P* and *Q*, start together at the top of a cliff at the same time, and each moves in a vertical line until it reaches the sea below. Particle *P* moves only downwards. Particle *Q* initially moves upwards.

The graph shows the displacements, in metres, of both particles above their starting point at time *t* seconds, until they reach the sea.

![Two displacement-time curves starting together at the origin and ending together at the same point below the time axis, one rising to a maximum before falling and the other falling throughout](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/038-two-displacement-time-curves-starting-together-a.png)

(i) Label the curves on the graph with *P* and *Q*.

(ii) Write down the height of the cliff.

(iii) One of the particles has a positive displacement for exactly half of the time it takes to reach the sea. Write down the time taken for each particle to reach the sea.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Particle *P* only moves downwards, so its displacement is never positive. Particle *Q* moves upwards first, so its curve rises above the time axis before falling

![Displacement-time graph with the curve that rises above the time axis labelled Q and the curve that only falls labelled P](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/039-displacement-time-graph-with-the-curve-that-rise.png)

**[B1]**

(ii)

Both particles reach the sea where the curves end, 64 m below the starting point

$64 \text{m}$

**[B1]**

(iii)

Only *Q* has a positive displacement, from $t = 0$ to $t = 4$, and that is half of its journey time

$2 \times 4$

$8 \text{seconds}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Both curves correctly labelled, *Q* on the curve that rises above the time axis and *P* on the curve that only falls.
> 
> **B1**: Correct height of 64 m.
> 
> **B1**: Correct time of 8 seconds.

parts.problemMd: Without performing any calculations, explain how you know that the two particles have the same average velocity over their motion.
parts.solutionMd:
The average velocity is the total displacement divided by the total time

*Both particles start at the top of the cliff and finish in the sea, so they have the same displacement of −64 m*

**[B1]**

*They start together and reach the sea at the same time, so they take the same time*

**Final answer:** **Equal displacements over equal times give equal average velocities**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A correct statement that both particles have the same displacement, since they start and finish at the same points.
> 
> **B1**: A correct statement that both take the same time, with the conclusion that their average velocities are therefore equal. Accept any equivalent wording. A response that computes either average velocity does not score this mark, since the question asks for an explanation without calculation.

parts.problemMd:
The displacement of particle *Q* is given by $s = A t ( B - t )$, where *A* and *B* are integers.

Find the greatest height of *Q* above the sea, and the time at which it reaches this height.
parts.solutionMd:
The curve for *Q* crosses the time axis at $t = 0$ and $t = 4$, so $B = 4$

*Q* reaches the sea at $t = 8$ with $s = - 64$. Substitute into $s = A t ( 4 - t )$

$- 64 = 8 A ( 4 - 8 )$

**[M1]**

$- 64 = - 32 A$

$A = 2$

**[A1]**

The curve is symmetrical, so its maximum is halfway between the zeros at 0 and 4

$t = \frac{0+4}{2}$

$2 \text{seconds}$

**[B1]**

Substitute $t = 2$ into $s = 2 t ( 4 - t )$

$s = 2 ( 2 ) ( 4 - 2 ) = 8$

![Displacement-time graph for both particles with dashed construction lines from the maximum of Q's curve down to the time axis and across to the displacement axis](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/040-displacement-time-graph-for-both-particles-with-.png)

The sea is 64 m below the starting point

$64 + 8$

$72 \text{m}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for *A*, substituting $t = 8$ and $s = - 64$ with $B = 4$ read from the zero at $t = 4$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct values $A = 2$ and $B = 4$.
> 
> **B1**: Correct time of 2 seconds, from the symmetry of the curve or from $\frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t} = 0$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct greatest height of 72 m above the sea, adding the height of the cliff to the greatest displacement of 8 m.

parts.problemMd:
A robot is tested for accuracy by being programmed to walk back and forth along a straight horizontal line.

In a three-part test the robot walks with constant velocities of $- 0 . 5 \text{m s}^{-1}$, $1 . 5 \text{m s}^{-1}$ and $- 1 \text{m s}^{-1}$, in that order. Over the first two parts together its average velocity is $0 . 7 \text{m s}^{-1}$. The last part lasts 10 seconds, and the final displacement of the robot from its starting point is 4 m.

Plot the displacement-time graph of the robot on the axes below, labelling the coordinates of the points where its velocity changes and the coordinates of its final position.

![Blank axes on a 1-unit grid with time in seconds from 0 to 34 on the horizontal axis and displacement in metres from −6 to 16 on the vertical axis](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/028-blank-axes-on-a-1-unit-grid-with-time-in-seconds.png)
parts.solutionMd:
Work backwards from the final position. The last part lasts 10 seconds at $- 1 \text{m s}^{-1}$

$- 1 \times 10 = - 10$

So at the end of the second part the displacement of the robot is

$4 + 10 = 14$

**[B1]**

The first two parts take the robot to 14 m at an average velocity of $0 . 7 \text{m s}^{-1}$, so together they last

$\frac{14}{0.7} = 20$

**[B1]**

Let the first part last *t* seconds, so the second part lasts $20 - t$ seconds. The displacements of the two parts add up to 14

$- 0 . 5 t + 1 . 5 ( 20 - t ) = 14$

**[M1]**

$- 0 . 5 t + 30 - 1 . 5 t = 14$

$2 t = 16$

$t = 8$

The first part therefore ends at $t = 8$ with displacement

$- 0 . 5 \times 8 = - 4$

**[A1]**

The second part ends at $t = 20$ with displacement 14, and the last part ends at $t = 30$ with displacement 4. Plot the points and join them with straight lines

![Displacement-time graph on the same grid, falling in a straight line from the origin to (8, −4), rising to (20, 14), then falling to (30, 4), with each of these points labelled with its coordinates](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/029-displacement-time-graph-on-the-same-grid-falling.png)

$( 8 ,  - 4 )$

$( 20 ,  14 )$

$( 30 ,  4 )$

**[B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct displacement of 14 m at the end of the second part, found by working back from the final displacement.
> 
> **B1**: Correct total time of 20 seconds for the first two parts, from the average velocity.
> 
> **M1**: Correct equation for the displacement over the first two parts, in one unknown time or as a pair of simultaneous equations.
> 
> **A1**: Correct values $t = 8$ and a displacement of −4 m at the end of the first part.
> 
> **B1**: Correct graph of three straight sections through (0, 0), (8, −4), (20, 14) and (30, 4), plotted accurately on the grid.
> 
> **B1**: All three coordinates (8, −4), (20, 14) and (30, 4) labelled on the graph.

parts.problemMd:
In a handicapped drag race two cars start side by side from rest, but car *A* is given a 2-second head start. Both cars accelerate in a straight horizontal line, and the first car to cross the finish line is declared the winner. Immediately after crossing the finish line each car deploys a parachute, enabling it to come to rest as quickly as possible.

The graph shows the velocities, in metres per second, of the two cars from the start of the race until they come to rest.

![Velocity-time graph for two cars, car A drawn as a solid line starting at the origin and car B as a dotted line starting 2 seconds later, each rising to a constant velocity, holding it, then falling to rest](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/022-velocity-time-graph-for-two-cars-car-a-drawn-as-.png)

Show that $V_{2} = 1 . 28 V_{1}$.
parts.solutionMd:
Each car begins to decelerate the moment it crosses the finish line, so both cars have covered the same distance by then: car *A* at 4.5 seconds and car *B* at 5.1 seconds

parts.problemMd:
The velocity-time graph below describes the motion of a particle moving in a straight line. Velocity is measured in metres per second and time in seconds.

![Velocity-time graph made of four straight sections, rising from the origin to V at time T, falling to the time axis, continuing below it to a minimum, then rising back to the time axis](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/052-velocity-time-graph-made-of-four-straight-sectio.png)

The final displacement of the particle from its starting position is −27 m, and the greatest magnitude of the acceleration of the particle during the motion is $1 . 5 \text{m s}^{-2}$.

Find the values of *V* and *T*.
parts.solutionMd:
The displacement is the area above the time axis minus the area below it, and both regions are triangles

![Velocity-time graph with the triangle above the time axis shaded, and the triangle below the time axis shaded in a darker tone](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/kinematics-graphs/assets/053-velocity-time-graph-with-the-triangle-above-the-.png)

The triangle above the axis has base $\frac{3}{2} T$ and height *V*. The triangle below has base $5 T - \frac{3}{2} T = \frac{7}{2} T$ and height $\frac{3}{4} V$

`\dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{3}{2}T\right)V - \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{7}{2}T\right)\left(\dfrac{3}{4}V\right) = -27`

**[M1]**

$\frac{3}{4} T V - \frac{21}{16} T V = - 27$

$- \frac{9}{16} T V = - 27$

$T V = 48$

**[A1]**

The magnitude of the acceleration is the steepness of each section

The steepest section runs from *T* to $\frac{3}{2} T$, where the velocity falls from *V* to 0 in $0 . 5 T$ seconds

$\frac{V}{0.5T} = 1 . 5$

**[M1]**

$V = 0 . 75 T$

Substitute this into $T V = 48$

$0 . 75 T^{2} = 48$

**[M1]**

$T^{2} = 64$

*T* is a time, so take the positive root

$T = 8$

**[A1]**

Substitute back to find *V*

$V = 0 . 75 \times 8$

$V = 6$

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The graph is only a sketch, so check that the section you took as steepest really is. With $T = 8$ and $V = 6$ the four sections have gradients of magnitude 0.75, 1.5, 0.409 and 0.265, so the greatest acceleration is indeed on the section from *T* to $\frac{3}{2} T$.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the final displacement, the area of the triangle above the axis minus the area of the triangle below it, equated to −27. Accept the equivalent equation with both signs reversed, equated to 27.
> 
> **A1**: Correct simplified equation $T V = 48$ or equivalent.
> 
> **M1**: Correct equation from the gradient of the steepest section, equated to 1.5.
> 
> **M1**: Correct method for solving the two equations simultaneously, substituting to form an equation in one unknown.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value $T = 8$. The negative root must be rejected, since *T* is a time.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value $V = 6$.

`\int_{4}^{5} (4t - t^{2}) \; \text{d}t = \left[2t^{2} - \dfrac{t^{3}}{3}\right]_{4}^{5}`

`= \left(2\left(5\right)^{2} - \dfrac{\left(5\right)^{3}}{3}\right) - \left(2\left(4\right)^{2} - \dfrac{\left(4\right)^{3}}{3}\right) \\ = \dfrac{25}{3} - \dfrac{32}{3} \\ = -\dfrac{7}{3}`

The particle is moving in the negative direction, so take the magnitude

$\text{Distance} = \frac{7}{3} \text{m}$

$a = \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$

**[M1]**

For the first 2 seconds of the motion, $t < 2$

$2 t < 4$

$2 t - 4 < 0$

**Final answer:** **The acceleration is negative for the first 2 seconds of the motion**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Differentiation of $v$ with respect to $t$, with the power of at least one term decreased by 1.
> 
> **B1**: A complete argument that $2 t - 4 < 0$ for $0 \leq t < 2$, with a conclusion. Accept an argument that $a$ is increasing and equals zero at $t = 2$, so it is negative before that time. Substituting a single value of $t$ does not score, since the result must hold throughout the first 2 seconds.

parts.problemMd:
An athlete training for the 100 m sprint aims to run according to the model

$s = 0 . 4 t^{2} + 3 . 5 t$

where $s$ m is the displacement of the athlete from the starting point at time $t$ seconds.

Find, according to the model, the time the athlete takes to complete the 100 m sprint. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
The athlete completes the sprint when $s = 100$

$0 . 4 t^{2} + 3 . 5 t = 100$

Rearrange to equal zero

$0 . 4 t^{2} + 3 . 5 t - 100 = 0$

This does not factorise, so use the quadratic formula

$t = \frac{-b\pm\sqrt{b^{2}-4ac}}{2a}$

`t = \dfrac{-3.5 \pm \sqrt{\left(3.5\right)^{2} - 4(0.4)(-100)}}{2(0.4)}`

**[M1]**

$t = \frac{-3.5\pm\sqrt{172.25}}{0.8}$

$t = 12 . 0305 \dots$* or *$t = - 20 . 7805 \dots$

Time cannot be negative, so reject the negative root

**Final answer:** $t = 12 . 0$** seconds (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Setting $s = 100$ and solving the resulting quadratic equation by any valid method.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 12.0, with the negative root rejected or ignored.

parts.problemMd: Show that, according to the model, the acceleration of the athlete is constant.
parts.solutionMd:
Differentiate the displacement to find the velocity

$v = \frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}$

$v = 0 . 8 t + 3 . 5$

**[M1]**

Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, so differentiate again

$a = \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$

$a = 0 . 8$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** **The acceleration does not depend on t, so it is constant**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Differentiation of $s$ with respect to $t$ to find the velocity, with the power of at least one term decreased by 1.
> 
> **M1**: Differentiation of the velocity with respect to $t$ to find the acceleration.
> 
> **B1**: Correct acceleration of 0.8 and a conclusion that it is constant because it does not depend on $t$.

parts.problemMd:
A home-made rocket is launched from rest at ground level at time $t = 0$ and moves vertically upwards. At time $t$ seconds after launch, the acceleration of the rocket is $a \text{m s}^{-2}$, where

$a = 40 + 6 t - t^{2}$

(i) Write down the acceleration of the rocket at launch.

(ii) Find the acceleration of the rocket when $t = 9$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

At launch $t = 0$, so only the constant term remains

$a = 40 \text{m s}^{-2}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Substitute $t = 9$ into the expression for the acceleration

`a = 40 + 6(9) - \left(9\right)^{2}`

**[M1]**

$a = 40 + 54 - 81$

$a = 13 \text{m s}^{-2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct acceleration of 40.
> 
> **M1**: Substitution of $t = 9$ into the expression for $a$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct acceleration of 13.

parts.problemMd:
(i) Find an expression for the velocity, $v \text{m s}^{-1}$, of the rocket in terms of $t$.

(ii) Find an expression for the height, $s$ m, of the rocket above the ground in terms of $t$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Integrate the acceleration to find the velocity

`v = \int (40 + 6t - t^{2}) \; \text{d}t`

$v = 40 t + 3 t^{2} - \frac{1}{3} t^{3} + c$

**[M1]**

The rocket starts from rest, so $v = 0$ when $t = 0$

`0 = 40(0) + 3\left(0\right)^{2} - \dfrac{1}{3}\left(0\right)^{3} + c`

$c = 0$

$v = 40 t + 3 t^{2} - \frac{1}{3} t^{3}$

**[A1]**

(ii)

Integrate the velocity to find the height

`s = \int \left(40t + 3t^{2} - \dfrac{1}{3}t^{3}\right) \; \text{d}t`

$s = 20 t^{2} + t^{3} - \frac{1}{12} t^{4} + k$

**[M1]**

The rocket starts at ground level, so $s = 0$ when $t = 0$

`0 = 20\left(0\right)^{2} + \left(0\right)^{3} - \dfrac{1}{12}\left(0\right)^{4} + k`

$k = 0$

$s = 20 t^{2} + t^{3} - \frac{1}{12} t^{4}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Integration of the acceleration with respect to $t$, with the power of at least one term increased by 1.
> 
> **A1**: Correct velocity $v = 40 t + 3 t^{2} - \frac{1}{3} t^{3}$, with the constant shown to be zero or correctly omitted.
> 
> **M1**: Integration of the velocity with respect to $t$, with the power of at least one term increased by 1.
> 
> **A1**: Correct height $s = 20 t^{2} + t^{3} - \frac{1}{12} t^{4}$, with the constant shown to be zero or correctly omitted. Accept equivalent forms such as $- \frac{t^{4}}{12}$.

parts.problemMd:
In a cheese-rolling competition, a cylindrical block of cheese rolls down a hill, starting from rest at the top of the hill. At time $t$ seconds, the acceleration of the cheese is modelled as $a \text{m s}^{-2}$, where

$a = 1 + 0 . 1 t$

for $0 \leq t \leq 20$. The cheese reaches the bottom of the hill when $t = 20$.

Find the velocity of the cheese when it reaches the bottom of the hill.
parts.solutionMd:
Integrate the acceleration to find the velocity

`v = \int (1 + 0.1t) \; \text{d}t`

$v = t + 0 . 05 t^{2} + c$

**[M1]**

The cheese starts from rest, so $v = 0$ when $t = 0$

`0 = 0 + 0.05\left(0\right)^{2} + c`

$c = 0$

$v = t + 0 . 05 t^{2}$

**[A1]**

Substitute $t = 20$

`v = 20 + 0.05\left(20\right)^{2}`

$v = 40 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Integration of the acceleration with respect to $t$, with the power of at least one term increased by 1.
> 
> **A1**: Correct velocity $v = t + 0 . 05 t^{2}$, with the constant shown to be zero or correctly omitted. Evaluating a definite integral from 0 to 20 is equally acceptable.
> 
> **A1**: Correct velocity of 40.

parts.problemMd: Find the length of the hill, as travelled by the cheese.
parts.solutionMd:
The cheese never changes direction, so integrate the velocity from part (a), $v = t + 0 . 05 t^{2}$, between the limits

`s = \int_{0}^{20} (t + 0.05t^{2}) \; \text{d}t`

`s = \left[\dfrac{t^{2}}{2} + \dfrac{t^{3}}{60}\right]_{0}^{20}`

**[M1 A1]**

Substitute the limits

`= \left(\dfrac{\left(20\right)^{2}}{2} + \dfrac{\left(20\right)^{3}}{60}\right) - 0 \\ = 200 + \dfrac{400}{3} \\ = 333.333\ldots`

**Final answer:** $\text{Length of hill} = 333 \text{m}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Integration of the velocity with respect to $t$, with the power of at least one term increased by 1.
> 
> **A1**: Correct integral $\frac{t^{2}}{2} + \frac{t^{3}}{60}$, or equivalent such as $\frac{0.05t^{3}}{3}$ for the second term.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 333. Accept the exact value $\frac{1000}{3}$.

parts.problemMd:
A high-speed train leaves a station from rest at time $t = 0$. Its displacement from the station at time $t$ seconds is $s$ m, where

$s = \frac{1}{k} t^{3}$

for $0 \leq t \leq 20$, and $k$ is a constant.

Find an expression, in terms of $t$ and $k$, for the velocity of the train for $0 \leq t \leq 20$.
parts.solutionMd:
Differentiate the displacement to find the velocity

$v = \frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}$

$v = \frac{3}{k} t^{2}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct velocity $v = \frac{3}{k} t^{2}$. Accept equivalent forms such as $\frac{3t^{2}}{k}$.

parts.problemMd:
The acceleration of the train is 0.6 $\text{m s}^{-2}$ when $t = 20$.

Find the value of $k$.
parts.solutionMd:
Differentiate the velocity from part (a), $v = \frac{3}{k} t^{2}$, to find the acceleration

$a = \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$

$a = \frac{6}{k} t$

**[M1 A1]**

Substitute $a = 0 . 6$ and $t = 20$

$0 . 6 = \frac{6}{k} ( 20 )$

$0 . 6 = \frac{120}{k}$

$k = \frac{120}{0.6}$

$k = 200$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Differentiation of the velocity with respect to $t$, with the power of $t$ decreased by 1.
> 
> **A1**: Correct acceleration $a = \frac{6}{k} t$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value of 200.

parts.problemMd: Find the distance travelled by the train in the first 20 seconds.
parts.solutionMd:
The train does not change direction, so substitute $k = 200$ and $t = 20$ into the displacement

`s = \dfrac{1}{200}\left(20\right)^{3}`

**[M1]**

$s = \frac{8000}{200}$

**Final answer:** $s = 40$** m**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Substitution of $t = 20$ and the value of $k$ found into the expression for $s$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct distance of 40.

parts.problemMd:
A particle $P$ moves in a straight line, starting from rest at a fixed point $O$. The displacement of $P$ from $O$ at time $t$ seconds is $s$ m, where

$s = 18 t^{2} - t^{3}$

(i) Find the displacement of $P$ from $O$ when $t = 3$.

(ii) Find the value of $t$, other than $t = 0$, at which $P$ is back at $O$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Substitute $t = 3$ into the expression for the displacement

`s = 18\left(3\right)^{2} - \left(3\right)^{3}`

**Final answer:** $s = 135$** m**

**[B1]**

(ii)

$P$ is at $O$ when its displacement is zero

$18 t^{2} - t^{3} = 0$

Factorise

$t^{2} ( 18 - t ) = 0$

**[M1]**

Since $t \neq 0$, $t^{2} \neq 0$, therefore

$18 - t = 0$

$t = 18$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct displacement of 135.
> 
> **M1**: Setting $s = 0$ and factorising, or otherwise solving the cubic equation.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value of 18.

parts.problemMd: Find the greatest displacement of $P$ from $O$ before it returns to $O$.
parts.solutionMd:
The greatest displacement is where $P$ is instantaneously at rest, so differentiate to find the velocity

$v = \frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}$

$v = 36 t - 3 t^{2}$

Set the velocity equal to zero

$36 t - 3 t^{2} = 0$

Factorise

$3 t ( 12 - t ) = 0$

**[M1]**

Since $t \neq 0$, $3 t \neq 0$, therefore

$12 - t = 0$

$t = 12$

**[A1]**

Substitute $t = 12$ into the expression for the displacement

`s = 18\left(12\right)^{2} - \left(12\right)^{3}`

$s = 2592 - 1728$

**Final answer:** $s = 864$** m**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Differentiation of $s$, with the power of at least one term decreased by 1, and the result set equal to zero and solved.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value of $t = 12$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct greatest displacement of 864.

parts.problemMd:
A go-kart manufacturer is testing a new model on a straight horizontal road. The go-kart starts from rest, and its velocity $v \text{m s}^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds is modelled by

$v = \frac{1}{10} t ( 36 - t )$

for $t \geq 0$.

Find the maximum velocity of the go-kart and the time at which it occurs. Justify that this is a maximum.
parts.solutionMd:
Expand the brackets so that each term is a power of $t$

$v = 3 . 6 t - 0 . 1 t^{2}$

Differentiate to find where the velocity is stationary
