$\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} = 3 . 6 - 0 . 2 t$

**[M1]**

Set the derivative equal to zero

$3 . 6 - 0 . 2 t = 0$

**[M1]**

$t = 18$

**[A1]**

Substitute $t = 18$ into the velocity

$v = \frac{1}{10} ( 18 ) ( 36 - 18 )$

$v = 32 . 4 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

To justify that this is a maximum, find the second derivative

$\frac{\text{d}^{2}v}{\text{d}t^{2}} = - 0 . 2$

**Final answer:** **The second derivative is negative, so the velocity is a maximum at t = 18**

**[B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The velocity is a negative quadratic that is zero at $t = 0$ and $t = 36$, so its maximum must lie midway between them, at $t = 18$. This gives you a quick check on your derivative.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Differentiation of $v$ with respect to $t$, with the power of at least one term decreased by 1.
> 
> **M1**: Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving for $t$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct time of 18.
> 
> **A1**: Correct maximum velocity of 32.4.
> 
> **B1**: A correct justification of the maximum, for example a negative second derivative, or a change in the sign of $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ from positive to negative, or the negative $t^{2}$ coefficient of the quadratic. Accept completing the square as an alternative method for the whole part.

parts.problemMd: The test ends when the go-kart next comes to rest. Find the time at which the test ends.
parts.solutionMd:
The go-kart is at rest when its velocity is zero

$\frac{1}{10} t ( 36 - t ) = 0$

**[M1]**

Reject $t = 0$, which is the start of the test

$36 - t = 0$

$t = 36$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Setting $v = 0$ and solving.
> 
> **A1**: Correct time of 36 only.

parts.problemMd:
A particle moves along a straight line. At time $t$ seconds, the acceleration of the particle is $a \text{m s}^{-2}$, where

$a = 6 - 3 t^{\frac{1}{2}}$

for $t \geq 0$. The velocity of the particle is 8 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ when $t = 4$.

Find an expression for the velocity of the particle in terms of $t$.
parts.solutionMd:
Integrate the acceleration to find the velocity

`v = \int \left(6 - 3t^{\frac{1}{2}}\right) \; \text{d}t`

Increase each power by 1 and divide by the new power

$v = 6 t - \frac{3t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}} + c$

**[M1]**

$v = 6 t - 2 t^{\frac{3}{2}} + c$

**[A1]**

Substitute $v = 8$ and $t = 4$ to find $c$, using $4^{\frac{3}{2}} = 8$

`8 = 6(4) - 2\left(4\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} + c`

**[M1]**

$8 = 24 - 16 + c$

$c = 0$

$v = 6 t - 2 t^{\frac{3}{2}}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Integration of the acceleration with respect to $t$, with the power of at least one term increased by 1.
> 
> **A1**: Correct integral $6 t - 2 t^{\frac{3}{2}}$, with a constant of integration.
> 
> **M1**: Substitution of $t = 4$ and $v = 8$ into the expression, which must include a constant, to find the constant.
> 
> **A1**: Correct velocity $v = 6 t - 2 t^{\frac{3}{2}}$. Accept equivalent forms such as $6 t - 2 t \sqrt{t}$.

parts.problemMd:
(i) Find the value of $t$, other than $t = 0$, at which the velocity of the particle is zero.

(ii) Hence state the set of values of $t$ for which the velocity of the particle is positive.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Set the velocity from part (a), $v = 6 t - 2 t^{\frac{3}{2}}$, equal to zero

$6 t - 2 t^{\frac{3}{2}} = 0$

Factorise, taking out the common factor $2 t$

`2t\left(3 - t^{\frac{1}{2}}\right) = 0`

**[M1]**

Since $t \neq 0$, $2 t \neq 0$, therefore

$3 - t^{\frac{1}{2}} = 0$

$t^{\frac{1}{2}} = 3$

Square both sides

$t = 9$

**[A1]**

(ii)

For $0 < t < 9$, $t^{\frac{1}{2}} < 3$, so both $2 t$ and $3 - t^{\frac{1}{2}}$ are positive

$0 < t < 9$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Setting $v = 0$ and taking out a factor of $t$ or $2 t$, or otherwise solving for $t^{\frac{1}{2}}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value of 9.
> 
> **B1**: Correct set of values $0 < t < 9$. Condone $0 \leq t \leq 9$ and accept an equivalent form, following through from the value found in part (i).

parts.problemMd:
A particle moves in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds, the velocity of the particle is $v \text{m s}^{-1}$, where

$v = 12 t - 2 t^{2}$

for $0 \leq t \leq 10$.

Sketch the velocity-time graph for the motion of the particle for $0 \leq t \leq 10$.
parts.solutionMd:
Find where the graph crosses the $t$-axis by setting $v = 0$

$12 t - 2 t^{2} = 0$

$2 t ( 6 - t ) = 0$

$t = 0$* or *$t = 6$

By symmetry, the maximum is halfway between the roots, at $t = 3$

`v = 12(3) - 2\left(3\right)^{2} = 18`

Find the velocity at the end of the interval, $t = 10$

`v = 12(10) - 2\left(10\right)^{2} = -80`

![Velocity-time graph of a downward-opening parabola starting at the origin, rising to a maximum at (3, 18), crossing the t-axis at t = 6 and ending at (10, −80)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/variable-acceleration/assets/005-velocity-time-graph-of-a-downward-opening-parabo.png)

**[B1 B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A downward-opening parabola starting at the origin.
> 
> **B1**: The graph crossing the $t$-axis at $t = 6$, with the maximum at $( 3 ,  18 )$ shown.
> 
> **B1**: The graph ending at $( 10 ,  - 80 )$, below the $t$-axis for $6 < t \leq 10$.

parts.problemMd: Show that the total distance travelled by the particle for $0 \leq t \leq 10$ is $\frac{632}{3}$ m.
parts.solutionMd:
The graph from part (a) crosses the $t$-axis at $t = 6$, so find the distance for each section separately

![Velocity-time graph of a downward-opening parabola starting at the origin, rising to a maximum at (3, 18), crossing the t-axis at t = 6 and ending at (10, −80)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/variable-acceleration/assets/006-velocity-time-graph-of-a-downward-opening-parabo.png)

Integrate the velocity between $t = 0$ and $t = 6$

`\int_{0}^{6} (12t - 2t^{2}) \; \text{d}t = \left[6t^{2} - \dfrac{2t^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{6}`

**[M1]**

Substitute the limits

`= \left(6\left(6\right)^{2} - \dfrac{2\left(6\right)^{3}}{3}\right) - 0 \\ = 216 - 144 \\ = 72`

**[A1]**

Integrate the velocity between $t = 6$ and $t = 10$

`\int_{6}^{10} (12t - 2t^{2}) \; \text{d}t = \left[6t^{2} - \dfrac{2t^{3}}{3}\right]_{6}^{10}`

**[M1]**

Substitute the limits

`= \left(6\left(10\right)^{2} - \dfrac{2\left(10\right)^{3}}{3}\right) - \left(6\left(6\right)^{2} - \dfrac{2\left(6\right)^{3}}{3}\right) \\ = -\dfrac{200}{3} - 72 \\ = -\dfrac{416}{3}`

The particle is moving in the negative direction, so take the magnitude

$\text{Distance} = \frac{416}{3}$

**[A1]**

Add the distances for the two sections

$72 + \frac{416}{3}$

$\text{Total distance} = \frac{632}{3} \text{m}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Integration of $v$, with the power of at least one term increased by 1.
> 
> **A1**: Correct distance of 72 for $0 \leq t \leq 6$.
> 
> **M1**: Splitting the motion at $t = 6$ and using the limits 6 and 10 in the integral.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value of $- \frac{416}{3}$, or its magnitude $\frac{416}{3}$, for $6 \leq t \leq 10$.
> 
> **B1**: The printed total reached by adding the two distances as positive values. Integrating from 0 to 10 in one step gives the displacement, $- \frac{200}{3}$, and scores the first M1 only.

parts.problemMd:
A particle moves along a straight line. At time $t$ seconds, the velocity of the particle is $v \text{m s}^{-1}$, where

$v = t - 4 t^{\frac{1}{2}} + 3$

for $t \geq 0$.

Find the values of $t$ at which the particle is instantaneously at rest.
parts.solutionMd:
The particle is at rest when its velocity is zero

$t - 4 t^{\frac{1}{2}} + 3 = 0$

Since `t = \left(t^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)^{2}`, this is a quadratic in $t^{\frac{1}{2}}$

`\left(t^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)^{2} - 4t^{\frac{1}{2}} + 3 = 0`

Factorise

`\left(t^{\frac{1}{2}} - 1\right)\left(t^{\frac{1}{2}} - 3\right) = 0`

**[M1]**

$t^{\frac{1}{2}} = 1$* or *$t^{\frac{1}{2}} = 3$

Square each value

**Final answer:** $t = 1$** and **$t = 9$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Setting $v = 0$ and solving as a quadratic in $t^{\frac{1}{2}}$, by factorising, by substitution or by any other valid method.
> 
> **A1**: Both values, $t = 1$ and $t = 9$.

parts.problemMd: Find the distance travelled by the particle while its velocity is negative.
parts.solutionMd:
Check the sign of the velocity between the two rest times by substituting $t = 4$

`v = 4 - 4\left(4\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} + 3 = -1`

The velocity is negative for $1 < t < 9$, so integrate it between these times

`\int_{1}^{9} \left(t - 4t^{\frac{1}{2}} + 3\right) \; \text{d}t = \left[\dfrac{t^{2}}{2} - \dfrac{4t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}} + 3t\right]_{1}^{9}`

**[M1]**

Simplify the middle coefficient

`= \left[\dfrac{t^{2}}{2} - \dfrac{8}{3}t^{\frac{3}{2}} + 3t\right]_{1}^{9}`

**[A1]**

Substitute the limits, using $9^{\frac{3}{2}} = 27$

`= \left(\dfrac{81}{2} - \dfrac{8}{3}(27) + 27\right) - \left(\dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{8}{3} + 3\right) \\ = -\dfrac{9}{2} - \dfrac{5}{6} \\ = -\dfrac{16}{3}`

The particle is moving in the negative direction, so take the magnitude

$\text{Distance} = \frac{16}{3} \text{m}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Integration of $v$, with the power of at least one term increased by 1, and the limits 1 and 9 used.
> 
> **A1**: Correct integral $\frac{t^{2}}{2} - \frac{8}{3} t^{\frac{3}{2}} + 3 t$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct distance of $\frac{16}{3}$. Accept answers which round to 5.33. A value of $- \frac{16}{3}$ left as the answer does not score, since a distance is asked for.

parts.problemMd:
A go-kart manufacturer is testing a new model on a straight horizontal road. The go-kart starts from rest, and its velocity $v \text{m s}^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds is modelled by

$v = \frac{1}{w} t^{2} ( 60 - t )$

for $0 \leq t \leq 60$, where $w$ is a constant.

Given that the maximum speed of the go-kart is 32 $\text{m s}^{-1}$, find the value of $w$ and the time at which the go-kart reaches its maximum speed.
parts.solutionMd:
Expand the brackets so that each term is a power of $t$

`v = \dfrac{1}{w}\left(60t^{2} - t^{3}\right)`

The maximum speed occurs where the rate of change of velocity is zero, so differentiate with respect to $t$

`\dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} = \dfrac{1}{w}\left(120t - 3t^{2}\right)`

**[M1]**

Set the derivative equal to zero

`\dfrac{1}{w}\left(120t - 3t^{2}\right) = 0`

Factorise

$3 t ( 40 - t ) = 0$

**[M1]**

Reject $t = 0$, which is the start of the motion

$40 - t = 0$

$t = 40$

**[A1]**

Substitute $t = 40$ and $v = 32$ into the velocity

`32 = \dfrac{1}{w}\left(40\right)^{2}(60 - 40)`

$32 = \frac{32000}{w}$

$w = 1000$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Differentiation of $v$ with respect to $t$, with the power of at least one term decreased by 1. The product rule is also acceptable.
> 
> **M1**: Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving for $t$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct time of 40, with $t = 0$ rejected or ignored.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value of $w = 1000$.

parts.problemMd:
(i) Find the maximum acceleration of the go-kart.

(ii) Justify that your answer to part (i) is a maximum.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The acceleration is the derivative of the velocity found in part (a), with $w = 1000$

`a = \dfrac{1}{1000}\left(120t - 3t^{2}\right)`

The maximum acceleration occurs where the rate of change of acceleration is zero

$\frac{\text{d}a}{\text{d}t} = \frac{1}{1000} ( 120 - 6 t )$

$120 - 6 t = 0$

$t = 20$

**[M1]**

Substitute $t = 20$ into the acceleration

`a = \dfrac{1}{1000}\left(120(20) - 3\left(20\right)^{2}\right)`

$a = \frac{2400-1200}{1000}$

$a = 1 . 2 \text{m s}^{-2}$

**[A1]**

(ii)

Find the second derivative of the acceleration

$\frac{\text{d}^{2}a}{\text{d}t^{2}} = - \frac{6}{1000}$

**Final answer:** **This is negative, so the acceleration is a maximum at t = 20**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Differentiation of the acceleration, set equal to zero and solved for $t$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct maximum acceleration of 1.2.
> 
> **B1**: A correct justification, for example a negative second derivative, a change in the sign of $\frac{\text{d}a}{\text{d}t}$ from positive to negative, or the negative $t^{2}$ coefficient of the quadratic.

parts.problemMd:
A home-made rocket is launched from rest at ground level at time $t = 0$ and moves vertically. At time $t$ seconds after launch, the acceleration of the rocket is $a \text{m s}^{-2}$, where

$a = 56 + t - t^{2}$

(i) Find an expression for the velocity of the rocket in terms of $t$.

(ii) Find the value of $t$, other than $t = 0$, at which the velocity of the rocket is zero. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Integrate the acceleration to find the velocity

`v = \int (56 + t - t^{2}) \; \text{d}t`

$v = 56 t + \frac{1}{2} t^{2} - \frac{1}{3} t^{3} + c$

**[M1]**

The rocket starts from rest, so $v = 0$ when $t = 0$

$c = 0$

$v = 56 t + \frac{1}{2} t^{2} - \frac{1}{3} t^{3}$

**[A1]**

(ii)

Set the velocity equal to zero and take out the factor $t$

`t\left(56 + \dfrac{1}{2}t - \dfrac{1}{3}t^{2}\right) = 0`

Since $t \neq 0$, the bracket is zero

$56 + \frac{1}{2} t - \frac{1}{3} t^{2} = 0$

Multiply through by $- 6$ to clear the fractions

$2 t^{2} - 3 t - 336 = 0$

Use the quadratic formula

`t = \dfrac{3 \pm \sqrt{\left(-3\right)^{2} - 4(2)(-336)}}{2(2)}`

$t = \frac{3\pm\sqrt{2697}}{4}$

Time cannot be negative, so take the positive root

$t = 13 . 7331 \dots$

**Final answer:** $t = 13 . 7$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Integration of the acceleration with respect to $t$, with the power of at least one term increased by 1.
> 
> **A1**: Correct velocity $v = 56 t + \frac{1}{2} t^{2} - \frac{1}{3} t^{3}$, with the constant shown to be zero or correctly omitted.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 13.7, from solving the quadratic, with the negative root rejected or ignored.

parts.problemMd: Find the greatest height reached by the rocket, giving your answer in kilometres correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Integrate the velocity from part (a), $v = 56 t + \frac{1}{2} t^{2} - \frac{1}{3} t^{3}$, to find the height

`s = \int \left(56t + \dfrac{1}{2}t^{2} - \dfrac{1}{3}t^{3}\right) \; \text{d}t`

$s = 28 t^{2} + \frac{1}{6} t^{3} - \frac{1}{12} t^{4} + k$

**[M1]**

The rocket starts at ground level, so $s = 0$ when $t = 0$

$k = 0$

$s = 28 t^{2} + \frac{1}{6} t^{3} - \frac{1}{12} t^{4}$

**[A1]**

The greatest height is when $v = 0$, so substitute the unrounded time from part (a), $t = 13 . 7331 \dots$

`s = 28\left(13.7331\ldots\right)^{2} + \dfrac{1}{6}\left(13.7331\ldots\right)^{3} - \dfrac{1}{12}\left(13.7331\ldots\right)^{4}`

**[M1]**

$s = 2748 . 31 \dots$

Divide by 1000 to convert to kilometres

**Final answer:** $\text{Greatest height} = 2 . 75 \text{km}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Integration of the velocity with respect to $t$, with the power of at least one term increased by 1.
> 
> **A1**: Correct height $s = 28 t^{2} + \frac{1}{6} t^{3} - \frac{1}{12} t^{4}$, with the constant shown to be zero or correctly omitted.
> 
> **M1**: Substitution of the time from part (a) into the expression for $s$.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 2.75, given in kilometres. Because the answer is asked for in kilometres, the unit must be km; 2750 m does not score this mark.

parts.problemMd:
A zip-wire runs in a straight horizontal line between two trees in a children's park. A child on the zip-wire leaves the first tree from rest at time $t = 0$. The velocity-time graph shows the motion of the child, where $v \text{m s}^{-1}$ is the velocity of the child at time $t$ seconds.

![Velocity-time graph on a grid. A curve rises from the origin to the point (4, 10), followed by a horizontal line at v = 10 from t = 4 to t = 16. A dashed vertical line at t = 16 runs down to v = −4, and a straight line then rises from (16, −4) to (20, 0)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/variable-acceleration/assets/003-velocity-time-graph-on-a-grid-a-curve-rises-from.png)

For $0 \leq t \leq 4$, the velocity is given by $v = 5 t^{\frac{1}{2}}$. The child reaches the second tree at $t = 16$ and rebounds from it, then moves back towards the first tree, coming to rest at $t = 20$.

(i) Find the distance between the two trees.

(ii) Find the distance of the child from the second tree when the child comes to rest.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The distance between the trees is the area under the graph up to $t = 16$, so first integrate the velocity for the curved section

`\int_{0}^{4} 5t^{\frac{1}{2}} \; \text{d}t = \left[\dfrac{5t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_{0}^{4}`

**[M1]**

`= \left[\dfrac{10}{3}t^{\frac{3}{2}}\right]_{0}^{4}`

Substitute the limits, using $4^{\frac{3}{2}} = 8$

$= \frac{10}{3} ( 8 ) - 0 \, = \frac{80}{3}$

**[A1]**

For $4 \leq t \leq 16$ the velocity is constant, so the area is a rectangle

$( 16 - 4 ) \times 10 = 120$

**[M1]**

Add the two areas

$\frac{80}{3} + 120 = \frac{440}{3} = 146 . 666 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{Distance between the trees} = 147 \text{m}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

After the rebound, the distance travelled is the area of the triangle from $t = 16$ to $t = 20$

$\frac{1}{2} \times ( 20 - 16 ) \times 4$

$\text{Distance from the second tree} = 8 \text{m}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Integration of $5 t^{\frac{1}{2}}$, with the power increased by 1, and the limits 0 and 4 used.
> 
> **A1**: Correct area of $\frac{80}{3}$ for $0 \leq t \leq 4$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct area of the rectangle for $4 \leq t \leq 16$ added to the curved area.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 147. Accept the exact value $\frac{440}{3}$.
> 
> **B1**: Correct distance of 8.

parts.problemMd: Find the acceleration of the child when $t = 1$.
parts.solutionMd:
Differentiate $v = 5 t^{\frac{1}{2}}$ to find the acceleration

$a = \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$

$a = \frac{5}{2} t^{-\frac{1}{2}}$

**[M1]**

Substitute $t = 1$

`a = \dfrac{5}{2}\left(1\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}`

$a = 2 . 5 \text{m s}^{-2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Differentiation of $5 t^{\frac{1}{2}}$, with the power decreased by 1.
> 
> **A1**: Correct acceleration of 2.5. Accept $\frac{5}{2}$.

parts.problemMd:
A bullet train leaves a station from rest at time $t = 0$. For $0 \leq t \leq 8$, the displacement of the train from the station is $s$ m, where

$s = \frac{3}{200} t^{3}$

During this time the acceleration of the train increases until it reaches its maximum value of 0.72 $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

Show that the train reaches its maximum acceleration when $t = 8$.
parts.solutionMd:
Differentiate the displacement to find the velocity

$v = \frac{\text{d}s}{\text{d}t}$

$v = \frac{9}{200} t^{2}$

**[M1]**

Differentiate again to find the acceleration

$a = \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$

$a = \frac{9}{100} t$

**[M1]**

Set the acceleration equal to its maximum value

$\frac{9}{100} t = 0 . 72$

**[M1]**

$t = \frac{72}{9}$

$t = 8$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Differentiation of $s$ to find the velocity, with the power of $t$ decreased by 1.
> 
> **M1**: Differentiation of the velocity to find the acceleration.
> 
> **M1**: Setting the acceleration equal to 0.72.
> 
> **B1**: The printed result $t = 8$ reached from correct working. Because the answer is given, the equation in $t$ must be seen. Substituting $t = 8$ into a correct acceleration to obtain 0.72 is equally acceptable.

parts.problemMd:
After reaching its maximum acceleration, the train continues to accelerate at 0.72 $\text{m s}^{-2}$ until its velocity reaches 75 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Find the time taken for the velocity of the train to increase to 75 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ at this constant acceleration.
parts.solutionMd:
Find the velocity of the train at $t = 8$, using $v = \frac{9}{200} t^{2}$ from part (a)

`v = \dfrac{9}{200}\left(8\right)^{2}`

$v = 2 . 88$

**[B1]**

The acceleration is now constant, so use $v = u + a t$ with $u = 2 . 88$, $v = 75$ and $a = 0 . 72$

$75 = 2 . 88 + 0 . 72 T$

**[M1]**

$T = \frac{72.12}{0.72}$

$T = 100 . 166 \dots$

**Final answer:** $T = 100$** seconds (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct velocity of 2.88 at $t = 8$.
> 
> **M1**: Correct use of $v = u + a t$ with $u$ equal to the velocity at $t = 8$, $v = 75$ and $a = 0 . 72$.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 100.

parts.problemMd:
The train then travels at a constant velocity of 75 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ for 10 minutes.

Find the displacement of the train from the station at the end of these 10 minutes. Give your answer in kilometres correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Sketch the velocity-time graph to organise the three stages of the motion

![Sketch, not to scale, of a velocity-time graph in three stages: a curve from the origin to (8, 2.88) labelled A, a straight line from (8, 2.88) to (108.17, 75) labelled B, and a horizontal line at v = 75 from t = 108.17 to t = 708.17 labelled C](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/variable-acceleration/assets/004-sketch-not-to-scale-of-a-velocity-time-graph-in-.png)

For stage $A$, substitute $t = 8$ into the displacement

`s_{A} = \dfrac{3}{200}\left(8\right)^{3} = 7.68`

For stage $B$, the acceleration is constant, so use $s = \frac{1}{2} ( u + v ) t$ with the unrounded time from part (b)

$s_{B} = \frac{1}{2} ( 2 . 88 + 75 ) ( 100 . 166 \dots )$

**[M1]**

$s_{B} = 3900 . 49$

For stage $C$, the velocity is constant for 600 seconds

$s_{C} = 75 \times 600 = 45000$

Add the three stages

$s = 7 . 68 + 3900 . 49 + 45000$

**[M1]**

$s = 48908 . 17$

Divide by 1000 to convert to kilometres

**Final answer:** $s = 48 . 9 \text{km}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Correct method for the displacement during the constant acceleration stage, using a constant-acceleration formula with the values from part (b), or the area of a trapezium.
> 
> **M1**: Adding the displacements for all three stages, including 7.68 for the first stage and 75 × 600 for the last.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 48.9, given in kilometres. Because the answer is asked for in kilometres, the unit must be km.

parts.problemMd:
A particle moves in a straight line. At time $t = 0$ it passes through a fixed point $O$ with velocity 36 $\text{m s}^{-1}$. For $t > 0$, the acceleration of the particle is $a \text{m s}^{-2}$, where

$a = 6 - 15 t^{-\frac{1}{2}}$

Find the values of $t$ at which the particle is instantaneously at rest.
parts.solutionMd:
Integrate the acceleration to find the velocity

`v = \int \left(6 - 15t^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) \; \text{d}t`

Increase each power by 1 and divide by the new power

$v = 6 t - \frac{15t^{\frac{1}{2}}}{\frac{1}{2}} + c$

**[M1]**

$v = 6 t - 30 t^{\frac{1}{2}} + c$

The velocity is 36 when $t = 0$

`36 = 6(0) - 30\left(0\right)^{\frac{1}{2}} + c`

$c = 36$

$v = 6 t - 30 t^{\frac{1}{2}} + 36$

**[A1]**

The particle is at rest when $v = 0$, so divide through by 6

$t - 5 t^{\frac{1}{2}} + 6 = 0$

Since `t = \left(t^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)^{2}`, this is a quadratic in $t^{\frac{1}{2}}$, so factorise

`\left(t^{\frac{1}{2}} - 2\right)\left(t^{\frac{1}{2}} - 3\right) = 0`

**[M1]**

$t^{\frac{1}{2}} = 2$* or *$t^{\frac{1}{2}} = 3$

Square each value

**Final answer:** $t = 4$** and **$t = 9$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Integration of the acceleration with respect to $t$, with the power of at least one term increased by 1.
> 
> **A1**: Correct velocity $v = 6 t - 30 t^{\frac{1}{2}} + 36$, including the constant from the initial velocity.
> 
> **M1**: Setting the velocity equal to zero and solving as a quadratic in $t^{\frac{1}{2}}$, by factorising, by substitution or by any other valid method.
> 
> **A1**: Both values, $t = 4$ and $t = 9$.

parts.problemMd: Find the total distance travelled by the particle for $0 \leq t \leq 16$.
parts.solutionMd:
Integrate the velocity from part (a), $v = 6 t - 30 t^{\frac{1}{2}} + 36$, to find the displacement

`s = \int \left(6t - 30t^{\frac{1}{2}} + 36\right) \; \text{d}t`

$s = 3 t^{2} - \frac{30t^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}} + 36 t + k$

**[M1]**

The particle is at $O$, so $s = 0$ when $t = 0$

$k = 0$

Simplify the middle coefficient

$s = 3 t^{2} - 20 t^{\frac{3}{2}} + 36 t$

**[A1]**

The particle changes direction at the rest times $t = 4$ and $t = 9$, so find its displacement at each of these times and at $t = 16$

`s(4) = 3\left(4\right)^{2} - 20\left(4\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} + 36(4) \\ = 48 - 160 + 144 \\ = 32`

**[M1]**

`s(9) = 3\left(9\right)^{2} - 20\left(9\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} + 36(9) \\ = 243 - 540 + 324 \\ = 27`

`s(16) = 3\left(16\right)^{2} - 20\left(16\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} + 36(16) \\ = 768 - 1280 + 576 \\ = 64`

**[A1]**

Add the size of the change in displacement for each stage

$32 + ( 32 - 27 ) + ( 64 - 27 )$

$= 32 + 5 + 37$

$\text{Total distance} = 74 \text{m}$

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Because the particle only changes direction at the rest times, you do not need three separate definite integrals: once you have $s$ as a function of $t$, the distance for each stage is just the difference between the displacements at its ends.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Integration of the velocity with respect to $t$, with the power of at least one term increased by 1.
> 
> **A1**: Correct displacement $s = 3 t^{2} - 20 t^{\frac{3}{2}} + 36 t$, with the constant shown to be zero or correctly omitted.
> 
> **M1**: Splitting the motion at the rest times and finding the displacement, or the definite integral of $v$, for each stage.
> 
> **A1**: Correct displacements of 32, 27 and 64, or correct stage distances of 32, 5 and 37.
> 
> **A1**: Correct total distance of 74. Evaluating the displacement at $t = 16$ alone, 64, gives the displacement rather than the distance and does not score this mark.

parts.problemMd:
A car travels along a straight horizontal road and passes a service station $S$ at time $t = 0$. The displacement of the car from $S$ at time $t$ seconds is modelled as $s$ m, where

`s = 0.4t\left(2t^{2} - 4t + 3\right)`

for $t \geq 0$.

Show that, according to the model, the car never returns to $S$.
parts.solutionMd:
Apart from $t = 0$, the car is at $S$ only if the bracket is zero

$2 t^{2} - 4 t + 3 = 0$

Find the discriminant of this quadratic

`b^{2} - 4ac = \left(-4\right)^{2} - 4(2)(3)`

$= 16 - 24 = - 8$

**[M1]**

*The discriminant is negative, so the quadratic has no real roots*

**Final answer:** **The displacement is zero only when t = 0, so the car never returns to S**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Setting $s = 0$ and considering the discriminant of $2 t^{2} - 4 t + 3$, or completing the square to give `2\left(t - 1\right)^{2} + 1`.
> 
> **B1**: A conclusion that there are no real roots other than $t = 0$, so the car never returns to $S$.

parts.problemMd: Show that the car is decelerating for the first $\frac{2}{3}$ seconds after passing $S$.
parts.solutionMd:
Expand the brackets so that each term is a power of $t$

$s = 0 . 8 t^{3} - 1 . 6 t^{2} + 1 . 2 t$

Differentiate to find the velocity

$v = 2 . 4 t^{2} - 3 . 2 t + 1 . 2$

**[M1]**

Differentiate again to find the acceleration

$a = 4 . 8 t - 3 . 2$

**[M1]**

Find where the acceleration is negative

$4 . 8 t - 3 . 2 < 0$

$t < \frac{2}{3}$

**[A1]**

Decelerating means the speed is decreasing, so check the sign of the velocity using its discriminant

`\left(-3.2\right)^{2} - 4(2.4)(1.2) = 10.24 - 11.52 = -1.28`

*The discriminant is negative and the coefficient of t² is positive, so v > 0 for all t*

**Final answer:** **For the first 2/3 seconds the velocity is positive and the acceleration is negative, so the car is decelerating**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Differentiation of $s$ to find the velocity, with the power of at least one term decreased by 1.
> 
> **M1**: Differentiation of the velocity to find the acceleration.
> 
> **A1**: Correct inequality $t < \frac{2}{3}$ from $4 . 8 t - 3 . 2 < 0$. Condone $t \leq \frac{2}{3}$.
> 
> **B1**: A complete argument that the velocity is positive throughout, for example by its discriminant or by completing the square, with a conclusion that the car is decelerating because the velocity and acceleration have opposite signs. Showing only that $a < 0$ does not earn this mark.

parts.problemMd:
A particle moves along a straight line. At time $t$ seconds, the velocity of the particle is $v \text{m s}^{-1}$, where

$v = t^{\frac{3}{2}} - 6 t + 9 t^{\frac{1}{2}}$

for $t \geq 0$.

Find the values of $t$ at which the particle is instantaneously at rest.
parts.solutionMd:
The particle is at rest when its velocity is zero

$t^{\frac{3}{2}} - 6 t + 9 t^{\frac{1}{2}} = 0$

Take out the common factor $t^{\frac{1}{2}}$

`t^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(t - 6t^{\frac{1}{2}} + 9\right) = 0`

**[M1]**

The bracket is a quadratic in $t^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and a perfect square

`t^{\frac{1}{2}}\left(t^{\frac{1}{2}} - 3\right)^{2} = 0`

**[M1]**

$t^{\frac{1}{2}} = 0$* or *$t^{\frac{1}{2}} = 3$

**Final answer:** $t = 0$** and **$t = 9$

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Because `\left(t^{\frac{1}{2}} - 3\right)^{2}` is never negative, the velocity touches zero at $t = 9$ without changing sign. The particle stops for an instant but does not reverse its direction.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Setting $v = 0$ and taking out a factor of $t^{\frac{1}{2}}$.
> 
> **M1**: Solving the remaining quadratic in $t^{\frac{1}{2}}$, by factorising, by substitution or by any other valid method.
> 
> **A1**: Both values, $t = 0$ and $t = 9$.

parts.problemMd: Find the set of values of $t$ for which the acceleration of the particle is negative.
parts.solutionMd:
Differentiate the velocity to find the acceleration

$a = \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$

$a = \frac{3}{2} t^{\frac{1}{2}} - 6 + \frac{9}{2} t^{-\frac{1}{2}}$

**[M1]**

The acceleration is negative when

$\frac{3}{2} t^{\frac{1}{2}} - 6 + \frac{9}{2} t^{-\frac{1}{2}} < 0$

Multiply through by $2 t^{\frac{1}{2}}$, which is positive for $t > 0$, so the inequality sign is unchanged

$3 t - 12 t^{\frac{1}{2}} + 9 < 0$

Divide through by 3

$t - 4 t^{\frac{1}{2}} + 3 < 0$

Factorise as a quadratic in $t^{\frac{1}{2}}$

`\left(t^{\frac{1}{2}} - 1\right)\left(t^{\frac{1}{2}} - 3\right) < 0`

**[M1]**

The product is negative between the roots

$1 < t^{\frac{1}{2}} < 3$

Square each part

$1 < t < 9$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Differentiation of $v$ with respect to $t$, with the power of at least one term decreased by 1.
> 
> **M1**: Forming $a < 0$ (or $a = 0$) and reducing it to a quadratic in $t^{\frac{1}{2}}$, for example by multiplying through by $2 t^{\frac{1}{2}}$, and finding the critical values.
> 
> **A1**: Correct set of values $1 < t < 9$. Condone $1 \leq t \leq 9$ and accept any equivalent form.

parts.problemMd:
A go-kart manufacturer is testing a new model on a straight horizontal road. The go-kart starts from rest, and its velocity $v \text{m s}^{-1}$ at time $t$ seconds is modelled by

`v = k\left(t^{3} - 20t^{2} + 100t\right)`

for $0 \leq t \leq 12$, and

$v = 12$

for $t > 12$, where $k$ is a constant. There is no instantaneous change in the velocity of the go-kart at $t = 12$.

Show that $k = 0 . 25$.
parts.solutionMd:
There is no instantaneous change in velocity at $t = 12$, so the first expression equals 12 when $t = 12$

`k\left(\left(12\right)^{3} - 20\left(12\right)^{2} + 100(12)\right) = 12`

$k ( 1728 - 2880 + 1200 ) = 12$

$48 k = 12$

$k = 0 . 25$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Setting the first expression equal to 12 at $t = 12$ and reaching $k = 0 . 25$ with the evaluation $48 k = 12$ seen. Because the answer is given, substituting $k = 0 . 25$ to show that $v = 12$ must be accompanied by a statement that the two expressions agree at $t = 12$.

parts.problemMd: Find the maximum velocity of the go-kart for $0 \leq t \leq 12$, and find the value of $t$, where $0 < t < 12$, at which the go-kart is instantaneously at rest.
parts.solutionMd:
With $k = 0 . 25$, differentiate the velocity to find where it is stationary

`\dfrac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t} = 0.25\left(3t^{2} - 40t + 100\right)`

**[M1]**

Set the derivative equal to zero

$3 t^{2} - 40 t + 100 = 0$

Factorise

$( 3 t - 10 ) ( t - 10 ) = 0$

**[M1]**

$t = \frac{10}{3}$* or *$t = 10$

**[A1]**

Find the velocity at each stationary value

`v\left(\dfrac{10}{3}\right) = 0.25\left(\left(\dfrac{10}{3}\right)^{3} - 20\left(\dfrac{10}{3}\right)^{2} + 100\left(\dfrac{10}{3}\right)\right) = \dfrac{1000}{27}`

`v(10) = 0.25\left(\left(10\right)^{3} - 20\left(10\right)^{2} + 100(10)\right) = 0`

The end values are $v ( 0 ) = 0$ and $v ( 12 ) = 12$, so the greatest velocity is at $t = \frac{10}{3}$

**Final answer:** $\text{Maximum velocity} = \frac{1000}{27} = 37 . 0 \text{m s}^{-1}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

The velocity is zero at $t = 10$, which lies in $0 < t < 12$

$t = 10$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Differentiation of $v$ with respect to $t$, with the power of at least one term decreased by 1.
> 
> **M1**: Setting the derivative equal to zero and solving the quadratic.
> 
> **A1**: Both values, $t = \frac{10}{3}$ and $t = 10$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct maximum velocity of $\frac{1000}{27}$. Accept answers which round to 37.0.
> 
> **B1**: Correct value $t = 10$. Accept this found directly by writing `v = 0.25t\left(t - 10\right)^{2}` and setting $v = 0$.

parts.problemMd:
A home-made rocket is launched from rest at ground level at time $t = 0$. It moves in a vertical straight line, first upwards and then back down to the ground. At time $t$ seconds after launch, the acceleration of the rocket is $a \text{m s}^{-2}$, taking upwards as positive, where

$a = 6 + \frac{1}{2} t - \frac{1}{2} t^{2}$

Find the total time for which the rocket is in the air. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Integrate the acceleration to find the velocity

`v = \int \left(6 + \dfrac{1}{2}t - \dfrac{1}{2}t^{2}\right) \; \text{d}t`

$v = 6 t + \frac{1}{4} t^{2} - \frac{1}{6} t^{3} + c$

**[M1]**

The rocket starts from rest, so $v = 0$ when $t = 0$

$c = 0$

Integrate the velocity to find the height

`s = \int \left(6t + \dfrac{1}{4}t^{2} - \dfrac{1}{6}t^{3}\right) \; \text{d}t`

$s = 3 t^{2} + \frac{1}{12} t^{3} - \frac{1}{24} t^{4} + k$

**[M1]**

The rocket starts at ground level, so $s = 0$ when $t = 0$

$k = 0$

$s = 3 t^{2} + \frac{1}{12} t^{3} - \frac{1}{24} t^{4}$

**[A1]**

The rocket lands when $s = 0$ again, so take out the factor $t^{2}$

`t^{2}\left(3 + \dfrac{1}{12}t - \dfrac{1}{24}t^{2}\right) = 0`

Since $t \neq 0$, the bracket is zero

$3 + \frac{1}{12} t - \frac{1}{24} t^{2} = 0$

Multiply through by $- 24$

$t^{2} - 2 t - 72 = 0$

Use the quadratic formula

`t = \dfrac{2 \pm \sqrt{\left(-2\right)^{2} - 4(1)(-72)}}{2}`

$t = 1 \pm \sqrt{73}$

Time cannot be negative, so take the positive root

$t = 9 . 5440 \dots$

**Final answer:** $t = 9 . 54$** seconds (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Integration of the acceleration with respect to $t$, with the power of at least one term increased by 1.
> 
> **M1**: Integration of the velocity with respect to $t$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct height $s = 3 t^{2} + \frac{1}{12} t^{3} - \frac{1}{24} t^{4}$, with both constants shown to be zero or correctly omitted.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 9.54, from solving $s = 0$ with $t \neq 0$ and the negative root rejected.

parts.problemMd: Find the total distance travelled by the rocket. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
The greatest height is where $v = 0$, so take out the factor $t$ from the velocity in part (a), $v = 6 t + \frac{1}{4} t^{2} - \frac{1}{6} t^{3}$

`t\left(6 + \dfrac{1}{4}t - \dfrac{1}{6}t^{2}\right) = 0`

Since $t \neq 0$, the bracket is zero

$6 + \frac{1}{4} t - \frac{1}{6} t^{2} = 0$

Multiply through by $- 12$

$2 t^{2} - 3 t - 72 = 0$

`t = \dfrac{3 \pm \sqrt{\left(-3\right)^{2} - 4(2)(-72)}}{2(2)}`

$t = \frac{3\pm\sqrt{585}}{4}$

Take the positive root

$t = 6 . 7966 \dots$

**[M1]**

Substitute the unrounded value into the height from part (a), $s = 3 t^{2} + \frac{1}{12} t^{3} - \frac{1}{24} t^{4}$

`s = 3\left(6.7966\ldots\right)^{2} + \dfrac{1}{12}\left(6.7966\ldots\right)^{3} - \dfrac{1}{24}\left(6.7966\ldots\right)^{4}`

$s = 75 . 833 \dots$

**[M1]**

The rocket falls the same distance back down, so double the greatest height

$2 \times 75 . 833 \dots = 151 . 66 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{Total distance} = 152 \text{m}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Setting the velocity equal to zero and solving to find the time of the greatest height.
> 
> **M1**: Substitution of the time into the expression for $s$ to find the greatest height.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 152. A value of 75.8, the greatest height alone, does not score this mark.

parts.problemMd:
In a cheese-rolling competition, a cylindrical block of cheese starts from rest at the top of a hill at time $t = 0$. It rolls down the hill and reaches the flat ground at the bottom when $t = 15$, then slows down along the flat ground. The acceleration of the cheese at time $t$ seconds is modelled as $a \text{m s}^{-2}$, where

$a = 0 . 2 t$

for $0 \leq t \leq 15$, and

$a = 9 - t$

for $15 < t \leq A$, where $A$ is a constant. There is no instantaneous change in the velocity of the cheese at $t = 15$, and the cheese comes to rest when its acceleration is $- 9 \text{m s}^{-2}$.

By first finding the value of $A$, find the total distance the cheese rolls before it comes to rest.
parts.solutionMd:
The cheese comes to rest when $a = - 9$

$9 - t = - 9$

$A = 18$

**[B1]**

For $0 \leq t \leq 15$, integrate the acceleration

`v = \int 0.2t \; \text{d}t`

$v = 0 . 1 t^{2} + c$

The cheese starts from rest, so $v = 0$ when $t = 0$

$c = 0$

$v = 0 . 1 t^{2}$

The velocity is positive, so the distance for this phase is the integral of $v$

`\int_{0}^{15} 0.1t^{2} \; \text{d}t = \left[\dfrac{t^{3}}{30}\right]_{0}^{15}`

**[M1]**

Substitute the limits

`= \dfrac{\left(15\right)^{3}}{30} - 0 \\ = 112.5`

**[A1]**

The velocity at $t = 15$ carries into the second phase

`v(15) = 0.1\left(15\right)^{2} = 22.5`

For $15 < t \leq 18$, integrate the new acceleration

`v = \int (9 - t) \; \text{d}t`

$v = 9 t - \frac{1}{2} t^{2} + c$

Use $v = 22 . 5$ when $t = 15$ to find $c$

`22.5 = 9(15) - \dfrac{1}{2}\left(15\right)^{2} + c`

**[M1]**

$22 . 5 = 135 - 112 . 5 + c$

$c = 0$

$v = 9 t - \frac{1}{2} t^{2}$

**[A1]**

Check that the cheese is at rest at $t = 18$

$v ( 18 ) = 162 - 162 = 0$

The velocity `v = t\left(9 - \dfrac{1}{2}t\right)` is positive for $15 < t < 18$, so integrate it for the distance

`\int_{15}^{18} \left(9t - \dfrac{1}{2}t^{2}\right) \; \text{d}t = \left[\dfrac{9}{2}t^{2} - \dfrac{1}{6}t^{3}\right]_{15}^{18}`

**[M1]**

Substitute the limits

$= ( 1458 - 972 ) - ( 1012 . 5 - 562 . 5 ) \, = 486 - 450 \, = 36$

Add the distances for the two phases

$112 . 5 + 36$

$\text{Total distance} = 148 . 5 \text{m}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Correct value $A = 18$.
> 
> **M1**: Integration of the first-phase acceleration, then integration of the velocity between 0 and 15.
> 
> **A1**: Correct distance of 112.5 for the first phase.
> 
> **M1**: Integration of $9 - t$ and use of the velocity at $t = 15$, or $v = 0$ at $t = 18$, to find the constant.
> 
> **A1**: Correct second-phase velocity $v = 9 t - \frac{1}{2} t^{2}$. The constant is fixed by a condition at $t = 15$ (or $t = 18$), not at the start of the motion, so it must be shown to be zero; omitting it does not earn this mark.
> 
> **M1**: Integration of the second-phase velocity between 15 and the value of $A$ found.
> 
> **A1**: Correct total distance of 148.5. Accept answers which round to 149.

parts.problemMd:
A high-speed train leaves a station from rest at time $t = 0$. Its displacement from the station at time $t$ seconds is $s$ m, where

$s = \frac{1}{p} t^{q}$

for $0 \leq t \leq 12$, and $p$ and $q$ are constants with $q > 1$.

In the first 10 seconds, the average velocity of the train is $\frac{5}{12} \text{m s}^{-1}$ and the average acceleration of the train is $\frac{1}{6} \text{m s}^{-2}$.

By first finding the values of $p$ and $q$, find an expression for the acceleration of the train for $0 \leq t \leq 12$.
parts.solutionMd:
Average velocity is the change in displacement divided by the time, with $s ( 0 ) = 0$

$\frac{s(10)-s(0)}{10} = \frac{5}{12}$

$\frac{10^{q}}{10p} = \frac{5}{12}$

$\frac{10^{q}}{p} = \frac{25}{6}$

**[M1]**

Differentiate $s$ to find the velocity

$v = \frac{q}{p} t^{q-1}$

**[M1]**

Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time, with $v ( 0 ) = 0$ since $q > 1$

$\frac{v(10)-v(0)}{10} = \frac{1}{6}$

$\frac{q\times10^{q-1}}{10p} = \frac{1}{6}$

$\frac{q\times10^{q-1}}{p} = \frac{5}{3}$

**[M1]**

Divide this equation by the first one, so that $p$ cancels

$\frac{q\times10^{q-1}}{10^{q}} = \frac{5}{3} \div \frac{25}{6}$

$\frac{q}{10} = \frac{2}{5}$

**[M1]**

$q = 4$

**[A1]**

Substitute $q = 4$ into the first equation

$\frac{10^{4}}{p} = \frac{25}{6}$

$p = \frac{6\times10000}{25}$

$p = 2400$

**[A1]**

Write the displacement with $p = 2400$ and $q = 4$

$s = \frac{1}{2400} t^{4}$

Differentiate twice to find the acceleration

$v = \frac{4}{2400} t^{3} = \frac{1}{600} t^{3}$

$a = \frac{3}{600} t^{2}$

**[M1]**

$a = \frac{1}{200} t^{2}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Forming an equation from the average velocity, using the displacement at $t = 10$ divided by 10.
> 
> **M1**: Differentiation of $s$ to give a velocity of the form $\frac{q}{p} t^{q-1}$.
> 
> **M1**: Forming an equation from the average acceleration, using the velocity at $t = 10$ divided by 10.
> 
> **M1**: Eliminating $p$ between the two equations, for example by division, to obtain an equation in $q$ only.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value $q = 4$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct value $p = 2400$.
> 
> **M1**: Differentiation of the displacement twice, or of the velocity once.
> 
> **A1**: Correct acceleration $a = \frac{1}{200} t^{2}$. Accept equivalent forms such as $\frac{t^{2}}{200}$ or $0 . 005 t^{2}$.

parts.problemMd:
A particle moves in a straight line, starting from a point $O$. At time $t$ hours after leaving $O$, the acceleration of the particle is $a \text{km h}^{-2}$, where

$a = \frac{1}{5} ( t - 11 )$

for $0 \leq t \leq 24$. When $t = 24$, the particle is back at $O$.

Show that the velocity, $v \text{km h}^{-1}$, of the particle at time $t$ hours is given by

`v = \dfrac{1}{10}\left(t^{2} - 22t + k\right)`

where $k$ is a constant to be found.
parts.solutionMd:
Integrate the acceleration to find the velocity

`v = \int \dfrac{1}{5}(t - 11) \; \text{d}t`

`v = \dfrac{1}{5}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}t^{2} - 11t\right) + c`

**[M1]**

Take out a factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ from the bracket

`v = \dfrac{1}{10}\left(t^{2} - 22t\right) + c`

**[A1]**

Integrate the velocity to find the displacement

`s = \dfrac{1}{10}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}t^{3} - 11t^{2}\right) + ct + d`

`s = \dfrac{1}{30}\left(t^{3} - 33t^{2}\right) + ct + d`

**[M1]**

The particle starts at $O$, so $s = 0$ when $t = 0$

$d = 0$

The particle is back at $O$ when $t = 24$

`\dfrac{1}{30}\left(\left(24\right)^{3} - 33\left(24\right)^{2}\right) + 24c = 0`

**[M1]**

$\frac{1}{30} ( 13824 - 19008 ) + 24 c = 0$

$- \frac{864}{5} + 24 c = 0$

$c = \frac{36}{5}$

Write $c$ with a denominator of 10 so it can go inside the bracket

`v = \dfrac{1}{10}\left(t^{2} - 22t\right) + \dfrac{72}{10}`

`v = \dfrac{1}{10}\left(t^{2} - 22t + 72\right)`

$k = 72$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Integration of the acceleration with respect to $t$, with the power of at least one term increased by 1.
> 
> **A1**: Correct velocity `\dfrac{1}{10}\left(t^{2} - 22t\right) + c`, including a constant.
> 
> **M1**: Integration of the velocity, including a term $c t$ from the constant.
> 
> **M1**: Using $s = 0$ at both $t = 0$ and $t = 24$ to form an equation for $c$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct $k = 72$, reaching the printed form of $v$ from exact working. Because the form of the answer is given, the value of the constant must be shown to come from $s ( 24 ) = 0$.

parts.problemMd: Find the exact total distance travelled by the particle for $0 \leq t \leq 24$.
parts.solutionMd:
Factorise the velocity from part (a) to find when the particle is at rest

$v = \frac{1}{10} ( t - 4 ) ( t - 18 )$

**[M1]**

Sketch the velocity-time graph to see where the particle changes direction

![Sketch of a velocity-time graph: an upward-opening parabola starting at v = 7.2 when t = 0, crossing the t-axis at t = 4 and t = 18, and rising again up to t = 24](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/kinematics-straight-line-motion/variable-acceleration/assets/001-sketch-of-a-velocity-time-graph-an-upward-openin.png)

Using $c = \frac{36}{5}$ and $d = 0$ from part (a), the displacement is

`s = \dfrac{1}{30}\left(t^{3} - 33t^{2} + 216t\right)`

Find the displacement at each reversal time, $t = 4$ and $t = 18$

$s ( 4 ) = \frac{1}{30} ( 64 - 528 + 864 ) = \frac{40}{3}$

$s ( 18 ) = \frac{1}{30} ( 5832 - 10692 + 3888 ) = - \frac{162}{5}$

**[M1 A1]**

The distance for each stage is the size of the change in displacement

`\dfrac{40}{3} + \left(\dfrac{40}{3} + \dfrac{162}{5}\right) + \dfrac{162}{5}`

$= \frac{40}{3} + \frac{686}{15} + \frac{162}{5}$

$\text{Total distance} = \frac{1372}{15} \text{km}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Factorising the velocity, or otherwise solving $v = 0$, to find the rest times 4 and 18.
> 
> **M1**: Splitting the motion at the rest times and finding the displacement at each, or the definite integral of $v$ for each stage.
> 
> **A1**: Correct displacements $\frac{40}{3}$ and $- \frac{162}{5}$, or correct stage distances $\frac{40}{3}$, $\frac{686}{15}$ and $\frac{162}{5}$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct exact total $\frac{1372}{15}$. A decimal answer such as 91.5 does not score this mark, since an exact value is asked for.

parts.problemMd:
State whether the quantity described in each of the following is a scalar or a vector.

(i) A motorcycle accelerates at 3.4 $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

(ii) A concert lasts 2 hours 53 minutes.

(iii) A train has an average speed of 28.4 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

(iv) A room is 3.95 m wide.

(v) A lift moves upwards at 2 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
parts.solutionMd:
A scalar has magnitude only; a vector has magnitude and a direction

(i)

Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, so it carries a direction

**Final answer:** **Vector**

**[B1]**

(ii)

Time has a magnitude but no direction

**Final answer:** **Scalar**

**[B1]**

(iii)

Speed is the rate at which distance is covered, with no direction attached

**Final answer:** **Scalar**

**[B1]**

(iv)

A width is a distance, so it has magnitude only

**Final answer:** **Scalar**

**[B1]**

(v)

A speed given together with a direction is a velocity

**Final answer:** **Vector**

**[B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> The quickest test is to ask whether reversing the direction of travel would change the quantity. A train that runs the same route backwards still has the same average speed, but its velocity changes sign, so speed is a scalar and velocity is a vector.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Vector. Acceleration is a vector quantity.
> 
> **B1**: Scalar. Time is a scalar quantity.
> 
> **B1**: Scalar. Speed is a scalar quantity, because no direction is given.
> 
> **B1**: Scalar. A width is a distance, which is a scalar quantity.
> 
> **B1**: Vector. "Upwards" gives the direction, so this is a velocity, which is a vector quantity.
> 
> A reason is not required; the single word scores. Accept "has magnitude only" for scalar and "has magnitude and direction" for vector as equivalent answers.

parts.problemMd:
A film crew record a cheetah running in a straight line. The cheetah covers 2400 m in a time of 150 s.

Find the average speed of the cheetah.
parts.solutionMd:
Average speed is the total distance travelled divided by the time taken

$\text{average speed} = \frac{\text{distance travelled}}{\text{time taken}} = \frac{2400}{150}$

**[M1]**

$16 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of average speed = distance ÷ time, with 2400 and 150 substituted. This mark is available even if the division is then carried out incorrectly.
> 
> **A1**: An answer which rounds to 16, in $\text{m s}^{-1}$. Units are not required for the mark.

parts.problemMd:
A box is pulled along a rough horizontal floor by a string. The diagram shows the four forces acting on the box, labelled A, B, C and D.

![A rectangular block resting on a horizontal line which is shaded to show it is rough. Four arrows are drawn from the block: arrow A points horizontally to the left, arrow B points vertically upwards, arrow C points up and to the right at an angle to the floor, and arrow D points vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/mechanics-toolkit/quantities-units-and-modelling/assets/007-a-rectangular-block-resting-on-a-horizontal-line.png)

Label each of the forces A, B, C and D with its name, choosing from: tension, friction, weight, normal contact force.
parts.solutionMd:
The string is attached at an angle and pulls the box forwards, so the arrow lying along the string is the tension

**Final answer:** **C is the tension**

The floor pushes the box away from its surface, at right angles to the floor

**Final answer:** **B is the normal contact force**

**[B1]**

The box is moving to the right along a rough floor, and friction always opposes the motion

**Final answer:** **A is the friction**

The weight of the box is the pull of gravity on it, acting vertically downwards

**Final answer:** **D is the weight**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Any two of the four forces correctly named.
> 
> **B1**: All four correctly named: A friction, B normal contact force, C tension, D weight.
> 
> Accept "normal reaction", "reaction" or "R" for the normal contact force, and "friction force" or "F" for friction. Accept "mg" or "gravity" for the weight. The names may be written on the diagram rather than listed.

parts.problemMd:
A box is pulled across a rough horizontal floor by a string.

In setting up a model of the motion, the box is treated as a particle and the string is treated as light and inextensible.

Explain what each of the following assumptions allows you to assume about the box or the string.

(i) The box is a particle.

(ii) The string is light.

(iii) The string is inextensible.

(iv) The floor is rough.
parts.solutionMd:
Each modelling word removes one complication from the situation, so state what it lets you ignore or treat as fixed

(i)

The word removes the box's size and shape from the problem

**Final answer:** **"Particle" means the box has no dimensions, so all the forces act at a single point**

**[B1]**

(ii)

No part of the tension is then used up supporting the string itself

**Final answer:** **"Light" means the string has no mass, so the tension is the same at every point along it**

**[B1]**

(iii)

The length of the string is then fixed

**Final answer:** **"Inextensible" means the string cannot stretch, so the box and the end of the string move with the same speed and acceleration**

**[B1]**

(iv)

A contact force then acts along the floor as well as at right angles to it

**Final answer:** **"Rough" means there is a frictional force on the box, acting along the floor and opposing the motion**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The box is treated as a single point, with its dimensions ignored, so all the forces act at that point.
> 
> **B1**: The string has no mass, so the tension is the same throughout its length. Accept "the tension at each end is the same".
> 
> **B1**: The string does not stretch, so the box and the end of the string have the same speed and the same acceleration. Accept "the length of the string stays the same".
> 
> **B1**: There is friction between the box and the floor. The direction (opposing the motion) is not required, but do not accept an answer which states the friction acts in the direction of motion.

parts.problemMd:
Draw a diagram to represent each of the following situations, labelling it with all the forces acting on the body in italics below.

Choose the force names from: air resistance, friction, normal contact force, tension, thrust, weight.

(i) A *child on a sledge* being pulled by a rope along a rough horizontal path.

(ii) A *crate* being pushed across a rough horizontal floor.
parts.solutionMd:
Take each body in turn, mark the forces that act on it and give each arrow a direction

(i)

The rope is attached in front of the sledge and pulls it along, so the force in the rope is a tension acting away from the sledge

The path is rough and the sledge is moving forwards, so friction acts backwards along the path

The ground pushes up at right angles to the path, and the weight of the child and sledge acts vertically downwards

![Force diagram for a child on a sledge on a rough horizontal path. Four arrows act on the sledge: tension forwards along the rope, friction backwards along the path, the normal contact force vertically upwards and the weight vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/mechanics-toolkit/quantities-units-and-modelling/assets/009-force-diagram-for-a-child-on-a-sledge-on-a-rough.png)

**[B1 B1 B1]**

(ii)

The crate is pushed from behind, so this force is a thrust acting forwards on the crate

The floor is rough and the crate moves forwards, so friction acts backwards

The floor pushes up at right angles to it, and the weight acts vertically downwards

![Force diagram for a crate on a rough horizontal floor. Four arrows act on the crate: thrust forwards, friction backwards, the normal contact force vertically upwards and the weight vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/mechanics-toolkit/quantities-units-and-modelling/assets/010-force-diagram-for-a-crate-on-a-rough-horizontal-.png)

**[B1 B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A diagram for the sledge showing the weight vertically downwards and the normal contact force vertically upwards.
> 
> **B1**: The tension marked on the diagram, acting forwards along the rope, away from the sledge.
> 
> **B1**: Friction marked, acting backwards along the path, opposing the motion. Do not award this mark if friction is drawn in the direction of motion.
> 
> **B1**: A diagram for the crate showing the weight vertically downwards and the normal contact force vertically upwards.
> 
> **B1**: The thrust marked, acting forwards on the crate.
> 
> **B1**: Friction marked, acting backwards along the floor. Do not award if drawn in the direction of motion.
> 
> The marks are for which forces are shown and which way they point, not for the quality of the drawing. Accept "normal reaction", "reaction" or "R"; accept "mg" or "gravity" for the weight; accept "push" or "driving force" for the thrust. A force may be named on the arrow or in a key beside the diagram. Air resistance is not required in either diagram, and including it does not lose a mark.

parts.problemMd:
Each day a train travels in a straight line between three stations A, B and C, as shown in the diagram.

![Three points labelled A, B and C marked in that order on a horizontal straight line, with an arrow above the line labelled "positive direction" pointing to the right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/mechanics-toolkit/quantities-units-and-modelling/assets/008-three-points-labelled-a-b-and-c-marked-in-that-o.png)

Starting at A the train travels directly to C. It then travels back to B before returning to its starting position at A.

Taking the positive direction as shown in the diagram, state whether each of the following is positive or negative.

(i) The displacement from A to C, and the displacement from B to A.

(ii) The velocity from A to C, and the velocity from C to B.
parts.solutionMd:
Displacement and velocity are both vectors, so in one dimension each one takes the sign of the direction of travel

(i)

Travelling from A to C moves along the line in the same sense as the arrow, while travelling from B to A moves back against it

**Final answer:** **A to C is positive, B to A is negative**

**[B1]**

(ii)

The velocity takes its sign from the direction of travel in the same way, and A to C follows the arrow while C to B runs against it

**Final answer:** **A to C is positive, C to B is negative**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Positive for the displacement from A to C and negative for the displacement from B to A. Both are needed for the mark.
> 
> **B1**: Positive for the velocity from A to C and negative for the velocity from C to B. Both are needed for the mark.
> 
> No reason is required; the words "positive" and "negative" score on their own. Accept the signs $+$ and $-$ in place of the words.

parts.problemMd:
State whether the quantity described in each of the following is a scalar or a vector.

(i) A golf ball is hit with a force of 17793 N.

(ii) A hot air balloon rises vertically with an acceleration of 2.8 $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

(iii) The acceleration due to gravity acts vertically downwards at 10 $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

(iv) A cyclist covers a distance of 3200 m.
parts.solutionMd:
A scalar has magnitude only; a vector has magnitude and a direction

(i)

A force acts in a particular direction, which is why forces are drawn as arrows on a force diagram

**Final answer:** **Vector**

**[B1]**

(ii)

Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, and here it is stated to be vertically upwards

**Final answer:** **Vector**

**[B1]**

(iii)

The statement gives both a size and a direction for the acceleration

**Final answer:** **Vector**

**[B1]**

(iv)

A distance covered says how far the cyclist has travelled but not in which direction

**Final answer:** **Scalar**

**[B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Part (iv) is the one to watch. Distance and displacement are easy to blur together, but only displacement records which way you went, so only displacement is a vector. If the question had said "moves 3200 m north" it would have been a displacement, and the answer would flip.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Vector. Force is a vector quantity.
> 
> **B1**: Vector. Acceleration is a vector quantity.
> 
> **B1**: Vector. Acceleration is a vector quantity, and a direction is given.
> 
> **B1**: Scalar. A distance is a scalar quantity, because no direction is given.
> 
> A reason is not required; the single word scores.

parts.problemMd:
A book of mass 0.6 kg rests in equilibrium on a horizontal table.

(i) Name the two forces acting on the book, and state the direction of each.

(ii) The table exerts a normal contact force on the book. State the force which forms a Newton's third law pair with this force, saying what exerts it, what it acts on, and in which direction it acts.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Gravity pulls the book downwards, and this force is the weight of the book

**Final answer:** **The weight, acting vertically downwards**

**[B1]**

The table is in contact with the book and pushes it away from the surface, at right angles to the surface

**Final answer:** **The normal contact force, acting vertically upwards**

**[B1]**

(ii)

Newton's third law pairs act on two different bodies, so the partner to the force the table exerts on the book is the force the book exerts on the table

**Final answer:** **The book exerts a force on the table, equal in magnitude and acting vertically downwards**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The weight, acting vertically downwards. Accept "mg" or "gravity". The direction is required.
> 
> **B1**: The normal contact force, acting vertically upwards. Accept "normal reaction", "reaction" or "R". The direction is required. Both forces may be shown on a diagram with arrows instead of being written out.
> 
> **B1**: The force exerted by the book on the table, equal in magnitude and acting vertically downwards. All three of what exerts it, what it acts on, and the direction are needed for the mark.
> 
> Do not accept "the weight of the book": the weight acts on the book, not on the table, so it is not the third law partner of a force the table exerts.

parts.problemMd:
A crate has a mass of 24 kg.

Take the acceleration due to gravity to be 10 $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

(i) Find the weight of the crate.

(ii) A student writes "the weight of the crate is 24 kg". Explain why this statement is wrong.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The weight of a body is the force of gravity acting on it, given by $W = m g$ with $m = 24$ and $g = 10$

$W = 24 \times 10$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** **240 N**

**[A1]**

(ii)

The kilogram measures how much matter a body contains, which is a different quantity from the force gravity exerts on it

**Final answer:** **Kilograms measure mass, not weight**

**[B1]**

Weight is a force, so it is measured in the unit used for every other force

**Final answer:** **Weight is a force and is measured in newtons**

**[B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> In everyday speech "weight" and "mass" are used interchangeably, but in mechanics they are different quantities in different units. The mass is what the question gives you; the weight is what you put into a force equation. Whenever a question hands you a mass in kilograms and you need a force, multiply by $g$ first.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of $W = m g$ with $m = 24$ and $g = 10$. The mark is for multiplying the mass by 10; it is available even if the arithmetic then goes wrong.
> 
> **A1**: 240, in newtons. Units are not required for the mark.
> 
> **B1**: A statement that kilograms are the unit of mass, not of weight. Accept "24 kg is the mass of the crate".
> 
> **B1**: A statement that weight is a force, measured in newtons. Both this and the previous mark may be earned in a single sentence which makes both points.
> 
> Accept an answer which makes the point by giving the correct version, provided both ideas appear, for example "the mass is 24 kg and the weight is 240 N, because weight is a force measured in newtons".

parts.problemMd:
Car A travels at a constant speed of 26 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Car B travels 5200 m in a time of 300 s.

Find the difference between the average speeds of the two cars, giving your answer correct to three significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Car A's speed is given, so start by finding Car B's average speed from the distance it covers and the time it takes

$\text{average speed of B} = \frac{5200}{300} = 17 . 333 \dots$

**[M1]**

Subtract the smaller speed from the larger one, keeping Car B's speed unrounded

$26 - 17 . 333 \dots = 8 . 666 \dots$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** **8.67 **$\text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> Rounding Car B's speed to 17.3 before subtracting gives 8.7, which is wrong in the third significant figure. Carry the full value through and round only once, at the very end.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of average speed = distance ÷ time for Car B, with 5200 and 300 substituted.
> 
> **M1**: Subtracting the two speeds, in either order. The mark is for the subtraction, so it is available from a wrong value for Car B's speed.
> 
> **A1**: An answer which rounds to 8.67. Units are not required. Do not award for 8.7, which comes from rounding Car B's speed before subtracting; an answer of −8.67 is acceptable, since a difference may be taken either way round.

parts.problemMd:
A snowboarder slides down a rough slope. The diagram shows the three forces acting, labelled A, B and C.

![A rectangular block on an inclined plane which rises from left to right. Three arrows act on the block: arrow A points up the slope, arrow B points away from the slope at right angles to it, and arrow C points vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/mechanics-toolkit/quantities-units-and-modelling/assets/003-a-rectangular-block-on-an-inclined-plane-which-r.png)

Label each of the forces A, B and C with its name, choosing from: friction, normal contact force, weight.
parts.solutionMd:
The snowboarder is sliding down the slope, and friction on a rough surface always opposes the motion, so it acts up the slope

**Final answer:** **A is the friction**

The slope pushes the snowboarder away from its surface, at right angles to the slope

**Final answer:** **B is the normal contact force**

**[B1]**

The weight is the pull of gravity, which acts vertically downwards whatever the slope is doing

**Final answer:** **C is the weight**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Any two of the three forces correctly named.
> 
> **B1**: All three correctly named: A friction, B normal contact force, C weight.
> 
> Accept "normal reaction", "reaction" or "R"; accept "F" for friction and "mg" or "gravity" for the weight. The names may be written on the diagram.

parts.problemMd:
A parachutist descends vertically with an open parachute. The diagram shows the two forces acting, labelled D and E.

![A particle descending below an open parachute canopy. Arrow D points vertically upwards and arrow E points vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/mechanics-toolkit/quantities-units-and-modelling/assets/004-a-particle-descending-below-an-open-parachute-ca.png)

(i) Label each of the forces D and E with its name.

(ii) The parachutist descends at a constant speed. State what this tells you about the two forces.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The parachute pushes against the air as it falls, and the air pushes back upwards on it, opposing the motion

**Final answer:** **D is the air resistance**

**[B1]**

The weight of the parachutist acts vertically downwards

**Final answer:** **E is the weight**

**[B1]**

(ii)

A constant speed in a straight line means there is no acceleration, so by Newton's second law the resultant force is zero

**Final answer:** **The air resistance and the weight are equal in magnitude**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: D is the air resistance. Accept "drag", "resistance" or "air resistance force".
> 
> **B1**: E is the weight. Accept "mg" or "gravity".
> 
> **B1**: The two forces are equal in magnitude, or equivalently that they balance and the resultant force is zero. Accept "they cancel out". Do not accept "there is no force acting".
> 
> The names in part (i) may be written on the diagram rather than listed.

parts.problemMd:
The slope in part (a) is now modelled as smooth.

(i) State which of the forces A, B and C is removed by this assumption, and describe the motion of the snowboarder that the model then predicts.

(ii) Give one reason why modelling a real snow slope as smooth may not be suitable.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

A smooth contact exerts no force along the surface, only at right angles to it

**Final answer:** **"Smooth" means the friction, A, is removed**

**[B1]**

The component of the weight down the slope is then the only force acting along the slope

**Final answer:** **The snowboarder accelerates down the slope, and the acceleration never decreases**

**[B1]**

(ii)

The smooth model is only reasonable when the frictional force is small compared with the other forces acting

**Final answer:** **A real slope does exert friction on the board, so the model predicts a larger acceleration than actually occurs**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The friction, A, is removed.
> 
> **B1**: The snowboarder accelerates down the slope with a constant acceleration, and does not slow down or reach a steady speed. Accept "there is a resultant force down the slope, so the snowboarder speeds up".
> 
> **B1**: Any statement that a real slope is not frictionless, together with a consequence for the model: that it overestimates the acceleration or the speed, or that it predicts the snowboarder never reaches a steady speed. The consequence is needed; "there would be friction" alone does not score.

parts.problemMd:
Two blocks A and B are attached by a light inextensible string which runs over a smooth pulley fixed at the edge of a table, as shown in the diagram. Block A accelerates along the smooth horizontal surface of the table in the direction shown, while block B moves towards the ground.

![A block labelled A on a horizontal table, connected by a string which runs horizontally to a pulley at the right-hand edge of the table and then vertically downwards to a hanging block labelled B. An arrow on the table shows A moving to the right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/mechanics-toolkit/quantities-units-and-modelling/assets/002-a-block-labelled-a-on-a-horizontal-table-connect.png)

State what each of the following assumptions allows you to assume in this model.

(i) A and B are both particles.

(ii) The surface of the table is smooth.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The word removes each block's size and shape from the problem

**Final answer:** **"Particle" means each block has no dimensions, so all the forces on it act at a single point**

**[B1]**

(ii)

A smooth contact exerts no force along the surface, only at right angles to it

**Final answer:** **"Smooth" means there is no friction between A and the table**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Each block is treated as a single point whose dimensions are ignored, so all the forces act at that point. Accept "the size and shape of the blocks do not matter".
> 
> **B1**: There is no frictional force between block A and the table.

parts.problemMd:
State what each of the following assumptions allows you to assume about the tension in the string, or about the motion of the two blocks.

(i) The string is light.

(ii) The string is inextensible.

(iii) The pulley is smooth.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

None of the tension is then used up supporting the string itself

**Final answer:** **"Light" means the string has no mass, so the tension is the same at both ends**

**[B1]**

(ii)

The two ends then stay the same distance apart along the string

**Final answer:** **"Inextensible" means the string cannot stretch, so A and B move with the same speed and the same acceleration**

**[B1]**

(iii)

A smooth pulley exerts no frictional force on the string passing over it

**Final answer:** **"Smooth" means the pulley exerts no friction on the string, so the tension is the same on both sides**

**[B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> These three assumptions are what let you write a single letter $T$ for the tension everywhere in the string and a single letter $a$ for the acceleration of both blocks. Without them you would need four separate unknowns, and connected-particle questions would be unsolvable!

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The string has no mass, so the tension is the same throughout its length, or at both ends.
> 
> **B1**: The string does not stretch, so A and B have the same speed and the same acceleration. Either "same speed" or "same acceleration" is enough.
> 
> **B1**: There is no friction between the string and the pulley, so the tension is the same on both sides of the pulley.
> 
> Award the marks for the consequence, not for restating the assumption. "The string has no mass" on its own does not score without what it allows.

parts.problemMd:
Draw a diagram to represent each of the following situations, labelling it with all the forces acting on the body in italics. In both cases air resistance is to be ignored.

Choose the force names from: friction, normal contact force, tension, thrust, weight.

(i) A *child* swinging on a rope swing, at the lowest point of the swing.

(ii) A *bowling ball* rolling along a horizontal lane, just as it strikes a skittle.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The rope is attached above the child and holds them up, so the force in the rope is a tension acting along the rope, upwards towards the point of support

The weight of the child acts vertically downwards

At the lowest point of the swing the rope is vertical, so both forces lie in the same vertical line, and nothing acts horizontally

![Force diagram for a child on a rope swing at the lowest point. The rope is vertical. Two arrows act on the child: the tension acting vertically upwards along the rope, and the weight acting vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/mechanics-toolkit/quantities-units-and-modelling/assets/005-force-diagram-for-a-child-on-a-rope-swing-at-the.png)

**[B1 B1 B1]**

(ii)

The lane pushes the ball upwards at right angles to it, and the weight of the ball acts vertically downwards

At the moment of contact the skittle pushes back on the ball, and this contact force acts horizontally, opposing the ball's motion

![Force diagram for a bowling ball on a horizontal lane at the moment it strikes a skittle. Three arrows act on the ball: the normal contact force from the lane vertically upwards, the weight vertically downwards, and the contact force from the skittle horizontally backwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/mechanics-toolkit/quantities-units-and-modelling/assets/006-force-diagram-for-a-bowling-ball-on-a-horizontal.png)

**[B1 B1 B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> There is no forward force on the child, even though the child is moving forwards. A force is needed to change motion, not to keep it going, so the only forces on a diagram are the ones something is actually exerting: here, gravity and the rope. Adding an arrow in the direction of travel is the commonest error on a force diagram, and it never scores. The one horizontal force that would genuinely act on a real swing is air resistance, backwards, which is why the question tells you to ignore it.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A diagram for the child showing the weight acting vertically downwards.
> 
> **B1**: The tension marked, acting along the rope away from the child, towards the point of support.
> 
> **B1**: The rope drawn vertical at the lowest point, with both forces in the same vertical line. Award this mark for a diagram in which the two arrows are drawn along the same line in opposite directions.
> 
> **B1**: A diagram for the ball showing the weight vertically downwards and the normal contact force vertically upwards.
> 
> **B1**: A horizontal contact force from the skittle marked on the ball. Accept "normal contact force", "reaction" or "force from the skittle".
> 
> **B1**: That contact force drawn acting backwards, opposing the ball's motion. Do not award if it is drawn in the direction of motion.
> 
> In (i) no horizontal force acts at all, because the rope is vertical at the lowest point and air resistance is ignored. In particular do not credit a force in the direction of motion: nothing is pushing the child forwards. Note also that the tension and the weight are not equal at this instant, so the child should not be described as being in equilibrium.
> 
> The marks are for which forces are shown and which way they point, not for the quality of the drawing. Accept "normal reaction", "reaction" or "R"; accept "mg" or "gravity" for the weight. Friction on the lane is not required in (ii), and including it does not lose a mark.

parts.problemMd:
(i) A dog on a skateboard rolls down a hill. In a first model the hill is treated as a smooth slope and the dog and skateboard together are treated as a particle.

State what the smooth assumption allows you to assume about the forces, and explain why the model becomes less reliable the longer the dog rolls.

(ii) A hot air balloon rises vertically towards its maximum height. A first model ignores air resistance.

Explain why ignoring air resistance is a poorer assumption for the balloon than it would be for a small dense object, and state what the balloon reaches that the model cannot predict.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

A smooth contact exerts no force along the surface, so nothing acts along the slope to oppose the motion

**Final answer:** **"Smooth" means there is no friction between the skateboard and the hill**

**[B1]**

With no friction, nothing opposes the component of the weight down the slope

**Final answer:** **The model predicts a constant acceleration, so the speed increases without limit**

**[B1]**

A real skateboard meets friction at the wheels and air resistance, and both grow in importance as the speed rises

**Final answer:** **The longer the roll, the faster the dog goes and the further the model's speed drifts above the real one**

**[B1]**

(ii)

Air resistance depends on how much surface the moving object presents to the air, and a balloon presents a very large one

**Final answer:** **The balloon is large, so the air resistance on it is large and cannot be treated as negligible**

**[B1]**

A small dense object has a large weight for its size, so the air resistance is small next to the other forces acting on it

**Final answer:** **For a small dense object the air resistance is negligible compared with its weight**

**[B1]**

Air resistance grows with speed until it balances the resultant of the other forces, at which point the acceleration is zero

**Final answer:** **The balloon reaches a constant maximum speed, which the model cannot predict**

**[B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> "Ignore air resistance" is not a free assumption; it is only reasonable when the resistance is small next to the other forces. Ask yourself whether the object is large and light, or small and dense. In a real exam question you will be told when to include air resistance, so you never have to make the judgement under exam conditions, but knowing why the instruction is there makes the models make sense.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: There is no friction between the skateboard and the hill. Accept "no resistance along the slope".
> 
> **B1**: The model gives a constant acceleration down the slope, so the predicted speed keeps increasing. Accept "the dog speeds up at a steady rate and never stops speeding up".
> 
> **B1**: Any statement that real resistances (friction at the wheels, or air resistance) grow with speed, so the difference between the model and the real motion widens as the roll continues. The idea that the error grows is needed; "there would really be friction" alone does not score.
> 
> **B1**: The balloon is large, so the air resistance acting on it is large and is not negligible.
> 
> **B1**: For a small dense object the air resistance is small compared with its weight, so ignoring it changes the answer very little. A comparison is needed, either explicitly against the balloon or against the object's own weight.
>
