> **B1**: The balloon reaches a constant maximum speed once the air resistance balances the other forces. Accept "terminal velocity" provided the reason accompanies it.

parts.problemMd:
A canal barge travels in a straight line between its home mooring and two locks, Lock A and Lock B, as shown in the diagram. The barge travels at 6 $\text{km h}^{-1}$ between home and Lock A, and at 4 $\text{km h}^{-1}$ between home and Lock B.

![Three points marked on a horizontal straight line, labelled Lock A, Home and Lock B from left to right, with the distance from Lock A to Home marked as 7 km and the distance from Home to Lock B marked as 3 km. An arrow above the line labelled "positive direction" points to the right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/mechanics-toolkit/quantities-units-and-modelling/assets/001-three-points-marked-on-a-horizontal-straight-lin.png)

Taking the positive direction as shown in the diagram, state the following.

(i) The velocity of the barge as it travels from home to Lock A.

(ii) The displacement of the barge from home once it reaches Lock A.
parts.solutionMd:
Velocity and displacement are both vectors, so each takes the sign of the direction of travel

(i)

Lock A lies to the left of home, so the barge travels against the positive direction

$- 6 \text{km h}^{-1}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Lock A is 7 km from home, again measured against the positive direction

$- 7 \text{km}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $- 6$, in $\text{km h}^{-1}$. The negative sign is essential; 6 without a sign does not score. Units are not required.
> 
> **B1**: $- 7$, in km. The negative sign is essential.

parts.problemMd:
The barge then returns home and travels on to Lock B, before returning home again.

Taking the same positive direction, state the following.

(i) The velocity of the barge as it travels from Lock B back to home.

(ii) The displacement of the barge from home once it has returned home for the second time.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Travelling from Lock B back to home moves against the positive direction

$- 4 \text{km h}^{-1}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Displacement is measured from the starting point to the finishing point, and the barge has finished where it began

$0 \text{km}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $- 4$, in $\text{km h}^{-1}$. The negative sign is essential.
> 
> **B1**: 0. Accept "zero". Do not accept 20 km, which is the total distance travelled, not the displacement.

parts.problemMd:
On the journey from Lock B back to home, the barge slows down steadily as it approaches its mooring.

Explain why the acceleration of the barge is positive during this part of the journey, even though the barge is decelerating.
parts.solutionMd:
The barge is travelling towards the left, so its velocity is negative throughout this stretch

$v = - 4$

**[B1]**

Slowing down means the speed falls towards zero

**Final answer:** **The velocity increases from −4 towards 0, so the acceleration is positive**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A statement that the velocity is negative on this stretch, because the barge is travelling in the negative direction.
> 
> **B1**: A statement that the velocity is increasing towards zero, so the acceleration is positive. Accept "the acceleration is opposite in direction to the velocity, and the velocity is negative, so the acceleration is positive".
> 
> Do not award the second mark for "deceleration means negative acceleration", which is the misconception the question is testing.

parts.problemMd:
(i) A puck slides across a horizontal ice rink after being hit. The ice is modelled as a smooth surface.

State the force that this assumption removes, name the forces that then act on the puck, and describe the motion that the model predicts.

(ii) A skydiver falls vertically after jumping from a plane, before the parachute is opened. A first model ignores air resistance.

Explain why this model is not suitable for the whole of the fall.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

A smooth contact is one where the surfaces exert no force along the surface, only at right angles to it

**Final answer:** **"Smooth" means the frictional force is removed**

**[B1]**

Only the pull of gravity and the push of the ice are left, and both of these are vertical

**Final answer:** **The weight and the normal contact force**

**[B1]**

These two vertical forces balance and nothing acts horizontally, so the resultant force on the puck is zero

**Final answer:** **The puck moves in a straight line with constant velocity, and never slows down**

**[B1]**

(ii)

Ignoring air resistance leaves the weight as the only force, so the model gives the same acceleration throughout the fall

$a = 10 \text{m s}^{-2}$

**[B1]**

A real skydiver meets a second force, which the first model leaves out

**Final answer:** **Air resistance acts upwards, opposing the motion, and increases as the speed increases**

**[B1]**

Once the air resistance has grown to balance the weight the resultant force is zero, which the model cannot reproduce

**Final answer:** **The model predicts a speed which increases without limit, but a real skydiver reaches a constant maximum speed**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Friction (between the puck and the ice) is removed.
> 
> **B1**: The weight and the normal contact force. Accept "reaction" for the normal contact force, and "mg" or "gravity" for the weight.
> 
> **B1**: The puck travels in a straight line at constant velocity, or equivalently that it never slows down and keeps moving forever. Accept "the resultant force is zero, so there is no acceleration".
> 
> **B1**: The model leaves the weight as the only force, giving a constant acceleration of $10 \text{m s}^{-2}$ throughout. Accept a statement that the acceleration is constant, without the value.
> 
> **B1**: A real skydiver experiences air resistance, which acts upwards, opposing the motion, and increases with speed. Both the direction and the fact that it increases with speed are needed.
> 
> **B1**: The model therefore predicts a speed increasing without limit, whereas the real skydiver reaches a constant maximum speed when the air resistance balances the weight. Accept "terminal velocity" as the name for that constant speed, but the name alone does not score without the reason.

parts.problemMd:
A particle rests in equilibrium on a smooth plane inclined at an angle to the horizontal. It is held in place by a string lying along a line of greatest slope, as shown.

![A particle on a plane inclined at an angle to the horizontal, rising from left to right. A string runs from the particle up the line of greatest slope. Three arrows act on the particle: P acts up the plane along the string; Q acts perpendicular to the plane, away from its surface; and R acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/mechanics-toolkit/quantities-units-and-modelling/assets/017-a-particle-on-a-plane-inclined-at-an-angle-to-th.png)

(i) Label each of the forces P, Q and R with its name.

(ii) Explain why no frictional force appears on the diagram.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The string runs up the line of greatest slope and holds the particle back, so the force in it is a tension acting up the slope

**Final answer:** **P is the tension**

**[B1]**

The plane pushes the particle away from its surface, at right angles to the plane

**Final answer:** **Q is the normal contact force**

The weight acts vertically downwards, not perpendicular to the plane

**Final answer:** **R is the weight**

**[B1]**

(ii)

A smooth contact is one which exerts no force along the surface, only at right angles to it

**Final answer:** **"Smooth" means there is no friction between the particle and the plane**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: P is the tension. Accept "T".
> 
> **B1**: Q is the normal contact force and R is the weight, both correct. Accept "normal reaction", "reaction" or "R" for Q, and "mg" or "gravity" for R.
> 
> **B1**: A statement that the plane is smooth, so no frictional force acts. Accept "a smooth surface exerts no force along the plane".

parts.problemMd:
A climber abseils down a vertical cliff face. The climber's feet remain in contact with the cliff and the rope is held taut.

![A climber in contact with a vertical cliff face, with a rope running up and away from the cliff. Four arrows act on the climber: W acts along the rope, upwards and away from the cliff; X acts horizontally, away from the cliff face; Y acts vertically upwards, parallel to the cliff face; and Z acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/mechanics-toolkit/quantities-units-and-modelling/assets/018-a-climber-in-contact-with-a-vertical-cliff-face-.png)

Label each of the forces W, X, Y and Z with its name.
parts.solutionMd:
The rope is taut and runs upwards to the anchor point, so the force in it is a tension acting along the rope, away from the climber

**Final answer:** **W is the tension**

The cliff face pushes the climber's feet away from the rock, horizontally and at right angles to the face

**Final answer:** **X is the normal contact force**

**[B1]**

The climber is sliding down the rock, so friction between the boots and the face acts upwards, opposing that motion

**Final answer:** **Y is the friction**

The weight acts vertically downwards

**Final answer:** **Z is the weight**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Any two of the four forces correctly named.
> 
> **B1**: All four correctly named: W the tension, X the normal contact force, Y the friction, Z the weight.
>

parts.problemMd:
An astronaut and her equipment have a combined mass of 80 kg.

On Earth the acceleration due to gravity is taken to be 10 $\text{m s}^{-2}$. On the Moon it is 1.6 $\text{m s}^{-2}$.

(i) Find the weight of the astronaut and her equipment on Earth, and their weight on the Moon.

(ii) State which of the mass and the weight is unchanged when the astronaut travels from the Earth to the Moon, and explain why.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The weight of a body is the force of gravity on it, given by $W = m g$

$W_{\text{Earth}} = 80 \times 10$

**Final answer:** **800 N**

**[B1]**

$W_{\text{Moon}} = 80 \times 1 . 6$

**Final answer:** **128 N**

**[B1]**

(ii)

Mass measures how much matter the body contains, and travelling to the Moon does not add or remove any of it

**Final answer:** **The mass is unchanged**

**[B1]**

Weight is a force, and it is found by multiplying that mass by the local value of $g$, which is smaller on the Moon

**Final answer:** **The weight changes because g is different, but the mass is a property of the body itself**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: 800, in newtons, from $80 \times 10$. Units are not required.
> 
> **B1**: 128, in newtons, from 80 × 1.6.
> 
> **B1**: The mass is unchanged.
> 
> **B1**: An explanation that mass is the amount of matter in the body and does not depend on location, while weight is the force $m g$ and depends on the local value of $g$. Both halves of the contrast are needed; "because gravity is weaker on the Moon" alone does not score, since it explains the weight but not the mass.

parts.problemMd:
A runner runs in a straight line from a point $O$ to a point $P$, a distance of 600 m, taking 200 s. She then turns and runs straight back from $P$ to $O$, taking 300 s.

Taking the direction from $O$ to $P$ as positive, find for the whole journey:

(i) the total distance travelled and the displacement from $O$;

(ii) the average speed and the average velocity.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Distance adds up every metre covered, whichever way the runner was facing

$\text{distance} = 600 + 600$

**Final answer:** **1200 m**

**[B1]**

Displacement records only where the runner finished relative to where she started, and she has returned to $O$

**Final answer:** **0 m**

**[B1]**

(ii)

Average speed uses the total distance and the total time, and the whole journey took $200 + 300 = 500$ s

$\text{average speed} = \frac{1200}{500}$

**Final answer:** **2.4 **$\text{m s}^{-1}$

**[B1]**

Average velocity uses the displacement over the same total time, and the displacement is zero

$\text{average velocity} = \frac{0}{500}$

**Final answer:** **0 **$\text{m s}^{-1}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: 1200, in metres.
> 
> **B1**: 0. Accept "zero". Do not accept 1200, which is the distance.
> 
> **B1**: An answer which rounds to 2.4, in $\text{m s}^{-1}$, from $1200 \div 500$. Follow through from a wrong total distance.
> 
> **B1**: 0. This mark requires the average velocity to be obtained from the displacement, so award it for $0 \div 500$ or for a clear statement that the displacement is zero and therefore so is the average velocity. Units are not required anywhere in this question.

parts.problemMd:
A car tows a trailer along a straight horizontal road. In one model the car and trailer are connected by a light rigid tow-bar; in another they are connected by a light rope. In both models the car and the trailer are treated as particles.

(i) State what modelling the tow-bar as light allows you to assume about the force in it, and what modelling the car and trailer as particles allows you to assume.

(ii) While the car is accelerating, state the direction of the force which the tow-bar exerts on the trailer, and name that force.

(iii) The driver now brakes sharply. Explain why the rigid tow-bar can slow the trailer down but a rope cannot.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

A light connector has no mass, so none of the force in it is used up accelerating the connector itself

**Final answer:** **"Light" means the tow-bar has no mass, so the force is the same at both ends**

**[B1]**

Treating each body as a particle removes its size and shape from the problem

**Final answer:** **"Particle" means each body has no dimensions, so all the forces on it act at a single point**

**[B1]**

(ii)

The trailer is speeding up, so there must be a resultant force on it in the direction of motion, and the tow-bar is the only thing pulling it forwards

**Final answer:** **Forwards, in the direction of motion, and the force is a tension**

**[B1]**

(iii)

Under braking the car slows first, so the trailer tends to run on and close the gap, which would compress the connector

**Final answer:** **A rigid tow-bar can be compressed, so it pushes backwards on the trailer**

**[B1]**

That backwards push on the trailer is a thrust rather than a tension, and only a rigid connector can provide one

**Final answer:** **The force in the tow-bar becomes a thrust**

**[B1]**

A rope carries a force only when it is taut, and it cannot be compressed

**Final answer:** **A rope would go slack, so it could exert no force on the trailer at all**

**[B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> This is the practical reason an exam question tells you which connector is used. With a rope you may only ever write a tension, so the rope can never slow the trailer down. With a rigid tow-bar the same letter can come out negative, and a negative answer is not a mistake; it means the force is a thrust.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The tow-bar has no mass, so the force in it is the same at both ends. Accept "the tension is the same throughout".
> 
> **B1**: The car and trailer are each treated as a single point with no dimensions, so all the forces on each act at that point.
> 
> **B1**: Forwards, in the direction of motion, and named as a tension. Both the direction and the name are needed.
> 
> **B1**: A statement that the trailer tends to catch up with the car under braking, so the tow-bar is compressed and pushes backwards on the trailer.
> 
> **B1**: That the force in the tow-bar is then a thrust. Accept "a compression" or "a negative tension".
> 
> **B1**: A rope cannot be compressed, so it would go slack and exert no force. Accept "a rope can only pull, never push".

parts.problemMd:
Draw a diagram to represent each of the following situations, labelling it with all the forces acting on the body in italics, and stating one modelling assumption you have made in each case.

Choose the force names from: air resistance, friction, normal contact force, tension, thrust, weight.

(i) A *lawnmower* being pushed along a horizontal lawn by a handle inclined to the horizontal.

(ii) A *bucket* being raised at a constant speed by a rope which passes over a fixed pulley.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The handle is inclined, so the push along it acts partly forwards and partly downwards into the lawn

The lawn is rough and the mower moves forwards, so friction acts backwards

The ground pushes up at right angles to it, and the weight acts vertically downwards

![Force diagram for a lawnmower on a horizontal lawn. Four arrows act on the mower: a thrust directed down along the inclined handle, friction backwards along the ground, the normal contact force vertically upwards and the weight vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/mechanics-toolkit/quantities-units-and-modelling/assets/015-force-diagram-for-a-lawnmower-on-a-horizontal-la.png)

**[B1 B1 B1]**

Treating the mower as a particle lets all four forces be drawn acting at a single point

**Final answer:** **"Particle" means the lawnmower has no dimensions, so all four forces act at one point**

**[B1]**

(ii)

The rope is taut and runs upwards from the bucket to the pulley, so the tension acts vertically upwards

The weight of the bucket acts vertically downwards, and no other force acts because the bucket touches nothing

![Force diagram for a bucket being raised by a vertical rope over a pulley. Two arrows act on the bucket: the tension acting vertically upwards along the rope and the weight acting vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/mechanics-toolkit/quantities-units-and-modelling/assets/016-force-diagram-for-a-bucket-being-raised-by-a-ver.png)

**[B1 B1]**

Modelling the rope as light and inextensible and the pulley as smooth lets the tension be the same all along the rope

**Final answer:** **"Light", "inextensible" and "smooth" together mean the tension is the same all along the rope**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A diagram for the mower showing the weight vertically downwards and the normal contact force vertically upwards.
> 
> **B1**: The thrust marked, acting along the handle, directed forwards and downwards. A force drawn horizontally does not score this mark.
> 
> **B1**: Friction marked, acting backwards along the ground, opposing the motion.
> 
> **B1**: One valid modelling assumption for the mower: that it is a particle, that the lawn is horizontal, or that air resistance is ignored.
> 
> **B1**: A diagram for the bucket showing the weight vertically downwards.
> 
> **B1**: The tension marked, acting vertically upwards along the rope.
> 
> **B1**: One valid modelling assumption for the bucket: that the rope is light, that it is inextensible, that the pulley is smooth, or that the bucket is a particle.
> 
> The diagram marks are for which forces are shown and which way they point, not for the quality of the drawing. Accept "normal reaction", "reaction" or "R"; accept "mg" or "gravity"; accept "push" or "driving force" for the thrust.

parts.problemMd:
A yo-yo moves in a straight line up and down a string of length 1 m. As it travels down the string it moves at 0.15 $\text{m s}^{-1}$, and as it returns towards the hand it moves at 0.12 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

To perform tricks the yo-yo stops at three points along the string. Stop 1 is a quarter of the way along the string and Stop 2 is four fifths of the way along it. At Stop 3 the string is fully extended. The trick "The Mechanic" runs Hand, Stop 2, Stop 1, Stop 3, Stop 1, Hand.

![A vertical line running downwards from a point labelled Hand, with three points marked on it in order labelled Stop 1, Stop 2 and Stop 3, Stop 3 being at the lower end](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/mechanics-toolkit/quantities-units-and-modelling/assets/019-a-vertical-line-running-downwards-from-a-point-l.png)

Taking the direction from the hand down the string as positive, state the velocity of the yo-yo:

(i) as it travels from Stop 2 to Stop 1;

(ii) as it travels from Stop 1 to Stop 3.
parts.solutionMd:
Stop 1 is a quarter of the way down and Stop 2 is four fifths of the way down, so Stop 2 is further from the hand than Stop 1

(i)

Moving from Stop 2 to Stop 1 is a move back towards the hand, which is against the chosen positive direction, at the return speed

**Final answer:** **−0.12 **$\text{m s}^{-1}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Moving from Stop 1 to Stop 3 is a move away from the hand, in the positive direction, at the downward speed

**Final answer:** **0.15 **$\text{m s}^{-1}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $- 0 . 12$, in $\text{m s}^{-1}$. The negative sign is essential. If the positive direction has instead been taken up the string, accept $+ 0 . 12$ provided that choice is stated or marked on the diagram.
> 
> **B1**: $0 . 15$, in $\text{m s}^{-1}$. If the positive direction has been taken up the string, accept $- 0 . 15$. The two answers must use the same convention as each other.

(i)

Displacement is the finishing position minus the starting position, with Stop 1 a quarter of the way down and Stop 3 at the full 1 m

$0 . 25 - 1$

**Final answer:** **−0.75 m**

**[B1]**

(ii)

Distance adds every stretch of string covered, whichever way the yo-yo was moving, so follow the trick leg by leg

$0 . 8 + 0 . 55 + 0 . 75 + 0 . 75 + 0 . 25$

**Final answer:** **3.1 m**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $- 0 . 75$, in metres. The negative sign is essential with the stated convention; accept $+ 0 . 75$ if the positive direction has been taken up the string. Do not accept 0.75 without a sign.
> 
> **B1**: An answer which rounds to 3.1, in metres. The five legs are Hand to Stop 2 (0.8), Stop 2 to Stop 1 (0.55), Stop 1 to Stop 3 (0.75), Stop 3 to Stop 1 (0.75) and Stop 1 to Hand (0.25). A negative answer does not score, since a distance cannot be negative.

parts.problemMd:
A block rests on a rough plane inclined to the horizontal. The angle of the plane is slowly increased until the block is on the point of slipping down the plane.

![A block on a plane inclined to the horizontal, rising from left to right, with the contact surface shaded to show it is rough. Three arrows act on the block: J acts up the plane, parallel to its surface; K acts perpendicular to the plane, away from its surface; and L acts vertically downwards](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/mechanics-toolkit/quantities-units-and-modelling/assets/014-a-block-on-a-plane-inclined-to-the-horizontal-ri.png)

(i) Label each of the forces J, K and L with its name.

(ii) State what "on the point of slipping" tells you about the frictional force.

(iii) State one modelling assumption that has been made about the block.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The block is on the point of sliding down the plane, so friction acts up the plane to oppose that impending motion

**Final answer:** **J is the friction, acting up the plane**

**[B1]**

The plane pushes the block away from its surface at right angles, and the weight acts vertically downwards whatever the plane is doing

**Final answer:** **K is the normal contact force and L is the weight**

**[B1]**

(ii)

On the point of slipping the block is in limiting equilibrium, which is the moment friction reaches the largest value it can supply

**Final answer:** **The friction is at its maximum value, so **$F = μ R$

**[B1]**

(iii)

Treating the block as a particle lets every force be drawn acting at a single point

**Final answer:** **"Particle" means the block has no dimensions, so every force acts at a single point**

**[B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> "On the point of slipping", "about to slip" and "in limiting equilibrium" all mean the same thing, and all of them are telling you to replace the inequality $F \leq μ R$ with the equation $F = μ R$.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: J is the friction, acting up the plane. The direction is required, since friction opposes the impending motion down the plane.
> 
> **B1**: K is the normal contact force and L is the weight, both correct. Accept "normal reaction", "reaction" or "R" for K, and "mg" or "gravity" for L. Award this mark only if both are correct.
> 
> **B1**: The friction has reached its maximum possible value, so $F = μ R$ rather than $F \leq μ R$. Either the words or the equation earns the mark; $F = μ R$ on its own is enough, since the equation itself states that the friction is at its maximum.
> 
> **B1**: Any one valid assumption: the block is a particle, the plane is a rigid straight surface, or air resistance is ignored.

parts.problemMd:
(i) Explain what is meant by a rough surface and by a smooth pulley, and give an example of a situation in which both would be used in the same model.

(ii) Explain what is meant by a light rigid tow-bar and by a light inextensible string, and state what each allows you to assume about the force it carries.

(iii) A rigid tow-bar can exert a thrust on the body it is attached to, but a string can never do so. Explain why.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

A rough surface is one which can exert a force along the surface as well as at right angles to it

**Final answer:** **"Rough" means the surface exerts a frictional force on a body sliding across it**

A smooth pulley exerts no frictional force on the string running over it

**Final answer:** **"Smooth" means the pulley exerts no friction on the string, so the tension is the same on both sides**

**[B1]**

Both appear together whenever a body is dragged along a rough surface by a string which changes direction

**Final answer:** **A box being pulled up a rough slope by a string running over a pulley at the top**

**[B1]**

(ii)

A light connector has no mass, so none of the force it carries is spent accelerating the connector itself

**Final answer:** **"Light" means the connector has no mass, so the force is the same at both ends**

**[B1]**

Rigid means the tow-bar keeps its length and its shape, while inextensible means the string cannot stretch

**Final answer:** **"Rigid" and "inextensible" both mean the length is fixed, so the two connected bodies move with the same speed and acceleration**

**[B1]**

(iii)

A thrust is a pushing force, so the connector would have to be shortened and push its ends apart

**Final answer:** **A rigid tow-bar keeps its length under compression, so it can push its ends apart**

**[B1]**

A string carries a force only while it is taut, and nothing stops it from becoming slack

**Final answer:** **A string goes slack rather than being compressed, so it can only ever pull**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Rough: the surface exerts a frictional force on a body moving, or tending to move, across it. And smooth pulley: no friction between string and pulley, so the tension is the same on both sides. Both halves are needed.
> 
> **B1**: Any example in which a body on a rough surface is connected by a string passing over a pulley. Accept a box on a rough table connected over a pulley at the edge to a hanging mass, or a body dragged up a rough slope.
> 
> **B1**: Light means the connector has no mass, so the force in it is the same at both ends. Accept "the tension is the same throughout".
> 
> **B1**: Rigid, or inextensible, means the length does not change, so the two connected bodies have the same speed and the same acceleration. Either "same speed" or "same acceleration" is enough.
> 
> **B1**: A rigid tow-bar keeps its length when compressed, so it can push its two ends apart.
> 
> **B1**: A string becomes slack rather than resisting compression, so it can only pull, never push. Accept "a string can only exert a force along itself when taut".

parts.problemMd:
![A basketball player shoots at a basket. A dashed curve shows the path of the ball: from the player's raised hands at A, up to its highest point at B, and down to the back of the metal rim of the basket at C, which is mounted on a vertical post](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/mechanics-toolkit/quantities-units-and-modelling/assets/011-a-basketball-player-shoots-at-a-basket-a-dashed-.png)

A basketball player takes a shot. Consider the ball at the following two instants.

At A, as the player takes the shot, with their hands still in contact with the ball.

At C, as the ball strikes the back of the metal rim of the basket.

Name all the forces acting on the ball at each of the two instants, stating the direction of each.
parts.solutionMd:
At A the ball is in contact with the player's hands, and the hands both support the ball and drive it upwards

**Final answer:** **At A: the weight, vertically downwards**

**Final answer:** **At A: the contact force from the hands, acting upwards and forwards**

**[B1 B1]**

At C the ball is touching the rim, so the rim pushes back on it, at right angles to the surface it strikes

**Final answer:** **At C: the weight, vertically downwards**

**Final answer:** **At C: the contact force from the rim, acting away from the rim, opposing the ball's motion**

**[B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The weight at A, acting vertically downwards. Accept "mg" or "gravity".
> 
> **B1**: The contact force from the hands at A, with a direction which is upwards, or upwards and forwards. Accept "normal contact force", "reaction", "push" or "thrust". A direction is required.
> 
> **B1**: The weight at C, acting vertically downwards.
> 
> **B1**: The contact force from the rim at C, acting away from the rim and opposing the ball's motion. Accept "normal contact force" or "reaction". A direction is required.
> 
> Air resistance is not required at either instant, and naming it does not lose a mark. Do not credit a force from the hands at C, or from the rim at A.

parts.problemMd: State three modelling assumptions you have made in answering part (a), and for each one state what it allows you to assume.
parts.solutionMd:
Treating the ball as a particle removes its size, so every force can be drawn acting at one point

**Final answer:** **"Particle" means the ball has no dimensions, so all the forces act at a single point**

**[B1]**

Ignoring air resistance leaves only the weight and the contact forces to be listed

**Final answer:** **Air resistance is ignored, so no resisting force acts on the ball**

**[B1]**

Treating the rim as rigid and smooth fixes the contact force at C to act at right angles to the surface

**Final answer:** **"Smooth" means the rim exerts no force along itself, so the contact force at C is perpendicular to it**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The ball is modelled as a particle, so its size and shape are ignored and all the forces act at a single point. Both the assumption and its consequence are needed.
> 
> **B1**: Air resistance is ignored, so no resisting force is included. Accept "the ball moves slowly enough that air resistance is negligible".
> 
> **B1**: Any third valid assumption with its consequence: the rim is smooth, so the contact force is perpendicular to it; the ball does not deform, so the contact acts at a single point; or the contact at C is instantaneous, so the ball's weight can be neglected during the impact.
> 
> Accept any three distinct assumptions, each with a stated consequence. An assumption stated without a consequence does not score.

parts.problemMd:
A boxer strikes a punch bag which hangs from the ceiling on a chain.

Draw a diagram showing all the forces acting on the *punch bag* at the moment the glove strikes it, labelling each force and choosing the names from: air resistance, friction, normal contact force, tension, thrust, weight.

State also one modelling assumption you have made, and what it allows you to assume.
parts.solutionMd:
The chain holds the bag up, so the force in it is a tension acting along the chain, away from the bag

The weight of the bag acts vertically downwards

The glove pushes horizontally on the bag at the moment of contact, so the bag is not in equilibrium and the chain swings away from the vertical

![Force diagram for a punch bag hanging from a chain at the moment a glove strikes it. Three arrows act on the bag: the tension along the chain, directed upwards and away from the direction of the punch; the weight vertically downwards; and the contact force from the glove, horizontal and in the direction of the punch](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/mechanics-toolkit/quantities-units-and-modelling/assets/012-force-diagram-for-a-punch-bag-hanging-from-a-cha.png)

**[B1 B1 B1]**

Treating the bag as a particle lets all three forces be drawn acting at a single point

**Final answer:** **"Particle" means the bag has no dimensions, so all three forces act at one point**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The weight marked, acting vertically downwards.
> 
> **B1**: The tension marked, acting along the chain away from the bag, towards the ceiling.
> 
> **B1**: The contact force from the glove marked, acting horizontally in the direction of the punch. Accept "normal contact force", "reaction", "thrust" or "push".
> 
> **B1**: One valid assumption with its consequence: the bag is a particle, so all the forces act at a point; the chain is light, so the tension is the same throughout; or air resistance is ignored.
> 
> The marks are for which forces are shown and which way they point, not for the quality of the drawing. A diagram which draws the chain vertical is not penalised, provided the three forces and their directions are correct.

parts.problemMd:
A cat bats at a piece of string which its owner holds at the upper end, letting the lower end hang freely.

Draw a diagram showing all the forces acting on the *string* at the moment the cat's paw touches it, labelling each force from the same list as in part (a).

State also one modelling assumption you have made, and what it allows you to assume.
parts.solutionMd:
The owner holds the upper end, so a tension acts along the string, upwards towards the hand

The weight of the string acts vertically downwards through its centre

The paw pushes sideways on the string where it touches, so the string swings away from the vertical

![Force diagram for a hanging string at the moment a cat's paw touches it. Three arrows act on the string: the tension acting upwards along the string towards the owner's hand, the weight acting vertically downwards, and the contact force from the paw acting horizontally in the direction the paw is moving](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/mechanics-toolkit/quantities-units-and-modelling/assets/013-force-diagram-for-a-hanging-string-at-the-moment.png)

**[B1 B1 B1]**

The diagram includes the weight of the string, so the assumption must be one which keeps it

**Final answer:** **"Inextensible" means the string does not stretch, so its length is fixed**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The tension marked, acting upwards along the string towards the owner's hand.
> 
> **B1**: The weight marked, acting vertically downwards. Alternatively, a response which has already assumed the string to be light may omit the weight, provided that assumption is stated; award this mark in that case.
> 
> **B1**: The contact force from the paw marked, acting horizontally in the direction the paw moves. Accept "normal contact force", "reaction", "thrust" or "push".
> 
> **B1**: One valid assumption with its consequence: the string is light, so its weight may be ignored; the string is inextensible, so its length is fixed; or the paw touches at a single point.

parts.problemMd:
A person stands on the horizontal floor of a lift. Two of the forces in this situation are:

- $P$, the normal contact force exerted by the floor on the person;
- $Q$, the weight of the person.

(i) Explain why $P$ and $Q$ are not a Newton's third law pair.

(ii) State the force which does form a Newton's third law pair with $P$, and state its direction.

(iii) The lift now accelerates upwards. State what happens to the magnitude of $P$ compared with $Q$, and state whether the pair you named in part (ii) remains equal in magnitude to $P$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

A Newton's third law pair consists of two forces which two bodies exert on each other, so the two forces always act on different bodies

**Final answer:** **P and Q both act on the person, so they act on the same body**

**[B1]**

(ii)

The partner to the force the floor exerts on the person is the force the person exerts back on the floor

**Final answer:** **The force exerted by the person on the floor, acting vertically downwards**

**[B1]**

(iii)

Accelerating upwards needs a resultant force upwards, and the only upward force on the person is the normal contact force

**Final answer:** **P becomes larger than Q**

**[B1]**

Newton's third law holds whatever the bodies are doing, so the pair is unaffected by the acceleration

**Final answer:** **The pair named in part (ii) stays equal in magnitude to P**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: Both forces act on the person, that is on the same body, whereas a third law pair acts on two different bodies. "They are different types of force" is also accepted, since the two forces in a Newton's third law pair are always of the same type.
> 
> **B1**: The force exerted by the person on the floor, acting vertically downwards. Both what it acts on and the direction are needed.
> 
> **B1**: $P$ becomes larger than $Q$. Accept a supporting reason such as "there must be a resultant force upwards", but the comparison alone scores.
> 
> **B1**: The pair remains equal in magnitude to $P$, because Newton's third law applies whether or not the bodies are accelerating.

parts.problemMd:
A stone is thrown vertically upwards from the edge of a lake. Its height above the water level, $h$ m, at time $t$ s after it is thrown is modelled by

$h = a t^{2} + b t + c$

where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are constants. Air resistance is ignored.

(i) State what the constant $c$ represents in this model.

(ii) Show that $a = - 5$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The stone is thrown at $t = 0$, and putting $t = 0$ into the model leaves only the constant term

$h = c$

**Final answer:** **The height of the stone above the water level at the moment it is thrown**

**[B1]**

(ii)

Taking upwards as positive, differentiate the height with respect to time to obtain the velocity

$\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} = 2 a t + b$

**[M1]**

Differentiate a second time to obtain the acceleration, which is constant

$\frac{\text{d}^{2}h}{\text{d}t^{2}} = 2 a$

The only force acting is the weight, so the acceleration is that due to gravity, acting downwards with $g = 10$

$2 a = - 10$

$a = - 5$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $c$ is the height of the stone above the water level when it is thrown, that is at $t = 0$. Accept "the initial height" or "the height of the point it is thrown from".
> 
> **M1**: Differentiating the given model with respect to $t$, with the power of at least one term reduced by 1. The mark is for the act of differentiating and is available from a slip in the coefficients.
> 
> **B1**: Reaching $a = - 5$ from a second differentiation and the statement that the acceleration is $- 10$. Since the answer is given, the working must be complete and exact: both differentiations and the equation $2 a = - 10$ must be seen. A solution which simply asserts that the coefficient of $t^{2}$ is $- \frac{1}{2} g$ does not score without the differentiation shown.

parts.problemMd: Explain why the model should not be used once $h$ becomes negative.
parts.solutionMd:
The height $h$ is measured above the water level, so a negative value of $h$ describes a stone below the surface of the lake

**Final answer:** **A negative value of h would place the stone under the water**

**[B1]**

The model was built with the weight as the only force acting, and that stops being true the moment the stone enters the water

**Final answer:** **Once in the water the stone also meets resistance and upthrust, so its acceleration is no longer −10**

**[B1]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> A model's domain is set by the assumptions behind it, not by the algebra. The quadratic will happily return a value of $h$ for $t = 100$, but the physical situation it describes ended when the stone hit the water. Always check what a formula is still allowed to describe.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A negative value of $h$ means the stone is below the water surface, since $h$ is measured above water level.
> 
> **B1**: The modelling assumption that the weight is the only force acting fails in the water, so the acceleration is no longer $- 10$. Accept a named additional force: resistance from the water, upthrust, or drag. A statement that the stone simply "stops" does not score without a reason.

parts.problemMd:
Three smooth spheres $P$, $Q$ and $R$, with masses 20 kg, 35 kg and $m$ kg respectively, are travelling in the same direction along a straight line with speeds 7 $\text{m s}^{-1}$, $u \text{m s}^{-1}$ and 10 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ respectively.

Given that $P$, $Q$ and $R$ all have the same momentum, find

(i) the value of $m$,

(ii) the value of $u$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity, and the spheres all move in the same direction, so equate the momentum of $P$ and the momentum of $R$

![Diagram of spheres P, Q and R moving to the right. P has mass 20 kg and speed 7 metres per second, Q has mass 35 kg and speed u metres per second, R has mass m kg and speed 10 metres per second](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/momentum/momentum-and-collisions/assets/031-diagram-of-spheres-p-q-and-r-moving-to-the-right.png)

$20 \times 7 = m \times 10$

**[M1]**

$140 = 10 m$

$m = 14$

**[A1]**

(ii)

Equate the momentum of $P$ and the momentum of $Q$

$20 \times 7 = 35 u$

**[M1]**

$140 = 35 u$

$u = 4$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Momentum of $P$ equated to momentum of $R$, each written as mass multiplied by speed.
> 
> **A1**: $m = 14$.
> 
> **M1**: Momentum of $Q$ equated to the momentum of $P$ or of $R$.
> 
> **A1**: $u = 4$.

parts.problemMd: Given that there are no collisions between any of $P$, $Q$ and $R$, state which sphere is travelling at the front, and which is travelling at the back.
parts.solutionMd:
The spheres move in the same direction along the same line, so for none of them to catch up with another, the fastest sphere must be at the front and the slowest at the back

The speeds are 7 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ for $P$, 4 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ for $Q$ and 10 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ for $R$

**Final answer:** **R is travelling at the front**

**[B1]**

**Final answer:** **Q is travelling at the back**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: $R$ identified as the sphere at the front.
> 
> **B1**: $Q$ identified as the sphere at the back. Follow through from an incorrect value of $u$ in part (a)(ii).
> 
> The two answers are marked independently. No working or reason is required.

parts.problemMd: A ball of mass 400 grams is travelling at a speed of 2 $\text{m s}^{-1}$. Calculate the momentum of the ball.
parts.solutionMd:
Convert the mass to kilograms, so that the momentum is in SI units

$400 \text{g} = 0 . 4 \text{kg}$

Use momentum $=$ mass $\times$ velocity

$\text{Momentum} = 0 . 4 \times 2$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** $\text{Momentum} =$** 0.8 **$\text{kg m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Mass multiplied by speed. Allow the mass in grams for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: 0.8. The mass must have been converted to kilograms, so 800 does not score this mark. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd: A car of mass $m$ kg travelling at a constant speed of 90 $\text{km h}^{-1}$ has momentum 32 500 $\text{kg m s}^{-1}$. Find the value of $m$.
parts.solutionMd:
Convert the speed to metres per second, to match the units of the momentum

$90 \text{km h}^{-1} = \frac{90\times1000}{60\times60} \text{m s}^{-1}$

$90 \text{km h}^{-1} = 25 \text{m s}^{-1}$

Use momentum $=$ mass $\times$ velocity

$m \times 25 = 32500$

**[M1]**

$m = 1300$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Momentum equated to $m$ multiplied by the speed, with an attempt to convert 90 $\text{km h}^{-1}$ to $\text{m s}^{-1}$.
> 
> **A1**: $m = 1300$.

parts.problemMd:
Two particles $P$ and $Q$, of masses 8 kg and 5 kg respectively, lie on a smooth horizontal surface. $Q$ is at rest and $P$ is moving directly towards $Q$ with speed 3 $\text{m s}^{-1}$. The particles collide directly. Immediately after the collision, $P$ continues to move in the same direction with speed 1 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Use the principle of conservation of linear momentum to find the speed of $Q$ immediately after the collision.
parts.solutionMd:
Take the direction in which $P$ is moving as positive, and let the velocity of $Q$ after the collision be $v \text{m s}^{-1}$

![Before and after diagram. Before: P, 8 kg, moves right at 3 metres per second; Q, 5 kg, is at rest. After: P moves right at 1 metre per second; Q moves right at v metres per second](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/momentum/momentum-and-collisions/assets/029-before-and-after-diagram-before-p-8-kg-moves-rig.png)

Momentum before the collision equals momentum after the collision, and $Q$ has no momentum before the collision because it is at rest

$8 \times 3 = 8 \times 1 + 5 v$

**[M1 A1]**

$24 = 8 + 5 v$

$5 v = 16$

**Final answer:** $v =$** 3.2 **$\text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of conservation of momentum with 3 non-zero terms. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation, $24 = 8 + 5 v$ or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: 3.2. The answer must be positive, since a speed is asked for.

parts.problemMd: Find the loss of kinetic energy of the system due to the collision.
parts.solutionMd:
Find the total kinetic energy before the collision, using $\text{KE} = \frac{1}{2} m v^{2}$. Only $P$ is moving

$\text{KE before} = \frac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 3^{2} = 36$

**[M1]**

Find the total kinetic energy after the collision, using the speed of $Q$ from part (a)

$\text{KE after} = \frac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 1^{2} + \frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 3 . 2^{2}$

$\text{KE after} = 4 + 25 . 6 = 29 . 6$

The loss of kinetic energy is the difference between the two totals

$\text{Loss of KE} = 36 - 29 . 6$

**Final answer:** $\text{Loss of KE} =$** 6.4 J**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of $\text{KE} = \frac{1}{2} m v^{2}$ for either particle, either before or after the collision.
> 
> **A1**: 6.4. Follow through from an incorrect speed in part (a). Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
Two particles $P$ and $Q$, of masses 10 kg and 16 kg respectively, are moving in the same direction along the same straight line on a smooth horizontal surface when they collide directly. Immediately before they collide, $P$ is moving with speed 13 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and $Q$ is moving with speed 1 $\text{m s}^{-1}$. Immediately after they collide, $Q$ is moving with speed 10 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Explain how you know that the direction of motion of $Q$ does not change as a result of the collision.
parts.solutionMd:
Before the collision both particles move in the same direction, and $P$ is faster, so $P$ must catch up with $Q$ from behind

![Before and after diagram. Before: P, 10 kg, moves right at 13 metres per second; Q, 16 kg, moves right at 1 metre per second. After: P has velocity v metres per second, drawn to the right; Q moves right at 10 metres per second](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/momentum/momentum-and-collisions/assets/030-before-and-after-diagram-before-p-10-kg-moves-ri.png)

**Final answer:** **Q is hit from behind by P, so it is pushed forwards and continues to move in the same direction**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: A correct explanation that $P$ collides with $Q$ from behind, so $Q$ is pushed in its original direction of motion. Accept an equivalent explanation, such as the collision force on $Q$ acting in its direction of motion.

parts.problemMd:
(i) Find the speed of $P$ immediately after the collision.

(ii) Explain how you know that the direction of motion of $P$ has been reversed.
parts.solutionMd:
![Before and after diagram. Before: P, 10 kg, moves right at 13 metres per second; Q, 16 kg, moves right at 1 metre per second. After: P has velocity v metres per second, drawn to the right; Q moves right at 10 metres per second](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/momentum/momentum-and-collisions/assets/030-before-and-after-diagram-before-p-10-kg-moves-ri.png)

(i)

Take the original direction of motion as positive, and let the velocity of $P$ after the collision be $v \text{m s}^{-1}$

Momentum before the collision equals momentum after the collision

$10 \times 13 + 16 \times 1 = 10 v + 16 \times 10$

**[M1 A1]**

$146 = 10 v + 160$

$10 v = - 14$

$v = - 1 . 4$

The speed is the magnitude of the velocity

**Final answer:** $\text{Speed of} P =$** 1.4 **$\text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

(ii)

**Final answer:** **The velocity of P after the collision is negative, so P is now moving in the opposite direction to the one taken as positive**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of conservation of momentum with 4 non-zero terms. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation, $146 = 10 v + 160$ or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: 1.4. The answer must be positive, since a speed is asked for; −1.4 does not score this mark.
> 
> **B1**: Reversal explained by the negative velocity (or negative momentum) of $P$ in the original direction of motion. Follow through from a negative velocity in part (i).

parts.problemMd:
Two particles $A$ and $B$, of masses 3 kg and $m$ kg respectively, are moving towards each other along a straight line on a smooth horizontal surface. Immediately before they collide, the speed of $A$ is 6 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and the speed of $B$ is 5 $\text{m s}^{-1}$. The particles collide directly. Immediately after the collision, $A$ continues to move in the same direction with speed 4 $\text{m s}^{-1}$, and the direction of motion of $B$ is reversed and its speed is 3 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Show that $m =$ 0.75.
parts.solutionMd:
Take the direction of motion of $A$ before the collision as positive, so $B$ has velocity $- 5 \text{m s}^{-1}$ before the collision and $+ 3 \text{m s}^{-1}$ after it

![Before and after diagram. Before: A, 3 kg, moves right at 6 metres per second; B, m kg, moves left at 5 metres per second. After: A moves right at 4 metres per second; B moves right at 3 metres per second](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/momentum/momentum-and-collisions/assets/033-before-and-after-diagram-before-a-3-kg-moves-rig.png)

Momentum before the collision equals momentum after the collision

$3 \times 6 + m \times ( - 5 ) = 3 \times 4 + m \times 3$

**[M1 A1]**

$18 - 5 m = 12 + 3 m$

$6 = 8 m$

$m = \frac{6}{8}$

**Final answer:** $m =$** 0.75**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of conservation of momentum with 4 non-zero terms. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation with the velocities of $B$ taking opposite signs, $18 - 5 m = 12 + 3 m$ or equivalent.
> 
> **B1**: $m = 0 . 75$ reached from correct working. As the answer is given, the equation and its rearrangement must be seen.

parts.problemMd: Find the change in momentum of $A$ due to the collision.
parts.solutionMd:
The change in momentum is the momentum after the collision minus the momentum before it, keeping the positive direction from part (a)

$\text{Change in momentum of} A = ( 3 \times 4 ) - ( 3 \times 6 )$

**[M1]**

$\text{Change in momentum of} A = - 6$

The negative sign means the change acts against the original direction of motion of $A$

$6 \text{kg m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

**Final answer:** **The change in momentum is in the opposite direction to the original motion of A**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Final momentum of $A$ minus initial momentum of $A$, using $m v - m u$ with the mass of $A$. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: A magnitude of 6. Units are not required.
> 
> **B1**: Direction stated as opposite to the original motion of $A$. Accept an answer of −6 with the positive direction clearly defined as the original motion of $A$.

parts.problemMd:
Safa and Adam each roll a ball towards the other along the same straight line on a smooth horizontal table. Adam's ball has mass 0.8 kg. Immediately before the balls collide, Safa's ball has speed 6 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and Adam's ball has speed 3 $\text{m s}^{-1}$. Immediately after the collision, the direction of motion of Safa's ball is reversed and its speed is 2 $\text{m s}^{-1}$. As a result of the collision, the magnitude of the momentum of Safa's ball decreases by 2.4 $\text{kg m s}^{-1}$.

Show that the mass of Safa's ball is 0.6 kg.
parts.solutionMd:
Let the mass of Safa's ball be $m$ kg. The magnitude of its momentum is its mass multiplied by its speed, whatever its direction

![Before and after diagram. Before: Safa's ball, m kg, moves right at 6 metres per second; Adam's ball, 0.8 kg, moves left at 3 metres per second. After: Safa's ball moves left at 2 metres per second; Adam's ball has velocity v metres per second, drawn to the right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/momentum/momentum-and-collisions/assets/032-before-and-after-diagram-before-safa-s-ball-m-kg.png)

$\text{Magnitude before} = 6 m$

$\text{Magnitude after} = 2 m$

**[M1]**

The magnitude decreases by 2.4

$6 m - 2 m = 2 . 4$

**[A1]**

$4 m = 2 . 4$

**Final answer:** $m =$** 0.6**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Both magnitudes of momentum written as mass multiplied by speed, $6 m$ and $2 m$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation, $6 m - 2 m = 2 . 4$ or equivalent. Treating the velocity after the collision as negative, giving $6 m - ( - 2 m ) = 2 . 4$, does not earn this mark, since the question describes a change in the magnitude of the momentum.
> 
> **B1**: $m = 0 . 6$ reached from correct working. As the answer is given, the equation must be seen.

parts.problemMd:
(i) Find the speed of Adam's ball immediately after the collision.

(ii) State whether the direction of motion of Adam's ball is changed by the collision.
parts.solutionMd:
![Before and after diagram. Before: Safa's ball, m kg, moves right at 6 metres per second; Adam's ball, 0.8 kg, moves left at 3 metres per second. After: Safa's ball moves left at 2 metres per second; Adam's ball has velocity v metres per second, drawn to the right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/momentum/momentum-and-collisions/assets/032-before-and-after-diagram-before-safa-s-ball-m-kg.png)

(i)

Take the original direction of motion of Safa's ball as positive, and let the velocity of Adam's ball after the collision be $v \text{m s}^{-1}$

Momentum before the collision equals momentum after the collision

$0 . 6 \times 6 + 0 . 8 \times ( - 3 ) = 0 . 6 \times ( - 2 ) + 0 . 8 v$

**[M1 A1]**

$3 . 6 - 2 . 4 = - 1 . 2 + 0 . 8 v$

$0 . 8 v = 2 . 4$

$v = 3$

$\text{Speed of Adam's ball} = 3 \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

(ii)

Adam's ball was moving in the negative direction before the collision, and $v$ is positive

**Final answer:** **The direction of motion of Adam's ball is changed (reversed) by the collision**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of conservation of momentum with 4 non-zero terms. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation, $3 . 6 - 2 . 4 = - 1 . 2 + 0 . 8 v$ or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: 3. The answer must be positive, since a speed is asked for.
> 
> **B1**: The direction of Adam's ball is changed. Follow through from the sign of the velocity found in part (i), provided the positive direction has been defined.

parts.problemMd:
Two small smooth spheres $A$ and $B$, of equal radius, are moving in the same direction along the same straight line on a smooth horizontal surface when they collide directly. The directions of motion of $A$ and $B$ are unchanged by the collision. Immediately before the collision, $A$ has speed 9 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and $B$ has speed 1 $\text{m s}^{-1}$. Immediately after the collision, $A$ has speed 1.8 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and $B$ has speed 5.8 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Given that the loss of kinetic energy of $A$ in the collision is 388.8 J, show that the mass of $A$ is 10 kg.
parts.solutionMd:
Let the mass of $A$ be $m_{A}$ kg. The loss of kinetic energy of $A$ is its kinetic energy before the collision minus its kinetic energy after, using $\text{KE} = \frac{1}{2} m v^{2}$

![Before and after diagram. Before: A moves right at 9 metres per second and B moves right at 1 metre per second. After: A moves right at 1.8 metres per second and B moves right at 5.8 metres per second](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/momentum/momentum-and-collisions/assets/034-before-and-after-diagram-before-a-moves-right-at.png)

$\frac{1}{2} m_{A} \times 9^{2} - \frac{1}{2} m_{A} \times 1 . 8^{2} = 388 . 8$

**[M1]**

$\frac{1}{2} m_{A} ( 81 - 3 . 24 ) = 388 . 8$

$38 . 88 m_{A} = 388 . 8$

$m_{A} = 10$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Loss of kinetic energy of $A$ written as $\frac{1}{2} m_{A} \times 9^{2} - \frac{1}{2} m_{A} \times 1 . 8^{2}$ and equated to 388.8.
> 
> **B1**: $m_{A} = 10$ reached from correct working. As the answer is given, the equation and a correct simplification must be seen.

parts.problemMd: Show that the mass of $B$ is 15 kg.
parts.solutionMd:
Take the direction of motion as positive and let the mass of $B$ be $m_{B}$ kg

Momentum before the collision equals momentum after the collision

$10 \times 9 + m_{B} \times 1 = 10 \times 1 . 8 + m_{B} \times 5 . 8$

**[M1 A1]**

$90 + m_{B} = 18 + 5 . 8 m_{B}$

$72 = 4 . 8 m_{B}$

$m_{B} = 15$

**[B1]**

parts.problemMd:

Immediately before this collision $C$ is at rest, and immediately after it $C$ moves with speed 3 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

(i) Calculate the speed of $B$ immediately after its collision with $C$.

(ii) State whether the collision between $B$ and $C$ changes the direction of motion of $B$.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Keep the same positive direction and let the velocity of $B$ after this collision be $v \text{m s}^{-1}$. $C$ is hit from behind, so it moves in the positive direction

![Before and after diagram for the collision of B and C. Before: B, 15 kg, moves right at 5.8 metres per second; C, 30 kg, is at rest. After: B has velocity v metres per second, drawn to the right; C moves right at 3 metres per second](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/momentum/momentum-and-collisions/assets/035-before-and-after-diagram-for-the-collision-of-b-.png)

Momentum before the collision equals momentum after the collision, and $C$ has no momentum before it

$15 \times 5 . 8 = 15 v + 30 \times 3$

**[M1]**

$87 = 15 v + 90$

$15 v = - 3$

$v = - 0 . 2$

The speed is the magnitude of the velocity

**Final answer:** $\text{Speed of} B =$** 0.2 **$\text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

(ii)

The velocity of $B$ is negative, so $B$ now moves in the opposite direction

**Final answer:** **The collision with C reverses the direction of motion of B**

**[B1]**

parts.problemMd: Explain why there will be another collision between $A$ and $B$.

After the first collision $A$ is still moving in the positive direction, behind $B$, and after hitting $C$ the sphere $B$ is moving in the negative direction

**[B1]**

parts.problemMd:
Two small smooth spheres $A$ and $B$, of equal radius and of masses $m$ kg and 1.5 kg respectively, are moving in the same direction along the same straight line on a smooth horizontal table when they collide directly. Immediately before they collide, $A$ is moving with speed 8 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and $B$ is moving with speed 3 $\text{m s}^{-1}$. Immediately after they collide, $A$ is moving with speed 1 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and $B$ is moving with speed 4 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ in its original direction.

Find the exact value of $m$ in each of the following cases.

(i) The direction of motion of $A$ is unchanged by the collision.

(ii) The direction of motion of $A$ is reversed by the collision.
parts.solutionMd:
Take the original direction of motion as positive. The two cases differ only in the sign of the velocity of $A$ after the collision

![Before and after diagram. Before: A, m kg, moves right at 8 metres per second; B, 1.5 kg, moves right at 3 metres per second. After in case (i): A moves right at 1 metre per second and B moves right at 4 metres per second. (i)

**[A1]**

> **A1**: $m = \frac{3}{14}$. Accept answers which round to 0.214.

parts.problemMd:
Two particles $A$ and $B$, of masses 0.6 kg and 1.4 kg respectively, are moving towards each other along a straight line on a smooth horizontal plane. Immediately before they collide, $A$ has speed 8 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and $B$ has speed 6 $\text{m s}^{-1}$. The particles collide directly and coalesce to form a particle $C$.

Find the speed and direction of motion of $C$ immediately after the collision.
parts.solutionMd:
Take the direction of motion of $A$ as positive, so $B$ has velocity $- 6 \text{m s}^{-1}$. The particles coalesce (stick together), so $C$ has mass $0 . 6 + 1 . 4 = 2$ kg; let its velocity be $v \text{m s}^{-1}$

![Before and after diagram. Before: A, 0.6 kg, moves right at 8 metres per second; B, 1.4 kg, moves left at 6 metres per second. After: the combined particle C, 2 kg, has velocity v metres per second, drawn to the right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/momentum/momentum-and-collisions/assets/023-before-and-after-diagram-before-a-0-6-kg-moves-r.png)

Momentum before the collision equals momentum after the collision

$0 . 6 \times 8 + 1 . 4 \times ( - 6 ) = 2 v$

**[M1]**

$4 . 8 - 8 . 4 = 2 v$

$v = - 1 . 8$

The speed is the magnitude of the velocity

**Final answer:** $\text{Speed of} C =$** 1.8 **$\text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

The velocity is negative, so $C$ moves against the original direction of $A$

**Final answer:** **C moves in the direction in which B was originally moving**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of conservation of momentum with 3 non-zero terms, using a combined mass of 2 kg. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: 1.8. The answer must be positive, since a speed is asked for.
> 
> **B1**: Direction given as the original direction of motion of $B$ (or opposite to the original motion of $A$). Accept the direction shown on a clearly labelled diagram. Taking $B$'s direction as positive, giving $v = 1 . 8$ in that direction, is equally acceptable.

parts.problemMd: Write down the momentum of $C$ immediately after the collision.
parts.solutionMd:
Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity, using the combined mass of 2 kg and the speed from part (a)

$\text{Momentum} = 2 \times 1 . 8$

**Final answer:** $\text{Momentum of} C =$** 3.6 **$\text{kg m s}^{-1}$

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: 3.6. Follow through as twice the speed found in part (a). Units and direction are not required; an answer of −3.6 consistent with a stated positive direction is also accepted.

parts.problemMd:
Two marbles $M$ and $N$, of masses 3 kg and $m$ kg respectively, are rolled towards each other along a straight line on a smooth horizontal table. The marbles are modelled as particles. Immediately before they collide, the speeds of $M$ and $N$ are 3 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and 5 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ respectively. The marbles collide directly and $M$ is brought to rest. Immediately after the collision, $N$ moves with speed 4 $\text{m s}^{-1}$.

Find the value of $m$.
parts.solutionMd:
$M$ is at rest after the collision and lies in the path of $N$, so $N$ cannot continue in its original direction: its direction of motion must be reversed

Take the direction of motion of $M$ as positive, so $N$ has velocity $- 5 \text{m s}^{-1}$ before the collision and $+ 4 \text{m s}^{-1}$ after it

![Before and after diagram. Before: M, 3 kg, moves right at 3 metres per second; N, m kg, moves left at 5 metres per second. After: M is at rest; N moves right at 4 metres per second](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/momentum/momentum-and-collisions/assets/024-before-and-after-diagram-before-m-3-kg-moves-rig.png)

Momentum before the collision equals momentum after the collision

$3 \times 3 + m \times ( - 5 ) = 3 \times 0 + m \times 4$

**[M1 A1]**

$9 - 5 m = 4 m$

$9 = 9 m$

$m = 1$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of conservation of momentum with 3 non-zero terms. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation with the velocities of $N$ before and after taking opposite signs, $9 - 5 m = 4 m$ or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: $m = 1$. The answer $m = 9$, from assuming $N$ keeps its original direction, does not score either A mark.

parts.problemMd:
Two particles $P$ and $Q$, of masses $3 m$ kg and $5 m$ kg respectively, are moving towards each other along the same straight line on a smooth horizontal plane. Immediately before they collide, the speed of $P$ is $3 u \text{m s}^{-1}$ and the speed of $Q$ is $2 u \text{m s}^{-1}$. The particles collide directly. Immediately after the collision, the speed of $P$ is halved and its direction of motion is reversed.

Find the speed of $Q$ immediately after the collision.
parts.solutionMd:
Take the original direction of motion of $P$ as positive. Then $Q$ has velocity $- 2 u$ before the collision, $P$ has velocity $- \frac{3}{2} u$ after it, and let $Q$ have velocity $v \text{m s}^{-1}$ after it

![Before and after diagram. Before: P, 3m kg, moves right at 3u metres per second; Q, 5m kg, moves left at 2u metres per second. After: P moves left at 1.5u metres per second; Q has velocity v metres per second, drawn to the right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/momentum/momentum-and-collisions/assets/025-before-and-after-diagram-before-p-3m-kg-moves-ri.png)

Momentum before the collision equals momentum after the collision

`3m \times 3u + 5m \times (-2u) = 3m \times \left(-\dfrac{3}{2}u\right) + 5mv`

**[M1 A1]**

Every term contains $m$, so divide through by $m$

$9 u - 10 u = - 4 . 5 u + 5 v$

$5 v = 3 . 5 u$

$\text{Speed of} Q = 0 . 7 u \text{m s}^{-1}$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of conservation of momentum with 4 non-zero terms. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation, $9 m u - 10 m u = - 4 . 5 m u + 5 m v$ or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: $0 . 7 u$, or $\frac{7}{10} u$. The answer must be positive and must include $u$.

parts.problemMd: State whether the direction of motion of $Q$ is changed by the collision.
parts.solutionMd:
$Q$ was moving in the negative direction before the collision, and its velocity $0 . 7 u$ after the collision is positive

**Final answer:** **The direction of motion of Q is changed (reversed) by the collision**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **B1**: The direction of $Q$ is changed. Follow through from the sign of the velocity found in part (a), provided the positive direction has been defined.

parts.problemMd:
Two small smooth spheres $A$ and $B$, of equal radius and of masses 5 kg and $m$ kg respectively, are moving in the same direction along a straight line on a smooth horizontal surface when they collide directly. Immediately after the collision, the speed of $A$ is 2 $\text{m s}^{-1}$, the speed of $B$ is 4 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and the direction of motion of $B$ is unchanged.

Find the two possible values of $m$.
parts.solutionMd:
Take the original direction of motion as positive. The direction of $A$ after the collision is not given, so its velocity is either $+ 2$ or $- 2 \text{m s}^{-1}$

![Before and after diagram. Before: A, 5 kg, moves right at 12 metres per second; B, m kg, moves right at 2 metres per second. After, if A is unchanged: A moves right at 2 metres per second and B moves right at 4 metres per second. After, if A is reversed: A moves left at 2 metres per second and B moves right at 4 metres per second](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/momentum/momentum-and-collisions/assets/022-before-and-after-diagram-before-a-5-kg-moves-rig.png)

If the direction of $A$ is unchanged, momentum before the collision equals momentum after the collision

$5 \times 12 + 2 m = 5 \times 2 + 4 m$

**[M1]**

$60 + 2 m = 10 + 4 m$

$m = 25$

**[A1]**

If the direction of $A$ is reversed

$5 \times 12 + 2 m = 5 \times ( - 2 ) + 4 m$

**[M1]**

$60 + 2 m = - 10 + 4 m$

$m = 35$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of conservation of momentum with 4 non-zero terms in either case. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: $m = 25$.
> 
> **M1**: Use of conservation of momentum for the other case, with the velocity of $A$ after the collision taking the opposite sign.
> 
> **A1**: $m = 35$.
> 
> The two values are marked independently.

parts.problemMd: Show that the smaller of the two possible losses of kinetic energy of the system due to the collision is 140 J.
parts.solutionMd:
Find the kinetic energy of $A$ before and after, using $\text{KE} = \frac{1}{2} m v^{2}$; this is the same in both cases

$\text{KE of} A \text{before} = \frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 12^{2} = 360$

$\text{KE of} A \text{after} = \frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 2^{2} = 10$

For $m = 25$, find the loss of kinetic energy of the system

`\text{Loss} = \left(360 + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 25 \times 2^2\right) - \left(10 + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 25 \times 4^2\right)`

**[M1]**

$\text{Loss} = 410 - 210 = 200$

For $m = 35$

`\text{Loss} = \left(360 + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 35 \times 2^2\right) - \left(10 + \dfrac{1}{2} \times 35 \times 4^2\right)`

$\text{Loss} = 430 - 290 = 140$

**[A1]**

Compare the two losses

$140 < 200$

**Final answer:** $\text{Smaller loss of KE} = 140$** J**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Total kinetic energy before minus total kinetic energy after, using $\text{KE} = \frac{1}{2} m v^{2}$, for either value of $m$.
> 
> **A1**: Both losses correct, 200 J and 140 J. Follow through from incorrect values of $m$ in part (a).
> 
> **B1**: 140 J identified as the smaller loss from a comparison of the two. As the answer is given, both losses must be seen; finding only the loss for $m = 35$ does not show that it is the smaller.

Show that there will be another collision between $A$ and $B$.
parts.solutionMd:

**[A1]**

parts.problemMd:
Given that $A$ and $B$ coalesce in this collision,

(i) show that the speed of the combined spheres immediately after the collision is 1.125 $\text{m s}^{-1}$,

(ii) show that the total loss of kinetic energy due to the three collisions is 6.38 J, correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

The spheres coalesce (stick together), so the combined sphere has mass $0 . 1 + 0 . 3 = 0 . 4$ kg; let its velocity be $V \text{m s}^{-1}$. Momentum before the collision equals momentum after the collision

$0 . 1 \times 1 . 5 + 0 . 3 \times 1 = 0 . 4 V$

**[M1]**

$0 . 45 = 0 . 4 V$

**Final answer:** $V =$** 1.125 **$\text{m s}^{-1}$

**[B1]**

(ii)

Before the three collisions only $A$ is moving, so find the initial kinetic energy using $\text{KE} = \frac{1}{2} m v^{2}$

$\text{Initial KE} = \frac{1}{2} \times 0 . 1 \times 12^{2} = 7 . 2$

**[M1]**

After all three collisions, $C$ moves at 1.5 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and the combined sphere moves at 1.125 $\text{m s}^{-1}$

$\text{Final KE} = \frac{1}{2} \times 0 . 5 \times 1 . 5^{2} + \frac{1}{2} \times 0 . 4 \times 1 . 125^{2}$

**[M1]**

$\text{Final KE} = 0 . 5625 + 0 . 253125 = 0 . 815625$

The total loss is the initial kinetic energy minus the final kinetic energy

$\text{Loss of KE} = 7 . 2 - 0 . 815625 = 6 . 384375$

**Final answer:** $\text{Loss of KE} =$** 6.38 J (3 s.f.)**

**[B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of conservation of momentum with 3 non-zero terms and a combined mass of 0.4 kg.
> 
> **B1**: 1.125 reached from correct working. As the answer is given, the equation must be seen.
> 
> **M1**: Initial kinetic energy of the system, $\frac{1}{2} \times 0 . 1 \times 12^{2}$.
> 
> **M1**: Final kinetic energy of the system, including both the kinetic energy of $C$ and that of the combined sphere.
> 
> **B1**: 6.38 reached from correct working, with a more accurate value such as 6.384 seen before rounding.
> 
> Finding the loss for each collision separately and adding the three losses is equally acceptable.

parts.problemMd:

A mass cannot be negative, so $R$ must move in the negative direction, the original direction of $Q$

$13 . 2 = 3 m$

**[A1]**

> **M1**: The direction of $R$ correctly determined as the original direction of $Q$. This may be by rejecting the negative mass from the other direction, or by arguing that $P$ cannot gain speed in its own direction in a head-on collision. This mark may be implied by a correct equation with $R$ in the direction of $Q$.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation, $6 - 15 m = - 7 . 2 - 12 m$ or equivalent.

parts.problemMd:
Lucy and Fran are driving monster trucks towards each other along the same straight line. The combined mass of Lucy and her truck is 5400 kg and the combined mass of Fran and her truck is 4700 kg. Immediately before the trucks collide, Lucy's truck is moving with speed 4 $\text{m s}^{-1}$ and Fran's truck is moving with speed 5 $\text{m s}^{-1}$. The trucks collide directly. The trucks are modelled as particles.

Immediately after the collision, the two trucks move in the same direction with the same speed.

(i) Find this speed.

(ii) State whose direction of motion has been reversed by the collision.

(iii) Calculate the change in momentum of Fran's truck due to the collision.
parts.solutionMd:
(i)

Take the direction of motion of Lucy's truck as positive, so Fran's truck has velocity $- 5 \text{m s}^{-1}$. After the collision both trucks have the same velocity, $v \text{m s}^{-1}$

![Before and after diagram. Before: Lucy's truck, 5400 kg, moves right at 4 metres per second; Fran's truck, 4700 kg, moves left at 5 metres per second. After: both trucks have the same velocity v metres per second, drawn to the right](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/momentum/momentum-and-collisions/assets/013-before-and-after-diagram-before-lucy-s-truck-540.png)

Momentum before the collision equals momentum after the collision

$5400 \times 4 + 4700 \times ( - 5 ) = 5400 v + 4700 v$

**[M1 A1]**

$21600 - 23500 = 10100 v$

$v = - \frac{1900}{10100} = - 0 . 18811 \dots$

The speed is the magnitude of the velocity

**Final answer:** $\text{Speed} =$** 0.188 **$\text{m s}^{-1}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

(ii)

The velocity is negative, so both trucks move in Fran's original direction after the collision

**Final answer:** **Lucy's direction of motion has been reversed**

**[B1]**

(iii)

The change in momentum is the momentum after minus the momentum before, for Fran's truck only. Keep the unrounded velocity

`\text{Change in momentum} = 4700 \times \left(-\dfrac{19}{101}\right) - 4700 \times (-5)`

**[M1]**

$\text{Change in momentum} = 22615 . 8 \dots$

The change is positive, so it acts in Lucy's original direction, against the motion of Fran's truck

**Final answer:** $22600 \text{kg m s}^{-1}$** (3 s.f.) in the opposite direction to the motion of Fran's truck**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of conservation of momentum with 4 non-zero terms and a common velocity after the collision. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation, $21600 - 23500 = 10100 v$ or equivalent.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 0.188. The answer must be positive, since a speed is asked for.
> 
> **B1**: Lucy. Follow through from the sign of the velocity found in part (i).
> 
> **M1**: Final momentum of Fran's truck minus its initial momentum, using its mass of 4700 kg and velocities of consistent sign.
> 
> **A1**: Answers which round to 22 600, with the direction stated as opposite to the motion of Fran's truck (or in Lucy's original direction). A signed answer consistent with a clearly defined positive direction is accepted. Units are not required.

parts.problemMd:
It is given instead that, immediately after the collision, the direction of motion of each truck is reversed and the two trucks have equal speeds.

Calculate this speed.
parts.solutionMd:
Keep Lucy's original direction as positive and let the common speed be $v \text{m s}^{-1}$. Both trucks reverse, so Lucy's truck now has velocity $- v$ and Fran's truck has velocity $+ v$

After: Lucy's truck moves left at v metres per second and Fran's truck moves right at v metres per second](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0c0f0e08045623dd9ae2cdca5bf5667330b83411/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-as-maths-20-mechanics/momentum/momentum-and-collisions/assets/014-before-and-after-diagram-before-lucy-s-truck-540.png)

$5400 \times 4 + 4700 \times ( - 5 ) = 5400 \times ( - v ) + 4700 v$

**[M1 A1]**

$- 1900 = - 700 v$

$v = \frac{19}{7} = 2 . 7142 \dots$

**Final answer:** $\text{Speed} =$** 2.71 **$\text{m s}^{-1}$** (3 s.f.)**

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Use of conservation of momentum with 4 non-zero terms and velocities of equal magnitude after the collision. Allow sign errors for this mark.
> 
> **A1**: Correct equation with the two velocities after the collision of opposite sign, each opposite to that truck's original velocity, $- 1900 = - 700 v$ or equivalent.
